note: THE CONTENT DOCUMENT — the course. This is the slot the course goes in: one document, loaded through src/lib/contentLoader.js and checked by src/lib/contentSchema.js, so adding the course is a data change here rather than a code change anywhere. The general-knowledge set that used to sit here came out for the beta (`git log -- src/content/test-content.json` is where it lives if it is ever wanted back); from 2026-09-21 it held the owner's own material; on 2026-10-03 all three chapters came out at his word and the replacement batches went in the same day, under chapter ids that had never existed. The `content.test` switch in src/lib/flags.js is on for everyone so every visitor loads it. Module NAMES are here and in src/data.js, and the two must agree: data.js is what the Flight Deck draws before this document arrives. Module CODES (M1–M4) never change — progress and saves are keyed to them.
contentModel: modules[] -> chapters[] -> lessons[] and one quiz per chapter. A chapter may also carry cards[] — its study-card set, same shape as a quiz question; without it the card set is the quiz's questions. A module may carry downloads[] — {id, title, file, pages}, a file under public/ offered as a plain download, never opened in the reader. notes, threads, replies, people and presence are the lesson surface's own rows. See contentSchema.js for the exact shape and the validator that enforces it.

questions.question: Compare the airfoils of a fixed-wing aircraft with those of a helicopter
options: Primarily the fuselage on the fixed-wing aircraft, the tail rotor on the helicopter
Primarily the wings on the fixed-wing aircraft, the main rotor on the helicopter
Primarily the propellers on the fixed-wing aircraft, the fuselage on the helicopter
questions.explain: The wings are the primary airfoil of a fixed-wing aircraft and the main rotor is the primary airfoil of the helicopter.

questions.question: The main rotor blades are the airfoils of a helicopter. Which of the two forces they produce holds the aircraft up against gravity?
options: Thrust
Drag
Lift
questions.explain: Of the two forces the airfoil produces, lift is the one the manual gives as counteracting gravity.

questions.question: A rotor blade is moving forward and downward through the air. In which direction does its relative wind act?
options: Backward and upward
Backward and downward
Forward and upward
questions.explain: The relative wind is always exactly opposite to the flight path of the blade, so forward and downward movement gives a backward and upward relative wind.

questions.question: Explain why the relative wind on a rotor blade changes when a hovering helicopter begins to move horizontally
options: The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the chord line of the rotor blade
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the span of the rotor blade
Movement of the helicopter through the air is one of the factors that affect it
questions.explain: Horizontal movement of the helicopter is one of the factors that affect the relative wind.

questions.question: A helicopter stands with its rotor stopped while wind blows over the blades. Which statement about the relative wind is correct?
options: The wind blowing over the blade creates the relative wind
The relative wind is created only by blade flapping
There is no relative wind because the rotor is stopped
questions.explain: Even with the rotor stopped, wind over the blade is airflow relative to the blade.

questions.question: Explain how one movement of the collective pitch control is able to change both the pitch angle and the angle of attack
options: It lifts the whole blade, moving the axis of rotation against the chord
It rotates the blade around the hub axis, moving the chord against each reference
It tilts the plane of rotation, moving the relative wind against the chord
questions.explain: Both angles are measured from the chord, so rotating the blade about the hub axis changes both.

questions.question: Why do the same factors that affect the relative wind also affect the angle of attack
options: Because the angle of attack depends upon the blade span
Because the angle of attack depends upon the relative wind
Because the relative wind depends upon the pitch angle
questions.explain: Angle of attack is measured to the relative wind, so what changes one changes the other.

questions.question: State what creates the relative wind on a helicopter hovering in completely still air
options: The wind speed and the wind direction
The turning of the rotor blades
The forward speed of the helicopter
questions.explain: With no wind and no forward speed, only the turning of the blades is left to produce the relative wind.

questions.question: The relative wind on a blade lies in the same direction as the plane of rotation and the pilot then increases the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It increases and stays equal to the pitch angle
It increases and becomes larger than the pitch angle
It stays constant while the pitch angle increases
questions.explain: With the relative wind in the plane of rotation the two angles are equal, and the angle of attack follows the pitch angle up.

questions.question: In the example wheel, an external force tries to turn the wheel around the input axis. Around which axis does the movement actually take place?
options: Only around the input axis
Only around the spin axis
Around the output axis
questions.explain: Because of precession the movement occurs around the output axis.

questions.question: A downward force is applied on the right side of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the output appear?
options: On the left side
Right in front
Right at the rear
questions.explain: 90° later in counterclockwise rotation from the right side is the front.

questions.question: State what happens to the direction in which lift acts on a blade when the relative wind changes direction
options: It changes with it, staying perpendicular to the relative wind
It stays fixed, remaining perpendicular to the plane of rotation
It changes with it, staying parallel to the relative wind
questions.explain: Lift is defined as perpendicular to the relative wind, so its direction follows the relative wind.

questions.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt to the left. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: Right in front
On the left side
Right at the rear
questions.explain: The output is wanted on the left; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the front.

questions.question: Explain why the torque of the main rotor must be counteracted before a flight is possible
options: Because the rotor blades would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the fuselage
Because the main rotor would otherwise produce thrust instead of lift
Because the fuselage would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the rotor blades
questions.explain: Torque makes the fuselage rotate opposite to the blades, so it must be counteracted before flight.

questions.question: A pilot raises the collective lever and the turning force on the fuselage rises. Why must the tail rotor thrust then change too?
options: Because it is what balances the drag of the main rotor
Because it is what compensates the torque on the airframe
Because it is what balances the lift of the main rotor
questions.explain: The tail rotor is what compensates the torque, so a change in torque has to be matched by a change in its thrust.

questions.question: State what the helicopter gains from being able to tilt its rotor plane slightly in any direction
options: Torque can act in all directions, giving heading control
Lift can act in all directions, giving collective control
Thrust can act in all directions, giving directional control
questions.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets the thrust act in any direction, which is how directional control is obtained.

questions.question: How do the rotors of a helicopter additionally ensure directional control
options: The rotor RPM is changed so thrust acts in all directions
The rotor plane may be tilted so thrust can act in all directions
Control surfaces on the rotor blades are deflected
questions.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets thrust act in any direction.

questions.question: During an autorotation after an engine failure, which statement about control is correct?
options: The helicopter is fully controllable and the pilot can choose the touchdown point
The helicopter is not controllable and lands wherever the descent takes it
Only the pedals remain effective and the touchdown point cannot be chosen
questions.explain: The manual says it is fully controllable and the pilot selects the touchdown location.

questions.question: Why must the rotor plane be tilted when changing from hover to forward flight
options: Because rotor thrust always acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
Because the tail rotor thrust acts in the direction of flight
Because the rotor RPM must be increased for forward flight
questions.explain: To point thrust forward, the plane must tilt, because thrust is perpendicular to it.

questions.question: State the penalty that follows from a helicopter rotor generating both lift and thrust by itself
options: Its rotor cannot be tilted out of the horizontal plane
Its torque reaction on the fuselage has to be counteracted
Its downwash cannot escape from under the fuselage
questions.explain: A powered rotor doing all the work also produces the torque reaction that must be counteracted.

questions.question: In straight-ahead flight the blade has minimum incidence in front and maximum incidence at the rear. What is the result for the rotor plane?
options: It tilts backward, giving lift and rearward thrust
It stays level, giving lift but no thrust
It tilts forward, giving lift and forward thrust
questions.explain: More lift at the rear and less at the front tilts the plane forward, producing lift and forward thrust.

questions.question: A pilot raises the collective lever to climb. The engine power changes and so does the torque effect on the fuselage. Which control must then vary the tail rotor thrust?
options: The tail rotor pedals
The collective lever
The cyclic pitch stick
questions.explain: Torque is compensated by the tail rotor, whose thrust the pilot varies with the pedals.

questions.question: A pilot pushes the left pedal forward during a hover and holds the new heading. What else now needs attention?
options: The rotor RPM, because the tail rotor pitch has changed
The pitch angle, because the collective lever has changed
The lateral drift, because the tail rotor thrust has changed
questions.explain: Tail rotor thrust is what produces the translating tendency, so changing it changes the drift the pilot must hold off.

questions.question: How is the collective pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By lifting or lowering the swash plate
By tilting the swash plate to one side
By rotating the stationary swash plate
questions.explain: Collective raises or lowers the swash plate.

questions.question: How is the cyclic pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By turning the stationary part
By lifting the whole swash plate
By tilting the swash plate
questions.explain: Cyclic tilts the swash plate.

questions.question: Explain why the two parts of the swash plate are held parallel but joined through a bearing
options: So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are fixed to the rotor mast
So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are turning with the rotor
So the rotor plane can be tilted without moving the control rods above it
questions.explain: The bearing lets the upper part turn with the rotor while the parallel lower part stays still, passing the input across.

questions.question: A technician watches the swash plate while a helper moves one cockpit control, and the whole swash plate moves up without tilting. Which control is being moved?
options: The collective lever
The tail pedals
The cyclic stick
questions.explain: Lifting the swash plate is collective; tilting would be cyclic.

questions.question: During a control check the swash plate tilts but its mean height does not change. Which pitch change is being made?
options: Tail rotor pitch change
Cyclic pitch change
Collective pitch change
questions.explain: Tilting the swash plate produces cyclic pitch change.

questions.question: A helicopter hovers on the spot in a steady strong wind. Why can its blades not all produce the same lift?
options: The wind raises the pitch angle on one half of the disc and lowers it on the other
The wind adds to the speed of one half of the disc and subtracts from the other
The wind increases the rotational speed of the whole rotor disc
questions.explain: Wind is a relative wind just like forward speed, so it adds on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

questions.question: In forward flight the retreating blade flaps down. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
It keeps its position in the plane
It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
questions.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, its CG moves outward, so it decelerates and lags.

questions.question: Identify on which blade flapping increases the angle of attack, and give the reason it has to
options: The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
The advancing blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too much lift
questions.explain: The retreating blade is short of lift, and flapping down raises its angle of attack and so its lift.

questions.question: A rotor head is built with no flapping hinges at all. How can dissymmetry of lift still be balanced on this rotor?
options: The lead-lag hinges let the blades move up and down instead
The feathering hinges let the blades change pitch instead
The blades themselves flex and absorb the forces acting on them
questions.explain: The manual allows blade properties that absorb the forces as the alternative to a flapping hinge.

questions.question: A helicopter is in steady forward flight and the pilot makes no control input at all. Is there still lead-lag movement, and why?
options: No, because lead-lag only follows a cyclic control input
Yes, because dissymmetry of lift keeps the blades flapping
Yes, because the collective lever holds the blades at a fixed pitch
questions.explain: Dissymmetry of lift makes the blades flap in forward flight even with no input, and flapping always makes lead-lag.

questions.question: Which turning force does a counterclockwise turning main rotor generate on the fuselage
options: A clockwise turning force
A counterclockwise turning force
A nose-down pitching force
questions.explain: The fuselage force is opposite, so clockwise.

questions.question: During hover flight, which two jobs does the tail rotor thrust perform
options: Maintain heading control and tilt the rotor disk
Generate lift and compensate main rotor torque
Compensate main rotor torque and maintain heading control
questions.explain: Tail rotor thrust compensates torque and maintains heading.

questions.question: What is translating tendency
options: The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
The drift caused by the thrust of the tail rotor
The drift caused by the ground effect air cushion
questions.explain: Translating tendency is the tail-rotor-thrust drift.

questions.question: How may the pilot prevent the lateral drift due to translating tendency
options: Tilt the main rotor disk slightly in the drift direction
Reduce the tail rotor thrust until the drift stops
Tilt the main rotor disk slightly opposite to the drift
questions.explain: The disk is tilted slightly opposite to the drift.

questions.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly forward
Slightly to the right
Slightly to the left
questions.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

questions.question: Explain why the reduced downward airflow in ground effect increases the angle of attack of the blades
options: The relative wind direction changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The plane of rotation changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The pitch angle changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
questions.explain: A slower downward airflow changes the relative wind, and the angle of attack is taken from the relative wind.

questions.question: State what the collective pitch controls once the engine has failed
options: The force that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
The tail rotor thrust that keeps the heading in the descent
The engine power that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
questions.explain: With no engine the collective no longer sets engine power; it controls the force that sustains rotor RPM.

cards.question: What is the primary airfoil of the helicopter
options: The tail rotor
The fuselage
The main rotor
cards.explain: The manual names the main rotor as the helicopter's primary airfoil.

cards.question: What is an airfoil by definition
options: Any surface which generates a useful static pressure of the air
Any surface which generates a useful dynamic reaction of the air
Only a wing surface which generates lift in forward flight
cards.explain: The manual defines an airfoil as any surface giving a useful dynamic reaction of the air.

cards.question: Which two forces are named as the useful reaction of the air on an airfoil
options: Thrust and weight
Lift and thrust
Lift and drag
cards.explain: The text names lift and thrust as the two forces needed for flying and manoeuvring.

cards.question: What is the leading edge of a rotor blade
options: The edge that cuts into the wind when the rotor is turning
The outer end of the blade opposite the root
The edge opposite the one that cuts into the wind
cards.explain: The leading edge cuts into the wind.

cards.question: What is the trailing edge of a rotor blade
options: The edge opposite the leading edge
The end attached to the rotor mast
The edge that cuts into the wind
cards.explain: The trailing edge is opposite the leading edge.

cards.question: What is the advancing blade
options: The blade at the tail boom
The backward moving blade
The forward moving blade
cards.explain: The blade moving forward is the advancing blade.

cards.question: What is the retreating blade
options: The backward moving blade
The forward moving blade
The blade over the cockpit
cards.explain: The blade moving backward is the retreating blade.

cards.question: What is the relative wind
options: The direction of the airflow with respect to the ground
The speed of the natural wind at the landing site
The direction of the airflow with respect to the rotor blade
cards.explain: Relative wind is airflow direction relative to the blade.

cards.question: How is the relative wind directed in relation to the flight path of the blade
options: Always perpendicular to the path
Always opposite to the flight path
Always along the same flight path
cards.explain: The relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

cards.question: What is the axis of rotation
options: The axis around which the rotor blades are turning
The plane formed by the average tip path
The line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
cards.explain: The rotor blades turn around the axis of rotation.

cards.question: What forms the plane of rotation
options: The chord line of the blades
The average tip path of the blades
The flapping hinges of the blades
cards.explain: The plane of rotation is formed by the average blade tip path.

cards.question: What is the pitch angle
options: The acute angle between the chord and the relative wind
The acute angle between the axis and the plane of rotation
The acute angle between the chord and the plane of rotation
cards.explain: Pitch angle is measured from the plane of rotation to the chord.

cards.question: Which cockpit control changes the pitch angle of all main rotor blades
options: The tail rotor pedals
The collective pitch control
The cyclic pitch stick
cards.explain: The collective pitch control changes the pitch angle.

cards.question: When is the angle of attack equal to the pitch angle
options: When the relative wind is parallel to the axis of rotation
When the relative wind is in the same direction as the plane of rotation
When the relative wind is perpendicular to the plane of rotation
cards.explain: If the relative wind lies in the plane of rotation, both angles use the same reference line.

cards.question: The pilot increases the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack
options: It is decreased
It remains unchanged
It is also increased
cards.explain: Pitch and angle of attack change together.

cards.question: State why a technician has to study the basic principles of helicopter flight
options: To calculate the lift and thrust produced by the main rotor blades
To obtain the flight crew licence required for ground running of the rotor
To understand the maintenance and troubleshooting practices on the systems
cards.explain: The manual gives understanding of maintenance and troubleshooting as the reason for studying the principles.

cards.question: Compare the airfoils of a fixed-wing aircraft with those of a helicopter
options: Primarily the propellers on the fixed-wing aircraft, the fuselage on the helicopter
Primarily the wings on the fixed-wing aircraft, the main rotor on the helicopter
Primarily the fuselage on the fixed-wing aircraft, the tail rotor on the helicopter
cards.explain: The wings are the primary airfoil of a fixed-wing aircraft and the main rotor is the primary airfoil of the helicopter.

cards.question: Why is the helicopter often referred to as a rotary-wing aircraft
options: Its primary airfoil is the tail rotor
Its primary airfoil is the main rotor
Its fuselage acts as a rotating wing
cards.explain: Because its main lifting surface is a rotating rotor, the helicopter is called rotary-wing.

cards.question: The main rotor blades are the airfoils of a helicopter. Which of the two forces they produce holds the aircraft up against gravity?
options: Lift
Thrust
Drag
cards.explain: Of the two forces the airfoil produces, lift is the one the manual gives as counteracting gravity.

cards.question: A rotor blade is moving forward and downward through the air. In which direction does its relative wind act?
options: Forward and upward
Backward and upward
Backward and downward
cards.explain: The relative wind is always exactly opposite to the flight path of the blade, so forward and downward movement gives a backward and upward relative wind.

cards.question: Explain why the relative wind on a rotor blade changes when a hovering helicopter begins to move horizontally
options: The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the chord line of the rotor blade
The horizontal movement of the helicopter changes the span of the rotor blade
Movement of the helicopter through the air is one of the factors that affect it
cards.explain: Horizontal movement of the helicopter is one of the factors that affect the relative wind.

cards.question: A helicopter stands with its rotor stopped while wind blows over the blades. Which statement about the relative wind is correct?
options: There is no relative wind because the rotor is stopped
The relative wind is created only by blade flapping
The wind blowing over the blade creates the relative wind
cards.explain: Even with the rotor stopped, wind over the blade is airflow relative to the blade.

cards.question: A helicopter is flying and the blades flap during each revolution, so each tip follows a slightly different path. Which path defines the plane of rotation?
options: The average tip path of the blades
The path of the blade roots
The highest tip path of the blades
cards.explain: The manual defines it by the average tip path.

cards.question: Explain how one movement of the collective pitch control is able to change both the pitch angle and the angle of attack
options: It lifts the whole blade, moving the axis of rotation against the chord
It tilts the plane of rotation, moving the relative wind against the chord
It rotates the blade around the hub axis, moving the chord against each reference
cards.explain: Both angles are measured from the chord, so rotating the blade about the hub axis changes both.

cards.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes pitch angle from angle of attack?
options: Pitch angle is referenced to the relative wind, angle of attack to the plane of rotation
Pitch angle is referenced to the axis of rotation, angle of attack to the span line
Pitch angle is referenced to the plane of rotation, angle of attack to the relative wind
cards.explain: Both use the chord, but pitch angle uses the plane of rotation and angle of attack uses the relative wind.

cards.question: Why do the same factors that affect the relative wind also affect the angle of attack
options: Because the angle of attack depends upon the relative wind
Because the relative wind depends upon the pitch angle
Because the angle of attack depends upon the blade span
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured to the relative wind, so what changes one changes the other.

cards.question: The pilot holds the pitch angle constant, but outside influences change the relative wind. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It stays constant, because the pitch is constant
It changes, because it depends on the relative wind
It becomes equal to the pitch angle of the blade
cards.explain: Angle of attack is also affected by relative wind changes, not only by pitch.

cards.question: Two reference dimensions of a rotor blade are quoted, one measured along the blade centreline and one across the blade section. Which pair is correct?
options: Span along the centreline, root across the section
Span along the centreline, chord across the section
Chord along the centreline, span across the section
cards.explain: Span runs root to tip along the centreline, and the chord runs leading edge to trailing edge across the section.

cards.question: A helicopter is in forward flight and one blade is on the advancing side. From which direction does the relative wind reach that blade?
options: Horizontally forward, with the blade movement
Horizontally backward, opposite to the blade movement
Backward and upward, across the blade movement
cards.explain: The advancing blade moves forward, and the relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

cards.question: A blade is moving forward and at the same time flapping upward. Applying the rule for relative wind, from which direction does the relative wind come?
options: Forward and downward
Backward and upward
Backward and downward
cards.explain: The relative wind moves exactly opposite to the blade path, so forward-and-upward blade motion gives a backward-and- downward relative wind.

cards.question: State what creates the relative wind on a helicopter hovering in completely still air
options: The forward speed of the helicopter
The turning of the rotor blades
The wind speed and the wind direction
cards.explain: With no wind and no forward speed, only the turning of the blades is left to produce the relative wind.

cards.question: A blade is set so that its chord lies exactly along the average tip path of the blades. What is its pitch angle?
options: Ninety degrees, because the chord and the axis of rotation coincide
Equal to the angle of attack, since the relative wind coincides
Zero, because the chord and the plane of rotation coincide
cards.explain: The pitch angle is measured between the chord and the plane of rotation, so a chord lying in that plane gives zero.

cards.question: On a turning blade the pitch angle and the angle of attack are found to be unequal. What does that tell you?
options: The blade is not fitted with a feathering hinge at its root
The relative wind is not in the direction of the plane of rotation
The collective pitch control has not been moved from its stop
cards.explain: The two angles are only equal when the relative wind lies in the plane of rotation, so unequal angles mean it does not.

cards.question: The relative wind on a blade lies in the same direction as the plane of rotation and the pilot then increases the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It stays constant while the pitch angle increases
It increases and stays equal to the pitch angle
It increases and becomes larger than the pitch angle
cards.explain: With the relative wind in the plane of rotation the two angles are equal, and the angle of attack follows the pitch angle up.

cards.question: Give the explanation for the angle of attack of a blade changing while the collective pitch control is held still
options: An outside influence has changed the chord of the blade
An outside influence has changed the plane of rotation
An outside influence has changed the relative wind
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured from the relative wind, so it changes when outside influences move the relative wind.

cards.question: What is lift
options: The force produced by torque reaction
The force that is produced by the airfoil
The force that is produced by gravity
cards.explain: Lift is the airfoil's force.

cards.question: In which direction does lift act in relation to the relative wind
options: Parallel to the relative wind
Opposite to the relative wind
Perpendicular to the relative wind
cards.explain: Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

cards.question: To which bodies does gyroscopic precession apply
options: All rotating bodies
Only the tail rotor
Only the main rotor
cards.explain: It applies to all rotating bodies, including both rotors.

cards.question: How is gyroscopic precession defined
options: The change of the rotational axis as a result of an external force
The change of the rotor RPM as a result of an external force
The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
cards.explain: Precession is a change of the rotational axis caused by an external force.

cards.question: Explain why gyroscopic precession has to be considered on the tail rotor as well as on the main rotor
options: Because the tail rotor blades have feathering hinges
Because the tail rotor turns opposite to the fuselage
Because the effect applies to every rotating body
cards.explain: The principle is stated to apply to all rotating bodies, which includes the tail rotor.

cards.question: In the example wheel, an external force tries to turn the wheel around the input axis. Around which axis does the movement actually take place?
options: Only around the input axis
Only around the spin axis
Around the output axis
cards.explain: Because of precession the movement occurs around the output axis.

cards.question: Why must the steering input to the rotor be applied 90° before the point where the tilt is wanted
options: Because the swash plate is mounted 90° to the rotor
Because the output occurs 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
Because the output occurs 90° later in the direction of rotation
cards.explain: Precession shifts the result 90° in the direction of rotation, so the input must lead by 90°.

cards.question: A downward force is applied on the right side of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the output appear?
options: Right in front
Right at the rear
On the left side
cards.explain: 90° later in counterclockwise rotation from the right side is the front.

cards.question: State what happens to the direction in which lift acts on a blade when the relative wind changes direction
options: It changes with it, staying perpendicular to the relative wind
It changes with it, staying parallel to the relative wind
It stays fixed, remaining perpendicular to the plane of rotation
cards.explain: Lift is defined as perpendicular to the relative wind, so its direction follows the relative wind.

cards.question: State what must happen to the plane of rotation when gyroscopic precession tilts the axis of rotation
options: It stays level, while the axis tilts away from it
It tilts with the axis, staying perpendicular to it
It tilts the opposite way, staying parallel to the axis
cards.explain: The plane of rotation is always perpendicular to the axis of rotation, so it tilts with the axis.

cards.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt backward for rearward flight. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: On the left side
Right at the rear
On the right side
cards.explain: The output is wanted at the rear; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the left side.

cards.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt to the left. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: On the left side
Right in front
Right at the rear
cards.explain: The output is wanted on the left; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the front.

cards.question: A downward force is applied at the rear of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the tip-path plane tilt down?
options: On the right side
Right in front
On the left side
cards.explain: 90° later than the rear in counterclockwise rotation is the right side.

cards.question: Which law explains torque reaction on a helicopter fuselage
options: Newton's Third Law
Newton's law of inertia
Newton's Second Law
cards.explain: Torque reaction is action and reaction, Newton's Third Law.

cards.question: In which direction does the helicopter fuselage tend to rotate due to torque
options: Around its lateral axis, nose down
In the same direction as the rotor blades
Opposite to the direction of the rotor blades
cards.explain: Action and reaction: the fuselage turns opposite to the rotor.

cards.question: Explain why the torque of the main rotor must be counteracted before a flight is possible
options: Because the fuselage would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the rotor blades
Because the main rotor would otherwise produce thrust instead of lift
Because the rotor blades would otherwise turn in the direction opposite to the fuselage
cards.explain: Torque makes the fuselage rotate opposite to the blades, so it must be counteracted before flight.

cards.question: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above and the tail rotor is not yet producing thrust. Which way does the fuselage tend to turn?
options: Not at all
Clockwise
Counterclockwise
cards.explain: The fuselage reaction is opposite to a counterclockwise rotor, so clockwise.

cards.question: A pilot raises the collective lever and the turning force on the fuselage rises. Why must the tail rotor thrust then change too?
options: Because it is what balances the lift of the main rotor
Because it is what balances the drag of the main rotor
Because it is what compensates the torque on the airframe
cards.explain: The tail rotor is what compensates the torque, so a change in torque has to be matched by a change in its thrust.

cards.question: Name what a gyrocopter in normal flight and a helicopter after an engine failure have in common
options: The rotor is held at a fixed pitch angle by the collective
The rotor is driven by the airflow in autorotation
The rotor is driven by the engine through the drive shafts
cards.explain: Both have an unpowered rotor kept turning by the airflow, which is autorotation.

cards.question: The lift-producing rotor of a gyroplane stays connected to the engine in flight. What follows from that?
options: The rotor torque has to be compensated
The rotor can no longer stall in flight
The rotor has to be tilted slightly aft
cards.explain: An engine-driven rotor produces a torque reaction on the airframe, so it must be compensated.

cards.question: Compare how the rotor of a gyrocopter and the rotor of a gyroplane receive their power in flight
options: The gyroplane rotor is driven by the airflow, the gyrocopter rotor shares the engine power
The gyrocopter rotor is driven by the airflow, the gyroplane rotor shares the engine power
Both rotors are driven by the airflow and the propellers share the engine power
cards.explain: The gyrocopter rotor is unpowered in flight while the gyroplane shares engine power between rotor and propellers.

cards.question: A convertiplane has accelerated to the airspeed at which its rotor turns freely in autorotation. What is then providing lift and what is providing thrust?
options: The wings give the lift, the rotor gives the thrust
The rotor gives the lift, the propellers or turbines give the thrust
The wings give the lift, the propellers or turbines give the thrust
cards.explain: Once the rotor autorotates it makes no lift, so the wings carry the aircraft and the propellers or turbines push it.

cards.question: Compare the rotor of a convertiplane in cruise with the rotor of a type 3 transformation helicopter in cruise
options: The type 3 rotor turns in autorotation, the convertiplane rotor is shut down and stowed
The convertiplane rotor turns in autorotation, the type 3 rotor is shut down and stowed
Both rotors turn in autorotation and carry part of the aircraft weight
cards.explain: The convertiplane rotor keeps turning in autorotation while the type 3 rotor is deactivated and stowed.

cards.question: What does lift counteract according to the helicopter description
options: Thrust
Torque
Weight
cards.explain: Lift counteracts weight.

cards.question: After an engine failure or broken drive shafts, how can a helicopter land safely
options: By using translating tendency
By performing an autorotation
By using ground effect
cards.explain: Autorotation allows a safe landing without engine power.

cards.question: How do helicopters change direction, unlike other aircraft
options: By changing the angle of the rotor blade plane
By changing the RPM of the main rotor
By deflecting control surfaces on the fuselage
cards.explain: Helicopters tilt the rotor blade plane instead of deflecting surfaces.

cards.question: The pilot moves the cyclic stick forward. What does the rotor plane do
options: It tilts backward
It tilts forward
It moves upward
cards.explain: Forward cyclic tilts the rotor plane forward.

cards.question: What does the pilot do to the main rotor blades by moving the collective lever upwards
options: Increases the pitch angle of all blades at the same time
Increases the pitch angle of each blade once per revolution
Tilts the rotor plane in the direction of flight
cards.explain: Collective up raises the pitch of all blades together.

cards.question: The pilot moves the collective lever upwards. What does the helicopter do
options: It descends
It climbs
It turns left
cards.explain: More pitch gives more lift and the helicopter climbs.

cards.question: Which control does the pilot use to turn the helicopter around the rotor mast axis
options: The collective lever
The cyclic pitch stick
The tail rotor pedals
cards.explain: Pedals turn the helicopter around the mast axis.

cards.question: What do the pedals change
options: The pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
The pitch angle of the main rotor blades
The tilt of the main rotor plane
cards.explain: Pedals change tail rotor blade pitch.

cards.question: State what the helicopter gains from being able to tilt its rotor plane slightly in any direction
options: Thrust can act in all directions, giving directional control
Torque can act in all directions, giving heading control
Lift can act in all directions, giving collective control
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets the thrust act in any direction, which is how directional control is obtained.

cards.question: Why does a helicopter need no pull or push propellers
options: Because the rotors generate both lift and thrust
Because the tail rotor generates the thrust
Because the rotors are driven by the airflow
cards.explain: The rotor provides both lift and thrust.

cards.question: How do the rotors of a helicopter additionally ensure directional control
options: The rotor plane may be tilted so thrust can act in all directions
The rotor RPM is changed so thrust acts in all directions
Control surfaces on the rotor blades are deflected
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets thrust act in any direction.

cards.question: During an autorotation after an engine failure, which statement about control is correct?
options: The helicopter is not controllable and lands wherever the descent takes it
The helicopter is fully controllable and the pilot can choose the touchdown point
Only the pedals remain effective and the touchdown point cannot be chosen
cards.explain: The manual says it is fully controllable and the pilot selects the touchdown location.

cards.question: Why must the rotor plane be tilted when changing from hover to forward flight
options: Because the rotor RPM must be increased for forward flight
Because the tail rotor thrust acts in the direction of flight
Because rotor thrust always acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
cards.explain: To point thrust forward, the plane must tilt, because thrust is perpendicular to it.

cards.question: How does cyclic control create different amounts of lift within the rotor plane
options: The rotor RPM is increased and decreased during each revolution
All blades change their pitch angle at the same time together
The blade changes its angle of incidence during each revolution
cards.explain: Cyclic changes the incidence per revolution, giving different lift around the disc.

cards.question: Explain why moving the collective lever also alters the torque effect on the fuselage
options: Because the movement of the lever also changes the tail rotor pitch
Because the movement of the lever also changes the engine power
Because the movement of the lever also tilts the rotor plane
cards.explain: The collective lever changes engine power as well as blade pitch, and with it the torque.

cards.question: Besides changing the blade pitch, which other effect does a movement of the collective lever have?
options: It changes engine power and causes effects like torque
It tilts the rotor plane and causes translating tendency
It changes tail rotor pitch and causes precession
cards.explain: Collective movement also changes engine power and torque effects.

cards.question: A pilot wants to yaw the helicopter around the rotor mast axis. How do the pedals bring this about?
options: They change the pitch angle of the main rotor blades and so vary its thrust
They change the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades and so vary its thrust
They tilt the tail rotor plane and so vary the direction of its thrust
cards.explain: Pedal movement changes tail rotor blade pitch, which varies tail rotor thrust and yaws the aircraft.

cards.question: How do the pedals vary the tail rotor thrust
options: By changing the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
By changing the RPM of the tail rotor drive shaft
By tilting the plane of rotation of the tail rotor
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust is varied via blade pitch.

cards.question: State the penalty that follows from a helicopter rotor generating both lift and thrust by itself
options: Its rotor cannot be tilted out of the horizontal plane
Its torque reaction on the fuselage has to be counteracted
Its downwash cannot escape from under the fuselage
cards.explain: A powered rotor doing all the work also produces the torque reaction that must be counteracted.

cards.question: Explain how a helicopter is able to fly sideways
options: The rotor plane is tilted sideways, so the thrust acts sideways
The tail rotor thrust is increased, so the fuselage is pushed sideways
The blade pitch is increased on one side, so the lift acts sideways
cards.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the plane sideways points the thrust sideways.

cards.question: Compare how the cyclic control and the collective control change the pitch angle of the main rotor blades
options: The collective changes it during each revolution, the cyclic changes all blades together
Both change it during each revolution, but only the cyclic changes all blades together
The cyclic changes it during each revolution, the collective changes all blades together
cards.explain: Cyclic pitch varies around the disc each revolution while collective pitch moves all blades by the same amount.

cards.question: A pilot pushes the cyclic stick forward to fly forward. Which chain of events takes place at the swash plate and the blades?
options: The swash plate is lifted, the control rods move and the blade pitch rises on every blade at once
The swash plate turns, the bell cranks move and the blade pitch is held through the revolution
The swash plate tilts, the control rods move and the blade pitch varies through the revolution
cards.explain: A cyclic input tilts the swash plate, which moves the control rods and varies blade pitch through each revolution.

cards.question: Explain why the rotor plane must be tilted when changing from a hover into forward flight, in terms of the law of acceleration
options: A force is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
A torque is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor mast
A force is needed in the direction of flight, and thrust acts parallel to the rotor plane
cards.explain: Accelerating forward needs a forward force, and the only way to point the thrust forward is to tilt the rotor plane.

cards.question: In straight-ahead flight the blade has minimum incidence in front and maximum incidence at the rear. What is the result for the rotor plane?
options: It tilts forward, giving lift and forward thrust
It tilts backward, giving lift and rearward thrust
It stays level, giving lift but no thrust
cards.explain: More lift at the rear and less at the front tilts the plane forward, producing lift and forward thrust.

cards.question: Explain why raising the collective lever makes the rotor produce more lift
options: The rotational speed of every blade rises, and with it the chord
The pitch angle of every blade rises, and with it the angle of attack
The plane of rotation of every blade rises, and with it the relative wind
cards.explain: More pitch means more angle of attack on every blade, so the rotor makes more lift.

cards.question: Identify which hinge allows the pitch change commanded from the cockpit and which allows the blade to move under aerodynamic forces
options: The feathering hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
The flapping hinge for the pitch change, the feathering hinge for the movement
The lead-lag hinge for the pitch change, the flapping hinge for the movement
cards.explain: Feathering hinges take the commanded pitch change, flapping hinges let the blade move under the air loads.

cards.question: A pilot raises the collective lever to climb. The engine power changes and so does the torque effect on the fuselage. Which control must then vary the tail rotor thrust?
options: The collective lever
The tail rotor pedals
The cyclic pitch stick
cards.explain: Torque is compensated by the tail rotor, whose thrust the pilot varies with the pedals.

cards.question: Explain why varying the tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter turn around the rotor mast axis
options: The thrust no longer exactly balances the torque reaction on the fuselage
The thrust no longer exactly balances the lift produced by the main rotor
The thrust tilts the main rotor disk away from the rotor mast axis
cards.explain: The tail rotor thrust is what holds the torque reaction in balance, so changing it lets the fuselage turn.

cards.question: A pilot pushes the left pedal forward during a hover and holds the new heading. What else now needs attention?
options: The pitch angle, because the collective lever has changed
The rotor RPM, because the tail rotor pitch has changed
The lateral drift, because the tail rotor thrust has changed
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust is what produces the translating tendency, so changing it changes the drift the pilot must hold off.

cards.question: How is the collective pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By rotating the stationary swash plate
By lifting or lowering the swash plate
By tilting the swash plate to one side
cards.explain: Collective raises or lowers the swash plate.

cards.question: How is the cyclic pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By tilting the swash plate
By lifting the whole swash plate
By turning the stationary part
cards.explain: Cyclic tilts the swash plate.

cards.question: In a hover with no wind, how does the lift of the rotor blades compare
options: The advancing blade generates more lift
The retreating blade generates more lift
All blades generate the same amount of lift
cards.explain: In a no-wind hover all blades have the same parameters.

cards.question: What is dissymmetry of lift
options: The difference in lift in and out of ground effect
The difference in lift between main and tail rotor
The difference in lift between advancing and retreating blade
cards.explain: The lift difference between advancing and retreating blade is dissymmetry of lift.

cards.question: Where does the blade's centre of gravity move when the blade flaps upwards
options: Closer towards the trailing edge
Closer towards the blade tip
Closer towards the rotational axis
cards.explain: Upward flapping brings the CG closer to the axis.

cards.question: Where does the blade's centre of gravity move when the blade flaps downwards
options: Closer to the blade tip
Closer to the rotational axis
Closer to the leading edge
cards.explain: Downward flapping moves the CG outward toward the tip.

cards.question: What happens to the angle of attack as the advancing blade flaps up
options: It increases
It stays the same
It decreases
cards.explain: Upward flapping decreases the angle of attack.

cards.question: What happens to the angle of attack as the retreating blade flaps down
options: It stays the same
It increases
It decreases
cards.explain: Downward flapping increases the angle of attack.

cards.question: Which two ways are given to achieve the flexibility for blade flapping
options: A lead-lag hinge or a larger and stiffer tail rotor
A flapping hinge or blade properties that absorb the forces
A feathering hinge or a stronger swash plate bearing
cards.explain: Either a flapping hinge or blades that absorb the forces.

cards.question: Compare what acts on the stationary part of the swash plate with what the rotating part acts on
options: The rotor head acts on it through a bearing; it drives the bell cranks through control rods
Control rods and bell cranks from the cockpit act on it; it drives the blades through control rods
Control rods from the blades act on it; it drives the cockpit controls through bell cranks
cards.explain: The cockpit acts on the stationary part and the rotating part is connected onward to the blades.

cards.question: Why does the swash plate have to act as an interface
options: It transfers torque between the main rotor and the tail rotor drive system
It transfers control signals between the stationary input system and the rotating rotor
It transfers engine power between the main gearbox and the rotating rotor mast
cards.explain: Cockpit inputs are stationary but the blades rotate, so the swash plate links the two.

cards.question: What is the direct result on the rotor blades when the swash plate moves?
options: The blades move forward and backward on lead-lag hinges
The control rods move and the blade pitch angle changes
The bearing locks and the blades stop their flapping
cards.explain: Swash plate motion moves control rods, which change pitch.

cards.question: A helicopter is hovering with no wind at all. Why is there no dissymmetry of lift in this condition?
options: There is no pitch angle on either blade, so both blades have the same parameters
There is no rotational speed at the blade tips, so both blades have the same parameters
There is no airstream from speed of flight, so both blades have the same parameters
cards.explain: Without the airstream caused by the speed of flight there is nothing to add to one blade and subtract from the other.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade produce more lift in forward flight
options: The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
Its pitch angle is increased by the collective
cards.explain: The airstream adds to its speed, giving more lift.

cards.question: Why does the retreating blade produce less lift in forward flight
options: Its pitch angle is reduced by the tail rotor pedals
The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
cards.explain: The airstream subtracts from its speed, giving less lift.

cards.question: Explain why an upward flapping rotor blade accelerates while the rotor RPM stays constant
options: Its centre of gravity moves closer to the trailing edge
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the rotational axis
cards.explain: A mass moved towards the centre of rotation tries to speed the rotation up, so the up-flapping blade accelerates.

cards.question: A mass point on a rotating disk is moved towards the edge of the disk. What happens to the rotational speed and why?
options: It decelerates, because the mass resists the tangential acceleration
It stays constant, because the rotor RPM is fixed by the engine
It accelerates, because the mass tries to hold its higher speed
cards.explain: Moving outward needs higher circumferential speed; inertia resists and slows the rotation.

cards.question: A mass point on a rotating disk is moved towards the centre of rotation. What does it do to the rotational speed?
options: It has no effect on the rotational speed
It tries to accelerate the rotational speed
It tries to decelerate the rotational speed
cards.explain: Moving inward, it keeps its higher speed and so accelerates the rotation.

cards.question: With constant rotor RPM, what does an upward flapping blade do
options: It accelerates and moves forward
It decelerates and moves backward
It accelerates and moves backward
cards.explain: Its CG moves inward, so it speeds up and leads.

cards.question: With constant rotor RPM, what does a downward flapping blade do
options: It decelerates and moves forward
It decelerates and moves backward
It accelerates and moves forward
cards.explain: Its CG moves outward, so it slows down and lags.

cards.question: Why is the installation of a lead-lag hinge required
options: Flapping blades accelerate or decelerate and move forward or backward
Flapping blades change their pitch angle during each revolution
Flapping blades change the direction of the torque reaction
cards.explain: The forward and backward blade movement caused by flapping must be allowed by a lead-lag hinge.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade flap up
options: It experiences increased relative wind and generates more lift
It experiences decreased relative wind and generates less lift
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
cards.explain: More relative wind means more lift, so it flaps up.

cards.question: The retreating blade experiences a decreased relative wind. Which sequence follows according to the manual?
options: Less lift, blade flaps down, angle of attack and lift increase
More lift, blade flaps up, angle of attack and lift decrease
Less lift, blade flaps up, angle of attack increases
cards.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, which raises angle of attack and lift.

cards.question: The advancing blade flaps up in forward flight. What finally happens to its lift?
options: The lift decreases as the angle of attack decreases
The lift stays constant as the pitch is constant
The lift increases as the angle of attack increases
cards.explain: Upward flapping reduces angle of attack and so lift.

cards.question: Is blade flapping alone sufficient to restore rotor balance
options: No, it helps to balance but is not sufficient
Yes, it fully restores rotor balance
No, it increases the dissymmetry of lift
cards.explain: Flapping helps but does not fully restore balance.

cards.question: Why must a rotor blade be able to move and occupy a new position
options: Because the swash plate rotates with the rotor
Because aerodynamic forces act on the rotor blade
Because the torque reaction turns the fuselage
cards.explain: Aerodynamic forces require the blade to move.

cards.question: Blade flapping compensates dissymmetry of lift. Which hinge lets the blade move up and down for this?
options: Feathering hinge
Lead-lag hinge
Flapping hinge
cards.explain: Flapping hinges allow the up-down movement.

cards.question: A pilot makes a cyclic control input. Which chain of effects follows according to the manual?
options: The tail rotor thrust changes, which generates torque
The swash plate lifts, which generates ground effect
The rotor plane tilts, which generates a lead-lag movement
cards.explain: Cyclic tilts the plane, and that generates lead-lag.

cards.question: Explain why the two parts of the swash plate are held parallel but joined through a bearing
options: So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are turning with the rotor
So the rotor plane can be tilted without moving the control rods above it
So the cockpit input can be passed to blades that are fixed to the rotor mast
cards.explain: The bearing lets the upper part turn with the rotor while the parallel lower part stays still, passing the input across.

cards.question: During a ground check the whole swash plate is seen to rise without tilting, and every blade takes a larger pitch angle. What will the helicopter do if this is done in flight?
options: It yaws left, because the tail rotor pitch is increased
It flies forward, because the rotor plane is tilted forward
It climbs, because all blades gain pitch together
cards.explain: Lifting the swash plate is a collective pitch increase, which makes more lift and a climb.

cards.question: Name the cockpit control that changes a blade pitch angle without acting through the main rotor swash plate
options: The cyclic stick, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
The pedals, which change the tail rotor blade pitch
The collective lever, which changes the main rotor blade pitch
cards.explain: The swash plate serves the main rotor blades, while the pedals act on the tail rotor blades.

cards.question: A technician watches the swash plate while a helper moves one cockpit control, and the whole swash plate moves up without tilting. Which control is being moved?
options: The cyclic stick
The collective lever
The tail pedals
cards.explain: Lifting the swash plate is collective; tilting would be cyclic.

cards.question: During a control check the swash plate tilts but its mean height does not change. Which pitch change is being made?
options: Collective pitch change
Tail rotor pitch change
Cyclic pitch change
cards.explain: Tilting the swash plate produces cyclic pitch change.

cards.question: State where on the rotor disc the highest airspeed occurs when a helicopter flies forward
options: At the tip of the advancing blade
At the root of the advancing blade
At the tip of the retreating blade
cards.explain: Speed rises towards the tip and the opposing airstream adds on the advancing side, so the advancing tip is fastest.

cards.question: A helicopter hovers on the spot in a steady strong wind. Why can its blades not all produce the same lift?
options: The wind raises the pitch angle on one half of the disc and lowers it on the other
The wind increases the rotational speed of the whole rotor disc
The wind adds to the speed of one half of the disc and subtracts from the other
cards.explain: Wind is a relative wind just like forward speed, so it adds on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

cards.question: A blade flaps up and therefore accelerates and moves forward in the plane of rotation. Which hinge has to allow this?
options: The lead-lag hinge
The flapping hinge
The feathering hinge
cards.explain: Movement forward and backward in the plane of rotation is taken by the lead-lag hinge.

cards.question: In forward flight the advancing blade flaps up. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
It keeps its position in the plane
cards.explain: The advancing blade flaps up, its CG moves inward, so it accelerates and moves forward.

cards.question: In forward flight the retreating blade flaps down. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
It keeps its position in the plane
It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
cards.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, its CG moves outward, so it decelerates and lags.

cards.question: Explain why blade flapping is described as a self-correcting effect
options: The blade with more lift flaps down, which reduces its angle of attack and its lift
The blade with more lift flaps up, which reduces its pitch angle and its lift
The blade with more lift flaps up, which reduces its angle of attack and its lift
cards.explain: The extra lift causes the up-flap, and the up-flap takes the angle of attack and the lift back down again.

cards.question: Identify on which blade flapping increases the angle of attack, and give the reason it has to
options: The advancing blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too much lift
The retreating blade, because it is the one producing too little lift
cards.explain: The retreating blade is short of lift, and flapping down raises its angle of attack and so its lift.

cards.question: Why does upward flapping reduce the angle of attack of the advancing blade, using the relative wind rule?
options: Moving up reduces the blade pitch angle
Moving up adds an upward relative wind component
Moving up adds a downward relative wind component
cards.explain: Relative wind is opposite to blade motion, so an upward-moving blade meets air from above, reducing the angle of attack.

cards.question: A rotor head is built with no flapping hinges at all. How can dissymmetry of lift still be balanced on this rotor?
options: The feathering hinges let the blades change pitch instead
The lead-lag hinges let the blades move up and down instead
The blades themselves flex and absorb the forces acting on them
cards.explain: The manual allows blade properties that absorb the forces as the alternative to a flapping hinge.

cards.question: A helicopter is in steady forward flight and the pilot makes no control input at all. Is there still lead-lag movement, and why?
options: Yes, because dissymmetry of lift keeps the blades flapping
No, because lead-lag only follows a cyclic control input
Yes, because the collective lever holds the blades at a fixed pitch
cards.explain: Dissymmetry of lift makes the blades flap in forward flight even with no input, and flapping always makes lead-lag.

cards.question: A pilot in forward flight moves the cyclic stick to the right. Which blade movement is produced in addition to the pitch change?
options: A feathering movement, because the rotor plane tilts
A lead-lag movement, because the rotor RPM changes
A lead-lag movement, because the rotor plane tilts
cards.explain: A cyclic input tilts the rotor plane and the tilt generates a lead-lag movement.

cards.question: Which turning force does a counterclockwise turning main rotor generate on the fuselage
options: A nose-down pitching force
A counterclockwise turning force
A clockwise turning force
cards.explain: The fuselage force is opposite, so clockwise.

cards.question: During hover flight, which two jobs does the tail rotor thrust perform
options: Compensate main rotor torque and maintain heading control
Maintain heading control and tilt the rotor disk
Generate lift and compensate main rotor torque
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust compensates torque and maintains heading.

cards.question: Within which height is a helicopter operating in ground effect
options: Within two rotor diameters
Within one rotor diameter
Within half a rotor diameter
cards.explain: In-ground effect is within one rotor diameter.

cards.question: How does the power required to hover in ground effect compare with hovering out of ground effect?
options: More power is required in ground effect
The same power is required in both
Less power is required in ground effect
cards.explain: Hovering in ground effect needs less power.

cards.question: During powered flight, how is the rotor drag overcome
options: With rotor inertia
With engine power
With upward airflow
cards.explain: In powered flight, engine power overcomes rotor drag.

cards.question: In which two failure cases must some other force sustain the rotor RPM
options: Engine failure or broken drive shafts
Swash plate failure or broken control rods
Tail rotor failure or broken pedals
cards.explain: Engine failure or broken drive shafts require another force.

cards.question: A helicopter is in a steady hover. Which two jobs is the thrust of the tail rotor doing at the same time?
options: Compensating the main rotor torque and preventing the lateral drift
Maintaining heading control and tilting the main rotor disk slightly
Compensating the main rotor torque and maintaining heading control
cards.explain: In the hover the tail rotor thrust both compensates the main rotor torque and maintains heading control; the drift it causes is held off with the main rotor disk instead.

cards.question: A helicopter in hover drifts sideways although torque is compensated. What causes this drift?
options: Gyroscopic precession
The thrust of the tail rotor
Dissymmetry of lift
cards.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust causes translating tendency.

cards.question: Which rotor thrust both compensates torque and causes translating tendency
options: The total rotor thrust
The tail rotor thrust
The main rotor thrust
cards.explain: The same tail rotor thrust compensates torque and causes the drift.

cards.question: Explain why ground effect becomes more pronounced the nearer the ground is approached
options: Because it is caused by the surface interfering with the rotor airflow pattern
Because it is caused by the surface increasing the pitch angle of the blades
Because it is caused by the surface reducing the rotational speed of the blades
cards.explain: The effect comes from the surface interfering with the rotor airflow, so it grows as the surface gets closer.

cards.question: What causes ground effect
options: Increased air density close to the ground surface
Interference of the surface with the rotor airflow pattern
Interference of the tail rotor with the main rotor airflow
cards.explain: The ground surface interferes with the rotor airflow.

cards.question: A helicopter hovering out of ground effect descends into an in-ground effect hover. What happens to blade efficiency and why?
options: It increases, because the reduced downward airflow increases the angle of attack
It decreases, because the increased downward airflow reduces the angle of attack
It increases, because the pilot must increase the pitch angle of the blades
cards.explain: Reduced downwash raises angle of attack and efficiency.

cards.question: Explain why a helicopter in autorotation has to descend
options: Because the engine power is needed to overcome the drag of the rotor blades
Because the collective pitch is lowered to its minimum stop during autorotation
Because the airflow up through the rotor in the descent supplies the energy
cards.explain: The upward airflow that keeps the rotor turning only exists while the helicopter is descending.

cards.question: What provides the energy to overcome blade drag and turn the rotor during autorotation
options: The tail rotor thrust through the gearbox
The engine power through the drive shafts
The airflow passing up through the rotor during descent
cards.explain: Upward airflow during descent drives the rotor.

cards.question: As altitude decreases in autorotation, what happens to the energy stored in the turning rotor?
options: More potential energy is converted into kinetic energy stored in the rotor
More kinetic energy is converted into potential energy of the helicopter
The stored rotor energy is lost to drag and the rotor comes to a stop
cards.explain: Descent converts potential into kinetic energy stored in the rotor.

cards.question: Why must the rotor RPM be sustained after an engine failure
options: So that a controlled flight can be continued to the ground
So that the tail rotor can be stopped during the descent
So that the engine can be restarted during the descent
cards.explain: Rotor RPM keeps the helicopter controllable to the ground.

cards.question: Name the cockpit control the pilot uses to hold off the drift caused by translating tendency
options: The cyclic stick, which tilts the main rotor disk
The pedals, which tilt the tail rotor thrust line
The collective lever, which lifts the main rotor disk
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor disk is a cyclic input, so the cyclic stick is the control that holds off the drift.

cards.question: Explain how tilting the main rotor disk stops the drift caused by the tail rotor
options: The lift then acts partly against the torque direction
The thrust then acts partly against the rotor mast axis
The thrust then acts partly in the opposite sideways direction
cards.explain: Thrust acts perpendicular to the rotor plane, so tilting the disk the other way points some thrust against the drift.

cards.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly to the right
Slightly forward
Slightly to the left
cards.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

cards.question: Explain why the reduced downward airflow in ground effect increases the angle of attack of the blades
options: The relative wind direction changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The plane of rotation changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
The pitch angle changes, and the angle of attack is measured from it
cards.explain: A slower downward airflow changes the relative wind, and the angle of attack is taken from the relative wind.

cards.question: A helicopter settles into a hover close to the ground and the pilot wants to stay there. Which lever does he move and what happens to the power needed?
options: He lowers the collective, and more power is needed
He lowers the collective, and less power is needed
He raises the collective, and more power is needed
cards.explain: Reducing blade pitch is done with the collective, and hovering in ground effect needs less power.

cards.question: A helicopter hovering just above the ground climbs slowly until it is just under one rotor diameter up. What has happened to ground effect?
options: It is stronger and still present
It is lost once the skids leave the ground
It is weaker but still present
cards.explain: Ground effect reaches to one rotor diameter and weakens with height, so it is still there but reduced.

cards.question: In ground effect the lift vector of the blades becomes more vertical. Why does that reduce the power the pilot needs?
options: More of the rotor force acts straight along the blade span
More of the rotor force acts straight against the weight
More of the rotor force acts straight against the drag
cards.explain: Lift is what overcomes weight, so a more vertical lift vector puts more of the rotor force where it is needed.

cards.question: A pilot descends from an out-of-ground effect hover into ground effect and wants to remain in the ground effect hover. What must he do and why?
options: Increase the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency decreases
Keep the blade pitch angle, because efficiency is unchanged
Reduce the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency increases
cards.explain: Entering ground effect raises angle of attack and efficiency, so pitch is reduced to stay in the hover.

cards.question: A helicopter hovers in ground effect and the pilot climbs out of ground effect without changing the collective. Based on the text, what happens to the power requirement to keep hovering?
options: It decreases
It stays the same
It increases
cards.explain: Hovering out of ground effect needs higher power than in ground effect.

cards.question: State what the collective pitch controls once the engine has failed
options: The engine power that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
The force that keeps the rotor turning in the descent
The tail rotor thrust that keeps the heading in the descent
cards.explain: With no engine the collective no longer sets engine power; it controls the force that sustains rotor RPM.

cards.question: An engine fails in cruise and the pilot chooses a field to land in. What makes that choice possible?
options: The rotor keeps turning at an RPM that provides aircraft control
The engine keeps turning at an RPM that provides hydraulic power
The rotor keeps turning at an RPM that provides enough lift to hover
cards.explain: Autorotation keeps the rotor at a controlling RPM, so the helicopter stays fully controllable and the pilot picks the spot.

cards.question: Explain why the kinetic energy stored in the turning rotor must not all be spent during the autorotative descent
options: It is needed to restart the engine before the touchdown
It is needed to cushion the touchdown near the ground
It is needed to drive the tail rotor during the touchdown
cards.explain: The stored rotor energy is what the pilot uses in the second phase to cushion the touchdown.

cards.question: An engine fails in cruise. In which order does the pilot use energy during the autorotation?
options: Rotor kinetic energy cushions the descent, then altitude drives the rotor at touchdown
Altitude drives the rotor in the descent, then rotor kinetic energy cushions touchdown
Engine power drives the rotor in the descent, then altitude cushions touchdown
cards.explain: Phase 1 converts altitude into rotor energy; phase 2 uses the rotor energy for touchdown.

questions.question: Which other name is given to closed loop control
options: correction
regulation
actuation
questions.explain: The manual gives regulation as the other name for closed loop control.

questions.question: Which quantity is denoted by Xw in the terms used for closed loop control
options: reference value
error
control value
questions.explain: Xw is the symbol given for the error in a closed loop system.

questions.question: For a P - Regulator, to what is the change in the output value always proportional
options: the magnitude of the input value
the rate of change of the input value
the change in the input value
questions.explain: A proportional regulator ties the change of its output directly to the change of its input.

questions.question: For an I - Regulator, to what is the rate of change of the output value proportional
options: the rate of change of its input value
the change in its output value
its input value
questions.explain: In an integral regulator it is how fast the output moves that follows the input.

questions.question: For a D - Regulator, to what is the output value proportional
options: the rate of change of the output value
the change in the input value
the rate of change of the input value
questions.explain: A differential regulator responds to how fast its input is changing.

questions.question: Under which condition does a P - Regulator generate a controller output value
options: an error value exists at its input
the error value at its input is zero
the input value is changing at a constant rate
questions.explain: No error at the input means no output from a proportional regulator.

questions.question: What are the three degrees of translatory freedom
options: the linear movements along the X, Y and Z axes
the rotations about the X, Y and Z axes
the linear movements along the roll and pitch axes
questions.explain: Translatory freedom is straight line movement along each of the three axes.

questions.question: For which systems is the conduct of flight decomposed into part-tasks in automatic flight guidance
options: the autopilot / flight director and the flight management system
the autopilot / flight director and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
the flight management system and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
questions.explain: The part-tasks are shared between the AP/FD and the ATHR.

questions.question: During climb, cruise and descent, how are the modes of the longitudinal channel and of the lateral channel chosen?
options: They are selected in a strict sequence by the system
They are selected together as a fixed combination
They are selectable independently from each other
questions.explain: In these phases the vertical and lateral modes are picked separately.

questions.question: Where do the legs of the standard instrument departure end
options: at the initial approach fix
at the active runway
at the airway system
questions.explain: The SID runs from the start of the flight plan up to the airway system.

questions.question: Which position sensors does the FMCS use to provide positioning and navigation automatically
options: DME/DME, VOR/DME, IRS and GPS
VOR/DME, ILS, radio altimeter and GPS
DME/DME, VOR/ILS, IRS and ATC
questions.explain: Those four sensor sources are the ones used for FMCS positioning.

questions.question: How does the flight management system relate to the autoflight system
options: an independent system not included in it
a subsystem which forms part of it
a regulator combination provided by it
questions.explain: The FMS stands outside the autoflight system as the term is used here.

questions.question: What is the objective of the managed automatic level of guidance
options: To let the crew leave the FMS profile at short notice
To relieve the crew of manual control tasks
To support the pilot flying with attitude commands
questions.explain: Relieving the crew of the manual control tasks is the objective given, which leaves them time to monitor the overall situation.

questions.question: At the managed manual level, what supplies the reference values and parameters used by the FD
options: the flight management system
the pilot at the control panel
the auto-thrust system
questions.explain: Managed manual means the FD is fed by the FMS while the pilot flies by hand.

questions.question: At the basic manual level, what does the pilot flying have to do?
options: Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by selecting modes and reference values
Maintain pitch and roll attitude by following the flight director commands
Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by manipulating the controls and thrust
questions.explain: With no autoflight support the pilot holds the values himself on the controls and the thrust levers.

questions.question: Which change to the flying properties of an aircraft is brought about by its flight condition regulators?
options: Increased accuracy of the position sensors
Increased damping of aircraft oscillations
Increased thrust rating in each flight phase
