questions.explain: Better damping of the aircraft's oscillations is one of the listed modifications.

questions.question: What decides whether disengagement follows an overpowering of the flight controls
options: The torque the limiter is built to pass and the airspeed
The circumstances of the input and the autopilot itself
The mode selected and the channel that is engaged
questions.explain: Disengagement is made conditional on both the pilot's input and the design of the autopilot.

questions.question: What happens to the AP engage switch when an interlock condition becomes invalid
options: It is held at its last selected mode
It is latched in the ON position
It is reset to the OFF position
questions.explain: Loss of a condition resets the engage switch to OFF.

questions.question: What supplies the force acting along the aircraft X-axis
options: Spoiler drag
Rudder deflection
Engine thrust
questions.explain: Thrust acts along the X-axis.

questions.question: What is the difference in role between primary and secondary control surfaces
options: Primary surfaces give lateral control, secondary surfaces change the longitudinal condition
Primary surfaces give trimming control, secondary surfaces change the dynamic condition
Primary surfaces give continuous control, secondary surfaces change the stationary condition
questions.explain: Primary surfaces are for continuous control; secondary surfaces change the stationary flight condition.

questions.question: A flight director mode is already active when the pilot engages the autopilot. How does the autopilot behave?
options: It drops the mode and reverts to pitch attitude hold at once
It takes the mode over and runs in the matching upper mode at once
It holds the mode armed until the basic mode is cancelled
questions.explain: An active FD mode is adopted by the autopilot, so no basic mode appears.

questions.question: A lasting pitch disturbance has to be compensated with the autopilot engaged. Why is the stabilizer used rather than holding the elevator deflected?
options: The elevator must keep its full travel for short term disturbances
The elevator must keep its neutral position for the gain schedule
The stabilizer must keep its full travel for long term disturbances
questions.explain: Holding the elevator deflected would eat into the travel it needs for gusts, so the stabilizer takes the standing load.

questions.question: The autopilot is disengaged after a long cruise during which auto-trim has been working. Why is there no abrupt pitch attitude change?
options: The elevator is already resting in its neutral position
The stabilizer is already resting in its neutral position
The elevator is already held by the torque limiter
questions.explain: With the standing moment carried by the stabilizer and the elevator at neutral, nothing springs back at disengagement.

questions.question: The angle of attack climbs past the maximum allowed value. What does the alpha trim subsystem do and for how long?
options: It drives the stabilizer leading edge up until the Mach number falls
It drives the stabilizer leading edge up until alpha falls below the curve
It drives the stabilizer leading edge down until alpha falls below the curve
questions.explain: Leading edge up is nose down, which unloads the angle of attack until it is back under the curve.

questions.question: An aircraft has a high longitudinal static stability. Why must the onset of auto-trim action be deferred?
options: Large stabilizer displacements are needed to counter long term disturbances
Small elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
Large elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
questions.explain: High stability makes the surfaces less effective, so ordinary gust corrections already use large deflections and trimming must wait.

questions.question: Why does an electronic integrator have to be added when an actuator motor is built into a servo loop
options: The motor loses the position feedback it needs for the loop
The motor loses its natural integral input/output behaviour
The motor loses its proportional input/output behaviour
questions.explain: Inside a servo loop the motor no longer integrates, so the behaviour must be restored electronically.

questions.question: The autopilot has just been engaged and no upper mode has been selected. Which attitudes do its two channels control straight away?
options: The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
The pitch channel the flight path, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the heading only
questions.explain: Each channel takes its basic mode at once, pitch attitude in pitch and roll attitude or heading in roll.

questions.question: A pilot holds a steady force on the control wheel in CWS. What do the inner loops make of it, and what does the aircraft do?
options: A proportional roll rate, which changes the attitude and the heading
A proportional roll angle, which changes the turn rate and the track
A fixed roll rate, which changes the heading but not the attitude
questions.explain: The force becomes a proportional roll rate, and a lasting roll rate changes the attitude and so the heading.

questions.question: A pilot applies force to the column and to the wheel at the same time in CWS. What two commands does the computer form from the sensor voltages?
options: A pitch attitude or a roll rate command
A pitch rate or a roll attitude command
A vertical speed or a turn rate command
questions.explain: The computer makes a pitch attitude command or a roll rate command out of the sensor voltage.

questions.question: A pilot wants a different target airspeed while supervisory override is available and the autopilot is holding the nose where it is. How can he obtain it?
options: By changing the pitch attitude manually at the control column
By changing the vertical speed target at the mode control panel
By changing the thrust setting manually at the power levers
questions.explain: With pitch attitude hold active, a manual pitch change is the way the pilot trades to a new speed.

questions.question: A meal is being served in the cabin and the pilot winds the outer knob below the heading window to its lower setting. What is he achieving?
options: A smaller maximum roll angle, which improves passenger comfort
A slower heading capture rate, which improves passenger comfort
A smaller maximum heading change, which improves passenger comfort
questions.explain: Reducing the maximum roll angle is what that knob does, and comfort is the stated reason for using it.

questions.question: The reference bank angle produced by the outer loop no longer matches the bank angle the aircraft is actually at. What does the inner loop do?
options: It commands a change in heading reference
It commands a change in roll attitude
It commands a change in rudder deflection
questions.explain: A difference between reference and actual roll angle makes the inner loop command a roll attitude change.

questions.question: The autopilot increases lift to hold altitude in a turn. Why must the thrust system then be brought in as well?
options: Because the extra lift brings extra drag, which would lower the airspeed
Because the extra bank brings extra slip, which would raise the fuel flow
Because the extra lift brings extra weight, which would lower the ceiling
questions.explain: More lift means more drag and a loss of speed, so a roll to thrust coupling adds thrust to hold the speed.

questions.question: Why does the autopilot have to treat interception and stabilization as two separate jobs?
options: The path is in segments, and each one has to be flown at a different airspeed
The path is in segments, and each must be caught without overshoot or offset
The path is continuous, but the sensors update at two different rates
questions.explain: Because the path is built of segments, each one has to be intercepted cleanly and then held.

questions.question: Both the pitch channel and the thrust system can hold the speed. Which of them gets the job, and why can they not share it?
options: The auto-thrust, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
The autopilot, because the flight management system cannot supply two targets
The autopilot, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
questions.explain: Only one may control speed, and the priority is given to the autopilot.

questions.question: Why can the altitude acquisition law not simply be left running until the selected level is reached?
options: Its transition follows an e-function, which would take an infinite time
Its gain is scheduled with airspeed, which would change during the capture
Its transition follows a ramp function, which would overshoot the level
questions.explain: The capture is exponential, so in theory it never quite arrives and must be terminated.

questions.question: When should a crew with only IAS hold available select it during a climb or a descent?
options: Once the new flight level has been selected
Before the thrust system reaches its climb limit
Once the new reference speed has been reached
questions.explain: Because it only freezes the current value, it is selected after the wanted speed has been reached.

questions.question: A Mach target is being flown at a high flight level. What does the reference speed marker on the primary flight display show?
options: An indicated airspeed, because the tape is in IAS at any altitude
A Mach number, because the tape follows the active reference
A calibrated airspeed, because the tape is in CAS at any altitude
questions.explain: The tape reads calibrated airspeed only, so a marker on it is a CAS value whatever the altitude or active reference.

questions.question: A crew wants to work to a Mach reference well below the normal transition height. What can they do and where?
options: Re-enter the target as a Mach number in the flight management system
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the altitude select display
questions.explain: The crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display allows a change over at any altitude.

questions.question: What does the PI behaviour of the outer loop prevent, and how
options: A standing speed error, by limiting the pitch attitude being commanded
A standing speed error, by integrating it into the attitude reference
An unstable speed loop, by integrating it into the thrust demand
questions.explain: Integrating the lasting error corrects the attitude reference until the error is removed.

cards.question: Which other name is given to closed loop control
options: regulation
actuation
correction
cards.explain: The manual gives regulation as the other name for closed loop control.

cards.question: Which quantity is denoted by Xw in the terms used for closed loop control
options: reference value
control value
error
cards.explain: Xw is the symbol given for the error in a closed loop system.

cards.question: Besides permanent monitoring of the control value, which feature is typical of closed loop control
options: its conversion by the controller into an input value
its feedback to and comparison with the reference value
its chain like sequence of effects through the actuator
cards.explain: Closed loop control is defined by feeding the control value back and comparing it with the reference value.

cards.question: Which feature is characteristic of open loop control
options: the comparison made at the controller input
the chain like sequence of effects
the permanent monitoring of the output
cards.explain: In open loop control the effects run in a chain from input to output with no return path.

cards.question: In a closed loop system the control value and the reference value are found to differ. What happens to that difference?
options: It is converted in the controller into an output which acts on the actuator
It is passed to the measurement unit and stored until the next comparison
It is converted in the actuator into an output which acts on the controller
cards.explain: The error goes to the controller, whose output drives the actuator.

cards.question: In a closed loop system, which quantity of the controlled system does the actuator alter
options: the disturbance acting on it is removed
its output, the control value, is modified
its input, the reference value, is modified
cards.explain: The actuator acts on the controlled system so that the control value changes.

cards.question: Which quantity is compared with the reference value only in a closed loop system?
options: The control value x
The disturbance z
The reference value w
cards.explain: In closed loop control the control value is permanently monitored, fed back and compared with the reference value; no such comparison exists in open loop control.

cards.question: In an open loop arrangement, on what does the controller output act?
options: On an actuator, which in turn acts on the system to be controlled
On the system to be controlled, which in turn acts on an actuator
On a measurement unit, which in turn acts on the reference value
cards.explain: The order runs controller, then actuator, then controlled system.

cards.question: When an open loop system must hold its output value constant while a disturbance acts, which condition is the reference value varied to reach
options: the effect of the controller output and that of the disturbance equalize each other
the controller output and the reference value become equal to each other
the disturbance is measured and fed back to the controller input for comparison
cards.explain: With no feedback the only way to hold the output is to trim the reference until the two effects cancel.

cards.question: A controlled system is acted on by disturbances whose effect cannot be predicted. Why is open loop control the wrong choice here?
options: It needs a measurement unit that unpredictable disturbances overload
It can only correct for what was allowed for in advance
It feeds the disturbance back and so amplifies the error further
cards.explain: Without feedback the correction must be worked out beforehand, which an unpredictable disturbance makes impossible.

cards.question: A gust disturbs an aircraft that is being regulated. How is that disturbance dealt with?
options: It is fed back to the controller input and so more or less equalized
It is removed by the actuator before it reaches the controlled system
It is predicted by the controller and allowed for before it arrives
cards.explain: Feedback carries the disturbance back to the controller input, where it is largely cancelled.

cards.question: Given that disturbances on aircraft systems cannot generally be predicted, what is the standing of open loop control principles for those systems
options: are applied to aircraft systems in place of regulation
make no sense for aircraft systems apart from a few exceptions
are used for aircraft systems wherever an actuator is fitted
cards.explain: Unpredictable disturbances rule open loop control out of aircraft systems, save for a few exceptions.

cards.question: For a P - Regulator, to what is the change in the output value always proportional
options: the change in the input value
the rate of change of the input value
the magnitude of the input value
cards.explain: A proportional regulator ties the change of its output directly to the change of its input.

cards.question: For an I - Regulator, to what is the rate of change of the output value proportional
options: its input value
the rate of change of its input value
the change in its output value
cards.explain: In an integral regulator it is how fast the output moves that follows the input.

cards.question: How are the six degrees of freedom of an aircraft in the air made up
options: two rotary and four translatory degrees of freedom
four rotary and two translatory degrees of freedom
three rotary and three translatory degrees of freedom
cards.explain: The six split evenly into three rotary and three translatory.

cards.question: Which axes do the three degrees of rotary freedom turn about
options: roll, pitch and yaw axes
roll, pitch and heading axes
longitudinal, lateral and flight path axes
cards.explain: Rotation takes place about the X or roll, Y or pitch and Z or yaw axes.

cards.question: What do flight parameters describe
options: the state of the autopilot regulators
the state of the aircraft fixed coordinate system
the state of motion of an aircraft
cards.explain: A flight parameter is a physical quantity that describes how the aircraft is moving.

cards.question: Which motions are described by flight condition parameters
options: translatory motions
rotary motions
oscillatory motions
cards.explain: Flight condition parameters belong to the rotary degrees of freedom.

cards.question: Into which two parts is the flight path of a transport category airplane separated
options: a rotary and a translatory profile
an inner and an outer profile
a horizontal and a vertical profile
cards.explain: The path is split into a horizontal profile and a vertical profile.

cards.question: Which autopilot channel is used to follow a vertical profile
options: lateral or roll channel
longitudinal or pitch channel
directional or yaw channel
cards.explain: The vertical profile is flown by the longitudinal, that is the pitch, channel.

cards.question: What causes P1 - and P2 - Behavior
options: inaccuracy in measurement within the control loop
a leap of the input value within the control loop
storage of energy within the control loop
cards.explain: It is energy stored in the loop that produces the P1 and P2 behaviours.

cards.question: A control loop contains one energy storage device. What does this produce?
options: An oscillation of the output value after a change of the input
A delay in the evolution of the output value
An output value that follows the input value without any delay
cards.explain: One storage device gives P1 behaviour, which is a lag in the output.

cards.question: A control loop contains two energy storage devices. What is the consequence?
options: Energy can flow to and fro, so the output value oscillates
Energy is dissipated, so the output value follows without delay
Energy is held fast, so the output value is merely delayed
cards.explain: Two storage devices let energy pass back and forth, which shows up as oscillation.

cards.question: Under which condition does a P - Regulator generate a controller output value
options: an error value exists at its input
the input value is changing at a constant rate
the error value at its input is zero
cards.explain: No error at the input means no output from a proportional regulator.

cards.question: A constant positive input value is applied to an I - Regulator. What does its output do?
options: It stays at its present magnitude
It increases linearly
It decreases linearly
cards.explain: With a steady positive input the integral regulator's output ramps up at a steady rate.

cards.question: The input value of an I - Regulator falls to zero. What becomes of its output value?
options: It remains constant at its present magnitude
It falls to zero together with the input value
It decreases linearly from its present magnitude
cards.explain: A zero input means the output stops moving but holds the level it has reached.

cards.question: What is the I - Regulator able to do that the P - Regulator cannot
options: produce an output without any error value at its input
completely compensate reference value changes or disturbances
produce an output before the error value has appeared
cards.explain: The integral regulator keeps acting until the difference is gone, which the proportional one cannot do.

cards.question: The input of a D - Regulator changes at a constant rate. What does the output value do?
options: It remains steady at one level
It theoretically becomes infinite
It increases linearly without limit
cards.explain: The differential regulator reacts to rate of change, so a steady rate gives a steady output.

cards.question: What are the three degrees of translatory freedom
options: the rotations about the X, Y and Z axes
the linear movements along the roll and pitch axes
the linear movements along the X, Y and Z axes
cards.explain: Translatory freedom is straight line movement along each of the three axes.

cards.question: Why does the pilot have two areas of responsibility at the same time?
options: Because the aircraft has two separate sets of flight controls
Because the aircraft has two different coordinate systems defined
Because the aircraft has two different kinds of degree of freedom
cards.explain: The rotary and translatory freedoms give rise to two separate jobs for the pilot.

cards.question: Which degrees of freedom are affected by the control inputs that stabilize the aircraft attitude about its centre of gravity
options: translatory degrees of freedom
rotary degrees of freedom
navigation objectives
cards.explain: Attitude about the centre of gravity is a rotary matter.

cards.question: Which degrees of freedom are affected by the inputs that guide the aircraft along a predetermined flight path
options: translatory degrees of freedom
rotary degrees of freedom
aircraft fixed coordinate system
cards.explain: Moving the aircraft along a path is linear motion, so it belongs to the translatory freedoms.

cards.question: Why is relieving the crew of monotonous flight path guidance tasks worthwhile?
options: Monotony makes the autopilot less accurate in holding the selected values
Monotony prevents the crew from entering reference values on the panel
Monotony deteriorates and limits the attention they pay to monitoring systems
cards.explain: Dull repetitive tasks eat into the attention the crew has left for watching the systems.

cards.question: Why can a human being reach its mental capacity in difficult flight phases
options: a multitude of reference values which have to be entered in sequence
a multitude of tasks which have to be carried out concurrently
a multitude of disturbances which have to be predicted in advance
cards.explain: It is the number of jobs that have to be done at the same time that over-stresses the pilot.

cards.question: Which direction is positive for the lateral axis in the aircraft fixed coordinate system
options: in the starboard direction
in the direction of flight
in the port direction
cards.explain: The lateral axis is counted positive to the right, that is to starboard.

cards.question: Which direction is positive for the vertical axis in the aircraft fixed coordinate system
options: downwards
in the direction of flight
upwards
cards.explain: The vertical axis is taken positive towards the ground.

cards.question: Why do the names of the body fixed coordinate axes refer to roll, pitch and yaw for auto flight purposes?
options: Because they refer to the linear motion along the respective axis
Because they refer to the rotary motion around the respective axis
Because they refer to the position of the centre of gravity
cards.explain: Each axis is named after the rotation that takes place about it.

cards.question: How is a predetermined condition or path realized in flight condition and flight path regulation
options: permanently selecting a new mode of operation for each flight parameter
permanently adapting the reference values to one or several flight parameters
permanently adapting one or several flight parameters to their reference values
cards.explain: The control values are continuously driven towards the reference values that were set.

cards.question: For which systems is the conduct of flight decomposed into part-tasks in automatic flight guidance
options: the flight management system and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
the autopilot / flight director and the flight management system
the autopilot / flight director and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
cards.explain: The part-tasks are shared between the AP/FD and the ATHR.

cards.question: What decides which flight parameters are controlled in a given flight phase?
options: The reference values entered for the AP/FD and the ATHR
The mode of operation selected for the AP/FD and the ATHR
The degree of automation achieved in that autoflight system
cards.explain: Selecting a mode of operation is what fixes the parameters to be controlled.

cards.question: On which other mode of operation does that of the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system depend
options: the autopilot's longitudinal channel
the autopilot's lateral channels
the flight director's roll channel
cards.explain: The thrust system follows whatever the vertical channel of the autopilot is doing.

cards.question: Besides controlling air speed, which other task is given to the ATHR system
options: sets a flight phase dependant altitude target
sets a flight phase dependant thrust rating
sets a flight phase dependant pitch attitude
cards.explain: Its other job is to set the thrust rating appropriate to the flight phase.

cards.question: During climb, cruise and descent, how are the modes of the longitudinal channel and of the lateral channel chosen?
options: They are selected together as a fixed combination
They are selectable independently from each other
They are selected in a strict sequence by the system
cards.explain: In these phases the vertical and lateral modes are picked separately.

cards.question: In a modern autoflight system, what can be said about the operating modes offered to the flight director?
options: Only the modes not available to the autopilot can be selected for it
Most of the modes available for the autopilot can be selected for it too
Only the basic modes of the autopilot can be selected for it
cards.explain: Modern systems let nearly the whole autopilot mode list be used by the flight director.

cards.question: How is the provision of reference values and the tuning of the VOR / ILS receivers allocated among the part-tasks
options: belongs to each part-task
belongs to the flight management system alone
belongs to the auto-thrust part-task only
cards.explain: Every part-task includes setting the reference values and tuning the navaids.

cards.question: The output of a control loop is found to oscillate after every input change. What must be provided and why?
options: Damping, because without it the loop will not be stable
A larger error value, because the controller then responds
A second energy store, because the loop then settles faster
cards.explain: Oscillation means P2 behaviour, and damping is what the manual makes mandatory for a stable loop.

cards.question: Why can a P - Regulator never completely compensate a change of the reference value or a disturbance?
options: Its output is proportional to how fast the error value is changing
Inaccuracies may show an error of zero while a real difference remains
Its output becomes infinite whenever the error value reaches zero
cards.explain: A proportional regulator needs an error to act, and measurement inaccuracy can hide a genuine one.

cards.question: Which regulator can produce a controller output from a very small error that persists for a sufficient period of time
options: P - Regulator, which can completely compensate the change
D - Regulator, which can completely compensate the change
I - Regulator, which can completely compensate the change
cards.explain: The integral regulator acts on tiny lasting errors and so removes the offset entirely.

cards.question: The input of a D - Regulator leaps from one constant value to another. What is the theoretical result at the output?
options: It becomes infinite
It becomes constant
It becomes zero
cards.explain: A step is an infinitely fast change, so a rate sensitive regulator gives an infinite output.

cards.question: Which regulator behaviour is used when an error just beginning to build up has to be removed very quickly
options: I - Regulator, whose output answers the rate of change
D - Regulator, whose output answers the rate of change
P - Regulator, whose output answers the rate of change
cards.explain: The differential regulator sees the error growing and reacts at once, which is its stated advantage.

cards.question: With one exception, direct inputs affecting the translatory degrees of freedom are not possible. How then is the flight path controlled?
options: Directly, through inputs applied to each of the three translatory axes
Indirectly, through inputs affecting initially the rotary degrees of freedom
Indirectly, through inputs affecting initially the centre of gravity position
cards.explain: The pilot has to change attitude first and let the path follow from it.

cards.question: Along which axis does engine thrust, the one direct input affecting a translatory degree of freedom, act
options: vertical or Z - axis
longitudinal or X - axis
lateral or Y - axis
cards.explain: Engine thrust pushes the aircraft straight along its longitudinal axis.

cards.question: An approach is to be flown in very low visibility. Why must the autoflight system fly it?
options: The thrust of the engines cannot be set manually in such conditions
The flight director cannot supply commands in such conditions
Regulations or limited perception prevent manual control in such phases
cards.explain: In these phases the rules, or simply what the pilot can see, rule manual control out.

cards.question: Why can the flight condition task and the flight path task not be clearly distinguished from each other in every case?
options: Any control of flight condition parameters uses the same regulator type
Any control of flight path parameters is carried out by the inner loop too
Any control of flight condition parameters always affects the flight path too
cards.explain: Changing attitude inevitably moves the aircraft, so the two tasks overlap.

cards.question: Which flight parameter influences the flight condition as well as the flight path and so blurs the division between the two tasks
options: the pitch attitude
the airspeed
the roll attitude
cards.explain: Airspeed is named as the parameter that belongs to both tasks.

cards.question: What makes it possible to guide a flight automatically from the initial climb out until the roll out after landing?
options: Adapting the reference values to the control values in every flight phase
Selecting a single control task that covers every one of the flight phases
Sequencing the different control tasks with respect to the required flight phases
cards.explain: Automatic guidance over a whole flight comes from running the control tasks in the order the phases need.

cards.question: A quantity describing a linear motion of the aircraft is to be regulated. Which part of the autopilot has this task?
options: The outer loops, since the quantity is a flight path parameter
The outer loops, since the quantity is a flight condition parameter
The inner loop, since the quantity is a flight path parameter
cards.explain: Linear motion means a flight path parameter, and flight path regulation is the outer loop task.

cards.question: A precision approach and landing is made up of a strict sequence of operating modes needing a series of different control parameters. What follows from this?
options: Mode sequencing is manual, so the pilot must select each mode in turn
Mode sequencing is automatic, so one button relieves the pilot to roll out
Mode sequencing is inhibited, so the approach mode holds to roll out
cards.explain: Because the modes must follow a fixed order, the system runs them itself after a single selection.

cards.question: Why is air speed monitored by the activated autoflight system to prevent upper and lower limits being exceeded?
options: Air speed is the only parameter the auto-thrust system can control
Air speed is a flight condition parameter of the rotary freedoms
Air speed is a decisive criterion for the amount of lift produced
cards.explain: Lift depends on speed, so the speed envelope has to be protected.

cards.question: Which flight phases make up the vertical structure of a flight plan
options: take-off, climb, cruise, descent and landing
take-off, climb, cruise, descent and approach
departure, climb, cruise, arrival and approach
cards.explain: The five vertical phases listed end with approach.

cards.question: What are the segments making up the lateral structure of a flight plan called
options: tracks
legs
fixes
cards.explain: The segments that make up the lateral structure are called legs.

cards.question: Into how many categories are all legs of a flight plan subdivided for procedural reasons
options: five categories
four categories
three categories
cards.explain: There are four leg categories.

cards.question: Which subsystems does the autoflight system comprise
options: autopilot, flight director and auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
autopilot, flight management system and auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
autopilot, flight director and flight management computer system
cards.explain: The three named subsystems make up the autoflight system.

cards.question: Which quantities are named in a flight plan for vertical flight path guidance
options: air speed or Mach number and heading
air speed or Mach number and altitude
ground speed or track angle and altitude
cards.explain: Vertical guidance is described by speed or Mach number together with altitude.

cards.question: What essentially determines the vertical flight path guidance written into a flight plan?
options: The intended route of the aircraft
The performance of the aircraft
The air traffic control clearances
cards.explain: What the aircraft can do sets the vertical profile.

cards.question: What mainly determines the lateral flight path guidance written into a flight plan?
options: The intended route and the air traffic control clearances
The performance of the aircraft and its thrust rating
The autopilot modes available for the roll channel
cards.explain: The lateral profile follows the route flown and what ATC clears.

cards.question: Besides air speed and thrust rating, what characterizes each vertical phase
options: heading, track angle or wind correction angle
pitch attitude, roll attitude or yaw attitude
altitude, climb or sink rate or flight path angle
cards.explain: Besides speed and thrust rating, each phase is set by altitude, climb or sink rate, or flight path angle.

cards.question: Which document describes both the vertical and the lateral flight path guidance for a flight from take-off to touch down
options: flight plan
flight profile
flight parameter list
cards.explain: It is the flight plan that sets out both the vertical and lateral guidance.

cards.question: Besides its direction, what defines a leg of a flight plan
options: the heading between two waypoints
the time between two waypoints
the distance between two waypoints
cards.explain: Distance between two waypoints plus direction is what defines a leg.

cards.question: Where do the legs of the standard instrument departure end
options: at the initial approach fix
at the active runway
at the airway system
cards.explain: The SID runs from the start of the flight plan up to the airway system.

cards.question: Which legs does the standard terminal arrival route comprise
options: from the initial approach fix to the airway system
from the initial approach fix to the active runway
from the airway system to the initial approach fix
cards.explain: The STAR takes the aircraft off the airways down to the initial approach fix.

cards.question: Which other legs are taken in by the leg category that ends at the active runway
options: all the legs of the arrival route
all the legs of the departure route
all the legs of a missed approach
cards.explain: The approach category also takes in the missed approach legs.

cards.question: Flying leg by leg, what must the pilot take into consideration when he selects the heading for each leg?
options: The initial approach fix
The flight path angle
The wind correction angle
cards.explain: Heading for a leg must allow for the wind correction angle.

cards.question: Which position sensors does the FMCS use to provide positioning and navigation automatically
options: DME/DME, VOR/DME, IRS and GPS
VOR/DME, ILS, radio altimeter and GPS
DME/DME, VOR/ILS, IRS and ATC
cards.explain: Those four sensor sources are the ones used for FMCS positioning.

cards.question: How does the flight management system relate to the autoflight system
options: a regulator combination provided by it
a subsystem which forms part of it
an independent system not included in it
cards.explain: The FMS stands outside the autoflight system as the term is used here.

cards.question: Which two tasks does the pilot have to fulfil during a flight
options: flight management and flight path control
flight path control and flight mode annunciation
flight management and flight condition damping
cards.explain: The pilot's two tasks are flight management and flight path control.

cards.question: Besides separately, how may each regulator offered by the autoflight system be used
options: in combination with the flight management computer system
in combination with the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
in combination with the measurement unit of the control loop
cards.explain: A regulator can work alone or together with the thrust system.

cards.question: Which parts of the system provide the combinations of regulators used for automatic vertical flight path guidance?
options: The AP/FD pitch channel and the auto-thrust system under AP/FD control
The AP/FD roll channel and the auto-thrust system under FMCS control
The AP/FD pitch channel and the flight management system under ATC control
cards.explain: Vertical guidance comes from the pitch channel together with the thrust system under AP/FD control.

cards.question: Apart from selected flight phases, for what may the combinations of regulators provided by the pitch channel be used
options: for the complete lateral structure
for the complete horizontal profile
for the complete vertical profile
cards.explain: They can cover single phases or the whole vertical profile.

cards.question: The roll channel of the autopilot/flight director is working as an independent subsystem. Why can it not guide the aircraft along a horizontal profile?
options: It needs the auto-thrust system to set a flight phase thrust rating
It needs inputs from the pilot or from a flight management computer system
It needs the pitch channel to be engaged in a vertical profile mode
cards.explain: On its own the roll channel has nothing to steer to, so it must be fed by the pilot or the FMCS.

cards.question: A waypoint is co-located with a VOR navaid. What does this allow the pilot to do?
options: Leave the roll channel to track the leg without any further input
Select the appropriate autopilot NAV mode to track a leg to or from it
Select the appropriate autopilot approach mode to capture the leg
cards.explain: A waypoint on a navaid lets the NAV mode of the autopilot track the leg.

cards.question: Why is leg by leg guidance described as semi-automatic flight guidance only?
options: The autopilot roll channel must be disengaged on each following leg
New parameters must be set up by the pilot before each following leg
New parameters must be set up by the FMCS before each following leg
cards.explain: The pilot has to reset the parameters at every waypoint, so the guidance is only half automatic.

cards.question: What becomes possible when an FMCS supplies all the inputs the AP/FD roll and yaw channel needs
options: shortly after take-off the aircraft can be guided along the flight plan automatically
shortly before each waypoint the pilot can set up the parameters for the next leg
shortly after take-off the roll channel can be operated as an independent subsystem
cards.explain: With the FMCS feeding the lateral channels, automatic guidance can begin soon after take-off.

cards.question: The accuracy of each sensor is permanently monitored. What does the FMCS then do with the information they give?
options: It blends it to calculate an accurate position in the earth coordinate system
It passes it unchanged to the roll channel as a wind correction angle
It selects the single most accurate sensor and discards the other information
cards.explain: The FMCS mixes all the position sources into one accurate FMS position.

cards.question: Which navigation parameters can the flight management computer system calculate from the change of the aircraft position
options: Mach number or flight path angle
ground speed or track
air speed or heading
cards.explain: Watching how the position moves gives ground speed and track.

cards.question: A flight is composed of a large number of very different route segments. What does the autoflight system therefore make available?
options: An appropriate regulator or combination of regulators for each route segment
An appropriate position sensor or combination of sensors for each route segment
An appropriate reference value or combination of values for each route segment
cards.explain: Because the segments differ so much, a matching regulator or set of regulators is offered for each.

cards.question: What is needed before extensive automatic flight guidance, a managed automatic flight, becomes possible?
options: Interaction of the flight director with the autopilot roll channel
Interaction of the autopilot with the auto-throttle system alone
Interaction of the flight management system with the autoflight system
cards.explain: Managed automatic flight comes only from the two systems working together.

cards.question: Particular route segments feature very different flight parameters. How may the pilot deal with a segment he does not wish to fly by hand?
options: Delegate the task to the flight management system working with the flight director
Delegate the task to the flight director working with the auto-thrust system
Delegate the task to the autopilot working with the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Handing the segment to the autopilot and auto-thrust system gives automatic guidance for that phase.

cards.question: What is indicated by a green flight mode annunciation in the uppermost display line of a primary flight display
options: a failed operating mode
an active operating mode
an armed operating mode
cards.explain: Green on the top line means the mode is active.

cards.question: At the managed automatic level of guidance, what supplies the reference values
options: the flight management system
the pilot at the control panel
the flight director channels
cards.explain: Managed means the FMS provides the reference values.

cards.question: With which systems does the highest present level of automatic flight combine the flight management system
options: autopilot and the flight director alone
autopilot and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
flight director and the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system
cards.explain: The top level is the FMS working with the autopilot and the thrust system.

cards.question: What does the operating mode selected on a mode control panel determine
options: the subsystem or combination of subsystems to be engaged
the reference value or combination of values to be entered
the regulator or combination of regulators to be activated
cards.explain: Choosing a mode is choosing which regulators run.

cards.question: What do the regulations demand regarding the operating states or modes of the autoflight subsystems?
options: Feedback to the pilot by colourful annunciators
Feedback to the flight management system by a data bus
Feedback to the pilot by an aural warning tone
cards.explain: The rules call for the modes to be annunciated to the pilot in colour.

cards.question: Where are the flight mode annunciators almost exclusively displayed in cockpits with an electronic flight instrument system
options: in the upper part of the primary flight display
in the lower part of the primary flight display
on backlit panels above the primary flight display
cards.explain: With EFIS the FMA sits at the top of the PFD.

cards.question: An operating mode has been selected but is waiting for an event before it takes effect. What is this mode said to be?
options: Armed
Engaged
Active
cards.explain: A mode waiting for an event to become active is armed.

cards.question: A pilot converting to another aircraft type cannot rely on the flight mode annunciator colours he is used to. Why not?
options: The colour scheme applies only to backlit panels in conventional cockpits
The colour of an annunciation depends on the reference value selected
There is no internationally agreed colour scheme for these annunciators
cards.explain: The manual states plainly that no internationally agreed colour scheme exists for flight mode annunciators.

cards.question: On what are the reference values supplied by the flight management system at the managed automatic level based
options: a stored flight plan which cannot be modified once in flight
the air traffic control clearances passed during the flight
a stored flight plan and any modifications made to it in flight
cards.explain: The FMS works to the stored plan including whatever the pilot has changed in flight.

cards.question: What is the objective of the managed automatic level of guidance
options: To support the pilot flying with attitude commands
To relieve the crew of manual control tasks
To let the crew leave the FMS profile at short notice
cards.explain: Relieving the crew of the manual control tasks is the objective given, which leaves them time to monitor the overall situation.

cards.question: At the selected automatic level, what supplies the reference values
options: the flight director from its selected modes
the flight management system from its flight plan
the pilot at the autoflight control panel
cards.explain: Selected means the pilot sets the reference values on the panel.

cards.question: At the managed manual level, what supplies the reference values and parameters used by the FD
options: the pilot at the control panel
the auto-thrust system
the flight management system
cards.explain: Managed manual means the FD is fed by the FMS while the pilot flies by hand.

cards.question: What is the objective of the managed manual level of guidance
options: To give the pilot flying pitch and roll commands that follow his own selections
To relieve the pilot flying of all manual control of pitch and roll
To give the pilot flying pitch and roll commands that follow the FMS flight plan
cards.explain: The flight director commands steer the hand flown aircraft along the FMS profile.

cards.question: Where do the flight director inputs come from at the selected manual level
options: supplied by the autopilot from its engaged basic modes
supplied to the panel by the flight management system
manually set up on the autoflight control panel by the pilot
cards.explain: In selected manual the pilot sets the FD modes and reference values himself.

cards.question: At the basic manual level, what does the pilot flying have to do?
options: Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by manipulating the controls and thrust
Maintain altitude, heading and airspeed by selecting modes and reference values
Maintain pitch and roll attitude by following the flight director commands
cards.explain: With no autoflight support the pilot holds the values himself on the controls and the thrust levers.

cards.question: What is the objective of the basic manual level of guidance
options: To fly the aircraft manually
To relieve the crew of manual control tasks
To support the pilot flying with attitude commands
cards.explain: The objective given for basic manual is simply to fly the aircraft by hand.

cards.question: At which level of guidance is the flight director off
options: selected manual
managed manual
basic manual
cards.explain: Basic manual is the single row with the flight director off.

cards.question: A blue annunciation appears in the second display line of a primary flight display. What does the pilot understand from it?
options: The mode is active and is already controlling the aircraft
The mode is armed and has been rejected by the autopilot
The mode is armed and is waiting for an event to become active
cards.explain: Amber, white or blue on the second line is the armed indication, and armed means waiting for an event.

cards.question: The crew must leave the FMS profile at short notice after an air traffic control request, but wishes to keep the autopilot flying. Which level of guidance do they use?
options: Managed automatic
Selected automatic
Selected manual
cards.explain: Selected automatic leaves the autopilot in control while the pilot supplies the reference values himself.

cards.question: Two levels of guidance both leave the autopilot in sole control of the aircraft. What separates them from each other?
options: Whether the flight director is switched on
Where the reference values come from
Whether the auto-thrust system is engaged
cards.explain: Managed automatic takes its references from the FMS, selected automatic from the pilot.

cards.question: The autopilot is off, the flight director is on and FMS guidance is in use. Which level of guidance is this?
options: Managed automatic
Managed manual
Selected manual
cards.explain: Autopilot off with flight director on and FMS guidance yes is the managed manual row.

cards.question: The autopilot and the auto-thrust system are on and there is no FMS guidance. Which level of guidance is this?
options: Selected manual
Managed automatic
Selected automatic
cards.explain: Autopilot on with no FMS guidance is the selected automatic row.

cards.question: How is the auto-throttle / auto-thrust system shown at the three levels of guidance where the autopilot is off
options: off in every case
on in every case
on or off
cards.explain: Wherever the autopilot is off, the thrust system may be either on or off.

cards.question: At which levels of guidance is FMS guidance shown as being in use?
options: Managed automatic and selected automatic
Managed automatic and managed manual
Selected automatic and selected manual
cards.explain: The two managed levels are the ones with FMS guidance.

cards.question: Which flight condition parameters belong to the rotary degrees of freedom
options: pitch attitude, roll attitude and vertical speed
pitch attitude, roll attitude and yaw attitude
pitch rate, roll rate and load factor
cards.explain: The three rotary parameters are pitch, roll and yaw attitude.

cards.question: What is the other name for yaw attitude
options: track
drift
heading
cards.explain: The manual gives heading as the other name for yaw attitude.

cards.question: In which two states of operation is activation of an autopilot normally possible
options: CMD and APPROACH
CWS/MAN and CMD
CWS/MAN and NAV
cards.explain: The two activation states are CWS/MAN and CMD.

cards.question: Basic modes refer to flight condition parameters, so what do they consequently control
options: translatory degrees of freedom
rotary degrees of freedom
flight path parameters
cards.explain: Flight condition parameters belong to the rotary freedoms, so basic modes control those.

cards.question: What is actually engaged when an autopilot is engaged
options: The clutch connecting the AP-servo with the primary controls
The servo valve connecting the AP-servo with the hydraulic supply
The torque limiter connecting the AP-servo with the trim actuator
cards.explain: Engagement is the closing of the clutch between the AP-servo and the primary flight controls.

cards.question: Which device lets the pilot overpower an engaged autopilot at any time
options: An engage interlock
An attitude command memory
A torque limiter
cards.explain: The torque limiter is what permits forceful pilot inputs to override the autopilot.

cards.question: What is the engage interlock circuit there to prevent
options: Activation of an upper mode before a basic mode is selected
Activation of a defective or not yet synchronized autopilot
Activation of the manual trim while the autopilot is engaged
cards.explain: That is the stated purpose of the interlock circuit.

cards.question: Which part of an autopilot is made up by the flight condition regulators
options: the simplest form of an autopilot
the outer control loop of an autopilot
the mode control panel of an autopilot
cards.explain: An attitude stabilising regulator on its own is the simplest autopilot there is.

cards.question: For what are the control conditions improved when flight condition regulators simplify and unify attitude control behaviour
options: the pilot or the outer control loops of the autopilot
the pilot or the measurement unit of the control loop
the flight management system or the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Both the pilot and the outer loops of the autopilot get an easier aircraft to control.

cards.question: Which change to the flying properties of an aircraft is brought about by its flight condition regulators?
options: Increased damping of aircraft oscillations
Increased thrust rating in each flight phase
Increased accuracy of the position sensors
cards.explain: Better damping of the aircraft's oscillations is one of the listed modifications.

cards.question: Besides neutral stability, which modification of control properties is brought about by flight condition regulators
options: control value monitoring
control wheel steering
control mode annunciation
cards.explain: Control wheel steering is named alongside neutral stability.

cards.question: Besides preventing skid or slip in circling flight, what do the flight condition regulators provide
options: compensation of the wind correction angle
compensation of the thrust rating change
compensation of the loss of lift
cards.explain: The loss of lift in a turn is compensated as well as the skid or slip.

cards.question: The autopilot has been activated in CWS/MAN. What can the pilot do and in which modes does the autopilot work?
options: It works in its upper modes and he can enter new reference values by hand
It works in its basic modes and he can influence the momentary attitude by hand
It works in the selected flight director modes and he must not touch the controls
cards.explain: In CWS/MAN the autopilot holds its basic modes while the pilot steers through it with the yoke.

cards.question: With the autopilot activated in CMD, which reference values does it use
options: held from the moment of engagement
stored in the flight management computer
set on the autoflight control panel
cards.explain: In CMD the references come from the autoflight control panel.

cards.question: Besides the flight phase, what else do the names given to operating modes refer to
options: the degree of freedom
the control value
the reference value
cards.explain: A mode is named after either the control value it holds or the flight phase it serves.

cards.question: Which regulator maintains the present heading in the basic mode heading hold
options: the roll regulator
the pitch regulator
the yaw regulator
cards.explain: Heading hold is carried out by the roll regulator.

cards.question: The basic modes of some autopilots are heading hold together with vertical speed. What does the pitch regulator then maintain?
options: The present pitch attitude
The present altitude
The present climb rate
cards.explain: In the vertical speed basic mode the pitch regulator holds the climb rate it has.

cards.question: The pilot pushes firmly on the control column while the autopilot is engaged. What happens to the auto-trim function?
options: It is switched over to its high trim speed
It is deactivated until the force is removed
It is transferred to the elevator actuator
cards.explain: Force on the control column deactivates auto-trim for as long as it is applied.

cards.question: What decides whether disengagement follows an overpowering of the flight controls
options: The mode selected and the channel that is engaged
The torque the limiter is built to pass and the airspeed
The circumstances of the input and the autopilot itself
cards.explain: Disengagement is made conditional on both the pilot's input and the design of the autopilot.

cards.question: Every engage interlock condition is satisfied as the pilot selects the autopilot on. What follows?
options: The servo clutches close and attitude control by the autopilot
The trim clutches close and stabilizer control by the pilot
The servo clutches open and manual control by the pilot
cards.explain: Meeting all conditions closes the servo clutches and hands attitude control to the autopilot.

cards.question: What happens to the AP engage switch when an interlock condition becomes invalid
options: It is held at its last selected mode
It is latched in the ON position
It is reset to the OFF position
cards.explain: Loss of a condition resets the engage switch to OFF.

cards.question: The engage interlock must establish that the autopilot is fit to take over. Which signals does it interrogate?
options: Only the systems and signals feeding the attitude command memory
Only the systems and signals of the outer flight path loops
All required systems and signals of the inner control loop
cards.explain: The interlock checks every required system and signal of the inner control loop before engagement is allowed.

cards.question: Why are flight condition regulators called basic regulators?
options: The outer control loops replace them whenever flight path control is required
The inner control loop uses them to achieve attitude control through flight path control
The outer control loops use them to achieve flight path control through attitude control
cards.explain: They are the building blocks the outer loops drive in order to steer the flight path.

cards.question: How are the problems of oscillation, gust effects and skid or slip actually solved?
options: By selecting an upper mode on the autoflight control panel
By controlling and damping the translatory motions of the aircraft
By controlling and damping the rotary motions of the aircraft
cards.explain: All of these are dealt with through control and damping of the rotary motions.

cards.question: The pilot makes a control input that induces a roll rate or a load factor. What does the flight condition regulator do with it?
options: It rejects the input until the autopilot has been disengaged
It transforms the input into the required dynamic behavior
It converts the input into a reference value for the outer loop
cards.explain: Secondary parameters commanded by the pilot are turned by the regulator into the dynamic behaviour wanted.

cards.question: Vertical speed is treated as a basic mode by some autopilots. Why is this called an exception?
options: Vertical speed is in fact named after a flight phase
Vertical speed is in fact a flight condition parameter
Vertical speed is in fact a flight path parameter
cards.explain: Basic modes normally hold flight condition parameters, and vertical speed is not one.

cards.question: An autopilot is engaged and no flight director modes had been selected beforehand. What happens?
options: Its basic modes are activated
Its upper modes are activated
It remains in CMD without any mode
cards.explain: With no prior flight director selection the autopilot comes up in its basic modes.

cards.question: An autopilot in a basic mode is holding the attitude the aircraft had about its lateral axis. Which basic mode is in use?
options: Pitch attitude hold
Roll attitude hold
Heading hold
cards.explain: The lateral axis is the pitch axis, so holding attitude about it is pitch attitude hold.

cards.question: The aircraft is circling and the autopilot holds the bank it has. Which basic mode is this and which regulator carries it out?
options: Roll attitude hold, carried out by the roll regulator
Heading hold, carried out by the roll regulator
Roll attitude hold, carried out by the yaw regulator
cards.explain: Holding the present bank in a turn is roll attitude hold, done by the roll regulator.

cards.question: The yaw damper drops out in flight while the autopilot is engaged. What is the consequence for the autopilot?
options: An upper mode is lost, so the autopilot reverts to a basic mode
An interlock condition is lost, so the autopilot disengages
A reference value is lost, so the autopilot re-synchronizes
cards.explain: Yaw damper engagement is an interlock condition, and losing any condition disengages the servo clutches.

cards.question: A crew member operates the manual trim while trying to engage the autopilot. Why will the autopilot not engage?
options: An active manual trim input is an interlock condition not met
An active manual trim input saturates the trim integrator
An active manual trim input resets the attitude command memory
cards.explain: The interlock requires that no manual trim be active, so the engage logic is blocked.

cards.question: What supplies the force acting along the aircraft X-axis
options: Engine thrust
Spoiler drag
Rudder deflection
cards.explain: Thrust acts along the X-axis.

cards.question: About which axis do the ailerons generate their moments
options: The vertical axis
The longitudinal axis
The lateral axis
cards.explain: Aileron moments act about the longitudinal axis and are called roll moments.

cards.question: Thrust is counted as a primary control alongside the control surfaces. What singles it out from them?
options: It is the only control effective at low dynamic pressure
It is the only way to supply energy to an aircraft
It is the only control that acts without a moment arm
cards.explain: Thrust is treated as a primary control because it alone supplies energy to the aircraft.

cards.question: What job does the stabilizer do among the primary control surfaces
options: It trims out a roll-moment generated by aileron deflection
It trims out a pitch-moment generated by elevator deflection
It trims out a yaw-moment generated by rudder deflection
cards.explain: The stabilizer trims out the pitch moment the elevator has produced.

cards.question: An engine failure leaves a thrust asymmetry in the cruise. Which primary control surface is held deflected to trim it out?
options: The ailerons
The stabilizer
The rudder
cards.explain: A standing rudder deflection trims a thrust asymmetry.

cards.question: What is the difference in role between primary and secondary control surfaces
options: Primary surfaces give continuous control, secondary surfaces change the stationary condition
Primary surfaces give trimming control, secondary surfaces change the dynamic condition
Primary surfaces give lateral control, secondary surfaces change the longitudinal condition
cards.explain: Primary surfaces are for continuous control; secondary surfaces change the stationary flight condition.

cards.question: Flaps and slats are extended for landing. In which direction is the flight envelope being extended?
options: Towards higher altitudes
Towards lower velocities
Towards higher velocities
cards.explain: Secondary surfaces extend the envelope towards lower speeds for take-off and landing.

cards.question: An aircraft accelerates in level flight. Which quantity's rise makes its control surfaces more effective?
options: The static pressure
The dynamic pressure
The aircraft mass
cards.explain: Control surface effectiveness is proportional to dynamic pressure, which rises with speed.

cards.question: As the aircraft accelerates past a certain airspeed the maximum rudder deflection available is reduced. What is this limiting there to achieve?
options: It keeps the surface within its maximum deflection angle
It keeps the loads within the limits of structural strength
It keeps the yaw damper inside its authority
cards.explain: Because effectiveness grows with dynamic pressure, deflection is limited at speed to hold loads within structural limits.

cards.question: The ailerons are returned to neutral after a roll input. What does the aircraft then do?
options: It rolls back to a wings level attitude and stops circling
It keeps the roll attitude it has reached and circles
It keeps the roll rate it has reached and goes on rolling
cards.explain: Because roll response is integral, neutral ailerons leave the aircraft banked and turning.

cards.question: Why does roll attitude show an integral relation to a constant aileron deflection
options: The bank angle stays constant because the roll rate decays to zero
The bank angle keeps increasing because the roll rate stays constant
The bank angle keeps increasing because the roll rate keeps rising
cards.explain: A steady roll rate accumulates with time into a steadily changing bank angle, which is integration.

cards.question: Which pitch attitude does Pitch Attitude Hold maintain
options: The one held at the moment the mode is activated
The one scheduled for the present calibrated airspeed
The one held at the moment the flight director is selected
cards.explain: The reference is the attitude present when the mode becomes active.

cards.question: Which two phases are distinguished within the pitch regulator
options: Synchronization and trimming
Synchronization and control
Engagement and override
cards.explain: The two phases are synchronization and control.

cards.question: What is meant by a hard-over of a control surface
options: A deflection held beyond the trim threshold
A deflection that reverses the commanded direction
A full deflection through its whole travel range
cards.explain: A hard-over is a run of the surface through its whole travel.

cards.question: What does the auto-trim function trim out while the autopilot is engaged
options: Short term pitch disturbances
Long lasting pitch disturbances
Lateral trim asymmetries
cards.explain: Auto-trim deals with the lasting disturbances, not the short ones.

cards.question: Which aspects are covered by the term flying qualities
options: Controllability, maneuverability, damping and strength
Stability, controllability, trimmability and static margin
Stability, controllability, maneuverability and gust ride
cards.explain: Those four aspects are the ones listed.

cards.question: Which two pitch channel signals serve as the input to the auto-trim system
options: The attitude error or the elevator deflection
The pitch rate or the elevator deflection
The attitude error or the stabilizer position
cards.explain: Either the attitude error or the proportional elevator deflection is used.

cards.question: What happens to the centre of lift as the Mach number increases
options: It moves forward
It stays fixed
It moves aft
cards.explain: The centre of lift travels rearwards with rising Mach number.

cards.question: Which unstable condition does the Mach trim subsystem exist to avoid
options: Spiral divergence
Tuck under
Dutch roll
cards.explain: The condition is named tuck under.

cards.question: About which axis does Pitch Attitude Hold suppress disturbance moments
options: The longitudinal axis
The lateral axis
The vertical axis
cards.explain: Pitch moments act about the lateral axis.

cards.question: Under which condition does Pitch Attitude Hold come up as the basic mode at engagement
options: No upper modes are armed on the control panel
No manual trim input is being made by the pilot
No flight director modes are already active
cards.explain: The basic mode only appears if no FD mode is already running.

cards.question: What happens to the attitude command memory at the moment of engagement
options: Its output is interrupted and the momentary pitch angle is erased
Its input is interrupted and the momentary pitch angle is stored
Its input is restored and the momentary pitch angle is updated
cards.explain: Engagement freezes the memory, so the stored pitch angle becomes the reference.

cards.question: The pitch error is scaled against the present calibrated airspeed before it reaches the actuator. What does this achieve?
options: To obtain the same pitch attitude at all velocities
To obtain the same elevator deflection at all velocities
To obtain the same pitch rate at all velocities
cards.explain: The gain schedule keeps the pitch rate the same whatever the speed.

cards.question: How is the work divided between elevator and stabilizer against disturbances
options: The elevator takes short term, the stabilizer takes long term
The elevator takes long term, the stabilizer takes short term
The elevator takes gusts, the stabilizer takes attitude errors
cards.explain: Short term is the elevator's job, long term the stabilizer's.

cards.question: Mach trim and speed trim are both fitted to an aircraft. Which flying quality do they improve?
options: The static stability
The maneuverability
The gust ride qualities
cards.explain: Both are listed as static stability, that is longitudinal stability augmentation.

cards.question: What do the alpha trim and alpha/Mach trim systems improve
options: The spiral stability
The static stability
The maneuverability
cards.explain: These two are listed under maneuverability.

cards.question: Which two safety demands does auto-trim fulfil
options: The elevator keeps its travel range and its actuator is unloaded in steady flight
The elevator keeps its travel range and its actuator is loaded in steady flight
The stabilizer keeps its travel range and its actuator is unloaded in steady flight
cards.explain: Auto-trim keeps the elevator off its stops and keeps its actuator unloaded.

cards.question: What is the effect of using a non-retroactive gear to drive the stabilizer
options: The stabilizer returns to neutral if the autopilot fails
The stabilizer is driven by the elevator if the autopilot fails
The stabilizer stays in position if the autopilot fails
cards.explain: The non-retroactive gear acts as a mechanical lock holding the stabilizer where it was left.

cards.question: In which two ways can the integration needed by the auto-trim system be obtained
options: By the stabilizer position sensor or by the trim actuator motor
By the trim detector itself or by a distinct electronic integrator
By the trim actuator motor itself or by a distinct electronic integrator
cards.explain: Either the motor's own integral behaviour or a separate electronic integrator does it.

cards.question: The trim speed is set differently for cruise and for approach. What makes that necessary?
options: The effectiveness of stabilizer and elevator depends on airspeed
The effectiveness of stabilizer and elevator depends on flap position
The travel range of stabilizer and elevator depends on airspeed
cards.explain: Surface effectiveness varies with speed, so the trim rate is matched to it.

cards.question: Which trim speeds are used for cruise and for approach
options: Low trim speed for cruise, low trim speed for approach
High trim speed for cruise, low trim speed for approach
Low trim speed for cruise, high trim speed for approach
cards.explain: Cruise uses the low trim speed, approach the high one.

cards.question: What effect is produced by the rearward movement of the centre of lift
options: A pitch up effect, which would decrease the Mach number
A pitch down effect, which would decrease the Mach number
A pitch down effect, which would increase the Mach number
cards.explain: The nose drops and the aircraft accelerates further, which is why it is unstable.

cards.question: High pressure differences at the wing tips are to be avoided in high speed flight. How does alpha trim achieve this?
options: By limiting the maximum Mach number
By limiting the maximum stabilizer travel
By limiting the maximum angle of attack
cards.explain: It caps the angle of attack.

cards.question: What does the alpha trim subsystem compare its sensed position against
options: An aircraft specific curve
A Mach trim function memory
A stabilizer trim unit scale
cards.explain: Sensed alpha is compared with the type's own curve.

cards.question: A flight director mode is already active when the pilot engages the autopilot. How does the autopilot behave?
options: It takes the mode over and runs in the matching upper mode at once
It drops the mode and reverts to pitch attitude hold at once
It holds the mode armed until the basic mode is cancelled
cards.explain: An active FD mode is adopted by the autopilot, so no basic mode appears.

cards.question: Why is synchronization made one of the engage interlock conditions
options: It stops the actuators loading the trim system at engagement
It stops the actuators reaching their travel limits in the cruise
It stops the actuators moving the surfaces abruptly at engagement
cards.explain: An unsynchronized autopilot would throw the surfaces over at engagement, so the interlock holds engagement off until synchronization is achieved.

cards.question: During the synchronization phase the pitch regulator produces no actuator activity at all. Why is that so?
options: The momentary pitch angle is held at zero, so the error is zero
The momentary pitch angle is compared with itself, so the error is zero
The regulator output is clamped, so the actuator cannot respond
cards.explain: Both inputs to the summing point are the same signal, so the error is always zero.

cards.question: The pitch channel is said to behave like a PI-regulator. How is that behaviour produced?
options: The error goes direct to the elevator actuator and also to the gain schedule
The error goes direct to the stabilizer actuator and also to the auto-trim
The error goes direct to the elevator actuator and also to the auto-trim
cards.explain: Splitting the error between the elevator actuator and auto-trim gives proportional plus integral action.

cards.question: An increase in thrust upsets the balance of pitch moments in the cruise. How is this disturbance classed and what does holding the attitude then need?
options: Permanent, and a permanently generated additional moment
Short term, and a permanently generated additional moment
Permanent, and a momentary additional elevator deflection
cards.explain: A thrust change is a lasting disturbance, so the compensating moment must also be lasting.

cards.question: A lasting pitch disturbance has to be compensated with the autopilot engaged. Why is the stabilizer used rather than holding the elevator deflected?
options: The elevator must keep its full travel for short term disturbances
The elevator must keep its neutral position for the gain schedule
The stabilizer must keep its full travel for long term disturbances
cards.explain: Holding the elevator deflected would eat into the travel it needs for gusts, so the stabilizer takes the standing load.

cards.question: A flight augmentation system fitted to the aircraft is unserviceable before departure. What is the likely effect on the autopilot?
options: Its availability has no bearing because it works without the autopilot
Its availability is only required for the upper modes of the autopilot
Its availability is often a precondition for autopilot engagement
cards.explain: These systems are commonly wired into the autopilot interlock.

cards.question: The autopilot is disengaged after a long cruise during which auto-trim has been working. Why is there no abrupt pitch attitude change?
options: The elevator is already resting in its neutral position
The stabilizer is already resting in its neutral position
The elevator is already held by the torque limiter
cards.explain: With the standing moment carried by the stabilizer and the elevator at neutral, nothing springs back at disengagement.

cards.question: The Mach number rises in the cruise. Which way does the Mach trim drive the stabilizer and what does that counter?
options: Leading edge up, countering the pitch down effect
Leading edge down, countering the pitch up effect
Leading edge down, countering the pitch down effect
cards.explain: Stabilizer leading edge down opposes the nose-down tuck under tendency.

cards.question: The angle of attack climbs past the maximum allowed value. What does the alpha trim subsystem do and for how long?
options: It drives the stabilizer leading edge up until alpha falls below the curve
It drives the stabilizer leading edge up until the Mach number falls
It drives the stabilizer leading edge down until alpha falls below the curve
cards.explain: Leading edge up is nose down, which unloads the angle of attack until it is back under the curve.

cards.question: When is longitudinal stability considered to be present
options: When disturbances are counteracted by moments the stabilizer trim generates
When disturbances are counteracted by moments the trimmed aircraft induces itself
When disturbances are counteracted by moments the autopilot commands at once
cards.explain: Stability means the aircraft itself produces the restoring moments.

cards.question: Which roll angle criterion decides which basic roll mode is activated
options: Twenty-five degrees
Five degrees
Fifteen degrees
cards.explain: Five degrees of bank is the dividing value.

cards.question: Which control structure has one regulator supplying the reference value for a second regulator closer to the aircraft
options: Proportional or integral control
Multi-rate or sampled control
Multi-loop or cascade control
cards.explain: That arrangement is called multi-loop or cascade control.

cards.question: To which speed is the roll attitude adapted so that the rate of turn is held
options: The true airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
The indicated airspeed
cards.explain: The heading outer loop gain is scheduled on true airspeed.

cards.question: Which three arrangements let the pilot keep control with the autopilot engaged
options: Control wheel steering, heading selector and attitude command memory
Turn or pitch knob control, torque limiter and heading selector
Turn or pitch knob control, control wheel steering and heading selector
cards.explain: Those three are the realizations listed.

cards.question: On which autopilots is a heading selector always available
options: On all those with a heading hold mode
On all those with a heading indication at the mode controller
On all those with a heading select mode
cards.explain: It is always there when the autopilot has heading select.

cards.question: On which two factors does the trim threshold depend
options: Longitudinal static stability and flap position
Longitudinal static stability and dynamic pressure
Lateral static stability and dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Those are the two factors listed.

cards.question: What does the heading hold mode give the aircraft
options: Its missing positive spiral stability in roll
Its missing positive heading damping in yaw
Its missing positive static heading stability
cards.explain: Heading hold supplies the heading stability the airframe does not have.

cards.question: Roll attitude hold is running with the autopilot engaged. What else is needed to improve the neutral spiral stability?
options: Turn compensation and a slight increase in engine thrust
Turn compensation and a slight reduction in engine thrust
Yaw damping and a slight increase in engine thrust
cards.explain: Turn compensation from the pitch channel plus a small thrust increase during circling do this.

cards.question: What are the roll attitude and heading command memories supplied with during synchronization
options: The actual roll and heading angles
The actual roll rate and heading error
The reference roll and heading angles
cards.explain: They track the actual angles until engagement freezes them.

cards.question: How is the roll attitude error signal adapted to the airspeed
options: By a rate feedback in the roll regulator
By a gain schedule in the attitude limiter
By a gain schedule in the roll regulator
cards.explain: A gain schedule inside the roll regulator does the adaptation.

cards.question: What are control cascades primarily employed for
