options: Complex processes made up of parallel independent processes
Complex processes made up of a sequence of sub-processes
Simple processes whose control value cannot be measured
cards.explain: They suit processes that are a chain of sub-processes.

cards.question: What is done to the present bank angle before heading control commences
options: It is reduced to zero in a period of ten seconds
It is reduced to five degrees in a period of four seconds
It is reduced to zero in a period of four seconds
cards.explain: The wings are levelled over four seconds before heading control starts.

cards.question: What does the roll outer loop put out
options: The reference heading for the heading inner loop
The reference roll attitude for the roll inner loop
The aileron deflection for the roll servo loop
cards.explain: Its output is the reference roll attitude handed down to the inner loop.

cards.question: What does turning a turn or pitch knob do
options: It modifies the reference value for the roll or pitch inner loop
It modifies the actual attitude fed back to the inner loop
It modifies the gain schedule for the roll or pitch inner loop
cards.explain: The knob shifts the inner loop's reference value.

cards.question: Where is turn and pitch knob control almost exclusively found
options: On older control panels with no entry of reference values
On newer control panels with no entry of reference values
On older control panels with no heading select mode
cards.explain: It belongs to the older panels that had no way of entering reference values.

cards.question: The CWS mode is selected with the autopilot engaged. How does the pilot then fly the aircraft?
options: Around the autopilot by means of the primary manual controls
Through the autopilot by means of the attitude reference knobs
Through the autopilot by means of the primary manual controls
cards.explain: The manual inputs are routed through the autopilot.

cards.question: Which arrangement is CWS equivalent to on a fly-by-wire aircraft
options: Heading select mode
Side stick steering
Turn and pitch knob control
cards.explain: CWS corresponds to side stick steering on fly-by-wire types.

cards.question: Fuel is burnt off through a long cruise and the centre of gravity moves aft. What happens to the aircraft's reaction to elevator and stabilizer displacements?
options: It changes, because the static stability has increased
It changes, because the static stability has decreased
It is unaltered, because the trim threshold is held fixed
cards.explain: An aft CG lowers static stability, which alters how the aircraft answers elevator and stabilizer inputs.

cards.question: An aircraft has a high longitudinal static stability. Why must the onset of auto-trim action be deferred?
options: Small elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
Large stabilizer displacements are needed to counter long term disturbances
Large elevator displacements are needed to counter short term disturbances
cards.explain: High stability makes the surfaces less effective, so ordinary gust corrections already use large deflections and trimming must wait.

cards.question: An aircraft is loaded with the centre of gravity well forward. How does the trim detector behave?
options: It starts trimming only after the stabilizer has reached its limit
It starts trimming only after a relatively small elevator displacement
It starts trimming only after a relatively large elevator displacement
cards.explain: A forward CG raises the trim threshold, so trimming begins later.

cards.question: The elevator is oscillating slightly either side of the trim threshold. What stops the trim system becoming unstable?
options: Trimming is only allowed while the stabilizer position is changing
Trimming is only started at displacements above the drop out line
Trimming is only stopped at displacements below the drop out line
cards.explain: The drop out line sets a lower cut-off than the threshold, so small oscillations cannot chatter the system.

cards.question: Why does an electronic integrator have to be added when an actuator motor is built into a servo loop
options: The motor loses its natural integral input/output behaviour
The motor loses its proportional input/output behaviour
The motor loses the position feedback it needs for the loop
cards.explain: Inside a servo loop the motor no longer integrates, so the behaviour must be restored electronically.

cards.question: An aircraft without the autopilot engaged is upset in roll by a gust. What is the lasting result once it has settled?
options: It is wings level again and on its original heading
It holds the bank it reached and keeps turning
It is wings level again but on a different heading
cards.explain: Roll is self-recovering but heading is not, which is why heading hold is needed.

cards.question: The autopilot is engaged while the aircraft is banked three degrees. What does the autopilot do?
options: It holds the three degrees of bank and lets the heading run
It rolls back to wings level and holds the heading of that moment
It rolls back to wings level and holds the last selected heading
cards.explain: Under five degrees the bank angle criterion selects heading hold on the heading present at engagement.

cards.question: The autopilot is engaged while the aircraft is banked ten degrees. What does the autopilot do?
options: It rolls back to wings level, so the heading of that moment is held
It holds the bank angle, so the heading changes and the aircraft turns
It holds the bank angle, so the heading of that moment is held
cards.explain: At or above five degrees the bank is kept, which leaves the aircraft turning.

cards.question: The roll regulator on its own is proportional. Why does the roll inner loop as a whole show PI- behaviour?
options: The regulator integrates the roll attitude error into a roll rate
The airframe integrates the commanded roll rate into a roll angle
The airframe integrates the commanded roll angle into a heading
cards.explain: The proportional regulator plus the airframe's own integration of roll rate gives PI overall.

cards.question: A regulator has to control a process made up of a long chain of sub-processes. Why does it need many feedback loops?
options: It requires feedback about the actual state of each sub-process
It requires feedback to keep each sub-process gain identical
It requires feedback about the real control value from each loop
cards.explain: Each sub-process has to be reported back, which is why there is a loop for each.

cards.question: An aileron deflection is held in. What does the airframe do with it before a heading change appears?
options: A roll rate is integrated into a yaw rate, which gives lateral forces
A roll rate is integrated into a bank angle, which gives lateral forces
A bank angle is integrated into a roll rate, which gives lateral forces
cards.explain: The chain runs deflection to roll rate to bank angle to lateral force to heading change.

cards.question: The aircraft is to hold the same rate of turn but at a higher true airspeed. What must happen to the bank angle?
options: It has to be increased
It has to be held unchanged
It has to be decreased
cards.explain: Rate of turn at higher TAS needs more bank, which the outer loop gain schedule provides.

cards.question: The autopilot has just been engaged and no upper mode has been selected. Which attitudes do its two channels control straight away?
options: The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
The pitch channel the pitch attitude, the roll channel the heading only
The pitch channel the flight path, the roll channel the roll attitude or heading
cards.explain: Each channel takes its basic mode at once, pitch attitude in pitch and roll attitude or heading in roll.

cards.question: Where are the reference values generated when the autopilot is flown in CWS mode
options: By stored inputs from the flight management computer
By manual inputs on the control wheel or column
By preset inputs on the mode control panel display
cards.explain: In CWS the pilot's own hand input at the wheel or column is the reference value.

cards.question: Which devices at the flight controls sense a pilot manual input and turn it into an electrical signal
options: Force transducers, that is CWS sensors and dynamometric rods
Position pick-offs, that is synchros and resolver pick-ups
Rate sensors, that is tachometers and rate gyroscopes
cards.explain: The manual names the force transducers, called CWS sensors or dynamometric rods, as the force measuring devices.

cards.question: What output is given by a force transducer or a dynamometric rod
options: An electrical current proportional to the applied travel
A hydraulic pressure proportional to the applied force
An electrical voltage proportional to the applied force
cards.explain: Their output is a voltage that changes in proportion to the force applied at the input.

cards.question: What does an ordinary autopilot engaged in command mode do when control forces exceed a certain level
options: It reverts to armed
It disengages
It trims out the force
cards.explain: Without supervisory override the autopilot simply drops out when the control force is high enough.

cards.question: At which break out force does the pitch channel switch off pitch attitude hold
options: More than 20 newtons
More than 10 newtons
More than 50 newtons
cards.explain: The printed break out force is in excess of 20 newtons.

cards.question: A pilot has flown the aircraft to a different attitude in CWS mode and now takes his hands off the controls. What happens next?
options: The attitude before the input is recovered automatically by the autopilot control loops
The changed attitude or the new heading is maintained by the autopilot control loops
The autopilot disengages and the aircraft is left in manual control
cards.explain: Releasing the controls makes the newly attained attitude or heading the value the autopilot holds.

cards.question: Why do the manual controls end at positions equivalent to the pilot own inputs during CWS operation
options: Because they are locked by the autopilot engage clutch
Because they follow up the movements of the control surfaces
Because they are centred by springs inside the feel and centering unit
cards.explain: The controls are tied to the surfaces, so they end up in positions matching the input made.

cards.question: What does the autopilot do if the roll angle on release of the yoke is less than 5 degrees
options: It decreases the roll angle to wings level and holds the present heading
It keeps the present roll angle and holds the resulting turn rate
It decreases the roll angle to wings level and holds the previous heading
cards.explain: Below 5 degrees of bank the autopilot rolls level and enters Heading Hold on the heading reached.

cards.question: What does the autopilot maintain when the yoke is released at a bank between 5 degrees and the type maximum
options: The present turn rate
The present roll angle
The present heading
cards.explain: Between 5 degrees and the maximum the bank angle present at release is the value held.

cards.question: What supports the improvement of neutral spiral stability in roll when CWS is used
options: Automatic yaw damping and possibly auto-trim
Automatic lift compensation and possibly auto-brake
Automatic turn compensation and possibly auto-thrust
cards.explain: Turn compensation, with auto-thrust where fitted, is what supports the improved spiral stability.

cards.question: Dynamometric rods are found on some aircraft outside the autopilot altogether. In which system?
options: The yaw damper system
The auto-throttle system
The auto-brake system
cards.explain: The manual gives the auto-throttle as the other application for dynamometric rods.

cards.question: What does an autopilot allowing supervisory override do when it senses force at the flight controls
options: It stays engaged and transits to CWS mode
It disengages and hands control back to the pilot
It stays engaged and transits to heading hold mode
cards.explain: Supervisory override converts a force on the controls into a change to CWS rather than a disengagement.

cards.question: When does an autopilot with supervisory override return to command mode
options: As soon as the pilot input is terminated, reverting to its basic attitude modes
Only after the pilot reselects command mode on the mode control panel
As soon as the pilot input is terminated, keeping its previously selected modes
cards.explain: Ending the manual input is enough for the autopilot to go back to command with its earlier modes.

cards.question: What does the CWS sensor signal command at S1 during a pitch override input
options: A pitch rate proportional to the travel of the control column
An elevator deflection proportional to the force on the control column
A pitch attitude proportional to the force on the control column
cards.explain: The commanded quantity is a pitch attitude that follows the applied column force.

cards.question: What is held in the command memory of the pitch channel and what updates it during an override input
options: The elevator position reference, updated with the trim integrator output
The pitch rate reference, updated with the manually commanded rate
The pitch attitude reference, updated with the manually commanded attitude
cards.explain: The memory stores the pitch attitude reference and takes on the value the pilot commands by hand.

cards.question: What does the autopilot servo actuator do to the control column during a pitch override
options: It releases the column from the elevator so it can be moved freely
It tilts the column to a position matching the elevator deflection
It holds the column at the position the pilot has moved it to
cards.explain: The servo extends or retracts so the column sits where the elevator deflection corresponds.

cards.question: Besides the roll attitude, which additional quantity must be synchronized during a roll override input
options: The aircraft heading
The aircraft turn rate
The aircraft slip angle
cards.explain: In roll both the roll attitude and the heading have to be kept synchronized.

cards.question: A pilot holds a steady force on the control wheel in CWS. What do the inner loops make of it, and what does the aircraft do?
options: A fixed roll rate, which changes the heading but not the attitude
A proportional roll angle, which changes the turn rate and the track
A proportional roll rate, which changes the attitude and the heading
cards.explain: The force becomes a proportional roll rate, and a lasting roll rate changes the attitude and so the heading.

cards.question: A pilot rolls the aircraft past its maximum roll angle in CWS and then releases the yoke. What does the autopilot do?
options: It rolls the aircraft back to the maximum roll angle and maintains it
It rolls the aircraft back to wings level and maintains the heading reached
It holds the roll angle reached, beyond the maximum, until a new input
cards.explain: Beyond the limit the autopilot recovers to the maximum roll angle and holds it in Roll Attitude Hold.

cards.question: A pilot flying in CWS makes a stick input and lets go. Why does the aircraft stay where he put it instead of going back?
options: By artificial feel, so any stick input gives a rising stick force
By auto-trim, so any stick input gives a new trimmed pitch attitude
By turn compensation, so any stick input gives a constant pitch rate
cards.explain: Neutral pitch stability is built in, and auto-trim retrims the aircraft at whatever attitude the input produced.

cards.question: Why do the computed control forces felt by a pilot flying in CWS stay the same as the centre of gravity, speed and weight change?
options: Because neutral stability makes the artificial feel independent of them
Because the autopilot servo takes over the control loads created by them
Because the feel unit is rescheduled by the air data computer for them
cards.explain: Neutral stability is the reason the artificial feel forces do not change with CG, speed or weight.

cards.question: A pilot applies force to the column and to the wheel at the same time in CWS. What two commands does the computer form from the sensor voltages?
options: A pitch attitude or a roll rate command
A vertical speed or a turn rate command
A pitch rate or a roll attitude command
cards.explain: The computer makes a pitch attitude command or a roll rate command out of the sensor voltage.

cards.question: A pilot pushes the power levers forward while the thrust system is engaged. What do the rods fitted there sense and report?
options: They sense the lever travel and signal a thrust limit to the engine controller
They sense the pilot input and signal a servo fault to the thrust controller
They sense the pilot input and signal a pilot override to the thrust controller
cards.explain: The rods pick up the hand force on the levers and tell the thrust controller that the pilot is overriding.

cards.question: A pilot wants to nudge the aircraft while the autopilot is intercepting a localizer. What does supervisory override let him do?
options: He can recentre the controls during levelling off or an intercept without resynchronising them
He can correct the autopilot during levelling off or an intercept without disengaging it
He can retrim the autopilot during levelling off or an intercept without reselecting it
cards.explain: The point of supervisory override is that the pilot can help the autopilot without dropping it out.

cards.question: A pilot is pressing on the controls of an autopilot that allows supervisory override. What is the state of the autopilot while he does so?
options: The current modes are retained and the autopilot ignores the input
The current modes are cancelled and the autopilot must be resynchronized
The current modes are suspended but the autopilot stays synchronized
cards.explain: Modes are only suspended during the input, and the autopilot remains synchronized throughout.

cards.question: An aircraft in altitude hold is pushed into a climb by a pilot input at the column, and the column is then released. Which altitude does the autopilot now hold?
options: The altitude reached at the release of the control column
The altitude midway between the two, blended by the trim integrator
The altitude selected before the control column was moved
cards.explain: The value reached when the pilot lets go becomes the new reference for the suspended upper mode.

cards.question: The pilot reaches the speed he wanted and lets go of the control column after a supervisory override input. What does the pitch channel do at that moment?
options: It sees the sensor signal fall to zero and reactivates pitch attitude hold at once
It waits for the trim integrator to run out before any mode is reactivated
It sees the sensor signal fall to zero and reverts to the previous pitch attitude
cards.explain: Zero sensor signal is the trigger that immediately brings pitch attitude hold back.

cards.question: A CWS pitch input has left the elevator standing deflected to hold the new attitude. How is that lasting deflection dealt with?
options: It compensates lasting elevator deflections with the auto-trim system
It compensates lasting elevator deflections with the artificial feel unit
It compensates lasting speed errors with the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Auto-trim takes out the standing elevator deflection so the new attitude is held.

cards.question: A pilot wants a different target airspeed while supervisory override is available and the autopilot is holding the nose where it is. How can he obtain it?
options: By changing the thrust setting manually at the power levers
By changing the pitch attitude manually at the control column
By changing the vertical speed target at the mode control panel
cards.explain: With pitch attitude hold active, a manual pitch change is the way the pilot trades to a new speed.

cards.question: What does the heading indication at the mode controller show when power is first applied on the ground
options: Either the present heading or the runway heading
Either the present heading or the last selected heading
Either the last selected heading or the magnetic variation
cards.explain: At power up the display is either synchronized to the present heading or shows the last selection.

cards.question: Which heading do some autopilots display at their mode control panel when power is first applied on the ground
options: 180 degrees
000 degrees
360 degrees
cards.explain: The manual states that some autopilots display 000.

cards.question: How many control loops make up the heading select control cascade
options: Three
One
Two
cards.explain: The cascade is made up of two control loops.

cards.question: Which quantity acts as the control value of the outer loop in the autopilot lateral channel
options: Turn rate
Roll angle
Heading
cards.explain: Heading is named as the control value in this mode.

cards.question: What does the term cross coupling mean
options: The mutual influence of the aircraft axes when attitude or thrust is changed
The mutual influence of the control loops when a mode is reselected
The mutual influence of the control surfaces when a servo channel is engaged
cards.explain: Cross coupling is defined as one axis influencing another when attitude or thrust rating is changed.

cards.question: Under which conditions is a horizontal turn said to be coordinated
options: The aircraft neither climbs nor descends and holds its bank and thrust
The aircraft neither slips nor skids and holds its bank and turn rate
The aircraft neither slips nor skids and holds its altitude and airspeed
cards.explain: A coordinated horizontal turn is free of slip and skid and keeps altitude and airspeed.

cards.question: What does the autopilot do once the heading select mode is engaged
options: It turns the aircraft to the pre-selected heading and maintains it
It arms the mode until the pre-selected heading is reached
It turns the aircraft onto the present heading and then maintains it
cards.explain: Selecting the mode makes the autopilot fly to the pre-selected heading and then hold it.

cards.question: The crew has a heading mode running and air traffic control passes a different heading. When may the selected heading be altered?
options: At any time while the mode is active
Only after the mode has been reselected
Only after the first heading has been captured
cards.explain: The selected heading may be changed at any time while heading select is running.

cards.question: A crew look at the outer of the two concentric knobs under the selected heading display. What does it let them choose?
options: Selection of a reduced maximum turn rate
Selection of a reduced maximum roll angle
Selection of a reduced maximum pitch angle
cards.explain: The outer knob picks a lower limit for the maximum roll angle.

cards.question: A pilot selects the heading mode on the mode control panel. Which loop of the cascade is closed by that selection?
options: The inner loop
Both loops together
The outer loop
cards.explain: Selecting the mode closes the outer loop of the cascade.

cards.question: How is the actual value of the heading obtained for the outer loop
options: From a directional gyro or a radio magnetic indicator
From a compass system or an inertial reference system
From a compass system or an air data computer
cards.explain: The actual heading comes from a compass system or from the IRS.

cards.question: Where and how is the heading error formed
options: At S2 in the inner loop, by comparing actual with reference heading
At S1 in the outer loop, by comparing actual with reference heading
At S1 in the outer loop, by comparing actual with commanded roll angle
cards.explain: S1 in the outer loop is where actual and reference heading are compared.

cards.question: An aircraft shows cross coupling between its axes. Why must those effects be kept as small as possible?
options: They reduce the authority of the autopilot servo actuators
They stimulate motion in the affected degrees of freedom
They increase the control forces felt at the control column
cards.explain: They are undesirable because they set up motion in the degrees of freedom they affect.

cards.question: What does the design of a modern autoflight system ensure about its own cross couplings
options: They reproduce the cross coupling effects in the aircraft
They counteract the cross coupling effects in the aircraft
They are removed entirely from the control channels
cards.explain: The couplings built into the system are there to work against the ones the airframe produces.

cards.question: A turn is about to be started. What generates the rolling moment that begins it?
options: Deflection of the rudder
Deflection of the ailerons
Deflection of the elevator
cards.explain: The ailerons are deflected to produce the rolling moment that starts the turn.

cards.question: What forces the aircraft onto a circular flight path once it is banked
options: The vertical component of the tilted lift vector
The horizontal component of the tilted lift vector
The horizontal component of the total drag vector
cards.explain: Tilting the lift vector gives a horizontal component, and that is what curves the flight path.

cards.question: What is the single cause of both the lateral accelerations and the unfavourable aerodynamic effects in a turn
options: The existence of a slip angle
The existence of a roll rate
The existence of a pitch error
cards.explain: Both arise from a slip angle being present.

cards.question: An aircraft is turning with a slip angle present. How is that slip angle brought to zero?
options: By deflecting the spoilers in coordination with the rudder
By deflecting the elevator in coordination with the ailerons
By deflecting the rudder in coordination with the ailerons
cards.explain: Rudder deflection coordinated with the aileron deflection takes the slip out.

cards.question: A meal is being served in the cabin and the pilot winds the outer knob below the heading window to its lower setting. What is he achieving?
options: A smaller maximum roll angle, which improves passenger comfort
A slower heading capture rate, which improves passenger comfort
A smaller maximum heading change, which improves passenger comfort
cards.explain: Reducing the maximum roll angle is what that knob does, and comfort is the stated reason for using it.

cards.question: What is the heading error turned into before it leaves the outer control loop
options: An aileron position demand fed to the servo
A roll angle reference value fed to the inner loop
A roll rate reference value fed to the inner loop
cards.explain: The outer loop converts heading error into a roll angle reference for the inner loop.

cards.question: The reference bank angle produced by the outer loop no longer matches the bank angle the aircraft is actually at. What does the inner loop do?
options: It commands a change in rudder deflection
It commands a change in heading reference
It commands a change in roll attitude
cards.explain: A difference between reference and actual roll angle makes the inner loop command a roll attitude change.

cards.question: The autopilot banks the aircraft into a turn and must not let it descend. Why does the elevator have to be deflected as well?
options: Total drag must rise so the airspeed stays at the reference value
Total lift must rise so its vertical part still balances the weight
Total lift must fall so its horizontal part still curves the path
cards.explain: Banking tilts the lift, so total lift must be increased to keep the vertical part equal to the weight.

cards.question: An altitude or vertical speed controller is left to correct a turn on its own, with no lift compensation fitted. What is the consequence?
options: It reacts too late and causes large errors or even unstable pitch control
It reacts correctly but leaves a permanent slip angle in the turn
It reacts too early and causes a lasting offset from the reference value
cards.explain: Altitude and vertical speed change slowly, so the controller is late and large errors or instability follow.

cards.question: A turn is entered and the bank angle goes on increasing. How does the input the pitch channel receives from the lateral channel change?
options: It increases aileron deflection in proportion to the existing pitch angle
It increases elevator deflection in proportion to the existing roll angle
It increases elevator deflection in proportion to the existing turn rate
cards.explain: Lift compensation adds elevator in proportion to the bank angle to raise the vertical lift component.

cards.question: The autopilot increases lift to hold altitude in a turn. Why must the thrust system then be brought in as well?
options: Because the extra bank brings extra slip, which would raise the fuel flow
Because the extra lift brings extra weight, which would lower the ceiling
Because the extra lift brings extra drag, which would lower the airspeed
cards.explain: More lift means more drag and a loss of speed, so a roll to thrust coupling adds thrust to hold the speed.

cards.question: An operator asks what the airline gains from letting the altitude wander slightly instead of correcting it at once. What is the answer?
options: Fewer mode changes, so less wear occurs and comfort improves
Fewer thrust changes, so less fuel is burnt and comfort improves
Fewer altitude errors, so less drag is created and comfort improves
cards.explain: Trading energy cuts the number of thrust changes, which saves fuel and makes the ride smoother.

cards.question: Which three parameters are described as flight path parameters
options: Airspeed, pitch rate and yaw rate
Altitude, airspeed and track
Altitude, pitch and roll
cards.explain: Altitude, airspeed and track are the flight path parameters named.

cards.question: Which two things does the flight path controller do in place of the pilot
options: Intercepting a flight path and stabilizing on it
Selecting a flight path and displaying it
Trimming a flight path and recovering from it
cards.explain: The controller intercepts the flight path and then stabilizes the aircraft on it.

cards.question: From which two sources does the airspeed or Mach reference number come
options: Dialled by the pilot at the mode control panel or supplied by the ADC
Computed by the autopilot from the flight plan or supplied by the FMS
Dialled by the pilot at the mode control panel or supplied by the FMS
cards.explain: It is either dialled by hand on the mode control panel or passed over by the FMS.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the LVL/CH mode
options: To transfer the aircraft automatically to a higher or lower flight level
To transfer the aircraft automatically onto a selected vertical speed
To transfer speed control automatically to the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: The mode exists to take the aircraft automatically from one flight level to another.

cards.question: Which computer normally calculates the thrust limits for each flight phase
options: The flight control computer
The flight warning computer
The FADEC computer
cards.explain: The FADEC computer works out the thrust limits for each flight phase.

cards.question: Which form does the reference value take below a pressure altitude of about 26 000 feet
options: A true airspeed (TAS)
A Mach number (M or MMO)
An airspeed (IAS or CAS)
cards.explain: Below about 26 000 feet the reference is an airspeed.

cards.question: In which memory is the reference value stored
options: The speed and Mach memory
The altitude capture memory
The attitude command memory
cards.explain: It is held in the speed and Mach memory.

cards.question: What is the source of the control value used for airspeed or Mach number control
options: The air data computer
The flight management system
The inertial reference system
cards.explain: Calibrated airspeed or Mach comes from the air data computer.

cards.question: What part does the pilot himself play when he is flying the aircraft along its flight path by hand
options: He makes up a feedback path for the attitude command memory
He makes up an outer loop for the translatory degrees of freedom
He makes up an inner loop for the three rotational degrees of freedom
cards.explain: A hand-flying pilot is himself the outer loop for the translatory degrees of freedom.

cards.question: How did the term autopilot become established
options: From the automatic stability function of damping the aircraft about its axes
From the automatic trim function of relieving the loads at the control column
From the automatic pilot function of guiding the aircraft along its flight path
cards.explain: The name comes from the system doing the pilot's job of guiding the aircraft along the flight path.

cards.question: A flight path controller is doing its job on a normal sector. Which upper autopilot modes do its tasks correspond to?
options: Climb, cruise, hold, go around and automatic taxi
Takeoff, climb, descend, flare and automatic braking
Climb, enroute, descend, approach and automatic landing
cards.explain: Those five are the upper modes listed.

cards.question: What does a flight management system relieve the pilot of
options: Most manual control tasks, which it trims automatically
Most monitoring tasks, which it displays automatically
Most routine tasks, which it sequences automatically
cards.explain: The FMS takes over most routine tasks and sequences the events itself.

cards.question: An FMS is sequencing a flight path segment by segment. What does it do automatically at each one?
options: Choosing navigation aids and tuning their frequencies for each path segment
Choosing autopilot channels and testing their servos for each path segment
Choosing engine ratings and setting their thrust limits for each path segment
cards.explain: Selecting the right navigation aids and tuning them is the example given.

cards.question: Which quantities does a flight management system calculate for lowest fuel consumption
options: Optimal climb and sink rates, cruise altitudes and airspeeds
Optimal thrust limits, bleed air settings and flap schedules
Optimal bank angles, turn radii and track changes
cards.explain: Those are the optimal values the FMS works out for the lowest fuel burn.

cards.question: Between which two systems is permanent control of airspeed or Mach number divided
options: The flight management system and the flight warning system
The autopilot or flight director pitch channel and the auto-thrust system
The autopilot or flight director roll channel and the auto-trim system
cards.explain: Either the AP/FD pitch channel or the auto-throttle system does the speed control.

cards.question: How does the autopilot pitch channel control airspeed or Mach number
options: By altering the thrust rating through the power lever position
By altering the flight path angle through the aircraft's attitude
By altering the drag through the speed brake panel setting
cards.explain: The pitch channel changes the flight path angle by changing pitch attitude with the elevator.

cards.question: Which energy change and speed change occur at pitch up
options: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the aircraft slows down
Kinetic energy becomes potential energy and the aircraft speeds up
Kinetic energy becomes potential energy and the aircraft slows down
cards.explain: Pitching up trades speed for height, so the aircraft slows.

cards.question: How widely is the airspeed or Mach reference value applied once it is set
options: It is always applied to both speed control systems
It is always applied to the system holding priority only
It is always applied to the auto-thrust system only
cards.explain: The one reference value goes to both of the speed controlling systems.

cards.question: Under which condition does the autoflight system maintain the reference airspeed or Mach number during a level change
options: As long as no thrust or flight envelope limits are exceeded
As long as no altitude or vertical speed limits are exceeded
As long as no autopilot or auto-thrust channel has failed
cards.explain: The reference speed is held while thrust limits and envelope limits are respected.

cards.question: What does thrust alone have to overcome during an unaccelerated horizontal flight
options: Weight
Drag
Inertia
cards.explain: In level unaccelerated flight the thrust only has to balance the drag.

cards.question: Which system takes charge of airspeed or Mach number the moment a level change is triggered
options: The autopilot, which holds it by adjusting the thrust rating
The auto-thrust, which holds it by adjusting the thrust rating
The autopilot, which holds it by adjusting the flight path angle
cards.explain: At level change the autopilot always takes the speed and holds it with flight path angle.

cards.question: The crew select a higher flight level and trigger a level change. What thrust does the auto-thrust system set?
options: The cruise thrust for the present flight phase
The flight idle thrust for the present flight phase
The maximum thrust for the present flight phase
cards.explain: For a climb the system sets the maximum thrust applicable to the flight phase.

cards.question: What does the auto-thrust system do for a level change in the descending direction
options: It disengages until capture
It sets the flight idle rating
It sets the maximum continuous rating
cards.explain: A descent needs a lack of thrust, so flight idle is set.

cards.question: What do the thrust limits depend on
options: Actual gross weight and the amount of bleed air tapped from an engine
Actual air data and the amount of bleed air tapped from an engine
Actual air data and the amount of fuel remaining in the tanks
cards.explain: They depend on the air data of the moment and on how much bleed air is being taken.

cards.question: Why is the capture point needed
options: To give a smooth transition from a climb or descent to level flight
To give an accurate indication of the time left to the target level
To give a smooth transition from thrust mode to speed mode
cards.explain: It exists so that the levelling off at the selected flight level is smooth.

cards.question: The aircraft is in the capture phase and the altitude error is shrinking. How is the vertical speed brought down?
options: By decreasing the flight path angle in proportion to the decreasing altitude error
By decreasing the thrust rating in proportion to the decreasing altitude error
By decreasing the flight path angle in proportion to the decreasing speed error
cards.explain: The flight path angle is reduced in step with the shrinking altitude error.

cards.question: What happens to speed control when altitude acquisition becomes active
options: The pitch channel hands it to the thrust system, which goes to speed mode
The thrust system hands it to the pitch channel, which goes to speed mode
The pitch channel keeps it and the thrust system goes to thrust mode
cards.explain: The pitch channel is now needed for the capture, so speed passes to the thrust system in speed mode.

cards.question: Which is the only system performing speed control in IAS hold or Mach hold
options: The autothrottle system
The autopilot pitch channel
The flight management system
cards.explain: In this mode the autothrottle alone does the speed control.

cards.question: An autopilot offers only IAS hold and Mach hold. What is the limitation of that control mode?
options: It does not allow bracketing of a pre-selected reference speed
It does not allow a change over between speed and Mach
It does not allow the autothrottle to reach its thrust limit
cards.explain: There is no bracketing of a pre-selected reference speed in this mode.

cards.question: Which two names are used for the reference value according to where it comes from
options: Preset speed target or managed speed target
Selected speed target or managed speed target
Selected speed target or computed speed target
cards.explain: The two printed names are selected speed target and managed speed target.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs to the level at which speed control passes from airspeed to Mach number. What is that altitude called?
options: The capture or transition altitude
The crossover or changeover altitude
The optimum or cruise altitude
cards.explain: That altitude is called the cross or changeover altitude.

cards.question: How does the autoflight system stop an entered speed target from exceeding the flight envelope
options: By voting between the entered value and the computed limits
By warning the crew and leaving the entered value in force
By rejecting the entered value and reverting to the last valid one
cards.explain: The system votes between the entered value and the limits so the envelope is not exceeded.

cards.question: At which pressure altitude is the automatic change over performed during a climb or a descent
options: Approximately 26 000 feet
Approximately 36 000 feet
Approximately 18 000 feet
cards.explain: The printed altitude is approximately 26 000 feet.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through about 26 000 feet and the reference changes over by itself. Which system has done it?
options: The auto-throttle and auto-thrust system
The autopilot and flight director system
The air data and inertial reference system
cards.explain: The AP/FD system carries out the automatic change over.

cards.question: How is the airspeed and Mach control loop built up
options: An outer loop is added to the roll attitude controller
An inner loop is added to the altitude hold controller
An outer loop is added to the pitch attitude controller
cards.explain: The pitch attitude controller gains an outer loop to make the speed controller.

cards.question: Which autoflight mode sets up the airspeed and Mach outer control loop when it is selected
options: Heading select
Altitude hold
Level change
cards.explain: Selecting level change is what makes the mode logic build the outer loop.

cards.question: The speed controller is running in level change. Where is the speed error formed, and from what?
options: At S1, by comparing reference attitude with actual attitude
At S2, by comparing reference attitude with actual speed
At S2, by comparing reference speed with actual speed
cards.explain: S2 is the summing point where reference and actual speed are compared.

cards.question: Which item gives the airspeed controller its PI behaviour in the outer loop
options: The trim integrator
The pitch attitude limiter
The attitude integrator
cards.explain: The attitude integrator is what makes the outer loop proportional plus integral.

cards.question: What are the two jobs of the pitch attitude limiter
options: It curtails extreme commands and sets the gain schedule of the inner loop
It curtails the speed error and sets the timing and direction of the change
It curtails extreme commands and sets the timing and direction of the change
cards.explain: It both limits extreme attitude commands and governs when and which way the pitch change happens.

cards.question: What is the airspeed or Mach error converted into at the output of the outer loop
options: A thrust rating demand
A pitch attitude reference
An elevator position demand
cards.explain: The outer loop turns the speed error into a pitch attitude reference.

cards.question: Gusts push an aircraft away from its altitude and its track. Why can the inner control loops not put that right on their own?
options: The inner loops cannot compensate disturbances acting on the attitude
The inner loops cannot drive the control surfaces without a servo
The inner loops cannot compensate disturbances acting on the flight path
cards.explain: Inner loops stabilize attitude only, so outer loops are added for flight path disturbances.

cards.question: How is the path of an aircraft through the air affected in principle
options: By acting on the rotary degrees of freedom, that is by changing attitude
By acting on the aerodynamic configuration, that is by changing flap setting
By acting on the thrust setting, that is by changing engine rating
cards.explain: The aircraft is moved about its path by changing its attitude.

cards.question: Why does the autopilot have to treat interception and stabilization as two separate jobs?
options: The path is in segments, and each one has to be flown at a different airspeed
The path is continuous, but the sensors update at two different rates
The path is in segments, and each must be caught without overshoot or offset
cards.explain: Because the path is built of segments, each one has to be intercepted cleanly and then held.

cards.question: What must be in place before an FMS can guide an aircraft laterally and vertically from departure to destination?
options: A flight plan of waypoints and the relevant modes selected for the autoflight system
A flight plan of waypoints and the relevant frequencies tuned at the radio panel
A route clearance entered and the relevant altitudes set at the mode control panel
cards.explain: Both a waypoint flight plan and the FMS modes selected for the autoflight system are required.

cards.question: Both the pitch channel and the thrust system can hold the speed. Which of them gets the job, and why can they not share it?
options: The autopilot, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
The autopilot, because the flight management system cannot supply two targets
The auto-thrust, because the two systems cannot both control speed at once
cards.explain: Only one may control speed, and the priority is given to the autopilot.

cards.question: The autopilot pitch channel lowers the nose while it is controlling speed. What energy change takes place and what does the speed do?
options: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed increases
Potential energy becomes kinetic energy and the speed decreases
Kinetic energy becomes potential energy and the speed decreases
cards.explain: Pitching down converts height into speed, so the aircraft accelerates.

cards.question: The pilot selects altitude hold, so the pitch channel is now given another job. Who controls the speed and how?
options: The auto-thrust system, by drag control to a reference speed
The auto-thrust system, by thrust control to a reference speed
The flight management system, by thrust control to a reference speed
cards.explain: With the pitch channel busy, speed passes to the auto-thrust, which holds it with thrust.

cards.question: The autopilot pitch channel is taken off speed control and put onto altitude hold. What does that decide for the thrust system?
options: Its mode of operation, which the pitch channel determines
Its thrust limit, which the pitch channel then determines
Its engagement, which the pitch channel determines
cards.explain: In current systems what the pitch channel is doing sets the mode the thrust system runs in.

cards.question: The autopilot is controlling speed in level flight and the thrust is then increased. What does the autopilot do with the aircraft?
options: It increases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to accelerate
It decreases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to climb
It increases the flight path angle and the aircraft begins to climb
cards.explain: The autopilot holds speed by raising the flight path angle, so the surplus thrust becomes a climb.

cards.question: The thrust is reduced instead, with the autopilot still controlling speed. What follows?
options: The flight path angle is decreased and the aircraft descends at constant speed
The flight path angle is held and the aircraft decelerates in level flight
The flight path angle is increased and the aircraft descends at constant speed
cards.explain: A lack of thrust is answered by lowering the flight path angle, which gives a descent at the same speed.

cards.question: A level change climb is being flown. What decides the amount of pitch change and the climb rate that result?
options: Only on the pitch attitude limit applied by the autopilot pitch channel
Only on the altitude error between present and preselected flight level
Only on the surplus of thrust from the rating set by the thrust system
cards.explain: Both depend only on the surplus of thrust left after the thrust system has set its rating.

cards.question: How does the thrust system decide whether to apply its thrust limit or flight idle at the start of a level change?
options: It evaluates the sign of the altitude error, taken as preselected minus actual
It evaluates the sign of the speed error, taken as reference minus actual
It evaluates the size of the altitude error, taken as preselected minus actual
cards.explain: The sign of the altitude error tells the system whether the aircraft must go up or down.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing fast towards the selected level. How does its high vertical speed affect the point at which the capture starts?
options: The capture point is unaffected, being a fixed distance from the level
The capture point is placed further from the level, in proportion to it
The capture point is placed closer to the level, in proportion to it
cards.explain: The capture point is a vertical distance from the selected level set in proportion to the vertical speed of the moment.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the capture point during a level change climb. Which mode changes take place?
options: Level change is turned off and altitude acquisition is activated
Level change is turned off and altitude hold is activated
Level change is rearmed and altitude acquisition is turned off
cards.explain: At the capture point level change drops out and altitude acquisition takes over.

cards.question: Why can the altitude acquisition law not simply be left running until the selected level is reached?
options: Its gain is scheduled with airspeed, which would change during the capture
Its transition follows a ramp function, which would overshoot the level
Its transition follows an e-function, which would take an infinite time
cards.explain: The capture is exponential, so in theory it never quite arrives and must be terminated.

cards.question: A level change descent is in progress. Which thrust mode is shown, and which one would it be if the aircraft were climbing instead?
options: Speed mode now, and thrust at the climb limit for a climb
Thrust at idle now, and thrust at the climb limit for a climb
Thrust at the climb limit now, and thrust at idle for a climb
cards.explain: The descent leg runs at idle thrust and the climb leg at the climb thrust limit.

cards.question: When should a crew with only IAS hold available select it during a climb or a descent?
options: Once the new reference speed has been reached
Once the new flight level has been selected
Before the thrust system reaches its climb limit
cards.explain: Because it only freezes the current value, it is selected after the wanted speed has been reached.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through the changeover altitude with a speed target that was dialled in by hand. What becomes of the number in the window?
options: It is replaced by dashes until the pilot enters a Mach number
It is converted to the equivalent true airspeed and displayed there
It is converted to the equivalent Mach number and displayed there
cards.explain: At the transition the value is converted to the equivalent Mach number, and a value entered at the panel is shown there.

cards.question: The crew look at the speed window on the mode control panel and see dashes. What does that tell them?
options: The speed target is being supplied by the flight management system
The speed target has been lost and the autothrottle has disengaged
The speed target is outside the limits of the flight envelope
cards.explain: Dashes in the window mean the target is managed by the FMS rather than selected by hand.

cards.question: A Mach target is being flown at a high flight level. What does the reference speed marker on the primary flight display show?
options: A calibrated airspeed, because the tape is in CAS at any altitude
An indicated airspeed, because the tape is in IAS at any altitude
A Mach number, because the tape follows the active reference
cards.explain: The tape reads calibrated airspeed only, so a marker on it is a CAS value whatever the altitude or active reference.

cards.question: The actual speed differs from the stored reference when a speed mode is armed. Why is the stored value synchronized first, and how?
options: To avoid an envelope exceedance, by storing the actual value at mode activation
To avoid a hard over, by storing the actual value at mode activation
To avoid a hard over, by storing the envelope limit at mode activation
cards.explain: Synchronizing to the actual speed at activation stops the controller making a violent correction.

cards.question: The flaps and the landing gear are extended. Which of the two configuration speed limits does VMAX take?
options: The lower of VMO and MMO
The higher of VFE and VLE
The lower of VFE and VLE
cards.explain: For an extended flap, slat and gear configuration the printed rule takes whichever of VFE and VLE is the lower.

cards.question: A crew wants to work to a Mach reference well below the normal transition height. What can they do and where?
options: Re-enter the target as a Mach number in the flight management system
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the altitude select display
Press the crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display
cards.explain: The crossover pushbutton beside the speed and Mach display allows a change over at any altitude.

cards.question: Which parameter is held constant above the automatic change over level and which below
options: Mach number above and indicated airspeed below
True airspeed above and indicated airspeed below
Indicated airspeed above and Mach number below
cards.explain: Above the change over the Mach number is held and below it the indicated airspeed is held.

cards.question: What does the PI behaviour of the outer loop prevent, and how
options: A standing speed error, by integrating it into the attitude reference
A standing speed error, by limiting the pitch attitude being commanded
An unstable speed loop, by integrating it into the thrust demand
cards.explain: Integrating the lasting error corrects the attitude reference until the error is removed.

cards.question: A descent at a lower reference speed is commanded. In what order does the pitch controller act?
options: It pitches down first and then reduces the speed error to zero
It reduces the speed error and pitches down at the same time
It reduces the speed error to zero first and then pitches down
cards.explain: The speed error is taken out first, and only then does the aircraft pitch down.

cards.question: What is the result of changing pitch attitude whenever a speed error appears at a given thrust
options: The aircraft adopts a vertical speed that restores the reference altitude
The aircraft adopts a thrust rating that restores the reference speed
The aircraft adopts a flight path angle that restores the reference speed
cards.explain: Changing attitude puts the aircraft on the flight path angle that holds the reference speed for the thrust set.

questions.question: How many control loops make up the cascade used for closed loop control of vertical speed
options: One
Three
Two
questions.explain: The cascade for vertical speed has two loops.

questions.question: What does the vertical speed controller determine and pass on to the inner loop
options: A pitch attitude reference value
A vertical speed reference value
An elevator deflection angle
questions.explain: The outer loop controller sets an attitude reference which the inner loop then follows.

questions.question: What does the mode annunciation read while the level off mode is in use
options: ALT
LVL CHG
V/S = 0
questions.explain: The level off condition is annunciated as a commanded vertical speed of zero.

questions.question: What is true of the provisions protecting against violation of airspeed and Mach limits
options: They differ a lot between aircraft types
They are identical in every modern autoflight system
They apply only to the vertical speed mode
questions.explain: The provisions vary so much from one type to another that no single description covers them all.

questions.question: To what does the vertical speed reference value correspond in the altitude acquisition outer loop
options: The measured vertical speed
The altitude error
The selected altitude
questions.explain: Height still to go is converted directly into a commanded rate, which is why the rate falls as the gap closes.

questions.question: What does the vertical speed controller determine from the vertical speed error during an altitude acquisition?
options: The altitude reference value for the altitude memory
The pitch reference value for the pitch inner loop
The thrust rating for the autothrust system
questions.explain: The outer loop output is always an attitude reference handed to the inner loop.

questions.question: With which system does the profile or vertical navigation mode connect the autoflight system
options: The inertial reference system
The air data computer
The flight management system
questions.explain: Vertical navigation is flown on data the flight management system supplies, so the two are coupled.

questions.question: Over what span of a flight do the sequential segments of profile or vertical navigation guidance run
options: From after take off to the instrument approach
From the top of climb to the top of descent
From the capture point to the transition altitude
questions.explain: The sequential segments are stated as running from just after take off through to the approach.

questions.question: Below what size of airspeed disturbance is the soft altitude deviation permitted
options: 4 Kts
5 Kts
10 Kts
questions.explain: The allowance applies only to disturbances below four knots.

questions.question: What relation do the several operating modes covered by the generic vertical navigation term bear to one another
options: They have separate annunciations
They have identical meaning
They have opposing control laws
questions.explain: The listed names are different labels for the same thing.

questions.question: Where the autothrust system is working in thrust mode, what decides the source of the thrust ratings it uses?
options: The momentary vertical speed
The selected altitude
The type of aircraft
questions.explain: The source of the ratings varies from one aircraft type to another.

questions.question: Which unit is activated first on selection of the VOR mode to measure angular deviation from the pre- selected course
options: The course comparator
The capture detector
The lateral beam sensor
questions.explain: The lateral beam sensor is the device that watches the angular deviation while the mode is armed.

questions.question: A waypoint has to be passed at a given altitude with a given airspeed maintained during a climb. What does the flight management computer calculate?
options: An optimum flight path angle for the required thrust
An optimum vertical speed for the required altitude
An optimum thrust for the required flight path angle
questions.explain: The constraint fixes the path to be flown, so what the computer works out is the thrust that path needs.

questions.question: Apart from pressing the button again, how is the navigation mode terminated?
options: Automatically, as soon as another lateral mode is selected
Automatically, as soon as the cross-track distance grows again
Automatically, as soon as another vertical mode is selected
questions.explain: Two lateral modes cannot run together, so selecting another one ends this one.

questions.question: The radial deviation rate rises above eight millivolts per second. What does the roll controller do?
options: It transits to heading control and reverses the pre-selected course
It transits to heading control and maintains the present heading
It transits to capture control and re-intercepts the radial
questions.explain: A fast moving deviation signals the cone of confusion, so the controller freezes the heading and flies on.

questions.question: How does the washout let the VOR deviation prevail over the heading error on the long run
options: Only changes of VOR deviation are still compared with the heading error
Only changes of heading error are still compared with the VOR deviation
Both signals are compared but the heading error is given a lower gain
questions.explain: The washout passes only the changing part of the heading error, so the steady deviation signal dominates.

questions.question: Which inverter reverses the localizer deviation signal for a back beam approach
options: Inverter 1
Inverter 2
The rate taker
questions.explain: The deviation signal is reversed by Inverter 2, while Inverter 1 works on the heading error.

questions.question: The localizer mode has been selected on its own on the autoflight control panel as an independent lateral mode — which phase is left out?
options: The Localizer-Track Phase
The Capture Phase
The Approach-Track Phase
questions.explain: Selecting LOC as an independent lateral mode omits the Approach-Track Phase.

questions.question: Two aircraft intercept the same localizer from very different distances to the transmitter antenna — what does the adaptive capture threshold guarantee?
options: The same bank angle throughout the transition onto the beam for both
The same intercept angle onto the beam for both
The best possible beginning of the transition onto the beam for both
questions.explain: The threshold is written to be independent of range, so the turn-on point is right in either case.

questions.question: Why does a further 180° have to be subtracted from the heading error built on the preselected front course
options: Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the back course
Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the front course
Because the deviation bar has already been rotated by 180°
questions.explain: The usable heading error is referenced to the back course, so another 180° comes off.

questions.question: Which common mode is available for the flight director only
options: GO AROUND
TAKE OFF
ILS APPROACH/LAND
questions.explain: The take off mode is listed as a flight director function only.

questions.question: An automatic approach is being flown with the Approach mode engaged — which span of flight phases does it control?
options: From localizer intercept, via flare, until the take off mode is selected
From glide path intercept, via flare, until the end of the missed approach
From localizer intercept, via glide path intercept, until roll out
questions.explain: The mode runs from localizer intercept through glide path intercept to roll out.

questions.question: The Approach/Land mode is engaged at 200 ft AGL and the crew decides to discontinue the approach — which mode can still take over?
options: The heading select mode
The altitude hold mode
The Go Around mode
questions.explain: Go Around can supersede Approach/Land at any height, unlike other upper modes.

questions.question: An automatic landing is being flown and the glide path has just been left — what is held until the flare phase begins?
options: The momentary pitch attitude
The momentary sink rate
The momentary glide slope angle
questions.explain: The sink rate at that moment is frozen until the flare starts.

questions.question: Beam convergence has been left uncompensated on an ILS approach — how does the controller behave at long range and close in?
options: Sluggish far out and unable to hold the beam near the runway
Sluggish far out and prone to oscillation near the runway
Prone to oscillation far out and sluggish near the runway
questions.explain: Low gain far out makes it sluggish, and rising gain close in makes it oscillate.

questions.question: A glide slope deviation appears while an aircraft is in a steady descent — which loops detect it and act on it?
options: The pitch outer loop detects it and the pitch inner loop changes the pitch attitude
The pitch outer loop detects it and the pitch inner loop changes the sink rate
The pitch inner loop detects it and the pitch outer loop changes the sink rate
questions.explain: The outer loop sees the beam error and the inner loop carries out the sink rate change.

questions.question: From where does the preselected course reach the yaw channel as its reference value
options: From the flight management computer
From the inertial reference system
From the autoflight control panel
questions.explain: The crew sets the preselected course on the autoflight control panel and that is the yaw reference.

questions.question: A wind correction angle has been carried down the approach — what does yaw attitude or heading control do during the auto land?
options: It holds the wind correction angle until the nose gear is down
It aligns the longitudinal axis with the runway direction
It aligns the ground track with the runway centre line
questions.explain: The crab is taken out by yawing the aircraft onto the runway direction.

questions.question: Which signal guides the aircraft along the runway centre line after touch-down
options: The radio altitude signal
The glide path deviation signal
The localizer deviation signal
questions.explain: Roll out steering uses the localizer deviation.

questions.question: Which result is achieved by feeding the glide path receivers from the nose gear antennas on a heavy aircraft
options: It gets the same flare window as a smaller aircraft
It gets the same approach speed as a smaller aircraft
It gets a lower flare window than a smaller aircraft
questions.explain: Measuring from the nose gear lifts the aircraft virtually on the beam so the flare window matches a small aircraft's.

questions.question: The flare controller stops rounding the path off at its upper limit - what would happen beyond that limit?
options: The aircraft would risk a tail strike at touch down
The aircraft would risk a long float before touch down
The aircraft would risk a nose gear strike at touch down
questions.explain: Too much nose up at touchdown would put the tail on the runway.

questions.question: The auto-trim is switched off at the same time as the derotation - what would otherwise drive the trim?
options: A constant pitch error caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch rate caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch error caused by the stabilizer's positive moment
questions.explain: The elevator holds a steady nose down moment after derotation, and the standing pitch error that leaves would wake the trim system up.

questions.question: Why is the aircraft headed into the wind during a cross wind approach
options: To prevent a displacement from the localizer beam
To prevent a bank angle on the localizer beam
To prevent a lateral load on the landing gear
questions.explain: Crabbing into the wind stops the aircraft being blown off the beam, so it drifts along it instead.

questions.question: Why can the localizer deviation signal be used for the yaw control during the roll-out
options: The localizer is aligned with the preselected course
The localizer is aligned with the runway centre line
The localizer is aligned with the aircraft track
questions.explain: Because the beam lies along the centre line, a beam deviation is a centre line deviation.

questions.question: The aircraft is being steered along the centre line after landing - which two signals does the yaw controller process?
options: The heading error and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the glide path deviation
The crab angle and the localizer deviation
questions.explain: Both a heading error and a lateral displacement have to be removed, so both signals are used.

questions.question: Which name is given to the transition phase from an approach to a stabilized climb
options: A roll out manoeuvre
A go around manoeuvre
An align manoeuvre
questions.explain: That transition is exactly what is called a go around.

questions.question: A go around is selected on the approach - which three parts of the autoflight system come in together?
options: The pitch channel, the roll channel and the auto-thrust system
The pitch channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
The roll channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
questions.explain: Go around is a common mode and brings pitch, roll and the thrust system in together.

questions.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system and the crew wants a go around - what do they do with the power levers?
options: Push them to the TOGA detent
Pull them back to the idle detent
Press the TOGA switch on them
questions.explain: On an auto-thrust aircraft the levers are pushed into the TOGA detent.

questions.question: The go around controller rotates the aircraft to a fixed positive pitch attitude - what follows from that?
options: Lift increases and the momentary airspeed increases
Drag increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
Lift increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
questions.explain: More attitude means more lift, and more lift arrests the descent.

questions.question: Which angle appears when the airspeed reference is changed while the thrust is held constant
options: A correction angle that changes the present flight path angle
An error angle that changes the present angle of attack
A demand angle that changes the present pitch attitude
questions.explain: The speed error is worked off by a correction angle that tilts the flight path so the aircraft accelerates or decelerates.

cards.question: Which quantity does the vertical speed mode bracket and maintain
options: A pitch attitude value
A flight path bank angle
A climb or descend rate
cards.explain: The mode brackets and holds a vertical speed, which is the same thing as a climb or descend rate.

cards.question: Which system safeguards airspeed control automatically while the vertical speed mode is bracketing a rate
options: The autothrust system
The inertial reference system
The flight management system
cards.explain: The autothrottle/autothrust system is what keeps the airspeed safe while pitch holds the rate.

cards.question: How many control loops make up the cascade used for closed loop control of vertical speed
options: Three
One
Two
cards.explain: The cascade for vertical speed has two loops.

cards.question: Which unit supplies the controlled value used by the vertical speed outer loop?
options: The air data computer
The flight management system
The inertial reference system
cards.explain: Vertical speed is an air data parameter and comes from the air data computer.

cards.question: What decides how many ways there are of selecting the vertical speed mode on a given aircraft
options: The vertical speed value stored
The transition altitude in force
The type of autopilot installed
cards.explain: How many ways there are depends on which autopilot is fitted to the aircraft.

cards.question: Where the vertical speed mode is a basic mode, what alone is needed to maintain the momentary rate of climb
options: A target flight level is dialled up
The autopilot is disengaged
The autopilot is engaged
cards.explain: As a basic mode it needs no separate selection, so engaging the autopilot alone holds the rate the aircraft already has.

cards.question: The autopilot is holding a vertical speed as a basic mode and the crew want a different rate. How is a new reference value introduced?
options: By rotating the vertical speed knob on the control panel
By disengaging and re-engaging the autopilot at the new rate
By pressing the vertical speed button on the control panel
cards.explain: With the mode already running, turning the knob is what changes the reference value, and it may be done at any time.

cards.question: How is the vertical speed mode brought in where it is an upper mode rather than a basic one
options: It is maintained automatically by engaging the autopilot alone
It is armed by the air data computer at take off
It is selected explicitly at the control panel
cards.explain: An upper mode is not automatic, so the crew must select it deliberately on the panel.

cards.question: When may the reference rate be dialled up in the selection sequence for the vertical speed mode as an upper mode
options: Only once the target level is reached
Only before mode activation
Either before or after mode activation
cards.explain: The reference value may be set on either side of mode activation.

cards.question: At what point is the outer control loop closed during vertical speed control
options: When the target level is reached
At mode selection
When the capture point is reached
cards.explain: Selecting the mode is what closes the outer loop for vertical speed control.

cards.question: From where does the outer loop of the rate of climb mode obtain its reference value
options: The flight management computer
The altitude memory
The vertical speed memory
cards.explain: The stored reference for this mode is held in, and supplied from, the vertical speed memory.

cards.question: With what is the commanded rate of climb compared to give the output error of the outer loop in this mode
options: The pitch attitude measured by the inertial reference system
The target flight level set on the autoflight control panel
The actual vertical speed measured by the air data computer
cards.explain: An error is reference minus actual, and the actual rate is the air data computer measurement.

cards.question: What does the vertical speed controller determine and pass on to the inner loop
options: A pitch attitude reference value
A vertical speed reference value
An elevator deflection angle
cards.explain: The outer loop controller sets an attitude reference which the inner loop then follows.

cards.question: On an aircraft where vertical speed is a basic mode, an upper vertical mode is switched off in flight. Which mode does the autopilot then adopt?
options: Altitude acquisition mode
Altitude hold mode
Vertical speed mode
cards.explain: Where vertical speed is the basic mode, switching off any upper vertical mode leaves the autopilot in vertical speed.

cards.question: The vertical speed mode is an upper mode on the aircraft. Which action comes first in the sequence of events to be observed?
options: Pressing the vertical speed button
Selecting the target flight level
Arming the altitude acquisition mode
cards.explain: The printed sequence begins with selection of the wanted target flight level, before the mode is activated.

cards.question: What is synchronisation of the vertical speed reference value intended to prevent
options: A loss of the air data computer rate signal in flight
A reference value being changed after mode activation
Controller activity at the moment of mode activation
cards.explain: A stored value unlike the actual rate would make the controller act the instant the mode came in, and synchronisation removes that step.

cards.question: In the vertical speed mode the pitch attitude is altered. Why does the actual rate of climb then change?
options: Because the flight path angle changes at constant airspeed
Because the air data computer re-corrects its altitude output
Because the trim integrator alters the stabiliser setting
cards.explain: With speed held, a change of attitude becomes a change of flight path angle and therefore of rate of climb or descent.

cards.question: Through which intermediate quantity does a pitch attitude change act on the rate of climb
options: Roll attitude
Flight path angle
Altitude error
cards.explain: Attitude acts on the flight path angle first, and the rate of climb follows from that.

cards.question: To what value is the vertical speed reference set when the level off mode is selected
options: The momentary vertical speed
Zero
The last value held in memory
cards.explain: Levelling off means commanding no rate at all, so the reference becomes zero.

cards.question: What does the mode annunciation read while the level off mode is in use
options: V/S = 0
ALT
LVL CHG
cards.explain: The level off condition is annunciated as a commanded vertical speed of zero.

cards.question: An altitude has just been pre-selected at the autoflight control panel. What does the autoflight system annunciate?
options: ALT ACQ active
ALT active
ALT ACQ armed
cards.explain: Pre-selection arms the mode, so the armed annunciation appears first.

cards.question: The level off mode has just been selected during a climb. What does the vertical speed controller do?
options: It reduces the actual rate by half and then holds it
It holds the altitude reached when the mode was selected
It reduces the actual rate to zero and holds zero
cards.explain: The same controller drives the rate down to nothing and then keeps it there.

cards.question: What is true of the provisions protecting against violation of airspeed and Mach limits
options: They are identical in every modern autoflight system
They apply only to the vertical speed mode
They differ a lot between aircraft types
cards.explain: The provisions vary so much from one type to another that no single description covers them all.

cards.question: While a commanded climb rate is being held, over what does the task of the pitch channel take precedence
options: Speed controlled by the autothrust system
Track controlled by the roll channel
Altitude controlled by the altitude memory
cards.explain: The pitch channel holds the rate first, which is exactly why the speed can drift to a limit.

cards.question: Into what does the altitude acquisition mode transfer an aircraft out of a climb or descend
options: A pilot selected capture altitude or transition level
A pilot selected vertical speed or flight path angle
A pilot selected QNH-altitude or pressure altitude
cards.explain: The target is an altitude the pilot has set, read either against QNH or as a pressure altitude.

cards.question: When is the capture detector of the altitude acquisition mode activated
options: Only when the aircraft reaches the capture point
When an altitude is pre-selected on the panel
Only when the altitude hold mode becomes active
cards.explain: Dialling the altitude is enough to start the detector running, long before any capture.

cards.question: Together with the actual rate of climb, what else enters the continuous calculation of the capture point
options: The momentary airspeed error against the speed limit
The barometric correction applied by the air data computer
The momentary vertical distance to the selected altitude
cards.explain: The two quantities entering the calculation are the rate of closure and the height still to go.

cards.question: In which case is the altitude representing the capture point baro-corrected
options: When it is at or below the transition altitude
When it is at or above the selected flight level
When it is anywhere above the transition altitude
cards.explain: Below the transition altitude altitudes are flown on QNH, so the baro correction is applied.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the calculated capture point in a descent. What does the mode logic do?
options: It makes the altitude hold mode active instead
It makes the altitude acquisition mode active
It arms the altitude acquisition mode
cards.explain: Reaching the point is the capture condition, so the mode goes from armed to active.

cards.question: At what point is the outer control loop closed in the altitude acquisition mode
options: When the capture condition is met
When the tolerance band is reached
When an altitude is pre-selected
cards.explain: Arming only starts the detector, and the loop is not closed until the capture condition is met.
