cards.question: To what does the vertical speed reference value correspond in the altitude acquisition outer loop
options: The altitude error
The selected altitude
The measured vertical speed
cards.explain: Height still to go is converted directly into a commanded rate, which is why the rate falls as the gap closes.

cards.question: With what is the pre-selected altitude compared in S3 to form the altitude error
options: The aircraft's actual vertical speed
The aircraft's actual altitude
The baro-corrected capture altitude
cards.explain: An altitude error can only be the difference between the target altitude and the one being flown.

cards.question: What does the vertical speed controller determine from the vertical speed error during an altitude acquisition?
options: The pitch reference value for the pitch inner loop
The thrust rating for the autothrust system
The altitude reference value for the altitude memory
cards.explain: The outer loop output is always an attitude reference handed to the inner loop.

cards.question: Explain why selecting the level off mode needs no control loop of its own?
options: The altitude controller is used with a reference of zero
The autothrust system is used with a reference of zero
The vertical speed controller is used with a reference of zero
cards.explain: Level off changes nothing but the reference value: the same vertical speed controller works, now to a reference of zero.

cards.question: An aircraft climbing in vertical speed mode with a very high commanded rate reaches its lower speed limit. What happens to the pitch channel?
options: It switches over from vertical speed to airspeed/Mach control
It hands pitch control over to the autothrust system
It reduces the commanded vertical speed to zero and levels off
cards.explain: Envelope protection takes the rate target away from the pitch channel and gives it the speed target instead.

cards.question: The pitch channel has just reverted to speed control during a climb. What does the autothrust system do at the same moment?
options: It changes from thrust mode to speed mode and holds the commanded airspeed
It remains in speed mode and raises the commanded airspeed
It changes from speed mode to thrust mode and sets a thrust limit
cards.explain: The two channels swap jobs, so the autothrust gives up speed and goes to a fixed thrust rating.

cards.question: To which mode does the combination of pitch speed control and autothrust thrust control after a reversion correspond
options: Level change mode
Altitude hold mode
Altitude acquisition mode
cards.explain: Pitch flying the speed with a fixed thrust rating is what defines level change.

cards.question: After a reversion during a climb, by which pitch movement is the commanded reference speed reached again?
options: Pitch up
Pitch hold
Pitch down
cards.explain: The aircraft was slow, so lowering the nose trades height for the speed it needs.

cards.question: A descent is flown with a very high negative vertical speed command and the aircraft approaches its upper speed limit. What does the autoflight system do?
options: It reverts from vertical speed control to airspeed control
It reduces the commanded vertical speed until the limit clears
It transfers airspeed control to the pitch channel integrator
cards.explain: The same envelope protection works at the top of the range as at the bottom, so vertical speed gives way to speed.

cards.question: To what does the rating taken up after a reversion in the descent correspond
options: The thrust required for the commanded vertical speed
The minimum thrust previously set in vertical speed mode
The maximum thrust previously set in vertical speed mode
cards.explain: The rating taken up on reversion in a descent is the minimum thrust the autothrust had set in vertical speed mode, while trying not to exceed the upper speed limit.

cards.question: After a reversion during a descent, by which pitch movement is the commanded reference speed reached?
options: Pitch down
Pitch up
Pitch hold
cards.explain: The aircraft was fast, so raising the nose brings the speed back down to the target.

cards.question: An excessive vertical speed causes an automatic reversion to level change. What is retained and what is given up?
options: The speed target is retained and the flight path is modified
The flight path is retained and the speed target is modified
A new speed target is set and the flight path is retained
cards.explain: Envelope protection keeps the speed and lets the profile change, which is the whole point of the reversion.

cards.question: An aircraft is levelling off in altitude acquisition mode above the transition level. Which reference is the selected target expressed against?
options: A radio height above ground
A pressure altitude
A QNH corrected altitude
cards.explain: Above the transition level flight levels are flown on standard setting, so the target is a pressure altitude.

cards.question: Why is the capture point determined as a function of vertical speed rather than at a fixed distance?
options: So the autothrust system can hold a constant airspeed during the capture
So the altitude is reached without oscillating about it afterwards
So the capture point can always be baro-corrected by the air data computer
cards.explain: A high rate needs an earlier start, and scaling the point with rate is what stops the aircraft overshooting and hunting.

cards.question: Two aircraft level off at the same altitude but close on it at different vertical speeds. Which one starts its capture further out?
options: The one with the lower vertical speed
The one with the higher vertical speed
The one with the higher airspeed
cards.explain: Capture distance grows with vertical speed, so the faster approach needs the earlier start.

cards.question: A capture point is calculated above the transition altitude. What represents it, and why?
options: A radio height, because the air data computer cannot correct there
A pressure altitude, because no baro-correction is applied there
A QNH-altitude, because baro-correction is always applied above it
cards.explain: With no correction applied the value stays a pressure altitude.

cards.question: As an aircraft in altitude acquisition gets closer and closer to the pre-selected altitude, what happens to its rate?
options: It is held constant until the tolerance band
It becomes steadily greater
It becomes steadily less
cards.explain: The rate is held in proportion to the distance left, so as the distance shrinks the rate shrinks with it.

cards.question: In what time does the e-function representing the acquisition transition theoretically reach the final altitude
options: Infinite time
The time to the capture point
The time to the tolerance band
cards.explain: An exponential approach never quite arrives, which is exactly why a tolerance band has to be defined.

cards.question: The aircraft has just entered the tolerance band at the end of an altitude acquisition. Which mode becomes active and what is annunciated?
options: Vertical speed, annunciated V/S = 0
Altitude hold, annunciated ALT
Altitude acquisition, annunciated ALT ACQ
cards.explain: Acquisition hands over to hold at the edge of the band and the annunciation changes with it.

cards.question: On what condition does the comparator of the capture detector declare the altitude acquisition active
options: Distance to go equals the calculated capture distance
Distance to go exceeds the calculated capture distance
Distance to go equals the width of the tolerance band
cards.explain: Capture happens where the remaining distance has shrunk to the distance the detector has calculated.

cards.question: An aircraft is climbing in level change to a pre-selected flight level. Which mode is armed at that point?
options: Speed and Mach control
Altitude hold mode
Altitude acquisition
cards.explain: The acquisition is waiting for its capture condition, so it sits armed while the climb mode is active.

cards.question: During an altitude acquisition the autothrust holds a constant airspeed in speed mode. What is the effect of a pitch attitude change?
options: The flight path angle changes, which modifies vertical speed
The airspeed changes, which in turn modifies vertical speed
The altitude error changes, which in turn modifies pitch attitude
cards.explain: With speed pinned by the autothrust, attitude translates straight into flight path angle and so into rate.

cards.question: In which phases of a flight can the flight management system guide the aircraft in this mode?
options: Cruise, descend and landing
Take off, climb and cruise
Climb, cruise and descend
cards.explain: The three named phases are climb, cruise and descend.

cards.question: At what deviation from the FM-altitude is profile or VNAV altitude hold entered automatically
options: 20 ft
100 ft
50 ft
cards.explain: The printed figure for this transit is fifty feet.

cards.question: What does the ALT mode of the pitch channel maintain
options: A pre-selected pitch attitude or trim setting
A pre-selected rate or flight path angle
A pre-selected altitude or flight level
cards.explain: The mode is named for what it holds, which is the altitude or flight level already selected.

cards.question: What deviation from the pre-selected altitude do modern control laws permit
options: 50 ft
100 ft
40 ft
cards.explain: The printed allowance in the soft altitude mode is a hundred feet either side.

cards.question: With which system does the profile or vertical navigation mode connect the autoflight system
options: The flight management system
The air data computer
The inertial reference system
cards.explain: Vertical navigation is flown on data the flight management system supplies, so the two are coupled.

cards.question: Over what span of a flight do the sequential segments of profile or vertical navigation guidance run
options: From the top of climb to the top of descent
From after take off to the instrument approach
From the capture point to the transition altitude
cards.explain: The sequential segments are stated as running from just after take off through to the approach.

cards.question: How does the pilot give clearance for a flight level change demanded by the flight management system
options: By entering the new flight level into the flight management system
By pressing the profile button at the autoflight control panel
By selecting an appropriate altitude on the control panel
cards.explain: The altitude selector on the panel is the place where the crew confirm the clearance to the system.

cards.question: An aircraft in profile mode approaches the FM-altitude within fifty feet. What happens?
options: The system automatically arms altitude acquisition
The system automatically transits to altitude hold
The system automatically reverts to vertical speed
cards.explain: Fifty feet of deviation is the printed trigger for the automatic change into hold.

cards.question: In which mode does the autothrust system work while the altitude hold mode is active
options: Thrust mode
Speed mode
Idle mode
cards.explain: With the pitch channel holding height, the autothrust takes the speed and works to a speed target.

cards.question: The altitude hold button is pressed while the aircraft is climbing. Which altitude does the system then maintain?
options: The altitude momentarily reached
The altitude at which the climb began
The pre-selected altitude on the panel
cards.explain: A manual selection freezes whatever altitude the aircraft has at that instant.

cards.question: Under what condition does the altitude hold mode come in automatically?
options: On passing the transition altitude during a climb or descent
On approaching a pre-selected altitude with acquisition armed
On approaching a pre-selected altitude with acquisition active
cards.explain: The acquisition must already be running, not merely armed, for the hold to follow automatically.

cards.question: Why is the soft altitude mode not explicitly annunciated
options: It is an armed mode only and never an active one
It is subordinate to the altitude hold mode
It is a function of the altitude memory alone
cards.explain: It works underneath altitude hold rather than beside it, so it gets no annunciation of its own.

cards.question: Below what size of airspeed disturbance is the soft altitude deviation permitted
options: 10 Kts
4 Kts
5 Kts
cards.explain: The allowance applies only to disturbances below four knots.

cards.question: Why must the autoflight system have a pilot input before it starts a climb that the flight management system has requested?
options: To prevent the flight management system losing its reference
To prevent altitude changes being made without ATC-clearance
To prevent the autothrust system reverting to thrust mode
cards.explain: The pilot input stands in for the clearance, so the aircraft never changes level on its own.

cards.question: Where must both the panel selection and the FM-altitude lie before a climb to an FM-altitude is cleared
options: Above the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Exactly at the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Below the momentary altitude of the aircraft
cards.explain: Both targets have to lie above the aircraft before a climb can be cleared.

cards.question: How must the FM-altitude stand against the panel selection for a climb to be cleared
options: Exactly equal to it
Equal to or above it
Equal to or below it
cards.explain: In a climb the panel selection is the ceiling the crew have cleared, so the flight management target may not sit above it.

cards.question: Where must both the panel selection and the FM-altitude lie before a descent to an FM-altitude is cleared
options: Below the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Above the momentary altitude of the aircraft
Exactly at the momentary altitude of the aircraft
cards.explain: Both targets have to lie below the aircraft before a descent can be cleared.

cards.question: A descent to an FM-altitude is to be cleared. How must the FM-altitude stand against the panel selection?
options: Equal to or below it
Equal to or above it
Exactly equal to it
cards.explain: In a descent the panel selection is the floor the crew have cleared, so the flight management target may not sit below it.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs in profile mode with the panel selection above the level the flight management system is aiming for. Where does it level off?
options: At the FMS target level
At the selected flight level
Midway between the two levels
cards.explain: In a climb the aircraft stops at whichever of the two lies lower, which here is the flight management target.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs in profile mode with the panel altitude below the FMS target level. Where does it level off?
options: It continues the climb unrestricted
At the flight management target level
At the selected flight level
cards.explain: The crew input acts as the cleared ceiling, so the aircraft stops there.

cards.question: An aircraft descends in profile mode with the panel altitude above the FMS target level. Where does it level off?
options: At the transition level
At the selected flight level
At the flight management target level
cards.explain: In a descent the aircraft stops at whichever of the two lies higher, which here is the crew input.

cards.question: The altitude hold button is pressed during a descent. Why does the aircraft then have to acquire that altitude again?
options: Because the autothrust reverts to thrust mode and sets flight idle
Because the altitude memory is only synchronised once the button is released
Because it undershoots that altitude while still descending
cards.explain: The altitude is frozen while the aircraft is still going down, so it undershoots and then has to acquire that altitude again.

cards.question: In which condition is manual activation of the altitude hold mode mainly used
options: When the aircraft is in the capture phase
When the aircraft is already in level flight
When the aircraft is approaching a pre-selected altitude
cards.explain: If there is no rate to arrest there is nothing to overshoot, so the manual selection is clean.

cards.question: What is traded for what when the soft altitude mode lets the aircraft wander within its band?
options: Potential energy as altitude against kinetic energy as airspeed
Kinetic energy as thrust against potential energy as airspeed
Potential energy as airspeed against kinetic energy as altitude
cards.explain: Height is the potential energy and speed the kinetic energy, and the band lets one be swapped for the other.

cards.question: What is the immediate benefit of the energy trade allowed in the soft altitude mode
options: Fewer corrections of the altitude reference in memory
Fewer transient oscillations about the altitude
Fewer changes of engine thrust for airspeed control
cards.explain: Letting the altitude move absorbs the speed disturbance so the engines do not have to.

cards.question: Minimising thrust changes in the soft altitude mode smoothes thrust control. What two results does this bring?
options: Reduced fuel consumption and increased passenger comfort
Reduced engine wear and increased thrust response rate
Reduced altitude deviation and increased airspeed stability
cards.explain: The two stated results of the smoother thrust are less fuel burned and a smoother ride.

cards.question: The altitude hold mode is not yet active. What is the altitude memory doing?
options: It is updated permanently with the pre-selected altitude from the panel
It is updated permanently with the current air data altitude
It is holding the last altitude at which the mode was active
cards.explain: Continuous updating keeps the stored reference equal to the actual altitude so there is no step at engagement.

cards.question: After the flight path angle has changed in altitude hold, what is the order of the remaining effects
options: Thrust changes and then altitude changes
Altitude changes and then vertical speed changes
Vertical speed changes and then altitude changes
cards.explain: Rate comes before height, because altitude only moves once a rate exists.

cards.question: Why does the altitude hold loop need no intermediate rate command, unlike the altitude acquisition cascade?
options: Because its vertical speed is supplied by the autothrust system
Because its own controller sets the attitude reference directly
Because its reference value is not stored in any memory at all
cards.explain: Holding needs no rate step because the altitude controller produces the attitude reference itself.

cards.question: What relation do the several operating modes covered by the generic vertical navigation term bear to one another
options: They have separate annunciations
They have identical meaning
They have opposing control laws
cards.explain: The listed names are different labels for the same thing.

cards.question: Which mode has the same meaning as vertical navigation?
options: Altitude acquisition
Level off
Profile
cards.explain: Profile is one of the names printed for the same mode as vertical navigation; altitude acquisition and level off are separate pitch modes.

cards.question: Which phase follows the arm phase of the horizontal navigation mode
options: The active phase
The on course phase
The over station phase
cards.explain: This mode is printed as an arm phase followed by an active phase; on course and over station belong to the VOR mode.

cards.question: Above which radio height can the autopilot and flight director be coupled with the flight management system
options: 50 ft
100 ft
30 ft
cards.explain: The printed minimum radio height for coupling is thirty feet.

cards.question: How is a VOR radial described
options: A fixed line of position
A variable line of position
A fixed line of equal altitude
cards.explain: The radial is a line of position fixed in space relative to the station.

cards.question: How many sub-modes does the VOR controller have to distinguish
options: Four
Two
Three
cards.explain: Capture, on course and over station make three.

cards.question: The VOR mode has just been selected but the angular deviation limit has not yet been passed. What does the flight mode annunciator show?
options: VOR mode active
VOR capture phase
VOR mode armed
cards.explain: Until the limit is passed the mode is only waiting, so it reads armed.

cards.question: Which pair of values does the roll controller use as the criterion for transiting to the On-Course Phase
options: VOR deviation 5° and heading error 15°
VOR deviation 2° and heading error 10°
VOR deviation 15° and heading error 5°
cards.explain: The printed criterion is a VOR deviation of 5° or less together with a heading error of 15° or less.

cards.question: A steady heading error is sitting at the input of the washout — roughly which time constant governs how quickly it decays?
options: 200 sec
10 sec
100 sec
cards.explain: The printed figure for the washout time constant is approximately 100 sec.

cards.question: Which criterion is used to recognise the cone of confusion
options: A deviation signal change of more than 8 mV/sec or more than 0,2°/sec
A deviation signal change of more than 5 mV/sec or more than 0,8°/sec
A deviation signal change of more than 8 mV/sec or more than 0,5°/sec
cards.explain: Those are the two printed rates that define the cone of confusion.

cards.question: Which four sub-modes does managed level-change comprise
options: Climb, altitude hold, altitude constraint, descent
Climb, altitude acquisition, level off and descent
Climb, cruise, instrument approach and descent
cards.explain: Climb, altitude hold, altitude constraint and descent are the four sub-modes of managed level-change.

cards.question: Which two systems are coupled with the flight management system in all the vertical navigation modes
options: The air data computer and the inertial reference system
The roll channel of the autopilot and the yaw damper
The autopilot/director and the autothrust system
cards.explain: Both the guidance and the thrust systems have to be tied to the flight management system for automatic vertical guidance.

cards.question: In the vertical navigation modes, which channel performs the vertical guidance?
options: The roll channel
The pitch channel
The autothrust channel
cards.explain: Vertical guidance is a pitch task and thrust control is left to the autothrust.

cards.question: Which unit determines the speed and Mach reference values in the vertical navigation modes
options: The flight management system
The autothrust control system
The central air data computer
cards.explain: The targets come from the flight management system, which is what makes the guidance managed.

cards.question: Where the autothrust system is working in thrust mode, what decides the source of the thrust ratings it uses?
options: The type of aircraft
The selected altitude
The momentary vertical speed
cards.explain: The source of the ratings varies from one aircraft type to another.

cards.question: From the drift between the wanted on-track point and what else does the pilot work out a wind correction angle
options: The actual position
The desired track angle
The selected course
cards.explain: Drift is measured between where the aircraft should be and where it actually is.

cards.question: The capture phase of the navigation mode has just been entered. What is annunciated?
options: Heading select active
NAV active
NAV armed
cards.explain: Entering the capture phase makes the mode active, and the annunciation says so.

cards.question: Which unit directs the autoflight system to intercept and follow the track once the mode is active
options: The inertial navigation system
The capture detector
The flight management system
cards.explain: The flight management system holds the flight plan, so it is what directs the interception.

cards.question: With the help of which autopilot channel does the VOR mode intercept and follow a radial
options: The roll channel
The pitch channel
The yaw channel
cards.explain: A radial is a lateral path, so the roll channel flies it.

cards.question: Besides selecting an appropriate receiver frequency, what else is required before the VOR mode can be activated?
options: The intercept angle must be determined by selecting a track
The radial must be determined by selecting a heading
The radial must be determined by selecting a course
cards.explain: The radial is told to the system as a course set on the pre-selected course knob.

cards.question: In which order do the three VOR sub-modes follow the flight phase sequence
options: Arm, capture and over station
Capture, over station and on course
Capture, on course and over station
cards.explain: The aircraft joins the radial, tracks it, and only then passes the station.

cards.question: What is the capture phase of the VOR mode there to achieve?
options: Guidance of the aircraft along the radial with cross wind correction
Guidance of the aircraft through the area where the deviation is useless
Transfer from an intercept heading onto the radial without oscillations
cards.explain: Capture is the joining manoeuvre, and it must settle the aircraft on the radial cleanly.

cards.question: Besides guiding the aircraft on the radial from or to the station, what does the on course phase do
options: It corrects any deviation rate above the threshold
It corrects the pre-selected course for station passage
It corrects any cross wind disturbances
cards.explain: Tracking a radial means holding it against the wind, which is what this phase does.

cards.question: At approximately what angular deviation is the transfer to the pre-selected course said to start
options: 5 degrees
2 degrees
10 degrees
cards.explain: The printed figure for the early start is about two degrees of angular deviation.

cards.question: Which unit is activated first on selection of the VOR mode to measure angular deviation from the pre- selected course
options: The capture detector
The lateral beam sensor
The course comparator
cards.explain: The lateral beam sensor is the device that watches the angular deviation while the mode is armed.

cards.question: What becomes the controlled value of the third loop that augments heading control during the capture phase
options: The actual aircraft heading
The pre-selected course value
The actual VOR-radial
cards.explain: The outermost loop added at capture controls the radial the aircraft is actually on.

cards.question: With what is the pre-selected course compared to obtain the deviation used by the outermost VOR loop
options: The actual radial at the aircraft's position
The actual roll attitude from the gyros
The actual heading from the compass system
cards.explain: Deviation is the difference between the course wanted and the radial the aircraft is actually on.

cards.question: Why does the roll controller change over to the On-Course Phase once the preselected radial is almost reached
options: To hand the lateral guidance over to the heading hold controller
To increase the rate at which the heading error is reduced
To improve its behaviour with respect to cross wind disturbances
cards.explain: Cross wind disturbance behaviour is what the change of phase improves.

cards.question: An aircraft tracking a VOR radial meets a permanent cross wind component — what does comparing the VOR deviation with the heading error in S3 then produce?
options: A permanent loss of the VOR deviation signal
A permanent Stand-Off from the radial
A permanent oscillation about the radial
cards.explain: A standing cross wind leaves a residual difference in S3, and that residual is the permanent Stand-Off.

cards.question: Which heading error does the controller have to leave standing while an aircraft tracks a radial in a steady crosswind
options: The one equivalent to the wind correction angle
The one equivalent to the preselected course
The one equivalent to the VOR course deviation angle
cards.explain: The crab angle must be kept, so the heading error equal to the wind correction angle is left alone.

cards.question: An aircraft is established on a pre-selected radial in a steady crosswind — how does it travel along that radial?
options: Wings level, with the heading error equal to the wind correction angle
In small banked corrections, with the heading error slowly decaying
Wings level, with the heading error equal to the VOR deviation angle rate
cards.explain: Once the washout has settled the crab is held and no roll command remains, so the aircraft drifts wings level.

cards.question: An aircraft is passing the cone of confusion overhead a VOR — for how long after leaving that area does the deviation signal stay switched off?
options: A further 10 seconds
A further 20 seconds
A further 100 seconds
cards.explain: The printed period is the cone of confusion plus a further 20 seconds.

cards.question: What determines the operating mode of the autothrust system in the vertical navigation modes
options: The pitch channel
The roll channel
The air data computer
cards.explain: The pitch channel takes the lead and the autothrust mode follows from what pitch is doing.

cards.question: A waypoint has to be passed at a given altitude with a given airspeed maintained during a climb. What does the flight management computer calculate?
options: An optimum flight path angle for the required thrust
An optimum thrust for the required flight path angle
An optimum vertical speed for the required altitude
cards.explain: The constraint fixes the path to be flown, so what the computer works out is the thrust that path needs.

cards.question: By selecting what does the flight management system determine the control loops for the different flight phases
options: Appropriate reference altitudes for the altitude memory
Appropriate thrust ratings for the autothrust system
Appropriate pitch channel modes of the autopilot
cards.explain: The flight management system works by picking pitch channel modes, and those modes define the loops.

cards.question: A climb demanded by the flight management system will only be carried out by the autoflight system under which condition?
options: The pilot arms the vertical navigation mode on the panel
The pilot selects an appropriate altitude on the panel
The system confirms the altitude constraint is active
cards.explain: The crew altitude selection is the clearance the system insists on before it changes level.

cards.question: A fixed inertial flight path is being flown in heading select mode. Why must the heading reference be corrected from time to time?
options: Because the required value depends on the prevailing wind
Because the roll channel loses its attitude reference in a turn
Because the compass system drifts away from magnetic north
cards.explain: A heading only produces the wanted track for one particular wind, so it has to be reset as the wind changes.

cards.question: Besides an inertial system or a flight management system with position sensors, what third source makes automatic lateral guidance possible
options: A compass system with a heading hold function
A radio navigation system with track capability
An air data computer with altitude correction
cards.explain: The third option listed is a radio aid that defines a track, such as a radial or a localizer.

cards.question: An active flight plan was entered into the flight management system during cockpit preparation. How will the autopilot couple to it?
options: Only once the capture phase begins
Manually only, after take off
Automatically
cards.explain: An active flight plan already loaded before departure gives automatic coupling.

cards.question: Apart from pressing the button again, how is the navigation mode terminated?
options: Automatically, as soon as another vertical mode is selected
Automatically, as soon as the cross-track distance grows again
Automatically, as soon as another lateral mode is selected
cards.explain: Two lateral modes cannot run together, so selecting another one ends this one.

cards.question: How is a heading change actually brought about in the navigation mode?
options: By track error values fed to the roll channel inner loop
By heading reference values fed to the roll channel outer loop
By roll attitude reference values fed to the roll inner loop
cards.explain: The aircraft is turned by banking it, so the command reaching the inner loop is a roll attitude.

cards.question: Why does the VOR mode need a separate over station phase?
options: Because the deviation signal is useless in the cone of confusion
Because the pre-selected course must be reversed as the station is passed
Because the receiver frequency must be re-tuned as the station is passed
cards.explain: With no usable deviation overhead, the controller cannot keep steering on it and needs another rule.

cards.question: The radial deviation rate rises above eight millivolts per second. What does the roll controller do?
options: It transits to heading control and maintains the present heading
It transits to heading control and reverses the pre-selected course
It transits to capture control and re-intercepts the radial
cards.explain: A fast moving deviation signals the cone of confusion, so the controller freezes the heading and flies on.

cards.question: Why does the transfer onto the pre-selected course have to start early rather than at the course itself?
options: So the bracketing is soft and free of oscillations
So the flight mode annunciator can indicate the mode armed
So the lateral beam sensor has time to measure the deviation
cards.explain: Turning early gives room for a gentle turn that settles on the course instead of swinging through it.

cards.question: The aircraft passes the two degree angular deviation limit on its way to the radial. What does the lateral beam sensor do?
options: It switches the roll controller into the capture phase
It switches the roll controller into heading control
It switches the roll controller into the on course phase
cards.explain: The sensor passing its limit is the capture trigger, and it works through the operating mode logic.

cards.question: A signal used by the VOR mode becomes invalid in flight. What actually happens, given the permanent monitoring of signal validity?
options: The VOR mode is terminated
The VOR mode reverts to the capture phase
The VOR mode holds its last roll reference value
cards.explain: Monitoring drops the mode rather than letting it fly on a missing signal.

cards.question: A washout has been added to the navigation loop and the aircraft is tracking a radial in a steady crosswind — what is the relationship between the aircraft heading and the PSC?
options: The heading differs from the PSC by the measured VOR deviation angle
The heading is aligned with the PSC and the track is offset
The heading differs from the PSC by the wind correction angle
cards.explain: With the washout fitted the radial is tracked, so the crab is carried as a heading difference from the PSC.

cards.question: How does the washout let the VOR deviation prevail over the heading error on the long run
options: Both signals are compared but the heading error is given a lower gain
Only changes of VOR deviation are still compared with the heading error
Only changes of heading error are still compared with the VOR deviation
cards.explain: The washout passes only the changing part of the heading error, so the steady deviation signal dominates.

cards.question: The VOR deviation signal has been switched off and the heading error signal connected to S3 during the Over Station Phase — how does the controller then behave?
options: The navigation loop is off and it acts as a heading controller only
The navigation loop is off and it acts as a roll rate controller only
The heading loop is off and it acts as a navigation controller only
cards.explain: With the deviation signal gone and the washout bypassed, only the heading loop remains in use.

cards.question: Which kind of approach does the localizer mode support when it is used as an independent auto flight mode
options: A Non-Precision Approach
A fully automatic landing
A Precision Approach
cards.explain: Used on its own the localizer mode gives lateral guidance only, which is a Non-Precision Approach.

cards.question: Which flight mode annunciation belongs to the localizer Capture Phase
options: LOC (ACTIVE)
LOC (ARM)
LOC (TRACK)
cards.explain: The Capture Phase is annunciated as LOC (ARM).

cards.question: Which other name is given to the back beam of a localizer
options: The reciprocal localizer
The back course
The back radial
cards.explain: Back course is the alternative name for the back beam.

cards.question: Which two forms of guidance can the back beam mode provide
options: Autopilot guidance or radar vectoring
Flight director guidance or autopilot guidance
Flight director guidance or auto-thrust guidance
cards.explain: The mode works for either the flight director or the autopilot.

cards.question: A back beam approach is being set up on the HSI — by how much must the deviation scale and the deviation bar be rotated?
cards.explain: The printed rotation for a correct back beam indication is 180°.

cards.question: How many radials does a VOR provide compared with the number of beams a localizer transmitter generates
options: 360 radials against one beam
180 radials against one beam
36 radials against one beam
cards.explain: The page prints 360 radials for the VOR against a single localizer beam from the localizer transmitter.

cards.question: A crew selects Approach/Land on the autoflight control panel — what happens to the localizer mode?
options: It is inhibited until the glide path is captured
It is activated automatically as a submode
It must still be armed separately by its own key
cards.explain: As a submode of Approach/Land it comes up with that selection and needs no separate key.

cards.question: The lateral annunciation changes from armed to active — which phase has just begun?
options: The Capture Phase
The Loc-Track Phase
The Approach-Track Phase
cards.explain: That annunciation change marks the beginning of the Loc-Track Phase.

cards.question: What are angular deviations converted into during the Approach-Track Phase, and why
options: Into lateral distances, to counteract the beam convergence effect
Into lateral distances, to counteract the funnel effect
Into roll rate commands, to counteract the funnel effect
cards.explain: They become lateral distances, which is what counteracts the funnel effect.

cards.question: From which two quantities does the Capture Detector calculate the Capture Point
options: The heading error and the LOC deviation angle
The heading error and the LOC deviation rate
The roll attitude and the LOC deviation rate
cards.explain: Heading error and rate of change of localizer deviation are the two printed inputs.

cards.question: Why is the capture threshold of the localizer mode called adaptive
options: Because the capture point location depends particularly on the radio altitude
Because the capture point is reset each time the deviation changes sign
Because the capture point location depends particularly on the deviation rate
cards.explain: The threshold moves with the closure rate, which is why it is called adaptive.

cards.question: Which property of the aircraft are the Approach-Track control laws written to exploit
options: Its longitudinal stability
Its weather cock stability
Its spiral stability
cards.explain: Weather cock stability is the printed property relied on near the ground.

cards.question: Why does the back beam mode count as a Non-Precision Approach
options: Because no lateral guidance is available in this mode
Because the deviation signal polarity is inverted in this mode
Because no vertical guidance is available in this mode
cards.explain: Only lateral guidance exists on the back beam, so the approach is non-precision.

cards.question: A crew is setting up for a localizer back beam approach — which course must be set as the pre- selected course?
options: The runway heading plus 90°
The front course
The back course
cards.explain: The front course, not the back course, is what the system expects at the PSC.

cards.question: The deviation bar on the HSI has to read correctly during a back beam approach — how is the required 180° rotation obtained?
options: By setting the back course as the pre-selected course
By inverting the heading signal from the compass system
By setting the front course as the pre-selected course
cards.explain: Selecting the front course at the PSC rotates the scale and bar by 180°.

cards.question: What happens to the polarity of the localizer deviation signal on the back beam
options: It is inverted and the inversion has to be undone in the navigation loop
It is unchanged and the heading error is inverted instead
It is inverted and the inversion is left in place for the navigation loop
cards.explain: The mirror image situation inverts the signal, and the controller has to reverse that inversion.

cards.question: Which inverter reverses the localizer deviation signal for a back beam approach
options: Inverter 2
The rate taker
Inverter 1
cards.explain: The deviation signal is reversed by Inverter 2, while Inverter 1 works on the heading error.

cards.question: Which two signals are added to form the roll attitude reference value in the heading loop
options: The localizer deviation and the roll rate
The heading error and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the roll attitude error
cards.explain: The reference roll attitude comes from the sum of heading error and localizer deviation formed in S2.

cards.question: The localizer mode has been selected on its own on the autoflight control panel as an independent lateral mode — which phase is left out?
options: The Capture Phase
The Approach-Track Phase
The Localizer-Track Phase
cards.explain: Selecting LOC as an independent lateral mode omits the Approach-Track Phase.

cards.question: Two aircraft intercept the same localizer from very different distances to the transmitter antenna — what does the adaptive capture threshold guarantee?
options: The best possible beginning of the transition onto the beam for both
The same intercept angle onto the beam for both
The same bank angle throughout the transition onto the beam for both
cards.explain: The threshold is written to be independent of range, so the turn-on point is right in either case.

cards.question: The localizer deviation signal has just fallen to 60 mV during an intercept — what is now fed into the outer control loop?
options: The PSC error, through a wash out
The PSC error, directly without a wash out
The localizer deviation rate, through a wash out
cards.explain: Reaching that beam value starts the Loc-Track Phase, in which the PSC error enters through the wash out.

cards.question: The aircraft is in the Approach-Track Phase and a gust pushes the heading off — under what condition will the roll controller still act?
options: If the gust changes the bank angle or displaces it from the beam
If the gust changes the sink rate or displaces it from the beam
If the gust changes the bank angle or the heading error exceeds 0,5°
cards.explain: Only upsets that move the bank angle or move the aircraft off the beam are corrected.

cards.question: Why does a further 180° have to be subtracted from the heading error built on the preselected front course
options: Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the back course
Because the actual heading error has to be taken from the front course
Because the deviation bar has already been rotated by 180°
cards.explain: The usable heading error is referenced to the back course, so another 180° comes off.

cards.question: What is the inversion applied to the heading error of a back beam approach equivalent to
options: Addition of 180° to the heading error obtained at S2
Subtraction of 180° from the heading error obtained at S1
Subtraction of 180° from the localizer deviation obtained at S1
cards.explain: Inverter 1 reverses the sign, which amounts to taking 180° off the S1 heading error.

cards.question: The pilot is flying the back beam manually on the flight director and keeps the roll bar centred — what is the result?
options: There is no localizer deviation and the roll bar stays centred
There is no heading error and the back beam is tracked
There is no roll attitude error and the back beam is tracked
cards.explain: Centring the bar removes the roll attitude error, which is what the flight director displays.

cards.question: How does the sequence of effects of the flight director differ from that of the autopilot on a back beam approach
options: The pilot is directly involved as part of the navigation loop
The inner control loop is replaced by the roll attitude limitation
The pilot is directly involved as part of the inner control loop
cards.explain: With the flight director the pilot closes the inner loop himself.

cards.question: Which common mode is available for the flight director only
options: GO AROUND
TAKE OFF
ILS APPROACH/LAND
cards.explain: The take off mode is listed as a flight director function only.

cards.question: Below which height above ground can the Approach/Land or Go Around mode no longer be deactivated by pressing its button again
options: 400 ft
cards.explain: Four hundred feet above ground is the height given for this lock-out.

cards.question: Below which height above ground can the Approach or Land mode be left in only two ways
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: Five hundred feet is the height given with the JAR-AWO reference for this restriction.

cards.question: Which vertical flight mode annunciation appears once the prerequisites for the glide path mode are met
options: G/S - CAPTURE
G/P - ARM
G/P - ACTIVE
cards.explain: The armed condition is annunciated as G/P - ARM.

cards.question: Within which angular range is the glide path signal usable
cards.explain: The printed usable range of the glide path signal is plus or minus 0,5 degrees.

cards.question: Below which height AGL does beam convergence make direct glide path control by zeroing the angular deviation unworkable
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: Below fifteen hundred feet AGL the angular deviation can no longer be used directly, because of beam convergence.

cards.question: Which unit monitors the angular glide path deviation signal as soon as Approach/Land is selected
options: The capture point detector
The over station sensor
The vertical beam sensor
cards.explain: The vertical beam sensor watches the glide path deviation from the moment the mode is selected.

cards.question: Below which angular deviation does the vertical beam sensor trigger the glide path capture phase
cards.explain: Capture is triggered when the angular deviation falls below 0,2 degrees.

cards.question: An aircraft is at 300 ft AGL with the Approach/Land mode engaged and the crew presses the Approach button again — what happens?
options: The mode disengages immediately
The mode stays in operation
The mode reverts to the localizer submode
cards.explain: Below 400 ft the button press no longer deactivates the mode.

cards.question: What does a precision approach require on board the aircraft or on the ground
options: A glide path indicator showing deviation from the intended glide path
A localizer transmitter showing deviation from the runway centre line
A marker beacon showing the distance to the runway threshold
cards.explain: A precision approach is defined by a glide path indicator that permanently shows deviation from the intended glide path.

cards.question: What do all non-precision approaches have in common
options: They lack any lateral guidance
They lack any vertical guidance
They lack any distance information
cards.explain: The absence of vertical guidance is what makes an approach non-precision.

cards.question: The pilot decides to discontinue an approach — according to what must the missed approach be flown?
options: The procedures published in the aircraft flight manual or ATC guidance
The procedures stored in the flight management system or the approach plate
The procedures published in instrument approach charts or ATC guidance
cards.explain: Charted missed approach procedures or ATC guidance are the two printed sources.

cards.question: An automatic approach is being flown with the Approach mode engaged — which span of flight phases does it control?
options: From glide path intercept, via flare, until the end of the missed approach
From localizer intercept, via glide path intercept, until roll out
From localizer intercept, via flare, until the take off mode is selected
cards.explain: The mode runs from localizer intercept through glide path intercept to roll out.

cards.question: An aircraft is below the JAR-AWO height with the Land mode engaged — what are the only two ways of deactivating it?
options: Turning off the autopilot or turning off the auto-thrust
Selecting Go Around or turning off the autopilot
Selecting Go Around or selecting another vertical mode
cards.explain: Only a Go Around selection or switching the autopilot off removes the mode below that height.

cards.question: How are the terms Approach mode and Land mode related
options: They are equivalent names for the same mode
The land mode is a sub-mode of the approach mode
The approach mode is armed and the land mode is active
cards.explain: The two names stand for one and the same mode.

cards.question: Which two settings are a prerequisite before the glide path mode can work
options: The back course of the active runway and the runway heading at the PSC
The ILS frequency of the active runway and the runway heading at the PSC
The ILS frequency of the active runway and the decision height at the PSC
cards.explain: Both the ILS frequency and the runway heading at the PSC knob have to be set first.

cards.question: The aircraft is in altitude hold on the localizer and passes an angular deviation of approximately -0,2° — what happens?
options: Altitude hold switches off and the flare law is armed
Altitude hold switches off and a descent starts
Altitude hold is retained until the beam centre is reached
cards.explain: At about -0,2° the altitude hold drops out and the aircraft begins descending onto the beam.

cards.question: What does an angular deviation of approximately -0,2° correspond to on the glide path deviation indicator
options: Roughly one dot below
Roughly half a dot above
Roughly half a dot below
cards.explain: The page equates about -0,2° with roughly half a dot below on the indicator.

cards.question: An aircraft on an automatic approach descends through approximately 70 ft AGL — why is glide path control terminated at the latest here?
options: The radio altimeter becomes unreliable through ground reflections now
The glide path signal becomes unreliable through ground reflection
The glide path signal is outside its usable angular range
cards.explain: Ground reflection spoils the glide path signal, so control is dropped by about 70 ft.

cards.question: An aircraft holds a constant vertical distance from the glide path as it closes on the transmitter — what happens to the angular deviation?
options: It decreases permanently
It stays constant
It increases permanently
cards.explain: The same vertical offset subtends a larger angle as the range closes.

cards.question: Which name is given to the permanently increasing loop amplification of a closing glide path
options: Funnel effect
Beam convergence
Beam sensitivity
cards.explain: The effect of the permanently rising loop amplification is called beam convergence.

cards.question: Which two quantities does the first estimation method use to estimate the vertical glide path deviation
options: Angular deviation and radio height
Radio height and ground speed
Angular deviation and ground speed
cards.explain: The first method combines the angular deviation with radio height.

cards.question: Which quantity is fed back to form the inner loop of the glide slope mode
options: The radio height
The pitch attitude
The vertical speed
cards.explain: Sink rate feedback closes the inner loop.

cards.question: Why will an aircraft hold a constant sink rate during a steady descent without controller action
options: Because of its weather cock stability
Because of its inherent stability
Because of the pitch trim integrator
cards.explain: Inherent stability is the printed reason for the steady sink rate.

cards.question: The Approach/Land mode is engaged at 200 ft AGL and the crew decides to discontinue the approach — which mode can still take over?
options: The heading select mode
The altitude hold mode
The Go Around mode
cards.explain: Go Around can supersede Approach/Land at any height, unlike other upper modes.

cards.question: An automatic landing is being flown and the glide path has just been left — what is held until the flare phase begins?
options: The momentary pitch attitude
The momentary sink rate
The momentary glide slope angle
cards.explain: The sink rate at that moment is frozen until the flare starts.

cards.question: An autopilot is certified for category II approaches only — what must happen at 100 ft radio height?
options: It must be disengaged and the landing flown manually
It must be switched to the flare sub-mode for the landing
It must be disengaged and the flare flown by the flight director
cards.explain: A category II only autopilot comes out at 100 ft and the pilot flares and lands.

cards.question: Beam convergence has been left uncompensated on an ILS approach — how does the controller behave at long range and close in?
options: Sluggish far out and prone to oscillation near the runway
Sluggish far out and unable to hold the beam near the runway
Prone to oscillation far out and sluggish near the runway
cards.explain: Low gain far out makes it sluggish, and rising gain close in makes it oscillate.

cards.question: Why do estimation methods have to be used to compensate the apparent increase in amplification
options: The angular deviation from the G/P is generally not available
The vertical deviation from the G/P beam is generally not available
The slant range to the G/P-transmitter is generally not available
cards.explain: Without a true slant range the deviation cannot be computed exactly, so it is estimated.

cards.question: The second estimation method is in use and the aircraft passes the outer marker — what is started there, and what has to be known?
options: A time proportional estimation, with the distance from OM to the transmitter
A radio height proportional estimation, with the distance from OM to the threshold
A time proportional estimation, with the height of the aircraft over the marker
cards.explain: Passing the marker starts a time based estimate that relies on the known OM to transmitter distance.

cards.question: A glide slope deviation appears while an aircraft is in a steady descent — which loops detect it and act on it?
options: The pitch outer loop detects it and the pitch inner loop changes the pitch attitude
The pitch outer loop detects it and the pitch inner loop changes the sink rate
The pitch inner loop detects it and the pitch outer loop changes the sink rate
cards.explain: The outer loop sees the beam error and the inner loop carries out the sink rate change.

cards.question: The glide path is being intercepted from below and the angular deviation is decreasing — how does the pitch controller react after synchronization?
options: With a constant pitch attitude until the beam centre
With an increasing pitch-up
With an increasing pitch-over
cards.explain: Synchronization reverses what the raw sign would command, so the aircraft pitches over onto the beam.

cards.question: An aircraft intercepts the glide path from above — what does the controller command at synchronization?
options: A pitch-up, so the aircraft levels off above the glide path
A pitch-up, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
A pitch-over, so the aircraft flares onto the glide path
cards.explain: All signs invert from above, giving a pitch-up and a flare onto the beam.

cards.question: Below which height AGL does the auto-throttle or auto-thrust system reduce the thrust to idle
options: 15 ft
50 ft
120 ft
cards.explain: The printed height for thrust reduction to idle is 15 ft AGL.

cards.question: From which vertical speed to which vertical speed does the flare reduce the descent shortly before touchdown
options: From approx. -400 to -600 ft/min down to approx. -120 ft/min
From approx. -600 to -750 ft/min down to approx. -120 ft/min
From approx. -600 to -750 ft/min down to approx. -250 ft/min
cards.explain: Those are the printed glide path and touchdown sink rates.

cards.question: Which vertical speed is aimed for at landing to achieve a positive touch down
options: Approximately -20 ft/min
Approximately -300 ft/min
Approximately -120 ft/min
cards.explain: The aimed touchdown sink rate is about -120 ft/min.

cards.question: The landing controller is compensating for the ground effect - how much is added to the actual radio altitude?
options: Approximately 20 ft
Approximately 15 ft
Approximately 50 ft
cards.explain: About 20 ft of bias is added to the measured radio height.

cards.question: Which movement does the pitch rollout submode command directly after touch down on the main gear
options: A controlled decrease of the bank angle
A controlled decrease of the pitch attitude
A controlled increase of the pitch attitude
cards.explain: The submode lowers the nose by reducing the pitch attitude in a controlled way.

cards.question: Which annunciation does the flight mode annunciator display once the nose gear is being lowered onto the runway
options: ROLLOUT
FLARE-ACTIVE
LAND
cards.explain: ROLLOUT is shown once the pitch rollout submode runs.

cards.question: Which name is given to the angle between the aircraft heading and its track on a crosswind approach
options: Drift angle or lateral slip angle
Crab angle or wind correction angle
Course angle or bearing angle
cards.explain: That angle is the crab angle, also called the wind correction angle.

cards.question: An automatic landing is flown in a crosswind - below which radio height is the alignment carried out?
options: Below 50 ft
Below 30 ft
Below 15 ft
cards.explain: Alignment is carried out below 30 ft of radio height.

cards.question: From where does the preselected course reach the yaw channel as its reference value
options: From the flight management computer
From the autoflight control panel
From the inertial reference system
cards.explain: The crew sets the preselected course on the autoflight control panel and that is the yaw reference.

cards.question: A wind correction angle has been carried down the approach — what does yaw attitude or heading control do during the auto land?
options: It holds the wind correction angle until the nose gear is down
It aligns the longitudinal axis with the runway direction
It aligns the ground track with the runway centre line
cards.explain: The crab is taken out by yawing the aircraft onto the runway direction.

cards.question: Which signal guides the aircraft along the runway centre line after touch-down
options: The glide path deviation signal
The radio altitude signal
The localizer deviation signal
cards.explain: Roll out steering uses the localizer deviation.

cards.question: Why does a zero sink rate have to be avoided during the flare
options: To avoid a tail strike
To shorten the touch down zone
To assure a positive touchdown
cards.explain: Some sink rate must remain so that the aircraft actually touches down.

cards.question: The flare window is being computed during an automatic landing — which two momentary quantities determine it?
options: Radio height and ground speed
Vertical speed and pitch attitude
Vertical speed and ground speed
cards.explain: The flare window is computed from the momentary vertical speed and ground speed.

cards.question: Which pair of quantities does the controller use to calculate the path to be flown down to the touch down
options: The momentary landing gear height and the derived sink rate
The momentary pitch attitude and the derived ground speed
The momentary radio altitude and the derived crab angle
cards.explain: The landing path is built from the gear height over the runway together with the derived sink rate.

cards.question: Which change to the calculated landing path would the ground effect produce if it were left uncompensated
options: A flattening out of the path
A shortening of the path
A steepening of the path
cards.explain: Extra lift in ground effect reduces the sink rate, so the path would flatten out.

cards.question: Which change behind the wing produces the ground effect as the aircraft approaches the ground
options: The angle of down wash decreases
The angle of sweep decreases
The angle of down wash increases
cards.explain: Near the ground the down wash angle falls off, which raises the effective angle of incidence.

cards.question: Which moment follows from the increased arm to the centre of gravity together with the increased lift at the horizontal stabilizer
options: A pitch up moment
A yawing moment
A pitch down moment
cards.explain: More tail lift on a longer arm pushes the nose down.

cards.question: Which two modes must already be active as the precondition for a flare activation
options: Glideslope as the vertical and localizer as the lateral mode
Altitude hold as the vertical and heading select as the lateral mode
Localizer as the vertical and glideslope as the lateral mode
cards.explain: The flare only arms out of a coupled approach with the glideslope active vertically and the localizer active laterally.

cards.question: The main gear has just touched down at the end of an automatic landing - which capability is lost at that moment?
options: An automatic deceleration process
An automatic go around manoeuvre
An automatic rudder alignment
cards.explain: Once the main gear is down the automatic go around can no longer be flown.

cards.question: Which part of the autoflight system switches itself off automatically at the touch down of the main gear
options: The autopilot roll channel
The autopilot yaw channel
The auto-throttle
cards.explain: The autothrottle switches itself off at touchdown while the yaw channel carries on through the roll out.

cards.question: Which signal is produced when the actual vertical speed is subtracted from the commanded vertical speed
options: The reference signal for the pitch outer loop
The error signal for the pitch inner loop
The feedback signal for the trim integrator
cards.explain: That subtraction is what generates the error fed to the pitch inner loop.

cards.question: At the earliest the flare detector starts the flare 50 ft above the ground. Which quantity modifies that height?
options: The derived vertical speed
The H1 height bias
The ground speed
cards.explain: The earliest flare point is the 50 ft main gear height modified by the H1 height bias that forces a positive touch down.

cards.question: The flare detector rounds the flight path off continuously - which limit does it observe?
options: The upper bank angle limit
The upper pitch attitude limit
The upper sink rate limit
cards.explain: The rounding off is bounded by the upper pitch attitude limit.

cards.question: The remaining lift has to be killed after the touch down - which two actions do that?
options: Auto brake application and ground spoiler extension
Derotation and reverse thrust selection
Derotation and ground spoiler extension
cards.explain: Lowering the nose and putting the ground spoilers out are the two actions named.

cards.question: Why does the aircraft heading have to be brought onto the runway heading shortly before touch down
options: The nose wheel steering is available right after touch down
The rudder loses its effectiveness right after touch down
The landing gear is aligned with the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: The wheels point where the fuselage points, so any crab left on would take the aircraft off the runway.

cards.question: The decrab is being flown on an automatic landing - which reference is the heading aligned with?
options: The present track
The localizer deviation
The preselected course
cards.explain: The align phase flies the heading onto the preselected course.

cards.question: The preselected course is the reference for the align phase - what must the pilot check before the alignment?
options: That it agrees with the runway heading
That it agrees with the present heading
That it agrees with the localizer frequency
cards.explain: The align phase is only as good as the preselected course, so it must match the runway heading.

cards.question: Which channel and which surface does the align phase require
options: A yaw channel acting on the rudder
A yaw channel acting on the nose wheel
A roll channel acting on the ailerons
cards.explain: The decrab is flown by the yaw channel through the rudder.

cards.question: Which axis receives a coordinated input during the alignment, depending on the type of aircraft
options: The vertical axis
The roll axis
The pitch axis
cards.explain: Some aircraft add a coordinated roll input, the low wing method, with the decrab.

cards.question: The flight director is on when the yaw align phase begins - what changes on the display?
options: The roll bar is simply removed from view
The roll bar is replaced by a yaw bar
The pitch bar is replaced by a yaw bar
cards.explain: The roll bar gives way to a yaw bar as the align phase starts.

cards.question: A crosswind automatic landing is flown - what does the flight mode annunciator show as the yaw align phase begins?
options: ALIGN appears as the lateral mode
ROLLOUT appears as the lateral mode
Nothing at all is annunciated for it
cards.explain: The align phase gets no annunciation at all.

cards.question: The align controller needs the present heading - where does it come from?
options: A magnetic heading system or a radio altimeter
A magnetic heading system or an inertial reference system
A localizer receiver or an inertial reference system
cards.explain: Present heading comes either from the compass system or from the inertial system.

cards.question: An aircraft is landing with a tailwind, which has increased its sink rate — what does this do to the flare window?
options: It increases the height at which the flare begins
It leaves the flare height unchanged but steepens the flare
It decreases the height at which the flare begins
cards.explain: A faster descent raises the flare height so that there is more time to arrest the sink rate.

cards.question: What does the simplicity of the flare controller have to be traded off against
options: A relatively narrow touch down zone and a large variation in sink rate
A relatively wide touch down zone and a large variation in pitch attitude
A relatively wide touch down zone and a large variation in sink rate
cards.explain: The price of the simple law is a wide touchdown zone and a spread of touchdown sink rates.

cards.question: An aircraft is set down so softly that the weight on wheels signal is late - what does that cost on the landing roll?
options: The reverse thrust is inhibited
The braking action is delayed
The ground spoilers extend early
cards.explain: A late weight on wheels signal or a late wheel spin up both hold up the braking.

cards.question: Which property of the tyres impedes the directional control by the landing gear after a greaser landing
options: They can accept only a limited lateral force
They can accept only a limited vertical load
They can accept only a limited rolling velocity
cards.explain: The tyres can take only a limited lateral force, so the landing gear cannot steer the aircraft.

cards.question: The controller adds a height bias to the measured radio altitude close to the ground - what does this achieve at the wheels?
options: A thrust increase is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A pitch up is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
A sink rate is still commanded once the aircraft is on the ground
cards.explain: Because the controller thinks it is higher than it is, it keeps commanding a descent and so forces a positive touch down.

cards.question: An aircraft enters ground effect in the last feet of the flare - which set of changes follows?
options: More lift, less induced drag and the centre of lift further aft
Less lift, less induced drag and the centre of lift further aft
More lift, more induced drag and the centre of lift further forward
cards.explain: Ground effect gives more lift, less induced drag and moves the centre of lift rearwards.

cards.question: A heavy aircraft carries a second set of antennas at the nose landing gear - what is switched over once the gear is extended?
options: The glide path receivers go to the nose gear antennas
The localizer receivers go to the nose gear antennas
The radio altimeters go to the nose gear antennas
cards.explain: Gear extension switches the glide path receivers over to the antennas on the nose gear.

cards.question: Which result is achieved by feeding the glide path receivers from the nose gear antennas on a heavy aircraft
options: It gets a lower flare window than a smaller aircraft
It gets the same approach speed as a smaller aircraft
It gets the same flare window as a smaller aircraft
cards.explain: Measuring from the nose gear lifts the aircraft virtually on the beam so the flare window matches a small aircraft's.

cards.question: The flare controller stops rounding the path off at its upper limit - what would happen beyond that limit?
options: The aircraft would risk a nose gear strike at touch down
The aircraft would risk a long float before touch down
The aircraft would risk a tail strike at touch down
cards.explain: Too much nose up at touchdown would put the tail on the runway.

cards.question: Why does a vertical acceleration signal damp the activity of the flare controller
options: It lets the radio altitude be filtered smoothly
It lets disturbances be recognised early
It lets the sink rate be measured accurately
cards.explain: Seeing a disturbance early means the controller does not have to react violently later.

cards.question: Why does the remaining component of lift have to be decreased after the touch down
options: To increase rudder authority and yaw damping
To increase tyre life and brake cooling
To increase runway adhesion and brake efficiency
cards.explain: Killing the lift puts weight on the wheels so they grip and the brakes work.

cards.question: The auto-trim is switched off at the same time as the derotation - what would otherwise drive the trim?
options: A constant pitch error caused by the elevator's negative moment
A constant pitch error caused by the stabilizer's positive moment
A constant pitch rate caused by the elevator's negative moment
cards.explain: The elevator holds a steady nose down moment after derotation, and the standing pitch error that leaves would wake the trim system up.

cards.question: Why is the aircraft headed into the wind during a cross wind approach
options: To prevent a bank angle on the localizer beam
To prevent a lateral load on the landing gear
To prevent a displacement from the localizer beam
cards.explain: Crabbing into the wind stops the aircraft being blown off the beam, so it drifts along it instead.

cards.question: Why is the alignment left until shortly before the touch down
options: It minimizes the crosswind component
It minimizes the lateral drift
It minimizes the rudder deflection
cards.explain: Once the crab is taken out the aircraft starts drifting sideways, so the manoeuvre is kept short.

cards.question: Which comparison produces the control error used by the align controller
options: The present heading against the runway heading
The present heading against the present track
The localizer deviation against the runway heading
cards.explain: The align loop subtracts the measured heading from the runway heading set as preselected course.

cards.question: An aircraft on an automatic approach is in landing configuration and passing 200 ft radio height - what is the state of the align phase?
options: Armed but not yet active
Active and holding the runway heading
Neither armed nor active
cards.explain: The landing configuration arms the phase, but it only goes active below 30 ft, so at 200 ft it is still armed.

cards.question: An automatic landing is being flown onto the runway - which event starts the roll-out phase?
options: The compression of the nose gear
The touch down of the main gear
The extension of the ground spoilers
cards.explain: Roll out begins the moment the main gear is on the runway.

cards.question: The aircraft is decelerating on the runway under the yaw channel - which event ends the roll-out phase?
options: The lowering of the nose gear
The aircraft coming to a stop
The disengagement of the autopilot
cards.explain: Roll out runs until the crew disengages the autopilot.

cards.question: Which means takes over the directional control increasingly after the derotation
options: The differential braking
The nose wheel steering
The rudder deflection
cards.explain: Once the nose wheel is down it progressively takes over the steering.

cards.question: Why can the localizer deviation signal be used for the yaw control during the roll-out
options: The localizer is aligned with the preselected course
The localizer is aligned with the aircraft track
The localizer is aligned with the runway centre line
cards.explain: Because the beam lies along the centre line, a beam deviation is a centre line deviation.

cards.question: The aircraft is rolling out fast with the nose gear still off the ground - how is the direction held?
options: By rudder deflections and nose wheel steering
By nose wheel steering only
By rudder deflections only
cards.explain: With the nose off the ground only the rudder is available, and at that speed it still bites.

cards.question: The aircraft is being steered along the centre line after landing - which two signals does the yaw controller process?
options: The heading error and the localizer deviation
The heading error and the glide path deviation
The crab angle and the localizer deviation
cards.explain: Both a heading error and a lateral displacement have to be removed, so both signals are used.

cards.question: All three gears are on the runway during the roll-out - what else does the yaw channel now control?
options: The rudder trim actuator
The nose wheel steering
The main wheel brakes
cards.explain: Once the nose gear is down the same yaw channel steers it as well as the rudder.

cards.question: Which name is given to the transition phase from an approach to a stabilized climb
options: An align manoeuvre
A go around manoeuvre
A roll out manoeuvre
cards.explain: That transition is exactly what is called a go around.

cards.question: Which channel takes over the vertical guidance once the go around manoeuvre has started
options: The pitch channel
The roll channel
The yaw channel
cards.explain: Vertical guidance in a go around belongs to the pitch channel.

cards.question: Which form of control does the first go around concept activate at the start of the manoeuvre
options: Airspeed control to a fixed reference value
Vertical speed control to a fixed climb value
Pitch attitude control to a fixed positive value
cards.explain: The first concept rotates to and then holds a fixed nose up attitude.

cards.question: A go around is selected on the approach - which three parts of the autoflight system come in together?
options: The pitch channel, the roll channel and the auto-thrust system
The roll channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
The pitch channel, the yaw channel and the auto-thrust system
cards.explain: Go around is a common mode and brings pitch, roll and the thrust system in together.

cards.question: The crew changes the slat and flap setting during a go around - what happens to the airspeed reference values?
options: They have to be reselected by hand
They are frozen at the previous value
They are adapted automatically
cards.explain: The references follow the configuration without any crew action.

cards.question: A go around is being flown - what is the minimum climb rate that has to be observed?
options: 120 ft/min
600 ft/min
1200 ft/min
cards.explain: The minimum climb rate for the go around is 120 ft/min.

cards.question: Which minimum flight path angle has to be observed during a go around
cards.explain: Half a degree is the minimum flight path angle.

cards.question: Why does the airworthiness standard demand a minimum climb rate and a minimum flight path angle
options: To achieve obstacle clearance
To achieve a positive rate of climb
To achieve a stabilized airspeed
cards.explain: The minima exist so the aircraft will clear what is ahead of it.

cards.question: Which action triggers the go around mode on an aircraft fitted with an auto-throttle system
options: Pushing the power levers to the TOGA detent
Pressing the TOGA switch at the throttles
Selecting a higher altitude on the control panel
cards.explain: With an auto-throttle the trigger is the switch on the throttles; the detent belongs to an auto-thrust system.

cards.question: Which condition must be satisfied before the go around mode may be terminated
options: A minimum climb rate of 120 ft/min has to be passed
A minimum airspeed above the reference has to be passed
A minimum height above the ground has to be passed
cards.explain: The mode is locked in until a minimum height above the ground has been exceeded.

cards.question: Which thrust does the auto-throttle command when the go around mode becomes active
options: The maximum thrust available for five minutes
The maximum continuous thrust available in the climb
The reduced climb thrust available after flap retraction
cards.explain: Go around thrust is the five minute maximum rating.

cards.question: Which track does the roll channel maintain during the go around
options: The track of the runway centre line extended
The track it was following at the start of the manoeuvre
The track selected on the autoflight control panel
cards.explain: The roll channel simply holds whatever track was being flown when the go around began.

cards.question: Which penalty follows the inversion of a sink rate into a climb rate during the go around
options: The airspeed is reduced
The thrust is reduced
The pitch attitude is reduced
cards.explain: Turning a descent into a climb is paid for in speed.

cards.question: Between which climb rates does the transition from attitude guidance to speed guidance take place
options: 600 ft/min and 1200 ft/min
1200 ft/min and 1800 ft/min
120 ft/min and 600 ft/min
cards.explain: The changeover is spread continuously over 600 to 1200 ft/min of climb.

cards.question: Which flight condition makes the climb rate drop drastically during a go around
options: Wind shear or a downdraft
A thrust reduction or a bank
A flap or a gear retraction
cards.explain: Wind shear or a downdraft is the case given for a sudden loss of climb rate.

cards.question: Which principle is the speed reference control law built on
options: Total energy management
Total pressure management
Total thrust management
cards.explain: The alternative concept works from the total energy of the aircraft.

cards.question: Which two modes is the speed reference control law used for
options: The flight director land mode and the go around mode
The flight director take-off mode and the go around mode
The flight director take-off mode and the flare mode
cards.explain: The same law serves the take-off director and the go around.

cards.question: Which quantity is the potential flight path angle directly proportional to
options: The thrust setting on the actual flight path
