The acceleration on the actual flight path
The pitch attitude on the actual flight path
cards.explain: It is the acceleration along the path that the potential angle follows.

cards.question: Which property of the aircraft does the potential flight path angle reflect
options: Its total energy
Its potential energy only
Its kinetic energy only
cards.explain: The potential angle is a measure of the whole energy state, not one part of it.

cards.question: Which quantity is the correction angle proportional to
options: The flight path error
The speed error
The angle of attack
cards.explain: The correction angle is sized by the speed error.

cards.question: Which signal is formed at the last summing point and used as the reference for the pitch attitude controller
options: The difference of the actual and potential flight path angles
The sum of the flight path error and the correction angle
The sum of the pitch attitude and the angle of attack
cards.explain: S3 adds the correction angle onto the flight path error and the sum is the demand given to the pitch controller.

cards.question: A large thrust increase at the start of a go around produces a strong nose up moment - which limits must the controller watch?
options: The bank angle or sideslip limits
The pitch attitude or angle of attack limits
The flap or landing gear speed limits
cards.explain: The required thrust increase causes a large positive pitch moment, so the pitch attitude and angle of attack limits have to be observed.

cards.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system and the crew wants a go around - what do they do with the power levers?
options: Push them to the TOGA detent
Press the TOGA switch on them
Pull them back to the idle detent
cards.explain: On an auto-thrust aircraft the levers are pushed into the TOGA detent.

cards.question: Why is the trigger tied to uncompressed gears with slats and flaps extended
options: It prevents triggering with the autopilot engaged
It prevents triggering below the minimum height
It prevents triggering during other flight phases
cards.explain: The configuration test makes sure the mode can only come up where it belongs, on an approach.

cards.question: The aircraft touches down while a go around is being flown - what happens to the mode?
options: It stays active
It is terminated at once
It changes into the rollout mode
cards.explain: The mode survives a touch down, which is what makes a touch and go possible.

cards.question: The crew decides to level off and fly a radar heading after a go around - how is the mode taken out?
options: By selecting other upper modes for pitch and roll independently
By disengaging the autopilot and flying by hand
By selecting other upper modes for pitch and roll together
cards.explain: Picking a new upper mode ends the go around, and the vertical and lateral sides can be ended separately.

cards.question: The go around controller rotates the aircraft to a fixed positive pitch attitude - what follows from that?
options: Lift increases and the momentary airspeed increases
Drag increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
Lift increases and the momentary sink rate decreases
cards.explain: More attitude means more lift, and more lift arrests the descent.

cards.question: Which control replaces pitch attitude hold a short while after the start of the go around
options: Thrust control of the auto-throttle system
Airspeed control of the pitch channel
Vertical speed control of the pitch channel
cards.explain: Because the attitude hold is eating the speed, the pitch channel goes over to controlling airspeed.

cards.question: Airspeed control is running in a go around and the climb rate falls below 1200 ft/min - what does the vertical guidance do?
options: It reverts to pitch attitude control
It reverts to vertical speed control
It stays on airspeed control
cards.explain: Losing climb performance sends the channel back to holding attitude so lift is restored.

cards.question: Why does the aircraft keep climbing once the pitch controller holds a constant airspeed
options: The surplus of go around thrust gives a positive flight path angle
The surplus of lift gives a positive flight path angle
The surplus of go around thrust gives a positive pitch attitude
cards.explain: With the speed pegged, the spare thrust has nowhere to go but into climb angle.

cards.question: An aircraft is flying on a path whose angle equals its potential flight path angle - what are its errors?
options: Airspeed error at a maximum and flight path error at a maximum
Airspeed error zero and flight path error not zero
Airspeed error zero and flight path error zero
cards.explain: Flying at the potential angle means the energy is exactly balanced, so both errors vanish.

cards.question: Which angle appears when the airspeed reference is changed while the thrust is held constant
options: A demand angle that changes the present pitch attitude
An error angle that changes the present angle of attack
A correction angle that changes the present flight path angle
cards.explain: The speed error is worked off by a correction angle that tilts the flight path so the aircraft accelerates or decelerates.

cards.question: Go around is selected on an approach - which speed is captured in the memory as the speed target?
options: The minimum selectable speed
The actual airspeed at that moment
The approach reference speed
cards.explain: Selecting go around closes the switch that freezes the actual airspeed into the memory as the target.

questions.question: Which flight phases flight director modes are available for
options: All phases from engine start until engine shut down
Only the phases from climb until final approach
Almost all phases from take off until roll out
questions.explain: The printed span is take off to roll out, for almost all phases.

questions.question: Which three speeds the pilots determine at flight preparation for the take off phase
options: VR, V2 and VMAX
V1, V2 and VLS
V1, VR and V2
questions.explain: The three take off speeds named are V1, VR and V2.

questions.question: Which input a deflection of the roll bar to the right signifies
options: Left aileron, turn left
Right aileron, turn right
Right rudder, yaw right
questions.explain: A roll bar to the right asks for right aileron and a turn to the right.

questions.question: A take off is to be made at a visibility between 125 m and 75 m. Which indication gives the pilot his lateral guidance?
options: A pitch bar controlled by the radio altitude signal
A yaw bar controlled by the localizer deviation signal
A roll bar controlled by the runway heading signal
questions.explain: In that visibility band the yaw bar driven by localizer deviation provides the lateral guidance.

questions.question: When the pitch attitude to be adopted at VR is shown on the pitch bar
options: As soon as the gear struts extend, or at 35 ft above the runway
As soon as the thrust levers reach the TOGA detent, or at lift off
As soon as the take off mode is selected, or at a certain airspeed
questions.explain: Two implementations exist: at mode selection, or on passing a certain airspeed.

questions.question: Which airspeed the flight director commands for the initial climb at a normal take off
options: An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above VR
An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above V2
An actual airspeed equal to V2
questions.explain: On all engines the initial climb is flown 10 to 20 kts above V2.

questions.question: Which input lets the yaw controller recognise a departure from the runway centre line?
options: The localizer deviation signal
The supplied runway heading
The nose wheel steering position
questions.explain: Deviations from the centre line are seen in the localizer deviation signal.

questions.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system fitted. How can its throttles be moved?
options: Only manually
Only automatically
Manually or by the servomotor
questions.explain: With auto-thrust the levers move by hand only.

questions.question: What supported the development of the auto-thrust system
options: The introduction of the para visual display systems
The electronic control of modern turbofan engines
The derating of the turbine inlet temperature limits
questions.explain: FADEC engine control made the auto-thrust system possible, and the functions are often built into it.

questions.question: The system is working in speed or Mach mode. Where does its reference speed come from?
options: The autoflight control panel or the FMS
The autoflight control panel or the EEC
The air data computer or the FMS
questions.explain: The reference is either set on the control panel or supplied by the FMS.

questions.question: Which system holds priority for airspeed control
options: The flight management system computer
The autopilot or flight director pitch channel
The auto-throttle or auto-thrust system
questions.explain: Priority lies with the pitch channel of the autopilot or flight director.

questions.question: The crew has made no manual selection of the phase used for the rating — what else can supply it?
options: The autothrottle computer unit
The engine control computer
The flight management system
questions.explain: The flight phase comes either from the pilot or from the FMS.

questions.question: Thrust mode has just been selected — what does the determined thrust rating then serve as?
options: The reference for N1 closed loop control by the engine computer
The reference for N2 closed loop control by the autothrottle computer
The reference for fuel flow control by the hydromechanical unit
questions.explain: The rating becomes the N1 reference that the engine computer then closes the loop on.

questions.question: A technician finds no throttle servo motor on an auto-thrust aircraft — is that a defect?
options: Yes, the servo must drive the levers to the rating
No, the levers here are not driven automatically
Yes, without it the retard bias cannot operate
questions.explain: An auto-thrust system has no lever servo at all, so none is missing.

questions.question: The all weather approval holds good for which runways
options: Only those fitted with a roll out guidance system
Only those listed in the operator's own route manual
Those approved by the authority for that category
questions.explain: Approval follows the authority's own runway classification for the category.

questions.question: Dutch roll grows into a problem at high altitude for which reason
options: The rudder travel available falls off with altitude
The damping aerodynamic forces fall with altitude
The lift of the swept wing rises with altitude
questions.explain: Thin air means weaker aerodynamic damping, so the oscillation is no longer suppressed naturally.

questions.question: The aircraft accelerates in the cruise — what happens to the yaw rate signal passed on to the actuator?
options: It is held at its take-off value
It is built up as the speed rises
It is cut back as the speed rises
questions.explain: Inverse proportionality means the signal is reduced as speed increases.

questions.question: ILS precision approaches are subdivided into which categories
options: CAT A to CAT C
CAT I to CAT III
CAT I to CAT VIII
questions.explain: The subdivision runs from CAT I to CAT III.

questions.question: The minimum runway visual range required for a CAT III approach depends on which two things
options: The equipment carried and the autoland capability
The decision height and the alert height selected
The runway length and the approach lighting fitted
questions.explain: Installed equipment and autoland capability together fix the minimum RVR.

questions.question: An approach is planned to a decision height of 150 ft with a reported visual range of 400 m — which category applies?
options: CAT II
CAT III a
CAT I
questions.explain: A decision height between 200 ft and 100 ft with at least 300 m visual range is CAT II.

questions.question: Required ground equipment fails at a point below the alert height — what is the consequence?
options: The failure is ignored and the approach goes on
The approach reverts to a higher category minimum
A go around is initiated without any delay
questions.explain: At or below the alert height the failure is ignored.

questions.question: After a failure the weather allows a higher minimum and enough autoflight capability remains — what may the crew then do?
options: Descend below the alert height
Continue down to the original minimum
Fly that approach category instead
questions.explain: Both conditions together allow the higher minimum approach to be flown.

questions.question: The objective of CAT II autoflight operation is to hold which level of safety
options: One set by the aircraft manufacturer alone
One above that of manual flight operation
One equivalent to manual flight operation
questions.explain: The aim is equivalence with manual operation, under worse weather.

questions.question: A CAT III B minimum is set so as to secure which crew capability
options: Visual confirmation of the touch down point
Visual supervision of the roll out
Visual acquisition of the approach light system
questions.explain: The CAT III B minimum exists so the roll out can be watched.

questions.question: One of several parallel channels drops out and the output signal is unaffected — which redundancy is in use?
options: Active redundancy
Monitored redundancy
Passive redundancy
questions.explain: Only active redundancy keeps the output going with no switch over.

questions.question: Which wheel provision is required for an approach flown with no decision height
options: An autobrake disarm warning
An anti-skid braking system
A carbon brake wear indicator
questions.explain: An anti-skid braking system is one of the items listed for no decision height.

questions.question: An autopilot that detects its own failure and disengages itself is operated on its own. Which behaviour does the system then show?
options: fail operational behaviour
fail passive behaviour
fail safe behaviour
questions.explain: A single system able to detect and remove its own failure gives fail passive behaviour in single operation.

questions.question: A manufacturer limits the authority of its autopilot servos, but the aircraft has no manual control path strong enough to overrule the autopilot. Why is that not acceptable?
options: because the autopilot could then not recognize its own hard over
because the pilot could then not over-power the autopilot
because the servos would then not reach their full travel range
questions.explain: Authority limitation relies on the pilot being able to apply strong inputs and over-power the autopilot manually.

questions.question: A fail passive system must be able to disengage itself. How does it recognize that it has a failure?
options: by monitoring the hydraulic pressure at the actuator
by comparing the surface position with the commanded position
by comparing the two autopilot computers with each other
questions.explain: Recognition rests on the electrical comparison of actual surface position with commanded actuator position.

questions.question: In which respect a dual channel fail passive autopilot differs from two parallel fail safe autopilots
options: it drives one actuator only and needs no mechanical voting
it drives two actuators and needs a torque limiter
it drives three actuators and needs a mid-value voter
questions.explain: Parallel fail safe autopilots need mechanical voting against force conflicts, while the dual channel autopilot drives a single actuator and does not.

questions.question: Of the two fail operational architectures described, one of them needs mechanical voting to avoid force conflicts
options: parallel operation of two fail passive autopilots
single operation of one fail passive autopilot
triple operation with three fail safe autopilots
questions.explain: Three parallel fail safe autopilots drive their actuators together and need voting; two fail passive autopilots never drive together.

questions.question: Why a hybrid landing system counts as fail operational although its automatic landing system is only fail passive
options: the automatic landing system becomes fail operational below the alert height
the two autopilots of the system are voted mechanically
the guidance system allows the landing to be continued manually
questions.explain: The overall capability is kept by the independent guidance system letting the crew finish the landing by hand.

questions.question: Two fail passive autopilots and one auto-thrust system are operational. Which capability is displayed and which failure mode does the system have?
options: CAT 3 DUAL, and the system is fail operational
CAT 3 SINGLE, and the system is fail passive
CAT 2, and the system is fail operational
questions.explain: Two fail passive autopilots make the total system fail operational and give CAT 3 DUAL for CAT III B.

questions.question: Why does the autoland warning demand action at once rather than merely being noted by the crew?
options: because the warning sits on the glare shield
because the warning repeats every ten seconds
because it is a red warning
questions.explain: Its red colour is what classes it as requiring immediate action.

questions.question: What the collective pitch lever controls
options: the main rotor lift
the velocity vector
the tail rotor thrust
questions.explain: The collective pitch lever is the lift control.

questions.question: On which helicopters a twist grip throttle is found
options: on those powered by a piston engine
on those with a counter clockwise rotor
on those powered by a turbine engine
questions.explain: The twist grip throttle belongs to piston engined helicopters.

questions.question: A helicopter is to be moved along its velocity vector without any change of lift. Which control is used and what does it do to the rotor plane?
options: the collective lever, which tilts the rotor plane
the cyclic stick, which raises the whole rotor plane
the cyclic stick, which tilts the rotor plane
questions.explain: Velocity vector control belongs to the cyclic stick, which works by tilting the rotor plane.

questions.question: The cyclic stick is moved to the left-hand side. Which servo stays unenergized and which movement results?
options: the front servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
the front servo, and the helicopter moves nose down
the LH servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
questions.explain: A sideward input leaves the front servo unenergized and moves the helicopter sideward to the left.

questions.question: The pedal position is changed in flight. Which quantity at the tail rotor changes as a result of the blade pitch change?
options: the speed of the tail rotor
the torque of the main rotor
the thrust of the tail rotor
questions.explain: Changing tail rotor blade pitch changes the tail rotor thrust.

questions.question: How the pilot gets a feedback of the attitude change at his controls
options: through the cable system, driven by the main servos
through the trim actuators, driven by the control panel
through the rate gyros, driven by the SCAS computer
questions.explain: The main servos feed the movement back to the pilot controls through the cable system.

cards.question: Which two tasks the flight director accomplishes
options: Commands for manual control and monitoring of autopilot activities
Commands for manual control and automatic trim of the pitch axis
Monitoring of autopilot activities and selection of the thrust rating
cards.explain: The page names exactly these two tasks: commands for manual control, and monitoring of the autopilot.

cards.question: During which phases a yaw bar is displayed and the roll bar is removed
options: Flare below 50 ft radio height, climb and take-off
Align below 30 ft radio height, rollout and approach
Flare below 30 ft radio height, rollout and take-off
cards.explain: Those are the three phases printed for yaw bar display.

cards.question: Which bars display the attitude reference commands in an ADI or PFD
options: A pitch bar, a track bar and eventually a roll bar
A roll bar, a speed bar and eventually a yaw bar
A pitch bar, a roll bar and eventually a yaw bar
cards.explain: Pitch and roll bars, and possibly a yaw bar, carry the attitude reference commands.

cards.question: Which three speeds the pilots determine at flight preparation for the take off phase
options: V1, V2 and VLS
V1, VR and V2
VR, V2 and VMAX
cards.explain: The three take off speeds named are V1, VR and V2.

cards.question: At which height above the runway the take off safety speed has to be obtained with one engine inoperative
options: 35 ft
30 ft
50 ft
cards.explain: V2 is defined at 35 ft above the runway surface.

cards.question: Why the flight director indicators are overlaid on the artificial horizon
options: They display attitude commands affecting the rotary degrees of freedom
They display track commands affecting the lateral degrees of freedom
They display speed commands affecting the linear degrees of freedom
cards.explain: Because the commands concern the rotary degrees of freedom they belong on the artificial horizon.

cards.question: An aircraft with a crossbar flight director is following its defined flight path. Where do the two bars lie?
options: They rest at the upper edge of the own aircraft symbol
They lie apart at an equal distance above the horizon line
They intersect at the middle mark of the own aircraft symbol
cards.explain: On path the roll bar crosses the pitch bar at the middle mark of the aircraft symbol.

cards.question: Which rotations the yaw bar commands
options: Rotations around the vertical axis only
Rotations around the lateral axis only
Rotations around the longitudinal axis only
cards.explain: The yaw bar is restricted to rotations about the vertical axis.

cards.question: The yaw bar in the ADI deflects during the take off run. Which control inputs does the pilot make?
options: Elevator or stabiliser trim inputs
Rudder or nose wheel steering inputs
Aileron or roll spoiler inputs
cards.explain: Yaw bar commands are flown with rudder or nose wheel steering.

cards.question: Below 50 ft radio altitude on an autoland the flare, align and rollout modes are selected automatically. What part does the flight director then play?
options: It is removed from the display until roll out has ended
It serves only for commanding manual control inputs
It serves only for monitoring the autopilot
cards.explain: In the autoland modes the flight director is a monitoring display only.

cards.question: The autopilot is engaged and a lateral mode is chosen on the control panel. What happens to the flight director?
options: The selected mode also holds for the flight director
The flight director bars are biased out of view
The flight director reverts to its take off mode
cards.explain: A mode selected with the autopilot engaged applies to the flight director as well.

cards.question: During a flight path mode the aircraft adopts the commanded attitude. What do the command bars do?
options: They return immediately to their centre position
They stay deflected until the mode is deselected
They move to a steady offset from the centre
cards.explain: The bars show attitude error only, so they centre as soon as the error is gone.

cards.question: The pitch bar deflects upward. Which input does it call for?
options: Pull elevator, pitch up
Right aileron, turn right
Push elevator, pitch down
cards.explain: An upward pitch bar asks for elevator back pressure to pitch up.

cards.question: Which input a deflection of the roll bar to the right signifies
options: Left aileron, turn left
Right rudder, yaw right
Right aileron, turn right
cards.explain: A roll bar to the right asks for right aileron and a turn to the right.

cards.question: The yaw bar deflects to the left. Which input does that command?
options: Left aileron wheel, turn left
Left rudder pedal, yaw left
Right rudder pedal, yaw right
cards.explain: A yaw bar to the left asks for left rudder pedal to yaw left.

cards.question: The roll bar in the ADI deflects. Which autopilot signal does that deflection correspond to?
options: The attitude error computed in the roll outer control loop
The signal fed to the roll actuator in the outer heading loop
The signal fed to the roll actuator in the inner roll loop
cards.explain: The bar is driven by the same signal the autopilot would send to its roll actuator in the inner loop.

cards.question: Which action removes a roll attitude error that the flight director indicates
options: A reset made in the outer heading loop
A control input made by the pilot himself
A servo input made by the roll actuator
cards.explain: The flight director only displays the command; the correction comes from the pilot's own input.

cards.question: Why must an aircraft be able to hold different steady pitch attitudes?
options: They depend on thrust rating, bleed air load and temperature
They depend on runway heading, visibility and flap setting
They depend on airspeed, centre of gravity and gross weight
cards.explain: Airspeed, CG position and gross weight each change the steady attitude required.

cards.question: Why distances and airspeeds are laid down in the airworthy standards
options: To keep the engine ratings within their derated temperature limits
To guarantee a sufficient safety margin in all flight phases
To allow a take off at the lowest possible runway visibility
cards.explain: They exist to give a sufficient safety margin in every flight phase.

cards.question: Why an aircraft with a tricycle gear has to be rotated at VR
options: It accelerates at a low angle of attack and needs more lift
It accelerates on its nose gear and has to unload that gear
It accelerates at a high angle of attack and needs less drag
cards.explain: The ground run is at a low angle of attack, so rotation is needed to make enough lift.

cards.question: A flight director shows a roll attitude error and the pilot moves the wheel to follow it. Which part of the loop structure has the pilot just closed?
options: The inner control loop
The attitude limiter path
The outer heading loop
cards.explain: In flight director operation the pilot himself closes the inner loop that the autopilot servo would otherwise close.

cards.question: Why integration has to be avoided when a vertical mode drives the flight director pitch bar
options: The behaviour of the pilot cannot be predicted
The pitch bar signal is inverted before it is displayed
The outer loop error is already proportional to attitude
cards.explain: A pilot may react late or not at all, so an integrator cannot be used.

cards.question: What a delayed pilot reaction would do to the integrator in the outer loop
options: Drive it towards saturation and wind up the pitch bar
Hold it at a constant value and freeze the pitch bar
Drive it towards zero and centre the pitch bar
cards.explain: The integrator saturates, the bar winds up and the command becomes useless.

cards.question: Why the outer loop error cannot be used directly as the pitch attitude reference for the inner loop
options: A zero error would then demand a pitch attitude of 20 degrees
A zero error would then demand a constant pitch rate
A zero error would then demand a pitch attitude of 0 degrees
cards.explain: With the outer loop error as reference, zero error would force the attitude to zero as well.

cards.question: The outer loop error is zero and the aircraft is held at a pitch attitude inside the suppression range. Where does the flight director pitch bar sit?
options: Deflected fully up
Deflected fully down
In its neutral position
cards.explain: Eight degrees up lies inside the printed suppression range, so with no outer loop error the bar rests neutral.

cards.question: The aircraft pitches up beyond the suppression range. What is added to the pitch bar deflection?
options: An opposing command proportional to the exceeding angle
A command proportional only to the outer loop error
A fixed command until the attitude re-enters the range
cards.explain: Outside the range an opposing command sized by the exceeding angle is added to the bar.

cards.question: The pilot makes no input in answer to a short-term pitch bar deflection. What happens to the bar?
options: It returns to its initial position again
It stays deflected until the mode is reselected
It increases its deflection steadily
cards.explain: The washout lets the deflection decay back to the initial position.

cards.question: The pilot follows a short-term pitch bar deflection caused by a gust inside the suppression range. What keeps that deflection from winding up?
options: The integrator in the outer control loop
The washout in the pitch rate feedback path
The attitude limiter at the pitch bar output
cards.explain: The washout makes the pitch rate feedback decay, so no lasting build-up occurs.

cards.question: An engine fails while the aircraft is accelerating and is still below V1. What must be done?
options: The aircraft has to be rotated at once
The take off has to be continued
The take off has to be discontinued
cards.explain: Before V1 an engine failure obliges the crew to stop the take off.

cards.question: A caution is generated by the warning system just after V1 has been passed. What must be done?
options: The take off has to be discontinued
The aircraft has to be held on its main gear
The take off has to be continued
cards.explain: At or after V1 the take off is continued whatever the warning.

cards.question: An aircraft is in a V2 climb after an engine failure and below the acceleration altitude. What is the state of the gear and the flaps?
options: Gear retracted, take off flaps already retracted
Gear extended, take off flaps already retracted
Gear retracted, take off flaps still extended
cards.explain: The gear comes up but the take off flaps stay out until the acceleration altitude.

cards.question: Which system the take off mode is exclusively reserved for
options: The flight director
The auto-throttle
The autopilot
cards.explain: The take off mode belongs to the flight director alone.

cards.question: The take off mode has just been selected on the ground. Which flight director channels are activated?
options: The pitch channel and the roll channel
The pitch channel and the yaw channel
The roll channel and the yaw channel
cards.explain: Selection of the take off mode brings up the pitch and yaw channels.

cards.question: At which typical airspeed the rotation attitude is indicated on the pitch bar during the acceleration
options: Typically 80 kts
Typically 60 kts
Typically 100 kts
cards.explain: The printed typical value is 60 kts.

cards.question: From which parameters the potential flight path angle is calculated
options: Longitudinal acceleration, pitch rate and radio altitude
Longitudinal and vertical acceleration and angle of attack
Vertical acceleration, airspeed and angle of attack
cards.explain: Those three parameters are the printed inputs to the potential flight path angle.

cards.question: How the actual flight path angle is obtained
options: From the difference between pitch attitude and angle of attack
From the difference between pitch attitude and the threshold angle
From the sum of the pitch attitude and the angle of attack
cards.explain: It is the pitch attitude angle less the angle of attack.

cards.question: In which mode an armed auto-throttle system stays throughout the take off phase
options: Speed mode
Thrust mode
Mach mode
cards.explain: Through the whole take off the armed system remains in thrust mode.

cards.question: A take off is to be made at a visibility between 125 m and 75 m. Which indication gives the pilot his lateral guidance?
options: A roll bar controlled by the runway heading signal
A pitch bar controlled by the radio altitude signal
A yaw bar controlled by the localizer deviation signal
cards.explain: In that visibility band the yaw bar driven by localizer deviation provides the lateral guidance.

cards.question: Why supplemental display systems are fitted for low visibility take offs
options: They replace the artificial horizon during the take off run
They avoid a change between head-up and head-down views
They allow the roll bar to be shown below 30 ft radio height
cards.explain: They let the pilot see the guidance while still looking at the runway lighting.

cards.question: How the flight director is switched into take off mode
options: Pressing a NAV switch or pushing the levers into the idle detent
Arming the auto-thrust and selecting the departure runway by hand
Pressing a TOGA switch or pushing the levers into the TOGA detent
cards.explain: Either the TOGA switch or the TOGA detent selects the mode.

cards.question: The aircraft passes 30 ft radio height with no FMS flight plan active. Which lateral guidance does the roll bar give?
options: It maintains the runway centre line
It maintains the runway track
It maintains the heading entered on the control panel
cards.explain: Above 30 ft the roll bar holds the runway track until another lateral mode is chosen.

cards.question: When the pitch attitude to be adopted at VR is shown on the pitch bar
options: As soon as the take off mode is selected, or at a certain airspeed
As soon as the gear struts extend, or at 35 ft above the runway
As soon as the thrust levers reach the TOGA detent, or at lift off
cards.explain: Two implementations exist: at mode selection, or on passing a certain airspeed.

cards.question: Which airspeed the flight director commands for the initial climb at a normal take off
options: An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above V2
An actual airspeed 10 to 20 kts above VR
An actual airspeed equal to V2
cards.explain: On all engines the initial climb is flown 10 to 20 kts above V2.

cards.question: A take off run is in progress. Which reference does the pilot use to find the point of rotation?
options: Pitch bar position only
Airspeed only
Radio height only
cards.explain: The rotation point is set by airspeed alone, read from the ASI.

cards.question: Which two inputs the flight director needs for yaw bar control up to 30 ft radio height
options: Runway heading and localizer deviation
Runway heading and radio altitude
Localizer deviation and ground speed
cards.explain: Yaw bar control needs the runway heading and the localizer deviation.

cards.question: Why pitch attitude replaces angle of attack in that calculation during the take off phase
options: Because of the air flow conditions at that time
Because the angle of attack vanes are not yet heated
Because the inertial system is not yet fully aligned
cards.explain: The air flow conditions at take off make the angle of attack unusable, so pitch attitude is taken.

cards.question: Which autopilot mode the flight director take off yaw control mode is equivalent to
options: The autoland align mode
The autoland flare mode
The autoland roll-out mode
cards.explain: It is the same control arrangement as the autoland roll-out mode.

cards.question: Which input tells the yaw controller the direction in which the aircraft should be pointing?
options: The supplied runway heading
The localizer deviation signal
The radio height signal
cards.explain: Alignment with the runway comes from the supplied runway heading.

cards.question: Which input lets the yaw controller recognise a departure from the runway centre line?
options: The supplied runway heading
The localizer deviation signal
The nose wheel steering position
cards.explain: Deviations from the centre line are seen in the localizer deviation signal.

cards.question: The aircraft climbs through a radio altitude of 30 ft after lift off. What changes in the flight director?
options: The yaw channel is deactivated and the roll channel activated
The pitch channel is deactivated and the roll channel activated
The roll channel is deactivated and the yaw channel activated
cards.explain: At 30 ft the yaw channel drops out and the roll channel comes in at the same moment.

cards.question: Which guidance the yaw bar gives from brake release up to a radio height of 30 ft
options: A return to the runway track after a lateral mode change
A return to the runway centre line at any deviation
A turn onto the standard instrument departure
cards.explain: Up to 30 ft the yaw bar works the aircraft back onto the runway centre line.

cards.question: An FMS flight plan is active as the aircraft climbs through 30 ft radio height. What does the lateral command follow?
options: The standard instrument departure
The localizer of the departure runway
The runway centre line until 1500 ft
cards.explain: With an active flight plan the lateral command follows the SID instead of the runway track.

cards.question: An engine fails after V1. Which pitch attitude does the flight director command?
options: One that holds the rotation attitude until the acceleration altitude
One that reaches the safety speed at 35 ft and then holds it
One that reaches the safety speed plus 15 kts and then holds it
cards.explain: After an engine failure the commanded attitude reaches V2 at 35 ft and keeps it through the first and second segment climb.

cards.question: The pitch bar already shows a rotation attitude while the aircraft is still accelerating below VR. What must the pilot do?
options: Rotate the aircraft into the pitch bar
Reduce thrust until the rotation speed is reached
Disregard that pitch bar command
cards.explain: The flight director cannot find the rotation point, so a command before VR is ignored.

cards.question: The take off runway has been selected at flight preparation. How does the yaw channel obtain its two inputs?
options: From the IRS, which supplies the track and the drift angle
From the ADC, which supplies the heading and the deviation
From the FMS, which tunes the ILS and supplies the heading
cards.explain: The FMS tunes the ILS for the localizer deviation and reads the runway heading from its database.

cards.question: Heading mode is selected for lateral guidance after the yaw bar has been removed. Which heading is followed?
options: The heading at its activation or one entered on the panel
The heading of the standard instrument departure leg
The runway heading supplied by the navigation database
cards.explain: Heading mode follows either the heading at activation or the heading set on the control panel.

cards.question: During take off the potential flight path angle drops below the threshold while the speed is already above V2. What does the autoflight system do?
options: It raises the speed target by a further 15 kts
It reduces the speed target to the safety speed
It tries to maintain the speed held at engine failure
cards.explain: Above V2 the system holds the speed the aircraft had at the failure instead of reducing the target.

cards.question: The potential flight path angle falls below the threshold while the aircraft is still below the safety speed. What becomes the speed target?
options: VLS
VR
V2
cards.explain: The target is automatically reduced to V2.

cards.question: Which difference remains between that flight director mode and the equivalent autopilot mode
options: The rudder is driven directly by the yaw servo
The localizer deviation signal is not made use of
The pilot is actively involved in the control loop
cards.explain: The one difference is that the pilot sits in the loop.

cards.question: The pilot flies the yaw bar commands accurately during the take off run. What happens to the localizer deviation and the heading error?
options: Both are replaced by a roll demand
Both of them are progressively minimized
Both are frozen at their present values
cards.explain: Following the bar drives both the lateral deviation and the heading error towards zero.

cards.question: Which computer function determines the thrust ratings
options: The power management function of the engine computers
The thrust limit function of the flight management computers
The envelope protection function of the flight control computers
cards.explain: Ratings come from the power management function in the EEC or ECU.

cards.question: In which two areas an auto-throttle or auto-thrust system can relieve the pilot
options: Thrust control or airspeed control
Airspeed control or lateral guidance
Thrust control or pitch trim control
cards.explain: The two areas of relief are thrust control and airspeed control.

cards.question: Which two modes of operation an auto-throttle or auto-thrust system provides
options: Speed or Mach mode and retard mode
Thrust mode and alpha floor mode
Thrust mode and speed or Mach mode
cards.explain: The system offers a thrust mode and a speed or Mach mode.

cards.question: For how long the maximum take off thrust rating is basically available
options: 15 minutes
10 minutes
5 minutes
cards.explain: The printed basic limit is 5 minutes.

cards.question: Which rating is the highest thrust available without a time limit
options: Maximum take off thrust
Maximum continuous thrust
Maximum climb thrust
cards.explain: MCT is the highest thrust with no time limit attached.

cards.question: The auto-throttle system works in thrust mode provided the autopilot vertical mode is of which kind
options: An altitude hold mode
A speed or Mach mode
A vertical speed mode
cards.explain: Thrust mode is entered only while the pitch channel is holding speed or Mach.

cards.question: The rearward throttle movement to the idle position during cruise-descent and flare carries which name
options: Rate feedback
Torque limiter
Retard bias
cards.explain: The page names the drive back to idle in those two phases the retard bias.

cards.question: In an auto-thrust system the required rating mode is brought in by which action
options: A servo motor driving the thrust levers forward
The pilot setting the thrust levers by hand
The flight management system commanding the levers
cards.explain: The pilot picks the rating mode by hand on the levers.

cards.question: In speed or Mach mode the auto-throttle system holds which quantity
options: A pre-selected rating for the flight phase
A pre-selected airspeed or Mach number
A pre-selected Mach trim setting
cards.explain: The mode holds the speed or Mach value selected by the pilot or by the FMS.

cards.question: What the auto-thrust system does in place of moving the throttles
options: It controls the throttle cables over the FADEC
It controls the thrust over the servo clutch
It controls the thrust over a data bus
cards.explain: Thrust is commanded over a data bus rather than by moving the levers.

cards.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system fitted. How can its throttles be moved?
options: Manually or by the servomotor
Only automatically
Only manually
cards.explain: With auto-thrust the levers move by hand only.

cards.question: What the position of the throttles determines on an aircraft with an auto-thrust system
options: The reference speed used by the speed mode of the system
The thrust rating and so the limits for that flight phase
The thrust demand sent straight to the fuel control unit
cards.explain: Lever position picks the rating, which sets the thrust limits for the phase.

cards.question: What supported the development of the auto-thrust system
options: The introduction of the para visual display systems
The electronic control of modern turbofan engines
The derating of the turbine inlet temperature limits
cards.explain: FADEC engine control made the auto-thrust system possible, and the functions are often built into it.

cards.question: Which demands the auto-thrust system was introduced to meet
options: Higher thrust ratings and a shorter take off run
Lower fuel burn and a wider speed envelope
Lower complexity and a better man/machine interface
cards.explain: It answered the demand for less complexity and a better man/machine interface.

cards.question: Which settings can be made in thrust mode
options: Thrust ratings or alpha floor
Reference speed or Mach number
Thrust ratings or thrust idle
cards.explain: Thrust mode sets either a rating, that is a thrust limit, or thrust idle.

cards.question: What is obtained when thrust idle is set
options: A thrust that just balances the aerodynamic drag
Only residual thrust from an idling engine
The lowest rating allowed for that flight phase
cards.explain: Thrust idle leaves only the residual thrust of the idling engine.

cards.question: The system is working in speed or Mach mode. Where does its reference speed come from?
options: The autoflight control panel or the EEC
The air data computer or the FMS
The autoflight control panel or the FMS
cards.explain: The reference is either set on the control panel or supplied by the FMS.

cards.question: Which low speed value the protective functions keep the aircraft away from
options: VR
V1
VLS
cards.explain: VLS is the low speed limit the system protects.

cards.question: With respect to what the overspeed protection works
options: Altitude and the slat/flap or landing gear configuration
Angle of attack and the pitch attitude during the approach
Airspeed and the thrust rating set for that flight phase
cards.explain: Overspeed protection takes account of altitude and the slat/flap or gear configuration.

cards.question: Which rule governs the control of airspeed by an autoflight system
options: The system with the smaller error controls it at any moment
Only one system can control it exclusively at any moment
Both systems control it together at any moment
cards.explain: Airspeed is controlled by one system at a time, never two.

cards.question: Which system holds priority for airspeed control
options: The auto-throttle or auto-thrust system
The autopilot or flight director pitch channel
The flight management system computer
cards.explain: Priority lies with the pitch channel of the autopilot or flight director.

cards.question: Why the maximum power available from a turbofan engine is reduced in service
options: To keep the thrust within the capacity of the data bus
To allow the thrust to be measured directly in flight
To reach acceptable life cycles for highly stressed parts
cards.explain: Continuous maximum thermodynamic power would wear the engine out quickly.

cards.question: Which parameter limits the thermodynamic power of a turbofan engine
options: The maximum low pressure rotor speed
The maximum engine pressure ratio
The maximum turbine inlet temperature
cards.explain: Turbine inlet temperature sets the thermodynamic ceiling, and is then derated.

cards.question: The auto-throttle is working in thrust mode. Why are N1 or EPR used as the reference values?
options: Thrust is a force and varies with the bleed air load in flight
Thrust is a force and is limited by the turbine inlet temperature
Thrust is a force and cannot be measured directly in flight
cards.explain: Thrust itself cannot be measured in flight, so derived parameters stand in for it.

cards.question: Which period most authorities apart from the FAA accept for engine failure performance calculations
options: 10 minutes of maximum take off thrust
5 minutes of maximum take off thrust
15 minutes of maximum continuous thrust
cards.explain: Those authorities allow 10 minutes of max take off thrust for that calculation.

cards.question: Conditions allow a reduced thrust take off. Why is that reduction recommended?
options: It shortens the take off run and lowers the noise footprint
It prolongs engine life and lowers the failure probability
It raises the thrust rating left available for the climb phase
cards.explain: Reduced thrust extends engine life and cuts the chance of a failure.

cards.question: How go around thrust is defined
options: The max climb rating corrected for the lower air density
The max continuous rating corrected for the higher altitude
The max take off rating corrected for the higher airspeed
cards.explain: It is the max take off rating adjusted for the greater airspeed in a go around.

cards.question: Idle thrust has to be set with care on every engine type, so what must it still guarantee?
options: Spool-up to go-around power in the regulated time
Minimum fuel flow throughout the whole descent
Bleed air delivery at the regulated cabin pressure
cards.explain: Idle may not be so low that the engine cannot spool up to go-around thrust in the required time.

cards.question: Idle thrust depends among other things on which characteristic of the engine fitted
options: Its compression characteristic
Its acceleration characteristic
Its bleed extraction characteristic
cards.explain: How fast the engine accelerates decides how low idle may be set.

cards.question: The permanent rating calculation takes account of which two inputs
options: Air data and bleed air demand
Thrust lever angle and fuel flow
Radio height and flap position
cards.explain: Those are the two inputs named for the rating calculation.

cards.question: The crew has made no manual selection of the phase used for the rating — what else can supply it?
options: The autothrottle computer unit
The engine control computer
The flight management system
cards.explain: The flight phase comes either from the pilot or from the FMS.

cards.question: Level change is engaged and the aircraft is descending — what thrust does the auto-throttle set?
options: The climb rating
The take-off rating
Idle
cards.explain: In a level change descent the auto-throttle sets idle thrust.

cards.question: Thrust mode is engaged on the auto-throttle — what type of control does the system itself apply?
options: Open loop control
Closed loop control
Cascaded loop control
cards.explain: In thrust mode the auto-throttle itself works open loop.

cards.question: Thrust mode has just been selected — what does the determined thrust rating then serve as?
options: The reference for fuel flow control by the hydromechanical unit
The reference for N2 closed loop control by the autothrottle computer
The reference for N1 closed loop control by the engine computer
cards.explain: The rating becomes the N1 reference that the engine computer then closes the loop on.

cards.question: The power management function works out the rating for which quantity
options: Each engine bleed demand
Each defined flight phase
Each throttle position
cards.explain: Power management maps throttle position to a rating, phase by phase is the other function.

cards.question: In an auto-thrust system which device turns lever position into the signal sent to the engine control unit
options: A rate gyro at the throttle quadrant
A torque limiter in the servo drive
An angle transducer at the levers
cards.explain: An angle transducer turns lever position into the TLA signal sent to the ECU.

cards.question: A technician finds no throttle servo motor on an auto-thrust aircraft — is that a defect?
options: Yes, without it the retard bias cannot operate
Yes, the servo must drive the levers to the rating
No, the levers here are not driven automatically
cards.explain: An auto-thrust system has no lever servo at all, so none is missing.

cards.question: The speed and Mach control structure is built on how many control loops
options: A single loop
Two cascaded loops
Three parallel loops
cards.explain: Speed and Mach control uses one single loop.

cards.question: The time response of the speed and Mach controller is fixed by which two factors
options: Thrust change dynamics and aircraft aerodynamics
Air data computer lag and thrust lever angle range
Servo rate feedback and clutch torque limiter setting
cards.explain: Those are the two things named as setting the controller response.

cards.question: The engine control input lever position is fed back to the servo — which effect is this meant to cut down?
options: Hysteresis from the mechanical components
Overshoot from the longitudinal acceleration
Drift from the air data computer
cards.explain: The position feedback is there to reduce mechanical hysteresis.

cards.question: Which components of the earlier auto-throttle installation become superfluous with auto-thrust
options: Servomotors, clutch mechanisms, cables and TOGA switches
Throttle levers, thrust limit displays and mode panels
Thrust rating computers, data buses and engine computers
cards.explain: Those mechanical items and the TOGA switches drop out with auto-thrust.

cards.question: Why does that relief only materialise when the pitch axis is also under autopilot control?
options: Thrust changes trim the aircraft out and automatic trim is needed
The autopilot has to hold the attitude while the levers are moving
The pitch channel supplies the reference speed to the thrust computer
cards.explain: Every thrust change puts the aircraft out of trim, and the automatic trim comes from the autopilot pitch channel.

cards.question: During an approach the angle of attack becomes extreme. Which protection acts and with which thrust?
options: Overspeed protection, with idle thrust
Alpha floor protection, with go around thrust
Low speed protection, with climb thrust
cards.explain: Alpha floor protection answers an extreme angle of attack by applying go around thrust.

cards.question: Which limits are still observed while the system works in the speed or Mach mode
options: The thrust ratings
The low speed limit
The take off rating
cards.explain: Thrust ratings are observed even when speed is being controlled.

cards.question: The pitch channel is given the task of holding a certain altitude. Which system then controls the airspeed?
options: The flight management system computer
The pitch channel, which keeps its priority
The auto-throttle or auto-thrust system
cards.explain: The pitch channel delegates speed control once it is busy with another task.

cards.question: The pitch channel is the system controlling the airspeed. In which mode is the auto-throttle then working?
options: Speed mode, setting the reference airspeed
Thrust mode, setting a rating or idle thrust
Mach mode, setting the cruise Mach number
cards.explain: When the pitch channel has the speed, the thrust system sits in thrust mode on a rating or idle.

cards.question: An aircraft takes off at a low mass from a long runway at a low air temperature. Which rating is recommended?
options: Maximum continuous thrust
Flexible take off thrust
Maximum take off thrust
cards.explain: Those conditions are exactly the case for the reduced, flexible take off rating.

cards.question: A go around is flown at go around thrust. For how long may that thrust be held?
options: Until climb thrust is set at the acceleration altitude
For as long as the approach has to be repeated
For the same period as maximum take off thrust
cards.explain: Go around thrust carries the same time limit as maximum take off thrust.

cards.question: The maximum take off thrust period has elapsed but maximum thrust is still needed. Which rating is used?
options: Maximum climb thrust
Maximum continuous thrust
Flexible take off thrust
cards.explain: That abnormal case is one of the two uses printed for maximum continuous thrust.

cards.question: The servo drive is running the throttles forward in thrust mode — when does the movement stop?
options: The power management value equals the rating reference
The thrust lever angle transducer reaches its forward stop
The engine reaches the commanded N1 at its control unit
cards.explain: The servo runs until the fed back power management value cancels the rating reference in the summing point.

cards.question: The aircraft climbs in thrust mode while pressure and temperature change — why do the throttles stay put?
options: Both functions work from the same input data
The retard bias holds the levers against the idle stop
The servo drive is declutched above the transition altitude
cards.explain: Both values move together, so their difference stays zero and no servo signal is produced.

cards.question: Two functions both work out ratings in thrust mode — what separates one from the other?
options: One uses the flight phase, the other the lever position
One works only in flight, the other works only on the ground
One uses the air data, the other uses the bleed demand
cards.explain: Rating calculation is keyed to the flight phase and power management to lever position.

cards.question: An aircraft has an auto-thrust system rather than an auto-throttle system — what is the practical difference?
options: Its ratings are worked out without an air data system
Its thrust is set without an engine control system
Its thrust levers are not moved by a servo system
cards.explain: The lever servo is exactly what an auto-thrust system does without.

cards.question: An integrating element is used in this mode in order to obtain which result
options: Less hysteresis in the linkage
A speed error of zero at the end
Faster throttle travel at large errors
cards.explain: Only an I-controller drives the remaining error to zero.

cards.question: Hysteresis is not limited and the speed error grows — what happens to the rate of throttle movement?
options: It rises in proportion to the error
It falls as the limiter takes over
It stays fixed until the error has gone
cards.explain: Rate feedback makes throttle speed directly proportional to the error.

cards.question: Adding the engine control input position feedback to the servo makes which further item necessary
options: A torque limiter behind the servo clutch
An electronic integrator ahead of the servo
A rate gyro ahead of the band pass filter unit
cards.explain: The feedback destroys the servo's own integrating action, so an electronic integrator must replace it.

cards.question: The compromise between precise speed control and smooth thrust is reached by feeding back which signal
options: Longitudinal acceleration
Actual pitch attitude angle
Actual throttle lever position
cards.explain: Longitudinal acceleration feedback is the means of reconciling the two demands.

cards.question: A higher reference has been commanded and the aircraft is still accelerating with the error already gone — what stops an overshoot?
options: The retard bias driving the throttles to idle
The acceleration bias on the speed error
The limiter holding the error at ten knots
cards.explain: The acceleration bias pulls the throttles back before the speed is reached.

cards.question: A head-on gust raises the indicated speed while the aircraft itself is slowing — what keeps the throttles still?
options: The integrator inside the speed controller
The hysteresis of the throttle control cables
The acceleration bias on the airspeed error
cards.explain: The acceleration bias cancels the false speed rise so the levers do not move.

cards.question: A gust suddenly raises the airspeed and no acceleration feedback is fitted — what would the throttles do?
options: An advance of the throttles
No movement of the throttles
A cut back of the throttles
cards.explain: The loop would read the gust as excess speed and close the throttles.

cards.question: On a jet aircraft the swept wing lowers which stability with respect to the lateral stability
options: The directional static stability margin
The vertical dynamic stability
The longitudinal dynamic stability
cards.explain: The swept wing costs longitudinal dynamic stability relative to the lateral.

cards.question: The oscillation caused by longitudinal dynamic instability takes place about which axes
options: The yaw and pitch axes
The pitch and roll axes
The yaw and roll axes
cards.explain: The motion is a combined yaw and roll oscillation.

cards.question: The angular velocity about the yaw axis is sensed by which device
options: An accelerometer
A rate gyro
A pitot probe
cards.explain: Yaw rate is picked up by a rate gyro.

cards.question: The band pass filter in the yaw damper suppresses which unwanted signals
options: Speed adaption signals from the air data computer
Rudder pedal movements made by the pilot
Structural oscillations sensed by the rate gyro
cards.explain: Airframe structural modes sensed by the gyro are filtered out.

cards.question: An all weather operation approval may be restricted in which two ways
options: In scope and in time
In crew and in aircraft
In altitude and in speed
cards.explain: Scope and time are the two named restrictions.

cards.question: Insufficient longitudinal dynamic stability spoils which two things
options: Controllability of the aircraft and passenger comfort
Accuracy of the ILS and of the automatic landing system
Range of the aircraft and the life of the engines
cards.explain: Both handling and passenger comfort suffer.

cards.question: A jet is rolling and slipping sideways in a repeating four second cycle — what is this motion called?
options: Dutch roll
Phugoid
Spiral dive
cards.explain: The combined roll and sideslip oscillation is named Dutch roll.

cards.question: A damper is fitted to stop the roll and slip motion of a swept wing jet — which surface does it move?
options: The rudder
The ailerons
The spoilers
cards.explain: The yaw damper works through the rudder.

cards.question: A yaw damper is required during which part of the flight
options: The flare
The take-off roll
The enroute phase
cards.explain: It is the cruise, at altitude, where the damper is needed.

cards.question: The yaw rate signal is adapted to airspeed in which manner
options: Directly proportional to the airspeed
Inversely proportional to airspeed
Independently of the airspeed
cards.explain: The adaptation is inversely proportional to speed.

cards.question: A constant yaw rate signal reaching the band pass filter is treated in which way
options: It is amplified
It is passed unchanged
It is damped out
cards.explain: A steady yaw rate is damped by the filter rather than fed through.

cards.question: The yaw damper actuator output is combined with which other demand at the mechanical summing point
options: The rudder pedal input
The speed adaption signal
The band pass filter output
cards.explain: Damper demand and pedal demand are summed before the rudder actuator.

cards.question: The yaw damper is making continuous rudder corrections in the cruise — what do the rudder pedals do?
options: They move in step with the rudder
They are locked until the damper drops out
Nothing, they stay where they are
cards.explain: In series mode a damper input does not move the pedals.

cards.question: An operator intends to fly in all weather conditions — which flight rules must its approval take in?
options: Instrument flight rules
Special visual flight rules
Visual flight rules
cards.explain: The approval must cover IFR flight before all weather operation can follow.

cards.question: An operator gains an all weather approval in its air operators certificate — what does that approval cover?
options: Each individual flight crew member
The aircraft type or series of types
Each individual aircraft registration
cards.explain: The approval is granted against a type or series of types.

cards.question: The all weather approval holds good for which runways
options: Only those listed in the operator's own route manual
Those approved by the authority for that category
Only those fitted with a roll out guidance system
cards.explain: Approval follows the authority's own runway classification for the category.

cards.question: Directional guidance for take-off in low visibility is covered by which subpart of the all weather operations requirements
options: Subpart 2
Subpart 4
Subpart 1
cards.explain: Subpart 4 deals with low visibility take-off guidance.

cards.question: Dutch roll grows into a problem at high altitude for which reason
options: The lift of the swept wing rises with altitude
The rudder travel available falls off with altitude
The damping aerodynamic forces fall with altitude
cards.explain: Thin air means weaker aerodynamic damping, so the oscillation is no longer suppressed naturally.

cards.question: The yaw damper becomes unserviceable during the cruise — what must then be done with the aircraft?
options: It has to climb to a higher altitude
It has to descend to a lower altitude
It has to slow to the minimum airspeed
cards.explain: Lower down the natural aerodynamic damping is strong enough.

cards.question: The aircraft accelerates in the cruise — what happens to the yaw rate signal passed on to the actuator?
options: It is cut back as the speed rises
It is built up as the speed rises
It is held at its take-off value
cards.explain: Inverse proportionality means the signal is reduced as speed increases.

cards.question: The pilot presses a rudder pedal while the yaw damper is working — how do the two demands reach the rudder?
options: They are added or subtracted at a summing point
The pedal demand switches the damper out of use
The damper demand overrides any pedal demand made
cards.explain: Both demands are summed, so neither cancels the other.

cards.question: ILS precision approaches are subdivided into which categories
options: CAT A to CAT C
CAT I to CAT III
CAT I to CAT VIII
cards.explain: The subdivision runs from CAT I to CAT III.

cards.question: A low visibility take-off is any take-off made below which runway visual range
options: 400 metres
300 metres
550 metres
cards.explain: Below 400 m RVR the departure counts as a low visibility take-off.

cards.question: The decision height is measured above which reference
options: The mean sea level datum
The runway threshold
The touch down zone
cards.explain: Decision height is referenced to the runway threshold.

cards.question: The alert height is defined by which party
options: The airport operator
The aircraft manufacturer
The national aviation authority
cards.explain: It is the manufacturer who sets the alert height.

cards.question: A system failure during an approach can be met by which three courses of action
options: Revert, divert or go straight in
Continue, descend or go straight in
Continue, revert or go around
cards.explain: Those three are the courses of action named.

cards.question: The reported runway visual range for departure is 350 metres — how is that take-off classified?
options: As an ordinary take-off
As a CAT II category take-off
As a low visibility take-off
cards.explain: 350 m is below the 400 m threshold, so the take-off is a LVTO.

cards.question: A CAT III b approach is being planned — what decision height condition applies?
options: No decision height and no visibility limit
Below 100 ft but not below 50 ft
Below 50 ft or no decision height
cards.explain: CAT III b covers decision heights under 50 ft and the no decision height case.

cards.question: An airport has no runway visual range measuring equipment — which value may be converted instead?
options: The decision height selected
The meteorological visibility
The cloud base height measured
cards.explain: Met visibility can be converted where no RVR equipment exists.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the decision height without the required visual reference — what must the crew do?
options: Continue down to the alert height
Revert to a lower category
Initiate a missed approach
cards.explain: Without the visual reference at decision height a missed approach is compulsory.

cards.question: The alert height is quoted in an aircraft's approach data — which approaches does it belong to?
options: CAT I approaches flown with the autopilot engaged
CAT III approaches with a fail-operational autoland
CAT II approaches with a fail-passive autoland fitted
cards.explain: The term belongs to fail-operational CAT III approaches.

cards.question: The value chosen for the alert height depends on what
options: The failure probability of the autoland
The reported runway visual range of the day
The landing distance available on the runway
cards.explain: The page ties the alert height to one thing only: the failure probability of the autoland system.

cards.question: The runway visual range refers to a pilot placed where
options: Over the threshold on the glide path
At the holding point beside the runway
On the centre line of the runway
cards.explain: The definition places the pilot on the runway centre line.

cards.question: The minimum runway visual range required for a CAT III approach depends on which two things
options: The equipment carried and the autoland capability
The decision height and the alert height selected
The runway length and the approach lighting fitted
cards.explain: Installed equipment and autoland capability together fix the minimum RVR.

cards.question: The crew needs to know the capability of their automatic landing system — where do they read it?
options: As an amber light on the ILS deviation alert
As an approach category on the flight annunciator
As a decision height index on the radio altimeter
cards.explain: Capability shows up as the available approach category on the flight mode annunciator.

cards.question: The crew decides to continue the planned approach after a failure — how far down may they go?
options: The alert height of the automatic landing system
The touch down zone marking on the runway
Its decision height or minimum descend altitude
cards.explain: Continue means fly the planned approach to its own minimum.

cards.question: A failure leaves the aircraft able to fly a lesser approach — what does reverting mean here?
options: Changing to a category the runway lighting supports
Changing to a category the remaining equipment allows
Changing to a category the reported weather would allow
cards.explain: Reversion is driven by what the surviving equipment can still do.

cards.question: A go around after a system fault is flown in order to do what
options: Reduce the landing weight before a second attempt
Investigate the failure and plan another approach
Allow the ground equipment to be reset by control
cards.explain: The go around buys time to look at the failure and reconfigure.

cards.question: Besides the type of failure, what else decides the action to be taken
options: The present position of the aircraft on approach
The category of runway lighting then in use
The age of the autoflight equipment then installed
cards.explain: Where the aircraft is on the approach matters as much as what failed.

cards.question: An approach is planned to a decision height of 150 ft with a reported visual range of 400 m — which category applies?
options: CAT II
CAT III a
CAT I
cards.explain: A decision height between 200 ft and 100 ft with at least 300 m visual range is CAT II.

cards.question: The reported runway visual range is 100 m and the decision height is 40 ft — which category covers it?
options: CAT III a
CAT III c
CAT III b
cards.explain: A decision height below 50 ft with a visual range between 200 m and 75 m falls in CAT III b.

cards.question: A failure appears in the redundant part of the autoland system above the alert height — what follows?
options: The approach is broken off and a go around flown
The approach reverts to the next higher category
The failure is ignored and the approach continued
cards.explain: Above the alert height such a failure forces a go around.

cards.question: Required ground equipment fails at a point below the alert height — what is the consequence?
options: A go around is initiated without any delay
The failure is ignored and the approach goes on
The approach reverts to a higher category minimum
cards.explain: At or below the alert height the failure is ignored.

cards.question: A CAT III A approach with a decision height below 100 ft is flown with a fail-passive landing system — what is the minimum visual range?
cards.explain: Every CAT III A column in the table shows 200 m.

cards.question: The automatic landing system is fail-passive and the decision height is below 50 ft — what visual range may be flown?
options: It is not authorised at all
It is authorised down to 75 metres
It is authorised down to 125 metres
cards.explain: In the fail-passive column of the table the row for a decision height below 50 ft reads 'Not authorized'.

cards.question: A CAT III B approach to a decision height below 50 ft with a fail-operational system and a fail-passive roll-out system needs which minimum visual range
cards.explain: Under the fail-operational landing system, the column for a fail-passive roll-out system gives 125 m at a decision height below 50 ft.

cards.question: An approach flown with no decision height is authorised only where the roll-out system holds which standard
options: Fail-safe
Fail-operational
Fail-passive
cards.explain: In the no decision height row only the fail-operational roll-out column carries a value; the fail-passive roll-out column reads 'Not authorized'.

cards.question: Two aircraft have a fail-operational landing system, one with a roll-out system and one without, both at a decision height below 50 ft — how do their minima differ?
options: Only the one without roll-out may fly the approach
Only the one with roll-out may fly the approach
Both may fly it to the same visual range
cards.explain: Without a roll-out system that decision height is not authorised at all.

cards.question: Reversion to another approach category may be considered only where the failure happens in which band
options: Above 1000 ft above the ground
At or below the alert height
Below 1000 ft above the ground
cards.explain: The general rule puts the reversion decision above 1000 ft AGL.

cards.question: A fail-operational autoflight system fails below 1000 ft but above the alert height — what action follows?
options: The approach continues to decision height
A reversion to CAT I is flown
A go around is executed
cards.explain: In that band any failure of a fail-operational system means a go around.

cards.question: After a failure the weather allows a higher minimum and enough autoflight capability remains — what may the crew then do?
options: Descend below the alert height
Continue down to the original minimum
Fly that approach category instead
cards.explain: Both conditions together allow the higher minimum approach to be flown.

cards.question: The objective of CAT II autoflight operation is to hold which level of safety
options: One set by the aircraft manufacturer alone
One equivalent to manual flight operation
One above that of manual flight operation
cards.explain: The aim is equivalence with manual operation, under worse weather.

cards.question: In a fail-safe system the output signal after a failure takes which state
options: An arbitrary but safe state
The last valid state before failure
A defined and equally safe state
cards.explain: Fail-safe gives an arbitrary state that is nevertheless safe.

cards.question: In a fail-passive system the output signal once the system has failed takes which state
options: A state within acceptable limits
A well defined failure state
An arbitrary but safe state
cards.explain: Fail-passive gives a defined, known failure state.

cards.question: The CAT II safety level depends partly on what the crew can see — which outside aid is named?
options: Approach and runway lighting
Ground radar surveillance cover
Runway friction measurement
cards.explain: Outside visual cues from the approach and runway lighting are listed.

cards.question: The aircraft reaches the decision height on a CAT II approach — what is the position regarding a manual landing?
options: It is allowed but is not compulsory
It is forbidden in every case
It is compulsory in every single case
cards.explain: CAT II minima permit a manual landing without requiring one.

cards.question: CAT III autoflight operation holds a safety level equivalent to manual flight under which conditions
options: The worst weather and visibility
Normal weather and visibility conditions
Conditions no worse than CAT II minima
cards.explain: CAT III carries that equivalence into the worst conditions.

cards.question: From a CAT III decision height a manual landing is possible to what extent
options: It is compulsory for the pilot flying
It is possible but is not compulsory
It is normally not possible at all
cards.explain: Unlike the lower categories, CAT III leaves no room for a manual landing from the decision height.

cards.question: An aircraft is to be certified for CAT III operation — which equipment is compulsory?
options: An automatic or hybrid landing system
A flight director approach coupler
A head-up ground roll guidance display
cards.explain: CAT III requires an automatic or hybrid landing system.

cards.question: How does the reliability demanded of CAT III systems compare with that demanded for CAT II?
options: It is somewhat lower still
It is considerably higher
It is very much the same
cards.explain: CAT III calls for considerably higher reliability than CAT II.

cards.question: A designer cuts the number of components in a system — why does availability improve?
options: Fewer components leave a faster response time
Fewer components leave fewer ways to fail
Fewer components leave a lower system weight
cards.explain: Less complexity means fewer ways for the system to fail.

cards.question: For CAT III operation the regulations demand redundant systems showing what
options: Automatic reset after every detected failure
Identical hardware from a single manufacturer
Defined behaviour for any conceivable failure
cards.explain: The behaviour at every conceivable failure must be defined.

cards.question: To behave passively when a fault appears a system needs which provision during normal operation
options: Periodic self testing carried out at every engine start
Manual selection of the standby channel by the crew
Permanent monitoring with suppression of any failure
cards.explain: Continuous monitoring plus suppression is what makes passive behaviour possible.

cards.question: A system that stays operative after a failure is described by which term
options: Failure suppressed
Failure tolerant
Failure neutral
cards.explain: Such a system is called failure tolerant.

cards.question: With passive redundancy a drop out of the main system causes what
options: A manual selection of the remaining system
An automatic shut down of all parallel systems
An automatic change to the redundant system
cards.explain: The change over happens automatically.

cards.question: In passive redundancy the system held in reserve carries which name
options: The hot standby system
The monitored main system
The active parallel system
cards.explain: The reserve system is called the hot standby.

cards.question: A main channel drops out and a reserve takes over automatically — what can be said of the system function afterwards?
options: The complete functionality is restored
Only the monitored functions are restored
Only half the functionality is restored
cards.explain: The standby restores the full function after the change over.

cards.question: For decision heights below 100 ft the two ILS receivers must feed the pilot stations in which way
options: Each pilot station from its own receiver
Both pilot stations from the same receiver
Both receivers into one combined display
cards.explain: The two stations must be fed from separate receivers.

cards.question: A decision height of 50 ft or greater is planned — what standard must the automatic landing system hold?
options: Fail-operational
Fail-safe
Fail-passive
cards.explain: At 50 ft and above a fail-passive landing system is enough.

cards.question: A decision height below 50 ft is planned — what standard must the automatic go-around system hold?
options: Fail-safe
Fail-operational
Fail-passive
cards.explain: The go-around system is required to be fail-passive there.

cards.question: For a no decision height approach the automatic ground roll control may hold which standards
options: Fail-operational or fail-passive
Fail-passive or fail-safe
Fail-operational or fail-safe
cards.explain: Either standard is accepted for the ground roll function.

cards.question: An approach with no decision height is to be flown — what provision is required for speed control?
options: Head-up speed guidance
