Manual throttle control only
Automatic throttle control
cards.explain: Automatic throttle control is on the no decision height equipment list.

cards.question: A CAT III A decision height is set so that the crew can judge which thing
options: Whether the autoland has dropped to fail-passive
Whether the roll out can be supervised visually throughout
Whether touch down will fall in the touch down zone
cards.explain: At CAT III A the crew can still see whether the aircraft will land in the zone.

cards.question: A CAT III B minimum is set so as to secure which crew capability
options: Visual confirmation of the touch down point
Visual acquisition of the approach light system
Visual supervision of the roll out
cards.explain: The CAT III B minimum exists so the roll out can be watched.

cards.question: Automatic guidance of the roll out until taxi speed is reached is demanded for which categories
options: CAT III B and CAT III C
CAT III A and CAT III B
CAT II and CAT III A
cards.explain: Flare and roll out guidance to taxi speed is listed for CAT III B and C.

cards.question: One of several parallel channels drops out and the output signal is unaffected — which redundancy is in use?
options: Monitored redundancy
Active redundancy
Passive redundancy
cards.explain: Only active redundancy keeps the output going with no switch over.

cards.question: An operator wants to certify a CAT II aircraft with no automatic throttle system — what must be shown?
options: That the engines accelerate within the regulated time
That speed can be held by hand without undue workload
That the autopilot can hold speed within ten knots
cards.explain: The way out is an in-flight demonstration of manual speed control.

cards.question: The number of ILS receivers and radio altimeters may have to be raised for which reason
options: To give an alert height indication at both stations
To give fail-operational capability where required
To give a roll out guidance display at both stations
cards.explain: Extra sensors are what makes a fail-operational installation possible.

cards.question: The decision height planned is below 50 ft — what standard must the automatic landing system then meet?
options: Fail-safe
Fail-passive
Fail-operational
cards.explain: Below 50 ft only a fail-operational landing or hybrid system will do.

cards.question: Which wheel provision is required for an approach flown with no decision height
options: An anti-skid braking system
An autobrake disarm warning
A carbon brake wear indicator
cards.explain: An anti-skid braking system is one of the items listed for no decision height.

cards.question: A no decision height approach is planned — what standard must the automatic landing system and the go-around system meet?
options: Fail-operational landing with fail-passive go-around
Fail-operational landing with fail-operational go-around
Fail-passive landing with fail-operational go-around
cards.explain: The landing system must be fail-operational while the go-around stays fail-passive.

cards.question: A fail-passive approach system without automatic landing is acceptable at 50 ft provided the aeroplane holds which property
options: A low approach speed and good manoeuvrability
A high approach speed and a long wheel base
A fail-operational go-around capability fitted
cards.explain: Those handling properties are what make the manual landing acceptable.

cards.question: Which system is defined as one comprising an automatic and/or a hybrid landing system
options: the guidance system
the landing system
the flight control system
cards.explain: That wording is the definition of the flight control system.

cards.question: Which equipment the term landing system covers
options: onboard equipment only
ground equipment only
onboard and ground equipment
cards.explain: The definition limits the term landing system to equipment carried on board.

cards.question: Which failure of a control surface can occur on a fail safe flight control system
options: a slow runaway of the control surface
a hard over of the control surface
a complete loss of control surface authority
cards.explain: A hard over of a control surface is named as the most important feature of the fail safe failure case.

cards.question: The autopilot runs a surface hard over while the aircraft is enroute. Within which time must the pilot be able to take over control?
options: 3 seconds
10 seconds
1 second
cards.explain: FAR 25 allows 3 seconds for the takeover enroute.

cards.question: Which kind of redundancy the parallel operation of two fail safe autopilots shows
options: standby redundancy
active redundancy
passive redundancy
cards.explain: Two fail safe autopilots working in parallel are described as active redundancy.

cards.question: Which arrangement inside one and the same autopilot gives fail passive behaviour
options: three actuators driven by a single channel
two independent channels working in parallel
two autopilots coupled rigidly together
cards.explain: Fail passive behaviour can come from two independent channels inside one autopilot.

cards.question: What the autopilot does when the comparison of its two channels detects a failure
options: it limits its authority
it reverts to one channel
it disengages
cards.explain: A detected failure disengages the autopilot.

cards.question: Which items the landing system comprises in accordance with JAR-AWO 321
options: all sensors, antennas and ground stations
all instruments, displays and ground transmitters
all sensors, instruments and power supplies
cards.explain: The equipment named in the definition is sensors, instruments and power supplies.

cards.question: What the differing architectures of the two major transport aircraft manufacturers are meant to realize
options: a lower weight of the autopilot installation
a common standard of autopilot engagement
failure modes acceptable for CAT III operation
cards.explain: The architectures exist to produce the fail passive or fail operational modes that CAT III operation accepts.

cards.question: Two fail passive single systems are operated together in dual operation. Which behaviour does the resulting system show?
options: fail safe behaviour
fail operational behaviour
fail passive behaviour
cards.explain: Dual operation of fail passive single systems yields fail operational behaviour.

cards.question: Why a hard over is not suppressed by a fail safe flight control system
options: because it cannot recognize the failure
because its servos have no force limiter
because its actuators have no clutch
cards.explain: Suppression is impossible because the system has no way of recognizing the failure.

cards.question: How the effect of a failure is limited on a fail safe system
options: by reducing the authority of the servos
by comparing the two autopilot channels
by voting between three actuator outputs
cards.explain: Reducing servo authority is the means given for limiting the failure effect.

cards.question: Under which condition authority limitation is allowed at all
options: only if a second autopilot is installed
only if the servos carry a torque limiter
only if a manual flight control system exists
cards.explain: A manual flight control system able to over-power the autopilot is the condition for allowing authority limitation.

cards.question: Which effect a failure of a fail passive flight control system has on the trim state and the flight path
options: neither of them is changed considerably
both of them are changed considerably
the trim state changes but the flight path does not
cards.explain: A fail passive failure leaves the trim state unchanged and causes no considerable deviation from flight path or attitude.

cards.question: What can no longer be carried out once a fail passive flight control system has failed
options: an automatic landing
a manual go around
an ILS approach
cards.explain: The printed definition says an automatic landing can no longer be performed.

cards.question: The fail passive automatic flight control system fails during an approach. What must happen then?
options: the system continues the approach and landing by itself
the pilot has to take over the control of the aircraft
the second autopilot takes over control and lands
cards.explain: On failure of a fail passive system the pilot has to take over control.

cards.question: How the independence of two autopilots working in dual operation is achieved
options: by one common computer serving both of the channels
by a common power supply feeding two sets of sensors
by separate supplies, sensors, computers and actuators
cards.explain: Independence comes from everything being separate: supplies, sensors, computers, actuators and cable ducts.

cards.question: Which causes make the rigidly coupled actuators of two autopilots work against each other
options: different reference values in the two sensor units
tolerances, pressure differences or poor adjustment
a delay between the two autopilot computers
cards.explain: Force conflicts are attributed to tolerances, pressure differences and poor adjustment.

cards.question: What is done for safety reasons in the two channels of one fail passive autopilot
options: the same hardware and the same programs in both lanes
one of the two channels is left unpowered as a spare
different hardware and different programming languages
cards.explain: The channels differ in hardware and in the programming language of the identical programs.

cards.question: A dual channel autopilot has produced an output in each of its channels. What happens to the two signals before the actuator sees them?
options: they are added together and then released
they are sent on separately to two actuators
they are compared for validity and then released
cards.explain: The outputs are compared for validity, and only then released to the actuator.

cards.question: By which three means fail passive behaviour is reached in a dual channel autopilot
options: mechanical voting, torque limiting and authority limiting
parallel processing, mutual monitoring and output comparison
active redundancy, crosstalk and autopilot synchronisation
cards.explain: Those three together are what makes the dual channel autopilot fail passive.

cards.question: An autopilot that detects its own failure and disengages itself is operated on its own. Which behaviour does the system then show?
options: fail operational behaviour
fail passive behaviour
fail safe behaviour
cards.explain: A single system able to detect and remove its own failure gives fail passive behaviour in single operation.

cards.question: A manufacturer limits the authority of its autopilot servos, but the aircraft has no manual control path strong enough to overrule the autopilot. Why is that not acceptable?
options: because the autopilot could then not recognize its own hard over
because the servos would then not reach their full travel range
because the pilot could then not over-power the autopilot
cards.explain: Authority limitation relies on the pilot being able to apply strong inputs and over-power the autopilot manually.

cards.question: A single autopilot suffers a failure that it cannot recognize at all. Which failure mode is that, and what can the control surface do?
options: fail passive, and the surface keeps its position
fail operational, and the landing is continued
fail safe, and a hard over of the surface is possible
cards.explain: Inability to recognize a failure is the mark of the fail safe mode, in which a hard over of the control surface can occur.

cards.question: A fail passive system must be able to disengage itself. How does it recognize that it has a failure?
options: by comparing the two autopilot computers with each other
by monitoring the hydraulic pressure at the actuator
by comparing the surface position with the commanded position
cards.explain: Recognition rests on the electrical comparison of actual surface position with commanded actuator position.

cards.question: During dual operation the two autopilot actuators try to deflect one surface in opposite directions. What does the surface do?
options: it follows the faster of the two actuators
it runs to its full deflection
it stays in its position
cards.explain: Opposing actuator commands are voted out, so the surface holds its position.

cards.question: Two fail safe autopilots drive one surface in dual operation. What does the feel system contribute?
options: the torque limit applied at the actuator clutch
the neutral reference for the deflection limiter
the third signal the mid-value voter needs
cards.explain: Mid-value voting needs three inputs, and with two autopilots the feel system provides the missing one.

cards.question: A fail passive autopilot built from two channels sends its signal to only one actuator. What follows for force conflicts?
options: force conflicts have to be limited by a voter
no force conflict can arise
a force conflict arises at every input
cards.explain: With a single actuator there is nothing to work against, so no force conflict occurs.

cards.question: In which respect a dual channel fail passive autopilot differs from two parallel fail safe autopilots
options: it drives three actuators and needs a mid-value voter
it drives two actuators and needs a torque limiter
it drives one actuator only and needs no mechanical voting
cards.explain: Parallel fail safe autopilots need mechanical voting against force conflicts, while the dual channel autopilot drives a single actuator and does not.

cards.question: What a fail operational flight control system does at any failure below the alert height
options: it continues the approach and lands automatically
it disengages and hands the approach to the pilot
it freezes the control surfaces in their position
cards.explain: Below the alert height the fail operational system carries on to an automatic landing and roll out.

cards.question: Of which two parts a hybrid landing system consists
options: a fail safe landing system and a mechanical voter
a fail operational landing system and a second autopilot
a fail passive landing system and a guidance system
cards.explain: The main system is a fail passive automatic landing system and it is supported by an independent guidance system.

cards.question: Which systems are usually used as the supporting system of a hybrid landing system
options: radio altimeter systems
yaw damper systems
head up guidance systems
cards.explain: Head up guidance systems are the usual supporting systems.

cards.question: Which failure mode the automatic landing system has after a failure has occurred
options: fail passive
fail safe
fail operational
cards.explain: The remaining system is fail passive once a failure has happened.

cards.question: Why mechanical voting has to be applied in triple operation
options: to detect a hard over of a surface
to limit the authority of the servos
to prevent force conflicts
cards.explain: Voting is applied for the same reason as in dual operation: to prevent force conflicts.

cards.question: Two autopilots run in parallel and each one disengages itself on its own failure. Which kind of redundancy does that architecture show?
options: active redundancy
passive redundancy
standby redundancy
cards.explain: This architecture is described as passive redundancy.

cards.question: The main system of a hybrid landing system fails on the approach. What does the supporting guidance system then allow?
options: automatic continuation of approach and landing
an automatic go around at the alert height
manual continuation of approach and landing
cards.explain: The supporting system lets the crew carry on manually after the main system has failed.

cards.question: Of which units the hybrid built from fail safe autopilots consists
options: three fail safe autopilots and one head up display
one fail safe autopilot and two flight director systems
two fail safe autopilots and one flight director system
cards.explain: It is built from two fail safe autopilots plus at least one flight director system.

cards.question: Of which units the hybrid system built around a fail passive autopilot consists
options: one fail passive autopilot and one flight director system
two fail passive autopilots and one flight director system
one fail passive autopilot and two head up displays
cards.explain: This architecture uses a single fail passive autopilot with at least one flight director system.

cards.question: A single autopilot fails below the alert height in a fail operational system. What can the crew still expect of the automatic system?
options: the system disengages and the approach has to be abandoned
the approach continues but the landing has to be flown manually
approach, flare, landing and roll out are completed automatically
cards.explain: Fail operational means the whole sequence down to roll out is still flown automatically.

cards.question: A fail operational system has already suffered one failure. What would a second failure mean now?
options: the landing is still completed, as the system stays fail operational
a hard over may occur, as the system is now fail safe
the pilot must take over, as the system is now fail passive
cards.explain: Once fail passive, a further failure means no automatic landing and the pilot has to take over.

cards.question: In a triple operation system one autopilot output drifts away from the other two. What does the mid- value voter do to the surface?
options: the surface follows the odd output until that autopilot is off
the surface follows the middle actuator and the odd output is lost
the surface takes the average, so the odd output shifts it
cards.explain: Mid-value voting passes only the middle signal, so a single deviating output is suppressed.

cards.question: Why two fail passive autopilots in parallel give a fail operational system
options: because both actuators drive the control surface together
because each one detects its own failure and disengages itself
because the two outputs are voted mechanically against each other
cards.explain: Self-detection and self-disengagement leave the healthy autopilot in control, which is fail operational behaviour.

cards.question: Two fail passive autopilots work in parallel on the same control train. Why can no force conflict arise there?
options: because only one actuator drives the surface at a time
because a mid-value voter selects the middle of the signals
because a torque limiter is fitted in each actuator clutch
cards.explain: At any instance only one actuator is driving, so nothing can work against it.

cards.question: One of two parallel fail passive autopilots detects its own failure during an automatic landing. What happens next?
options: both of them disengage and the pilot takes over
it disengages itself and the other one keeps control
the faulty one is voted out by the mechanical voter
cards.explain: The failed autopilot takes itself out and the remaining one continues to control the aircraft.

cards.question: Of the two fail operational architectures described, one of them needs mechanical voting to avoid force conflicts
options: triple operation with three fail safe autopilots
single operation of one fail passive autopilot
parallel operation of two fail passive autopilots
cards.explain: Three parallel fail safe autopilots drive their actuators together and need voting; two fail passive autopilots never drive together.

cards.question: Which behaviour the autopilot system of a hybrid built from two fail safe autopilots shows
options: fail passive, augmented by a flight director
fail safe, augmented by an auto-thrust system
fail operational, augmented by a flight director
cards.explain: Two fail safe autopilots make the autopilot system fail passive, and the flight director augments it.

cards.question: The autopilot of a hybrid landing installation fails on short final. How can the landing still be completed?
options: manually, following the supporting guidance system
automatically, after the voter has selected a channel
automatically, by the second autopilot taking over
cards.explain: The hybrid system's reserve is manual flight on the supporting guidance system, not a second automatic system.

cards.question: Why a hybrid landing system counts as fail operational although its automatic landing system is only fail passive
options: the guidance system allows the landing to be continued manually
the automatic landing system becomes fail operational below the alert height
the two autopilots of the system are voted mechanically
cards.explain: The overall capability is kept by the independent guidance system letting the crew finish the landing by hand.

cards.question: Where the autoland warning is displayed
options: in the glare shield, in the pilot's view
on the engine display of the lower screen
on the overhead panel above the pilots
cards.explain: It sits in the glare shield, inside the pilot's field of view.

cards.question: Which colour the autoland warning has
options: amber
red
white
cards.explain: The autoland warning is a red warning.

cards.question: Where components influencing CAT II and CAT III approach capability are specially marked
options: in column 1 of the operations manual part B
in column 3 of the minimum equipment list
in chapter 22 of the aircraft maintenance manual
cards.explain: The MEL marks them in its column 3.

cards.question: The capability logic has checked the serviceability of all required systems. Which supplies does it count as well?
options: the independent hydraulic and electrical power supplies
the independent pneumatic and electrical power supplies
the independent hydraulic and pneumatic power supplies
cards.explain: The number of independent hydraulic and electrical power supplies is counted as well.

cards.question: What the degree of redundancy determines
options: the decision height of the approach
the failure mode of the system
the alert height of the approach
cards.explain: Redundancy decides whether the system is fail safe, fail passive or fail operational.

cards.question: One fail passive autopilot or flight director is operational and the redundancy is limited. Which capability is reached?
options: CAT 3 SINGLE
CAT 2
CAT 1
cards.explain: With one fail passive autopilot or flight director and limited redundancy only CAT I is available.

cards.question: Which condition gives a capability of CAT 2
options: one fail passive autopilot with sufficient redundancy
two fail passive autopilots with sufficient redundancy
one fail passive autopilot with limited redundancy
cards.explain: CAT 2 needs one fail passive autopilot plus sufficient redundancy.

cards.question: The autoland warning comes on during an automatic approach. Which reaction is the normal one?
options: the initiation of a go around
a continuation of the approach to CAT I minima
the disengagement of one autopilot
cards.explain: A go around is the normal response to the autoland warning.

cards.question: The autoland warning comes on and the runway is clearly in sight. What is possible besides a go around?
options: an automatic landing
a manual landing
a second automatic approach
cards.explain: With visual conditions permitting, the landing may be completed manually.

cards.question: Above which difference of radio height between two radio altimeters the autoland warning comes on
options: 100 ft
10 ft
50 ft
cards.explain: The warning condition is a radio height difference of more than 10 ft.

cards.question: Required ground equipment fails while the aircraft is still above the alert height and the capability changes. What has to be done?
options: a go around has to be initiated
the autopilot has to be disengaged and the approach flown manually
the approach may be continued to CAT I minima
cards.explain: A capability change above the alert height requires a go around.

cards.question: A single failure occurs below the alert height and degrades the failure mode from fail operational to fail passive. What happens to the displayed capability?
options: it is replaced by a red warning
it is no longer changed
it drops by one category
cards.explain: Below the alert height the capability is frozen even though the failure mode degrades.

cards.question: A single failure below the alert height degrades the failure mode, yet the capability stays as it was. Why is it kept?
options: because the autoflight system still performs its duty
because the ground equipment can no longer be monitored
because the autopilot can no longer be disengaged
cards.explain: The capability stays because the system is still doing its job after the single failure.

cards.question: One fail passive autopilot and one auto-thrust system are operational. Which capability is displayed?
options: CAT 3 SINGLE
CAT 3 DUAL
CAT 2
cards.explain: That combination gives CAT III A, displayed as CAT 3 SINGLE.

cards.question: Two fail passive autopilots and one auto-thrust system are operational. Which capability is displayed and which failure mode does the system have?
options: CAT 3 SINGLE, and the system is fail passive
CAT 3 DUAL, and the system is fail operational
CAT 2, and the system is fail operational
cards.explain: Two fail passive autopilots make the total system fail operational and give CAT 3 DUAL for CAT III B.

cards.question: Why does the autoland warning demand action at once rather than merely being noted by the crew?
options: because the warning repeats every ten seconds
because it is a red warning
because the warning sits on the glare shield
cards.explain: Its red colour is what classes it as requiring immediate action.

cards.question: What the collective pitch lever controls
options: the main rotor lift
the velocity vector
the tail rotor thrust
cards.explain: The collective pitch lever is the lift control.

cards.question: What the cyclic pitch stick controls
options: the main rotor lift
the velocity vector
the tail rotor thrust
cards.explain: The cyclic stick controls the velocity vector.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is moved forward. Which movement of the helicopter results?
options: a tail down movement
a nose down movement
a left sideward movement
cards.explain: Forward cyclic gives a nose down movement.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is moved rearward. Which movement of the helicopter results?
options: a right sideward movement
a nose down movement
a tail down movement
cards.explain: Rearward cyclic gives a tail down movement.

cards.question: Through which servo the pedals act
options: the front servo
the LH servo
the yaw servo
cards.explain: Pedal inputs pass through the yaw servo.

cards.question: What a twist grip throttle is
options: a rotary trim controller at the cyclic pitch stick
a rotary rpm controller at the collective pitch lever
a friction lock fitted at the pedal unit
cards.explain: It is the rotary rpm control sitting on the collective pitch lever.

cards.question: On which helicopters a twist grip throttle is found
options: on those powered by a piston engine
on those powered by a turbine engine
on those with a counter clockwise rotor
cards.explain: The twist grip throttle belongs to piston engined helicopters.

cards.question: Which stability a helicopter has around its longitudinal, lateral and vertical axes
options: positive stability around the longitudinal axis only
no positive stability around any of them
positive stability around the vertical axis only
cards.explain: The helicopter has no positive stability about any of the three axes.

cards.question: Which sensors a helicopter stabilization system uses
options: rate gyros
accelerometers
pressure transducers
cards.explain: Rotation rates about pitch, roll and yaw are sensed by rate gyros.

cards.question: The collective pitch lever is raised. How is the pitch angle of the main rotor blades changed?
options: on all blades at once and by the same amount
on half of the blades at once and by the same amount
on each blade in turn and by a different amount
cards.explain: Collective input acts on every blade simultaneously and equally.

cards.question: How the cyclic stick produces a variation of the rotor blade pitch angle
options: by changing the pitch of all the blades equally
by tilting the main rotor plane around the X or Y axis
by changing the thrust produced by the tail rotor
cards.explain: The cyclic tilts the rotor plane about the X or Y axis.

cards.question: Only the front servo is driven by a control input. Around which axis is the rotor plane tilted?
options: the vertical axis, Z-Z'
the lateral axis, Y-Y'
the longitudinal axis, X-X'
cards.explain: The front servo tilts the rotor plane about the lateral Y-Y' axis.

cards.question: Which servos tilt the rotor plane around the longitudinal axis
options: the front and yaw servos
the front and LH servos
the LH and RH servos
cards.explain: The LH and RH servos work the longitudinal X-X' axis.

cards.question: What the up and down movement of the swash plate is called
options: lateral pitch variation
collective pitch variation
cyclic pitch variation
cards.explain: That up and down movement is the collective pitch variation.

cards.question: The swash plate is moved up from its initial position. Which quantity at the rotor changes?
options: the angle of attack of the rotor blades
the length of the blade lever rods
the rotational speed of the main rotor
cards.explain: Moving the swash plate up and down alters the blades' angle of attack.

cards.question: What decides about which axis the swash plate is tilted
options: the position of the two pedal units
the movement direction of the cyclic stick
the amount of collective pitch applied
cards.explain: The tilt axis follows the direction in which the cyclic stick is moved.

cards.question: The swash plate is to be tilted about the lateral axis. Which servo is energized on its own?
options: the LH servo
the front servo
the yaw servo
cards.explain: Only the front servo is energized for a tilt about the lateral axis.

cards.question: A sideward movement is commanded. How are the LH and RH servos driven for it?
options: concurrently, with equal signals in opposite directions
one after the other, with signals of different magnitude
concurrently, with equal signals in the same direction
cards.explain: They get equal signals at the same time, but run opposite to each other.

cards.question: Which movement of the swash plate a diagonal cyclic stick movement produces
options: an up and down movement without any tilt
a combined tilt about both of the axes
a tilt about the lateral axis only
cards.explain: A diagonal input tilts the swash plate proportionally about both axes at once.

cards.question: The pilot presses one of the pedals. What is changed at the tail rotor?
options: the rotational speed of the tail rotor
the diameter of the tail rotor disc
the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
cards.explain: The pedals set tail rotor blade pitch.

cards.question: Around which axis the tail rotor allows the helicopter to be controlled
options: the vertical axis
the lateral axis
the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust gives control about the vertical axis, that is yaw control.

cards.question: What gives an aeroplane the stability a helicopter lacks
options: the rate gyros feeding its stabilization computer
the dihedral and sweep of the wing and the stabilizers
the attenuation signals sent to its control servos
cards.explain: Wing dihedral and sweep together with the stabilizers give the fixed wing aircraft its stability.

cards.question: Why stabilization systems have been developed for helicopters
options: to allow the main rotor to be driven at a lower speed
to let the pilot concentrate on navigation and supervision
to raise the maximum forward speed of the helicopter
cards.explain: They relieve the pilot of the constant control task so he can attend to navigation and supervision.

cards.question: The SCAS has received a rate signal from one of the gyros. What does it drive with its attenuation signal?
options: the servo valves of the control servos
the main servo input levers directly
the trim actuators of the cyclic stick
cards.explain: The attenuation signals go to the servo valves of the control servos.

cards.question: Which stability the helicopter shows once the stabilization system is working
options: neutral stability
positive stability
negative stability
cards.explain: With the stabilization system active the helicopter exhibits neutral stability.

cards.question: What holds the cable system of the main rotor controls in position
options: the control servos
the motion transducers
the trim actuators
cards.explain: The control servos hold that cable system in position.

cards.question: The control servos of a stabilized helicopter are driven by the SCAS computer. What do they move?
options: the swash plate directly
the main servo input levers
the trim control panel switches
cards.explain: The control servos act on the main servo input levers.

cards.question: The pilot returns the cyclic stick to its neutral position. What does the output of the motion transducer do?
options: it reaches its maximum
it becomes zero
it reverses its sign
cards.explain: At neutral the motion transducer output is zero.

cards.question: From which sources the stored reference value is obtained
options: from the motion transducers, via the trim actuator units
from the rate gyros, via the stability augmentation computer
from the attitude and heading gyros, via the synchronizer
cards.explain: It comes from the pitch-roll attitude gyro and the heading gyro through the synchronizer control unit.

cards.question: To which fixed wing function this way of controlling the helicopter is comparable
options: to the yaw damper
to control wheel steering
to the autothrottle
cards.explain: The text compares it to control wheel steering.

cards.question: What is compared with each other in the flight path control of a helicopter
options: the trim signals with the outputs of the motion transducers
the commanded path with the signals of the three rate gyros
the planned path and altitude with the momentary path parameters
cards.explain: Planned path and altitude are compared against the momentary path parameters.

cards.question: A flight path error has been worked out on a helicopter flying an upper mode. Where is it superimposed on the stabilization signals?
options: in the SCAS computer
in the synchronizer control unit
in the trim control panel
cards.explain: The superposition happens inside the SCAS computer.

cards.question: Through which item each trim signal reaches its trim actuator
options: the respective motion transducer
the synchronizer control unit
the stability augmentation computer
cards.explain: Trim signals pass through the synchronizer control unit on their way to the trim actuator.

cards.question: A helicopter is to be moved along its velocity vector without any change of lift. Which control is used and what does it do to the rotor plane?
options: the cyclic stick, which raises the whole rotor plane
the cyclic stick, which tilts the rotor plane
the collective lever, which tilts the rotor plane
cards.explain: Velocity vector control belongs to the cyclic stick, which works by tilting the rotor plane.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is moved to the left-hand side. Which servo stays unenergized and which movement results?
options: the front servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
the front servo, and the helicopter moves nose down
the LH servo, and the helicopter moves left sideward
cards.explain: A sideward input leaves the front servo unenergized and moves the helicopter sideward to the left.

cards.question: The helicopter is to be moved sideward to the right. Around which axis must the swash plate tilt, and which units do it?
options: the longitudinal axis, by the front servo alone
the lateral axis, by the front servo alone
the longitudinal axis, by the LH and RH servos
cards.explain: Sideward movement comes from a tilt about the longitudinal axis, produced by the LH and RH servos.

cards.question: The pedal position is changed in flight. Which quantity at the tail rotor changes as a result of the blade pitch change?
options: the torque of the main rotor
the thrust of the tail rotor
the speed of the tail rotor
cards.explain: Changing tail rotor blade pitch changes the tail rotor thrust.

cards.question: With speed already established the cyclic stick is moved back. Which pair of reactions does that give?
options: a climb like an airplane, with speed being gained
a climb like an airplane, with speed being lost
a descent like an airplane, with speed being lost
cards.explain: With speed on, a rearward cyclic input gives an airplane like climb and the speed falls off.

cards.question: With speed established the left pedal is applied on such a helicopter. Which pair of reactions results?
options: a yaw to the left, with a little speed increase
a yaw to the right, with a little speed drop
a yaw to the left, with a little speed drop
cards.explain: Left pedal with speed on yaws the helicopter left and costs a little speed.

cards.question: What follows from the helicopter having no positive stability
options: its rotor speed has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its attitude has to be controlled permanently by the pilot
its trim actuators have to run permanently in flight
cards.explain: Without inherent stability the pilot has to control the attitude all the time.

cards.question: How the pilot gets a feedback of the attitude change at his controls
options: through the cable system, driven by the main servos
through the rate gyros, driven by the SCAS computer
through the trim actuators, driven by the control panel
cards.explain: The main servos feed the movement back to the pilot controls through the cable system.

cards.question: The cyclic stick is returned to neutral after a manoeuvre. What does the SCAS computer do with the attitude reached at that moment?
options: it passes it to the trim actuators as a trim command
it stores it as the reference value to be maintained
it compares it with the planned flight path of the mission
cards.explain: The momentary attitude becomes the new reference the stabilization system holds.

cards.question: A helicopter flying with its stabilization system engaged is disturbed in roll. How is that disturbance countered?
options: the trim actuator returns the cyclic stick to its neutral position
the motion transducer stores a new attitude as the reference
the sensed rate drives the control servos to compensate the motion
cards.explain: The rate gyro signal goes through the SCAS to the control servos, and the main servos compensate the motion.

cards.question: A pilot input and the stabilization signals are present at the same time. How does the SCAS computer handle them?
options: it passes only the larger of the two signals to the servos
it overlays the attitude reference and stabilization signals
it blocks the stabilization signals while the pilot inputs
cards.explain: The two are overlaid on each other inside the computer rather than one replacing the other.

cards.question: A helicopter loses its stability augmentation in flight. Which quality does it lose, and what does the pilot have to do?
options: positive stability, and he must retrim the controls permanently
neutral stability, and he must hold the rotor speed permanently
neutral stability, and he must control the attitude permanently
cards.explain: The neutral stability is what the system provided, and without it the pilot is back to controlling the attitude all the time.

questions.question: Which minimum period must a required public address system stay powerable after the shutdown or failure of all engines and auxiliary power units
options: At least 10 minutes
At least 5 minutes
At least 3 minutes
questions.explain: The specification sets a time duration of at least 10 minutes.

questions.question: A cabin crew member takes a microphone out of its stowage. Within what time must the public address system be able to operate?
options: 10 seconds
5 seconds
3 seconds
questions.explain: The specification allows 3 seconds from removal of the microphone.

questions.question: From how many flight crew member stations in the pilot compartment must the public address system be accessible for immediate use
options: Two
Three
One
questions.explain: The specification names each of two flight crew member stations.

questions.question: Which subsystem makes recorded audio selectable at each passenger seat
options: The Passenger Entertainment System
The Passenger Address System
The Passenger Services System
questions.explain: Selectable recorded entertainment audio at the seat is the Passenger Entertainment System.

questions.question: Which kind of system is the nice system
options: A modular analogue cabin lighting system
A modular IP based cabin management system
A centralised IP based flight management system
questions.explain: The nice system is a modular, IP based cabin management system.

questions.question: Which cabin functions can the crew and the passengers reach through the nice system
options: Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access
Window-shades, galley power, audio/video and seat heating
Illumination, cabin pressure, audio/video and internet access
questions.explain: Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access are the cabin functions printed.

questions.question: What does an ADI display
options: The compass and the indications from the radio navigation systems
The artificial horizon and the indication from the flight director system
The artificial horizon and the indication from the radio altimeter
questions.explain: The ADI combines attitude with flight director guidance.

questions.question: Into which two kinds of devices is aircraft monitoring divided
options: Flight monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Airframe monitoring devices and standby devices
Airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
questions.explain: Aircraft monitoring covers airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices.

questions.question: Which task do EICAS and ECAM perform in the modern cockpit
options: They perform maintenance data recording
They perform aircraft monitoring
They perform flight monitoring
questions.explain: EICAS and ECAM are the names given to the aircraft monitoring instruments.

questions.question: A pilot reads his magnetic heading and a VOR course deviation from one round instrument. Which indicator is he using?
options: The HSI
The variometer
The ADI
questions.explain: The HSI is the instrument that combines compass and radio navigation information.

questions.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
options: Only temperature becomes lower
All three become lower
All three become higher
questions.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

questions.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
questions.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

questions.question: A crew selects QNH on both altimeters. In which phases of flight is this setting used?
options: During cruise, above transition altitude and above transition level
During landing and take-off, up to transition altitude and below transition level
During landing and take-off, above transition altitude and above transition level
questions.explain: QNH belongs to the low level phases, below the transition altitude or level.

questions.question: What is the transition altitude
options: Prior to landing, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
questions.explain: The transition altitude is the climb-out point for changing to the standard setting.

questions.question: Which transponder requirement applies to an aircraft flying in RVSM airspace?
options: It must transmit altitude and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit altitude and be connected to the radio altimeter
It must transmit heading and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
questions.explain: The transponder must report altitude taken from the altitude measurement unit.

questions.question: Under which conditions does an airspeed indicator with bellows show the real speed of the aircraft
options: At mean sea level with compressibility corrected
At cruise altitude with standard conditions
At mean sea level with standard conditions
questions.explain: The bellows instrument is only true at mean sea level in standard conditions.

questions.question: Which calculation is made between EAS and TAS
options: A density calculation
A static source correction
A compressibility correction
questions.explain: The last step of the chain is the density calculation.

questions.question: The aneroid barometer takes its name from a neros, not fluid, because its sensing element is
options: a small capsule made of thin metal
a vertical tube filled with a fluid
a curved tube with an oval cross section
questions.explain: An aneroid barometer senses pressure with a thin metal capsule and so needs no liquid at all.

questions.question: What is the amount of tube tip movement proportional to
options: The applied pressure
The signal frequency
The tube temperature
questions.explain: Tip travel is proportional to the applied pressure.

questions.question: Which effect does friction have in the transfer mechanism of an aneroid instrument
options: It raises the capsule hysteresis
It damps the capsule stroke
It falsifies the measured result
questions.explain: Friction in the mechanism corrupts the reading.

questions.question: An altimeter fails in cruise and the aircraft loses its RVSM capability. Which action is required?
options: A change of the altimeter setting to QNH
A descent to the transition level
A quick exit of RVSM airspace
questions.explain: Losing RVSM capability means the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace quickly.

questions.question: A standby airspeed indicator with bellows and the airspeed readout of the glass cockpit are read at the same moment and differ. Which airspeeds are the two showing?
options: Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and true airspeed on the glass cockpit
Calibrated airspeed on the bellows instrument and indicated airspeed on the glass cockpit
Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and calibrated airspeed on the glass cockpit
questions.explain: A bellows instrument shows the indicated airspeed, while the glass cockpit indication is the calibrated airspeed.

questions.question: An electronic pressure sensor delivers an output frequency that depends on the input pressure. This sensor is
options: the piezoresistive transducer, the most commonly used type
the pressure cell transducer, the most commonly used type
the vibrating transducer, the most commonly used type
questions.explain: The vibrating transducer is named as the most commonly used type and it is the one whose output frequency depends on the input pressure.

questions.question: A pressure sensor consists of a chamber made of silicon, only a few millimetres in size. It is
options: the micromechanical transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the vibrating transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the micromechanical transducer, built as a liquid-based chamber
questions.explain: The micromechanical transducer is the aneroid-type chamber made of silicon whose structure is only a few millimetres in size.

questions.question: The pitot probe of a simple system becomes completely blocked while the static system stays clear. Which of the three supplied instruments is affected?
options: The airspeed indicator
The altimeter
The vertical speed indicator
questions.explain: Of the three instruments only the airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure, so only it depends on the pitot probe.

questions.question: Which instrument of the simple system needs a pressure connection in addition to the static system
options: The vertical speed indicator
The airspeed indicator
The altimeter
questions.explain: The altimeter and vertical speed indicator use static pressure only, while the airspeed indicator also needs pitot pressure.

questions.question: The Captain moves the handle of the alternate static source selector valve to its other position. Which static pressure then reaches his instruments?
options: The pitot pressure of his own system
His own static pressure system
The copilot's static pressure system
questions.explain: The valve exists so that the Captain can take his static pressure from the copilot's system instead of his own.

questions.question: A helicopter cannot keep its static ports in air that is free of rotor downwash. Which fitting deals with this?
options: A drain hole at each static port
Special cover plates at the static ports
Electrically heated static ports
questions.explain: The cover plates are fitted for exactly this purpose, to compensate the effects of the strong rotor downwash at the ports.

questions.question: A slow-flying propeller plane and a jet aeroplane near the speed of sound differ in one of the listed static source error factors above all. Which factor is that?
options: The position of the nose gear
The mach number
The position of the flaps
questions.explain: The two cases are set apart by how near the speed of sound they fly, which is the mach number among the listed factors.

questions.question: In the relation Ptot = q + ps, the quantity ps is delivered to the instrument from
options: The drain hole of the pitot tube
The pitot probe
The static ports
questions.explain: The static pressure ps used in the relation is the pressure measured at the static ports.

questions.question: A pitot tube delivers the pressure present in its cylindrical pipe throughout the flight. What must be supplied in addition before a speed can be obtained?
options: The total air temperature from a temperature probe
The static pressure from the static ports
A second total pressure from another pitot tube
questions.explain: The pitot tube gives total pressure only, and the static pressure from the static ports has to be subtracted from it to get the ram pressure.

questions.question: An aircraft type is to take both the ram pressure and the static pressure needed for speed indication from one single ram air tube. Which probe is used?
options: A Prandtl tube
A multi function probe
A pitot tube
questions.explain: The Prandtl tube is the single ram air tube that supplies both of these pressures.

questions.question: An aircraft with a modern EFIS carries two pneumatic back up instruments. Which of them has to be connected to the pitot system?
options: Both of them equally
The standby altimeter
The standby airspeed indicator
questions.explain: An airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure as well as static pressure, while an altimeter uses static pressure only.

questions.question: A technician must check the mouth of a static port and also damage to the skin around it. Where are the two sets of limits found?
options: The port mouth limits in ATA chapter 34 and the skin damage limits in the structure chapter or the SRM
Both the port mouth limits and the skin damage limits in ATA chapter 34
The port mouth limits in the structure chapter or the SRM and the skin damage limits in ATA chapter 34
questions.explain: The mouth of the port is covered by ATA chapter 34, while skin damage is covered by the structure chapter or the SRM.

questions.question: The same static line leak is considered in an unpressurized aircraft and in a pressurized one. How does the altimeter behave in each case?
options: It decreases the indication in the unpressurized aircraft and slightly increases it in the pressurized one
It slightly increases the indication in both aircraft
It slightly increases the indication in the unpressurized aircraft and decreases it in the pressurized one
questions.explain: On PDF page 432 the leak into an unpressurized cabin lowers the pressure in the lines, so the altimeter reads slightly higher; on this page the cabin pressure raises the line pressure, so it reads lower.

questions.question: The reason why the airspeed indication falls to zero with a pitot leakage in an unpressurized cabin
options: Static and pitot pressure become nearly the same
The static pressure becomes much greater than the pitot pressure
The pitot pressure rises with the cabin pressure
questions.explain: The airspeed indicator works on the difference between the two pressures, which is now almost nil.

questions.question: The instruments disturbed by a leakage in the pitot system alone compared with a leakage in both the pitot and the static system
options: The airspeed indicator and the altimeter, compared with the airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication
The airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication, compared with the airspeed indicator alone
The airspeed indicator alone, compared with the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the vertical speed indication
questions.explain: PDF page 436 prints that a pitot leak affects the airspeed indicator only, and this page adds the altimeter and the vertical speed indication once the static system leaks as well.

questions.question: An aircraft cruises at constant altitude and constant airspeed with a blocked static system and then begins a climb. What does the altimeter do?
options: It jumps once and then follows the climb correctly
It continues to display the same altitude
It begins to increase its indication as the climb starts
questions.explain: The trapped static pressure cannot change, so the altimeter holds the same altitude in level flight and through the climb.

questions.question: The airspeed indication with a blocked static system during a climb compared with a descent
options: Decreasing during both the climb and the descent
Decreasing during the climb and increasing during the descent
Increasing during the climb and decreasing during the descent
questions.explain: PDF page 440 prints the decreasing indication in the climb and this page the increasing one in the descent, because the trapped static pressure stays fixed while the total pressure falls and then rises.

questions.question: The airspeed indication during a descent with a blocked static system compared with a completely blocked pitot tube
options: Decreasing with the blocked static system and increasing with the blocked pitot tube
Increasing with both blockages
Increasing with the blocked static system and decreasing with the blocked pitot tube
questions.explain: PDF page 442 prints the increasing indication with the static side blocked, while this page prints the decreasing one with the pitot side blocked, because the rising static pressure then drives the instrument.

cards.question: Which minimum period must a required public address system stay powerable after the shutdown or failure of all engines and auxiliary power units
options: At least 10 minutes
At least 3 minutes
At least 5 minutes
cards.explain: The specification sets a time duration of at least 10 minutes.

cards.question: Which aggregate period of announcements by flight and cabin crew members is contained within the required powering duration
options: At least 5 minutes
At least 10 minutes
At least 3 minutes
cards.explain: An aggregate of at least 5 minutes of crew announcements sits inside the 10 minutes.

cards.question: On which technology is the Cabin Intercommunication Data System based
options: A hardwired relay logic
An analogue amplifier chain
A microprocessor
cards.explain: The CIDS is described as a microprocessor based system.

cards.question: How many subsystems make up the Advanced Cabin Entertainment/Service System
options: Four
Seven
Five
cards.explain: Five subsystems are listed for the ACESS.

cards.question: Which subsystem broadcasts flight deck announcements, flight attendant announcements and boarding music to the cabin
options: The Cabin Interphone System
The Passenger Address System
The Passenger Entertainment System
cards.explain: Those announcements and the boarding music are broadcast through the Passenger Address System.

cards.question: A restraining means is fitted to a megaphone. Which paragraph of the design specification sets the inertia forces it must withstand?
options: CS 25.1421, Megaphones
CS 25.1423, Public Address System
CS 25.561, Emergency Landing Conditions
cards.explain: The megaphone paragraph itself refers the inertia forces out to CS 25.561.

cards.question: All engines and auxiliary power units have failed. Beyond the announcement time, what further powering does the specification call for?
options: A standby period for other essential loads on the same source
A standby period for further announcements by the cabin crew
A standby period for the crew member interphone system
cards.explain: An additional standby duration is required for the other loads on that source that are essential to safety of flight.

cards.question: An announcement is made on a required public address system. Where in the aeroplane must it be intelligible?
options: At all passenger seats, galleys and flight crew seats and work stations
At all passenger seats, lavatories and cabin crew seats and work stations
At all passenger seats, lavatories and flight crew rest compartments
cards.explain: Intelligibility is demanded at the passenger seats, the lavatories and the cabin crew seats and work stations.

cards.question: Which other system must a required public address system be able to work independently of
options: Any required passenger entertainment system
Any required cabin crew member call system
Any required crew member interphone system
cards.explain: Independence is demanded specifically from any required crew member interphone system.

cards.question: Which emergency exits must have a microphone readily accessible to the seated cabin crew member
options: Required floor-level exits with an adjacent cabin crew seat
Required floor-level exits with an adjacent passenger seat
Required overwing exits with an adjacent cabin crew seat
cards.explain: The requirement is written for required floor-level exits that have an adjacent cabin crew member seat.

cards.question: Which three things does the Cabin Intercommunication Data System do to the cabin systems it serves
options: Controls, tests and monitors them
Controls, records and displays them
Tests, records and announces them
cards.explain: Control, test and monitor are the three functions printed for the CIDS.

cards.question: Which users are the cabin systems handled by the Cabin Intercommunication Data System dedicated to
options: Cabin attendant and passenger use
Cabin attendant and ground service use
Flight crew and ground crew use
cards.explain: The cabin systems concerned are those dedicated to cabin attendant and passenger use.

cards.question: Where does the audio of the Passenger Address System go
options: To the passenger headphones and the flight deck speakers
To the cabin speakers and the passenger headphones
To the cabin speakers and the attendant handsets
cards.explain: PA audio is fed to the cabin speakers and to the passenger headphones.

cards.question: Video, announcements and recorded audio all have to reach a seat. Which subsystem controls and distributes them to it?
options: The Passenger Entertainment System
The Cabin Interphone System
The Passenger Services System
cards.explain: All three are routed to the seat through the Passenger Entertainment System.

cards.question: Smoke is picked up by a lavatory smoke detector. Which cabin subsystem takes that signal and gives the annunciation?
options: The Cabin Interphone System
The Cabin Lighting System
The Passenger Services System
cards.explain: The interface to the lavatory smoke detector for smoke detection annunciation is a feature of the Passenger Services System.

cards.question: The flight deck needs to speak to the load cargo master. Which subsystem carries that call?
options: The Passenger Address System
The Cabin Interphone System
The Cabin Configuration System
cards.explain: Flight deck to load cargo master is one of the calls made through the Cabin Interphone System.

cards.question: Which lights are controlled by the Cabin Lighting System
options: The passenger call lights
The passenger reading lights
The ceiling and wash lights
cards.explain: The ceiling and wash lights are in the Cabin Lighting System list.

cards.question: Besides the ceiling, wash and night illumination lights, which further lights does the Cabin Lighting System control
options: The crew rest and reading lights
The lavatory call and seat row lights
The lavatory and crew rest lights
cards.explain: The lavatory and crew rest lights complete the Cabin Lighting System list.

cards.question: Which benefit does the Cabin Configuration System give an airline
options: Fault reporting of the whole cabin to the flight deck
Interior changes with minimal hardware changes
Entertainment audio selectable at every seat
cards.explain: The CCS lets the airline change the interior configuration with minimal hardware changes.

cards.question: How is an airplane interior configuration change accomplished through the Cabin Configuration System
options: By modifying the ACESS configuration database
By reprogramming each passenger service unit
By exchanging the configuration pins of the cabin wiring
cards.explain: Configuration changes are made by modifying the ACESS configuration database.

cards.question: A new cabin configuration has to be prepared before it is loaded. Which equipment creates the ACESS configuration database?
options: An on-board cabin configuration module
An on-ground personal computer software
An on-board central maintenance computer
cards.explain: The Airplane Configuration System that creates the database is an on-ground PC software.

cards.question: An operator wants to alter its speaker volume zones and its smoking areas. Where are those settings held?
options: In the ACESS Test System memory
In the ACESS configuration database
In each passenger service unit
cards.explain: Speaker volume zones and smoking areas are among the items held in the ACESS configuration database.

cards.question: Which cabin items can be arranged through the ACESS configuration database
options: The chime tone and the ceiling light brightness
The seat recline limits and the galley loads
The PA areas and the chime mute zones
cards.explain: PA areas and chime mute zones are printed in the list of configurable items.

cards.question: Which test of the ACESS Test System runs on-line and continuously
options: The built-in test equipment test
The built-in test
The programming test
cards.explain: The built-in test is the on-line continuous one, while the BITE is off-line.

cards.question: A major fault is found by the ACESS Test System. Besides the Cabin Configuration/Test Module, where is it reported?
options: To the passenger service units and the attendant call panels
To the airplane configuration system and the ground station
To the EICAS/EFIS interface units and the maintenance computers
cards.explain: Major faults go on to the EIUs and the CMCs as well as to the CCTM.

cards.question: The same power source that feeds the public address system also feeds other loads that stay powered when every other source is inoperative. How must that be treated?
options: Those other loads are shed for the whole powering duration
Those other loads are taken into account in the powering duration
Those other loads are transferred to the crew interphone supply
cards.explain: The duration must be achieved while considering the other loads left on the same source.

cards.question: A microphone has been left out of its stowage and unused at a cabin crew station. What must the public address system do in that condition?
options: Alert the flight deck
Stay serviceable
Mute the cabin loudspeakers
cards.explain: No unused, un-stowed microphone may render the system inoperative, so it must remain serviceable.

cards.question: Two required floor-level exits lie close together and each has an adjacent cabin crew member seat. When may one microphone serve both exits?
options: When the two exits are on the same side of the fuselage
When the seated crew members can talk unassisted
When the two crew member seats face in the same direction
cards.explain: One microphone may cover several exits only if their proximity allows unassisted verbal communication between the seated cabin crew members.

cards.question: Two operators want the cabin of the same aeroplane arranged to suit their own service. What does the CIDS design philosophy give them?
options: A fixed configuration set once by the airframe manufacturer
Flexibility without complex and time expensive hardware changes
Flexibility gained by exchanging the cabin wiring looms
cards.explain: The CIDS is designed for high flexibility so that complex and time expensive hardware changes are not needed.

cards.question: Which of these systems is a subsystem of the Advanced Cabin Entertainment/Service System
options: The Cabin Configuration System
The ACESS Test System
The Cabin Lighting System
cards.explain: The Cabin Lighting System is one of the five subsystems, while the other two are special features.

cards.question: Which two items are the special features of the integrated cabin entertainment and service system rather than its subsystems
options: The Passenger Services System and the Passenger Address System
The Cabin Configuration System and the ACESS Test System
The Cabin Lighting System and the Cabin Interphone System
cards.explain: The CCS and the ATS are named as the two special features added to the five subsystems.

cards.question: A reading light and a night illumination light both fail in the same cabin section. Why are two different subsystems involved?
options: Reading lights belong to the services system and night illumination to the address system
Reading lights belong to the lighting system and night illumination to the services system
Reading lights belong to the services system and night illumination to the lighting system
cards.explain: Reading lights sit under the Passenger Services System while night illumination sits under the Cabin Lighting System.

cards.question: Which kind of system is the nice system
options: A modular IP based cabin management system
A centralised IP based flight management system
A modular analogue cabin lighting system
cards.explain: The nice system is a modular, IP based cabin management system.

cards.question: For which aircraft is the nice cabin management system offered
options: Regional commuter aircraft
Long range freighter aircraft
VIP and government aircraft
cards.explain: The system is offered for VIP and government aircraft.

cards.question: Which cabin functions can the crew and the passengers reach through the nice system
options: Window-shades, galley power, audio/video and seat heating
Illumination, cabin pressure, audio/video and internet access
Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access
cards.explain: Illumination, window-shades, audio/video and internet access are the cabin functions printed.

cards.question: Further functions are to be added to an existing nice installation. Which protocol makes the system easy to expand?
options: The standard TCP/IP protocol
The ARINC 429 protocol
The spanning tree protocol
cards.explain: Expandability comes from the use of the standard TCP/IP protocol.

cards.question: To which two subgroups can every instrument of the classical cockpit be assigned
options: Airframe monitoring and aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring and engine monitoring
Flight monitoring and aircraft monitoring
cards.explain: The text splits classical cockpit instruments into flight monitoring and aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: To which group does the artificial horizon indicator ADI belong
options: Flight monitoring
Airframe monitoring
Aircraft monitoring
cards.explain: The ADI is listed among the flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: A panel layout is described as Basic T. Which four instruments form that T?
options: Attitude indicator, altimeter, compass and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass
cards.explain: The four instruments arranged in the T shape are the airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass; turn coordination and vertical speed sit below them.

cards.question: Where is the attitude indicator located in the Basic T configuration
options: In the middle at the bottom
On the left at the top
In the middle at the top
cards.explain: The Basic T places the attitude indicator centrally at the top of the group.

cards.question: The group of instruments which the standby set of a modern cockpit duplicates is
options: airframe monitoring
flight monitoring
engine monitoring
cards.explain: Altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass are all listed as flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: An exhaust gas temperature indicator is fitted in a classical cockpit. Which group and subdivision does it belong to?
options: Aircraft monitoring, as an engine monitoring device
Aircraft monitoring, as an airframe monitoring device
Flight monitoring, as a pressure monitoring device
cards.explain: Exhaust gas temperature indicators are named as engine monitoring devices under aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: Into which two kinds of devices is aircraft monitoring divided
options: Airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Flight monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Airframe monitoring devices and standby devices
cards.explain: Aircraft monitoring covers airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices.

cards.question: Why do the aircraft monitoring systems of the modern cockpit carry different names such as EICAS or ECAM
options: Because the name depends on the display size
Because the name depends on the flight phase
Because the name depends on the aircraft type
cards.explain: The text states that aircraft monitoring instruments have different names depending on aircraft type.

cards.question: Which task do EICAS and ECAM perform in the modern cockpit
options: They perform maintenance data recording
They perform flight monitoring
They perform aircraft monitoring
cards.explain: EICAS and ECAM are the names given to the aircraft monitoring instruments.

cards.question: Why is the CMS counted as part of aircraft monitoring
options: Because it delivers information to the flight crew
Because it delivers information to the maintenance personnel
Because it delivers information to the standby instruments
cards.explain: The CMS is used for aircraft monitoring because it delivers information to maintenance personnel.

cards.question: The electronic displays of a glass cockpit are lost in flight. Which speed and attitude information remains available from the standby set?
options: Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and heading from the standby horizon
Mach number from the standby machmeter and attitude from the standby horizon
Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and attitude from the standby horizon
cards.explain: The standby set contains an airspeed indicator and a horizon, but no machmeter.

cards.question: A fuel pressure indication changes during flight. Which value is the instrument responding to?
options: Pressure of fluids
Earth's magnetism
Pressure of air
cards.explain: Fluid pressure is listed separately from air pressure as a value that operates instruments.

cards.question: Of the two combined indicators, the one that adds the flight director indication and the one that adds radio navigation indications are
options: the ADI and the HSI respectively
the HSI and the ADI respectively
the ADI and the magnetic standby compass respectively
cards.explain: The ADI adds the flight director indication to the artificial horizon; the HSI adds radio navigation indications to the compass.

cards.question: A pilot reads his magnetic heading and a VOR course deviation from one round instrument. Which indicator is he using?
options: The variometer
The HSI
The ADI
cards.explain: The HSI is the instrument that combines compass and radio navigation information.

cards.question: A glass cockpit aircraft has no separate round flight instruments. Which statement describes the arrangement of the flight parameters?
options: They are laid out on the PFD and correspond to the Basic T configuration
They are laid out on the PFD in a configuration that replaces the Basic T
They are laid out on the navigation display in Basic T configuration
cards.explain: The PFD keeps the Basic T arrangement rather than abandoning it.

cards.question: An aircraft presents its altimeter, airspeed indicator and artificial horizon indicator on electronic displays. To which system of the modern cockpit are these instruments assigned?
options: EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System)
EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
CMS (Central Maintenance System)
cards.explain: All three named instruments are listed as flight monitoring instruments, and flight monitoring instruments go to the EFIS.

cards.question: The standby devices of a modern cockpit cover all but one of the flight parameters shown on the PFD. The parameter left without a standby device is
options: altitude
airspeed
vertical speed
cards.explain: The standby set holds altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass, so of the PFD parameters only vertical speed has no standby device.

cards.question: An engineer needs aircraft system information for troubleshooting rather than an indication meant for the crew. Which aircraft monitoring system delivers it?
options: The ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitoring)
The EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
The CMS (Central Maintenance System)
cards.explain: The CMS is the aircraft monitoring system that delivers information to the maintenance personnel.

cards.question: An instrument is to be fitted in the middle at the top of a Basic T panel and must also display the indication from the flight director system. Which indicator is required?
options: The attitude director indicator ADI
The horizontal situation indicator HSI
The turn coordination indicator
cards.explain: The middle top position of the Basic T carries the attitude indicator, and the ADI is the attitude indicator that also shows the flight director indication.

cards.question: What is the proportion of nitrogen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Nitrogen makes up 78% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: What is the proportion of oxygen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Oxygen makes up 21% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: An air data system is being described to a student. Which two measurements does flight monitoring require?
options: Static pressure and dynamic pressure
Dynamic pressure and air temperature
Static pressure and air density
cards.explain: Flight monitoring is built on the two pressures, static and dynamic.

cards.question: What is the other name for dynamic pressure
options: Atmospheric pressure
Barometric pressure
Ram pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is the ram pressure produced by the aircraft's motion.

cards.question: What does HUD stand for
options: Heading Up Display
Head Unit Display
Head Up Display
cards.explain: HUD is short for Head Up Display.

cards.question: The transition level is the specified last usable flight level. By what minimum margin must it lie above the 5000 ft MSL level
options: 500 ft
cards.explain: The manual requires at least 1000 ft of margin above the 5000 ft MSL level.

cards.question: How does the temperature behave with increasing height in the troposphere
options: It decreases by 6.5 °C every 100 metres
It increases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
It decreases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
cards.explain: The troposphere lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m of climb.

cards.question: The air data measurement also called atmospheric pressure and the one also called ram pressure are
options: the static pressure and the total pressure respectively
the dynamic pressure and the static pressure respectively
the static pressure and the dynamic pressure respectively
cards.explain: The manual gives atmospheric pressure as the other name for static pressure and ram pressure as the other name for dynamic pressure.

cards.question: The two indications that become possible once temperature is applied as a corrective value are
options: airspeed and vertical speed
barometric altitude and true airspeed
true airspeed and static air temperature
cards.explain: Temperature as a corrective value makes true airspeed and static air temperature available.

cards.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
options: Only temperature becomes lower
All three become lower
All three become higher
cards.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

cards.question: True airspeed and static air temperature are to be indicated as well. Which value must be applied as a corrective?
options: Humidity
Temperature
Density
cards.explain: Temperature is the corrective value that makes TAS and SAT available.

cards.question: A pneumatic instrument is calibrated in the workshop. Which values form the basis of that calibration?
options: The actual airfield values at the time of installation
The tropopause values of the standard atmosphere
The standard atmosphere values at mean sea level
cards.explain: Calibration is referred to the ISA mean sea level values.

cards.question: Why has the international standard atmosphere been established
options: To set the pressure scale of the altimeter before every flight
To predict the weather conditions along a planned route
To compare flight performance under greatly differing conditions
cards.explain: The ISA exists so performance figures can be compared on a common basis.

cards.question: In a modern indicating system all the air data information is presented
options: on separate electrical instruments
on one screen called the HUD
on one screen called the PFD
cards.explain: Modern indicating systems gather all the air data information onto the PFD.

cards.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
cards.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

cards.question: The one of the two transition terms that applies prior to landing is
options: the flight level
the transition level
the transition altitude
cards.explain: The transition altitude belongs to the climb after take-off and the transition level to the approach prior to landing.

cards.question: A barometric altimeter is set to QFE while the aircraft stands on the airfield. What does it indicate?
options: Current flight level
Airfield elevation
Zero altitude
cards.explain: With QFE set the reading starts from the airfield, so it is zero on the ground.

cards.question: A crew selects QNH on both altimeters. In which phases of flight is this setting used?
options: During cruise, above transition altitude and above transition level
