cards.question: The indication of the vertical speed indicator during a descent with a blocked static system
options: A steady rate of descent
A zero rate
A steady rate of climb
cards.explain: The trapped static pressure never changes, so the VSI sees no rate at all.

cards.question: What a completely blocked pitot tube means
options: The drain hole is blocked and the inlet is open
The inlet and the drain hole are blocked
The inlet is blocked and the drain hole is open
cards.explain: Complete blockage covers both the inlet and the drain hole.

cards.question: A pitot tube is completely blocked by ice. Which instruments are not affected?
options: The altimeter and the airspeed indicator
The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator
The airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indicator
cards.explain: Those two run on static pressure, which the pitot blockage does not touch.

cards.question: The pitot inlet is blocked by ice but the water drain hole is still open. What does the airspeed indication do?
options: It decreases to zero
It increases into the overspeed region
It stays unchanged at the last value
cards.explain: With pitot pressure equal to static pressure the airspeed indicator reads zero.

cards.question: The indications fluctuate during a check of the pitot static system. What does this show?
options: The presence of ice at the static port
The presence of water in them
The presence of a leak in them
cards.explain: Fluctuating indications are the sign of water lying in the pipes.

cards.question: A pitot line leaks inside an unpressurized cabin. What does the airspeed indication do?
options: It decreases to zero
It increases into the overspeed region
It stays at the value flown when the leak started
cards.explain: With the pitot line open to the cabin the airspeed indication falls away to zero.

cards.question: The reason why the airspeed indication decreases when both the pitot and the static system leak
options: Pitot and static pressure tend to be the same
The total pressure in the pitot line is trapped at a constant value
The static pressure in the lines rises above the pitot pressure
cards.explain: Both lines fill with the same cabin pressure, so the difference the indicator works on shrinks.

cards.question: The effect on the airspeed indication of a leakage in both the pitot and the static system
options: It is not affected
It decreases
It increases
cards.explain: With both lines open to the same cabin pressure the difference shrinks and the indication falls.

cards.question: Both the pitot system and the static system are leaking. What do the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator show?
options: Correct indications, because the two leaks cancel each other
The same results as for a leakage in the static system
The same results as for a leakage in the pitot system
cards.explain: Those two instruments see only static pressure, so the static leak result still applies.

cards.question: The indications with a blocked static system while the aircraft flies at constant altitude and constant airspeed
options: The airspeed indication slowly decreases
There are no changes in the indication
The altitude indication slowly increases
cards.explain: Nothing changes while the trapped static pressure still matches the real one.

cards.question: The static system is blocked and the aircraft climbs. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: An increasing airspeed indication
Zero airspeed
A decreasing airspeed indication
cards.explain: In the climb the falling total pressure works against a trapped static pressure, so the reading drops.

cards.question: The indications of the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator with a blocked static system, during a climb and during a descent
options: The same altitude and a vertical speed of zero
The same altitude and a vertical speed that follows the aircraft
A changing altitude and a vertical speed of zero
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the frozen altitude and zero vertical speed for the climb and this page the same pair for the descent, since both instruments work from the trapped static pressure.

cards.question: The static system is blocked and the aircraft descends. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: A decreasing airspeed indication
An increasing airspeed indication
Zero airspeed
cards.explain: In the descent the rising total pressure works against a trapped static pressure, so the reading climbs.

cards.question: The reason why the airspeed indicator reacts like an altimeter when the pitot tube is totally blocked
options: Total and static pressure become nearly equal, so the indication falls away
The static pressure is trapped, so only the changing total pressure moves the indication
The total pressure is trapped, so only the changing static pressure moves the indication
cards.explain: With the total pressure held fixed the indication is driven only by static pressure, which is what an altimeter responds to.

cards.question: The indication of the airspeed indicator during a climb with a totally blocked pitot tube
options: It increases and can reach the overspeed region
It stays at the speed flown when the blockage occurred
It decreases and can reach zero
cards.explain: With trapped total pressure and falling static pressure the indication runs up.

cards.question: The behaviour of the airspeed indicator when the pitot tube is totally blocked
options: It reacts like a vertical speed indicator
It reacts like an altimeter
It reacts like a turn coordinator
cards.explain: Its reading now follows altitude change instead of speed.

cards.question: The indication of the airspeed indicator during a descent with a totally blocked pitot tube
options: It decreases to a lower indicated airspeed
It remains at the value held during cruise
It increases to a higher indicated airspeed
cards.explain: The rising static pressure against a trapped total pressure drives the reading down.

cards.question: The pitot pressure when the pitot tube inlet is blocked but the water drain hole is still open
options: It stays at the value it had before the blockage
It increases to the value of the total pressure
It decreases to the value of the static pressure
cards.explain: The open drain lets the trapped pressure bleed down to static.

cards.question: The reason why the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator are not affected by a blocked pitot inlet
options: They get both pitot and static pressure
They only get pitot pressure
They only get static pressure
cards.explain: Both instruments are fed from the static system alone.

cards.question: The reason why water can be present in the pressure pipes
options: They are not drained on a regular basis
They are capped for protection during testing
Their test fittings are used to simulate altitude and speed
cards.explain: The pipes are not drained routinely, so water can collect in them.

cards.question: The static ports of a cold aeroplane are capped and the aircraft is moved into a warm hangar. What happens in the static system?
options: The pressure increases
The pressure decreases
The pressure stays the same
cards.explain: Warming the trapped air in a sealed static system raises its pressure.

cards.question: The ram pressure when both the pitot inlet and the drain are iced over
options: It depends on the altitude
It is always zero
It is constant at every altitude
cards.explain: With the total pressure held fixed, only the static pressure varies, so ram pressure follows altitude.

cards.question: A pitot line is leaking inside the cabin. How does the airspeed indication behave in an unpressurized aircraft compared with a pressurized one?
options: It is unpredictable in the unpressurized aircraft and decreases to zero in the pressurized one
It decreases to zero in both aircraft
It decreases to zero in the unpressurized aircraft and is unpredictable in the pressurized one
cards.explain: With no cabin pressure the two pressures equalise and the indication falls to zero, while cabin pressure makes the result depend on altitude and cabin pressure.

cards.question: The reason why the airspeed indication falls to zero with a pitot leakage in an unpressurized cabin
options: The static pressure becomes much greater than the pitot pressure
Static and pitot pressure become nearly the same
The pitot pressure rises with the cabin pressure
cards.explain: The airspeed indicator works on the difference between the two pressures, which is now almost nil.

cards.question: A pitot line leaks inside a pressurized cabin. What can be said about the airspeed indication?
options: It always falls to zero, because pitot and static pressure become equal
It is unpredictable, because it depends on altitude and cabin pressure
It always rises, because the cabin pressure is higher than the static pressure
cards.explain: With a pressurized cabin the two varying pressures make the indication unpredictable.

cards.question: The instruments disturbed by a leakage in the pitot system alone compared with a leakage in both the pitot and the static system
options: The airspeed indicator alone, compared with the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the vertical speed indication
The airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication, compared with the airspeed indicator alone
The airspeed indicator and the altimeter, compared with the airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication
cards.explain: PDF page 436 prints that a pitot leak affects the airspeed indicator only, and this page adds the altimeter and the vertical speed indication once the static system leaks as well.

cards.question: Both the pitot system and the static system leak inside an unpressurized cabin. What does the altimeter do?
options: It slightly increases the indicated altitude
It slightly decreases the indicated altitude
It holds the altitude it had when the leakage started
cards.explain: This page refers the altimeter back to the static leakage result, and PDF page 432 prints that result for an unpressurized cabin as a slightly increased indicated altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at constant altitude and constant airspeed with a blocked static system and then begins a climb. What does the altimeter do?
options: It begins to increase its indication as the climb starts
It continues to display the same altitude
It jumps once and then follows the climb correctly
cards.explain: The trapped static pressure cannot change, so the altimeter holds the same altitude in level flight and through the climb.

cards.question: The reason why the airspeed indication decreases during a climb with a blocked static system
options: The total pressure and the static pressure both decrease together
The total pressure from the pitot tube stays constant while the static pressure decreases
The total pressure from the pitot tube decreases while the trapped static pressure stays constant
cards.explain: Only the total pressure falls; the blocked static side cannot follow it.

cards.question: The airspeed indication with a blocked static system during a climb compared with a descent
options: Decreasing during both the climb and the descent
Decreasing during the climb and increasing during the descent
Increasing during the climb and decreasing during the descent
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the decreasing indication in the climb and this page the increasing one in the descent, because the trapped static pressure stays fixed while the total pressure falls and then rises.

cards.question: The reason why the airspeed indication increases during a descent with a blocked static system
options: The total pressure and the static pressure both increase together
The trapped static pressure increases while the total pressure remains constant
The total pressure from the pitot tube increases while the trapped static pressure remains constant
cards.explain: Only the total pressure rises; the blocked static side stays where it was.

cards.question: Two aircraft climb, one with a blocked static system and one with a completely blocked pitot tube. What does the airspeed indicator show in each?
options: A decreasing indication in both aircraft
A decreasing indication with the blocked static system and an increasing indication with the blocked pitot tube
An increasing indication with the blocked static system and a decreasing indication with the blocked pitot tube
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the decreasing indication with the static side blocked, while this page prints the increasing one with the pitot side blocked, because the falling static pressure then drives the instrument.

cards.question: The airspeed indication during a descent with a blocked static system compared with a completely blocked pitot tube
options: Decreasing with the blocked static system and increasing with the blocked pitot tube
Increasing with the blocked static system and decreasing with the blocked pitot tube
Increasing with both blockages
cards.explain: PDF page 442 prints the increasing indication with the static side blocked, while this page prints the decreasing one with the pitot side blocked, because the rising static pressure then drives the instrument.

cards.question: The pitot tube becomes totally blocked in cruise and the thrust is then increased to accelerate. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: A rise in the indicated speed
A fall of the indicated speed to zero
No change in the indicated speed
cards.explain: At constant altitude neither pressure changes, so the reading is frozen whatever the thrust.

cards.question: The pitot inlet of an aircraft is found blocked by ice. Which indication shows that the water drain hole is still open?
options: The airspeed indication increases into the overspeed region
The airspeed indication decreases to zero
The airspeed indication stops responding to changes of thrust
cards.explain: With the drain open the pitot pressure falls to static and the indication drops to zero, which a completely blocked tube does not do.

cards.question: The pitot pressure and the airspeed indication when the pitot inlet is iced over but the drain is free
options: The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
The pitot pressure remains constant and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication increases
cards.explain: The open drain lets the pitot pressure fall to static pressure, leaving no difference for the indicator to show.

cards.question: Two pitot probes are examined, one iced at the inlet only and one iced at the inlet and the drain. What does each condition say about the heating?
options: Defective or deactivated heating for the inlet only, and insufficient heating when both are iced
Insufficient heating for the inlet only, and defective or deactivated heating when both are iced
Insufficient heating in both conditions
cards.explain: Ice at the inlet alone points to heating that is too weak, while ice at both openings points to heating that is defective or switched off.

cards.question: The pitot inlet is iced over but the drain is free. What does this tell you about the heating?
options: The heating is defective or deactivated
The heating is working correctly
The heating is insufficient
cards.explain: Ice only at the inlet points to heating that is working but not enough.

cards.question: Both the pitot inlet and the drain are iced over. What does this say about the heating and the pitot pressure?
options: The heating is defective or deactivated and the pitot pressure remains constant
The heating is insufficient and the pitot pressure falls to static pressure
The heating is defective or deactivated and the pitot pressure falls to static pressure
cards.explain: Complete icing means the heating has failed or is off, and the sealed pitot pressure cannot change.

questions.question: The quantity measured in the barometric method of determining altitude
options: Satellite signal delay
Air pressure
Radio wave delay
questions.explain: The barometer method measures air pressure; the other two quantities belong to the radio altimeter and to GPS.

questions.question: The quantity measured by a radio altimeter
options: Static air pressure
Gravitation model deviation
Radio wave delay
questions.explain: The radio altimeter works on the delay of the radio wave, not on pressure.

questions.question: One of the factors on which the choice of altimeter depends
options: The transition level at the destination
The number of static ports fitted
The tolerance values required by law
questions.explain: Legal tolerance values are one of the three listed selection factors.

questions.question: The pressure decrease that corresponds to an altitude increase of 30 ft at low altitude
options: 10 hPa
1 hPa
30 hPa
questions.explain: The printed relationship at low altitude is 30 ft per 1 hPa.

questions.question: How the information about the actual pressure related to sea level reaches the crew
options: By the ATC transponder system
By radio communication or by data link
By the encoding altimeter
questions.explain: The setting value is passed to the aircraft by radio or data link.

questions.question: How the interior of a barometric altimeter casing is connected
options: To the outside air via the pitot system
To the outside air via the static system
To a sealed reference vacuum
questions.explain: Outside air reaches the inside of the case through the static system.

questions.question: The reason why an encoding altimeter is fitted with electrical connectors
options: To drive the additional bellows inside the instrument
To provide the ALT signal for the ATC transponder system
To receive the reference pressure from an air data computer
questions.explain: The electrical connectors carry the ALT signal that the ATC transponder system needs.

questions.question: The capsule of an airspeed indicator sits inside a sealed casing. Which pressure acts inside that casing?
options: Total pressure from the pitot system
Static pressure from the static system
Dynamic pressure from the pitot system
questions.explain: The casing is fed from the static system, so static pressure surrounds the capsule.

questions.question: In an airspeed indicator the difference between total pressure and static pressure gives
options: Total pressure
Dynamic pressure
Static pressure
questions.explain: Total pressure minus static pressure is by definition the dynamic pressure.

questions.question: A crew wants a minimum speed indication in the cockpit. On which aircraft is it available, and where is it shown?
options: Only on piston engine aircraft, as a red line on the airspeed indicator
On all jet aircraft, as a coloured band on the airspeed indicator scale
Only on aircraft with a glass cockpit, on the speed tape of the PFD
questions.explain: The minimum speed indication is a glass cockpit feature shown on the PFD speed tape.

questions.question: The air density correction applied to airspeed depends on
options: Pressure and temperature
Temperature and aircraft weight
Pressure and humidity
questions.explain: The manual states air density depends on pressure and temperature.

questions.question: What does the shock formation caused by compression of the air do to the airflow and the forces on the aircraft
options: It prevents laminar airflow, decreases drag and decreases lift
It prevents laminar airflow, increases drag and decreases lift
It prevents turbulent airflow, decreases drag and increases lift
questions.explain: The page states shock formation stops laminar flow, raises drag and lowers lift.

questions.question: An aircraft approaches its speed limit at low altitude. What sets that limit?
options: The static pressure which acts on the aircraft structure
The maximum allowed mach number
The dynamic pressure which acts on the aircraft structure
questions.explain: VMO is a structural limit set by dynamic pressure.

questions.question: An aircraft climbs steadily and the MMO limit falls. Why does it fall?
options: Because the dynamic pressure decreases
Because the speed of sound decreases
Because the compressibility error increases
questions.explain: The falling speed of sound is the stated reason.

questions.question: An aircraft with an IVSI enters and leaves a turn with a high bank angle. What should be expected?
options: An inaccurate vertical speed indication, because any vertical acceleration affects the piston
A correct vertical speed indication, because the piston compensates for bank angle
A total loss of indication, because the piston is locked by the acceleration
questions.explain: Any vertical acceleration acts on the piston, so turn entry and exit give a wrong reading.

questions.question: How is pressure balanced out in a diaphragm variometer
options: Via a calibrated orifice in the centre of the diaphragm
Via a capillary tube between the diaphragm and the casing
Via the air gap between the diaphragm and the casing
questions.explain: Balancing takes place through the air gap between diaphragm and casing.

questions.question: The airspeed value that the temperature display is used to determine
options: TAS
EAS
IAS
questions.explain: Temperature is one of the inputs needed for true airspeed.

questions.question: The aircraft on which the simple OAT indicating system is used
options: Supersonic transport aeroplanes
Large commercial jet aeroplanes
Small propeller driven aeroplanes and helicopters
questions.explain: The simple system is restricted to small propeller driven aeroplanes and helicopters.

questions.question: How SAT is obtained in a fast aeroplane
options: It is calculated by an air data computer
It is read directly from the total air temperature probe
It is read directly from a flush skin probe
questions.explain: SAT cannot be measured directly in flight, so the ADC calculates it from other data.

questions.question: An aeroplane accelerates to a higher mach number while the static air temperature stays the same. What happens to the gap between TAT and SAT?
options: It grows, because the ram rise depends on the mach number
It shrinks, because the probe recovers less of the airflow at high speed
It stays the same, because the ram rise depends only on the static air temperature
questions.explain: The gap between TAT and SAT is the ram rise, and that grows with mach number.

questions.question: A TAT indication sits hard against its lower stop and does not move. Which fault fits this picture?
options: A failure of the probe heating
A break in the measuring wire
A short circuit in the measuring wire
questions.explain: Only the short circuit, giving 0 ohm, parks the indication at the lower stop.

questions.question: A static port feeding one of an aircraft's two air data computers becomes blocked. Why does the other computer still give a correct altitude?
options: Each of the two air data computers has a separated pitot and static system of its own
Each of the two air data computers corrects its own static source error from the Mach number
The two air data computers share one pitot and static system through a crossfeed valve
questions.explain: Because the two computers have separate pitot and static systems, a blockage in one system cannot reach the other computer.

questions.question: The Mach module of an analogue air data computer fails. Why is the static source error correction affected as well?
options: The correction depends primarily on the calibrated airspeed, which comes from that module
The correction depends on the static pressure, which is routed through that module
The correction depends primarily on the Mach number, which comes from that module
questions.explain: Static source error depends first of all on Mach number, and that value is supplied by the Mach module.

questions.question: The STDBY flag is in view on a servo corrected altimeter. What does this tell the engineer about how the instrument is working?
options: The correction is deactivated and the instrument is working from the synchrotel alone
The correction is active and the instrument is following the air data computer
The correction is deactivated and the instrument is working purely mechanically
questions.explain: The STDBY flag goes with the correction being deactivated, and in that condition the instrument works purely mechanically.

questions.question: In an electrical altimeter, the element that blocks the coarse synchro value on small changes of height and the element that suppresses the fine value on large changes
options: The HIGH LEVEL detector blocks the coarse value and the baro correction suppresses the fine value
The HIGH LEVEL detector blocks the coarse value and the LIMITER suppresses the fine value
The LIMITER blocks the coarse value and the HIGH LEVEL detector suppresses the fine value
questions.explain: On small changes the HIGH LEVEL detector blocks the coarse value, and on large changes the LIMITER suppresses the fine value.

questions.question: An air data computer stops working altogether. What is seen on the Mach/airspeed indicator?
options: No flag at all, because the indicator holds the last values received
A red flag for the Mach value only, because CAS is taken from a capsule
A red flag for each value, because the valid discretes are no longer transmitted
questions.explain: Loss of the valid discrete for a value raises the red flag for that value.

questions.question: How does the air data computer obtain true airspeed from equivalent airspeed?
options: It replaces the standard density used before with the real density
It replaces the standard pressure used before with the real pressure
It adds the static source error correction to the equivalent airspeed
questions.explain: The step from EAS to TAS is the substitution of real air density for standard density.

questions.question: The inputs a digital air data computer takes from the aircraft sensing elements, and the form in which its computed values leave it
options: Pitot pressure, static pressure and dynamic pressure in, digital data on several data busses out
Pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature in, analogue signals on separate wires out
Pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature in, digital data on several data busses out
questions.explain: The computer is fed with pitot pressure, static pressure and temperature, and sends its computed values out digitally on several data busses; dynamic pressure is not sensed but worked out from the two pressures.

questions.question: The air data computers have failed, yet the digital vertical speed indicator still gives a usable indication. Why?
options: It normally works from the static pressure rate measured in the indicator itself
It normally works from the vertical speed output of the air data computer
It normally works from the inertial vertical speed signal of the inertial reference unit
questions.explain: The normal source is the IRU, so the indication survives the loss of the air data computers.

questions.question: The altitude shown on the primary flight displays disagrees with the standby instrument. Which settings should be compared?
options: The baro correction on the EFIS control panel and the BARO setting on the standby instrument
The baro correction on the EFIS control panel and the air data source selection
The BARO setting on the standby instrument and the selected altitude on the mode control panel
questions.explain: The displays and the standby instrument take their barometric reference from separate controls, so a disagreement points to the two settings being different.

questions.question: Both navigation displays of a glass cockpit aircraft fail while the primary flight displays stay serviceable. Which air data value is no longer indicated?
options: The true airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
The barometric altitude
questions.explain: The navigation display carries the true airspeed and no other air data, and it has replaced the separate TAS indicators, so losing it loses the TAS indication.

questions.question: An aircraft uses air data modules at its probes and ports. Which equipment must still be supplied by pneumatic tubes?
options: The standby instruments
The air data inertial reference units
The primary flight displays
questions.explain: Everything else is fed by data bus; the standby instruments keep their pneumatic supply.

questions.question: A GNADIRU is fitted but the aircraft has no air data computer as a separate box. How does the unit obtain its pressures?
options: From pneumatic tubes run from the probes to the unit in the avionics bay
From air data modules placed as near as possible to the pitot and static sensors
From the inertial reference section, which derives them from acceleration
questions.explain: The air data section works like a digital air data computer but is fed digitally by modules mounted close to the probes and ports.

questions.question: An aircraft is cruising at high altitude. Which of the two speed limits is the governing one there?
options: MMO, because at higher altitudes the limit depends on the maximum allowed Mach number
VMO, because the compressibility error of the indicated airspeed grows with altitude
VMO, because at higher altitudes the dynamic pressure on the structure is greatest
questions.explain: VMO is the structural limit that rules low down; higher up the Mach limit becomes the lower of the two.

questions.question: An integrated standby instrument system fails completely. Which standby indications are lost?
options: Standby altitude, standby attitude and standby airspeed
Standby altitude, standby attitude and standby heading
Standby altitude, standby airspeed and standby vertical speed
questions.explain: One unit does the work of the three separate standby instruments, so all three indications go together.

questions.question: The relationship between angle of attack and the lift acting on the wings
options: the greater the angle of attack, the smaller the lift
the greater the angle of attack, the greater the lift
the lift is independent of the angle of attack
questions.explain: Lift rises with angle of attack, up to the individual maximum for the profile.

questions.question: The quantity sensed by an angle of attack wind vane on the side of the fuselage, and the quantity sensed by a lift transducer below the forward wing surface
options: The vane senses the angle of the air stream, the transducer changes in the stagnation point
The vane senses the angle of the air stream, the transducer a pressure difference between two rows of holes
The vane senses changes in the stagnation point, the transducer the angle of the air stream
questions.explain: The wind vane senses the angle of the air stream directly, while the lift transducer senses changes in the direction and intensity of the stagnation point.

questions.question: The angle of attack indication of an aeroplane is rising towards alpha max. What is about to happen at the wing?
options: The airflow can no longer follow the upper surface of the wing and separation occurs
The airflow can no longer follow the lower surface of the wing and separation occurs
The airflow over the wing speeds up and the lift goes on rising
questions.explain: The indication shows the actual angle of attack, and at alpha max the airflow cannot follow the upper surface of the wing and separates.

questions.question: In flight the maximum possible angle of attack for the flap position in use is exceeded. What happens?
options: The flaps extend automatically
An amber lamp illuminates and a chime sounds
A motor shakes the control column
questions.explain: Exceeding the flap dependent maximum angle drives the stick shaker motor.

questions.question: In the stall warning management computer, the value corrected by the signals from the ADC and the value corrected by the IRS
options: M and CAS from the ADC correct the maximum angle of attack, the IRS corrects the flap position signal
M and CAS from the ADC correct the maximum angle of attack, the IRS corrects the pitch limit signal
M and CAS from the ADC correct the pitch limit signal, the IRS corrects the maximum angle of attack
questions.explain: The ADC signals M and CAS correct the maximum angle of attack, while the pitch limit signal is corrected by the IRS.

cards.question: The quantity measured in the barometric method of determining altitude
options: Satellite signal delay
Radio wave delay
Air pressure
cards.explain: The barometer method measures air pressure; the other two quantities belong to the radio altimeter and to GPS.

cards.question: The quantity measured by a radio altimeter
options: Static air pressure
Radio wave delay
Gravitation model deviation
cards.explain: The radio altimeter works on the delay of the radio wave, not on pressure.

cards.question: One of the factors on which the choice of altimeter depends
options: The transition level at the destination
The tolerance values required by law
The number of static ports fitted
cards.explain: Legal tolerance values are one of the three listed selection factors.

cards.question: The type of indication listed besides double pointer, triple pointer and drum-type
options: Altitude indication on the baro scale
Altitude indication on the transponder
Altitude indication on the PFD
cards.explain: The fourth kind of indication listed is the altitude display on the PFD.

cards.question: The shape of the ISA pressure graph at low altitudes
options: Nearly linear
Strongly exponential
A series of steps
cards.explain: Close to the ground the pressure against altitude curve is nearly a straight line.

cards.question: The pressure decrease that corresponds to an altitude increase of 30 ft at low altitude
options: 10 hPa
30 hPa
1 hPa
cards.explain: The printed relationship at low altitude is 30 ft per 1 hPa.

cards.question: What the baro set knob gives the altimeter
options: A new reference pressure
A new static pressure source
A new scale calibration in metres
cards.explain: The knob only changes the reference pressure the indication is based on.

cards.question: The crew is preparing for departure. Which pressure do they set on the altimeters?
options: The actual pressure related to sea level
The standard pressure of the ISA
The actual pressure at ground level
cards.explain: Before takeoff the reference is the actual sea level pressure, which is the QNH setting.

cards.question: The name given to the reference pressure used for QNE
options: Ambient
Standard
Nautical
cards.explain: The 1013 hPa reference is called standard.

cards.question: Who may select the barometric correction on an altimeter, besides the pilots
options: Maintenance personnel
Air traffic control
The air data computer
cards.explain: The manual names pilots and maintenance personnel as the ones who select the baro correction.

cards.question: How a barometer determines altitude
options: By using the decrease in pressure with increasing altitude
By using the increase in pressure with increasing altitude
By using the delay of a reflected radio wave
cards.explain: Pressure falls as altitude rises, and the barometer uses that relationship.

cards.question: A method of determining altitude uses the WGS84 gravitation model as its reference instead of the ground. Which method is it?
options: Radio altimeter
GPS
Barometer
cards.explain: WGS84 is the reference of the GPS method; the barometer uses pressure and the radio altimeter uses the ground.

cards.question: How the interior of a barometric altimeter casing is connected
options: To the outside air via the pitot system
To a sealed reference vacuum
To the outside air via the static system
cards.explain: Outside air reaches the inside of the case through the static system.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs. What happens inside its barometric altimeter?
options: Pressure decreases, the bellows contract and the pointer rises
Pressure decreases, the bellows expand and the pointer rises
Pressure increases, the bellows expand and the pointer falls
cards.explain: Falling pressure around the capsule lets the bellows expand, which drives the pointer up the scale.

cards.question: The reason for mounting 2 or 3 bellows in series in an altimeter
options: To allow the case to be sealed against static pressure
To balance the mechanism against acceleration
To obtain a more exact indication
cards.explain: Several capsules in series give more movement and therefore a more exact indication.

cards.question: An altitude indicator has no pneumatic connection at all, only wiring. Which technology is it?
options: An instrument with static pressure input
An indicator with electrical input from an air data computer
A drum-type instrument with static pressure input
cards.explain: Without a static connection the altitude information can only come electrically from an air data computer.

cards.question: The construction feature that distinguishes an encoding altimeter
options: Additional bellows and electrical connectors
An additional static port and a drum
Additional pointers and a second baro scale
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter carries extra bellows and electrical connectors on top of the normal altimeter.

cards.question: An encoding altimeter puts out an ALT signal. Which system receives it?
options: The ATC transponder system
The air data computer
The static system
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter feeds the ALT signal to the ATC transponder.

cards.question: Why is an encoding altimeter connected to the ATC transponder system?
options: So that ground control can be informed about the altitude of the aircraft
So that the crew can be informed about the ground pressure
So that the transponder can set the baro correction of the altimeter
cards.explain: The purpose of the ALT signal is to pass the aircraft altitude to ground control.

cards.question: The aircraft in which encoding altimeters are found
options: All aircraft fitted with an air data computer
Some small aircraft
Only aircraft without a transponder
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter is described as a fit found in some small aircraft.

cards.question: The reason why an encoding altimeter is fitted with electrical connectors
options: To provide the ALT signal for the ATC transponder system
To receive the reference pressure from an air data computer
To drive the additional bellows inside the instrument
cards.explain: The electrical connectors carry the ALT signal that the ATC transponder system needs.

cards.question: How the baro set knob works in a pneumatic indicator
options: It directly turns the whole altimeter mechanism
It moves the bellows stack alone
It sends a correction signal to the air data computer
cards.explain: In a pneumatic instrument the setting is made mechanically by turning the whole mechanism.

cards.question: A new reference pressure is selected on an electrical altitude indicator. How is the correction made?
options: Electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer
Mechanically, by turning the whole altimeter mechanism
Pneumatically, by an additional set of bellows
cards.explain: Electrical indicators have no mechanism to turn, so the correction is done electrically.

cards.question: An airport lies well above sea level and the altimeter is set to QNH. What does the instrument show on the ground?
options: The altitude of the airport related to mean sea level
The height of the aircraft above the runway
Zero feet
cards.explain: With sea level as the reference, an airport above sea level indicates its own elevation.

cards.question: The aircraft is descending and reaches the Transition Level. What do the pilots do with the altimeters?
options: They adjust them to 1013 hPa
They adjust them to the actual pressure at the destination airport
They adjust them to the pressure used at the departure airport
cards.explain: At the Transition Level the standard setting is replaced by the destination setting.

cards.question: How a new reference pressure is applied in a pneumatic altimeter compared with an electrical indicator
options: By turning the whole altimeter mechanism, compared with a correction made electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer
By a correction made electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer, compared with turning the whole altimeter mechanism
By turning the whole altimeter mechanism, in the pneumatic indicator and in the electrical indicator alike
cards.explain: The pneumatic instrument is re-referenced mechanically, the electrical one electrically inside itself or through an air data computer.

cards.question: The baro correction that makes the altimeter read zero on the ground
options: QNE
QFE
QNH
cards.explain: QFE uses the ambient pressure at ground level, so the indication on the ground is zero.

cards.question: The level to which the pressure used for QFE is related
options: The standard atmosphere
Mean sea level
Ground level
cards.explain: QFE is the ambient pressure at ground level, unlike QNH which is related to mean sea level.

cards.question: An aircraft is in flight with QFE set on its altimeter. What does the indication represent?
options: The height above mean sea level
The altitude in the standard atmosphere
The height above the ground
cards.explain: With the ground as reference the instrument shows height above the ground.

cards.question: Why do pilots of medium and large aircraft normally not use QFE?
options: The QFE value is not transmitted by data link
They can use a radio altimeter system
Their baro scales cannot be set that low
cards.explain: A radio altimeter already gives the height above the ground, so the QFE setting is not needed.

cards.question: An aircraft in flight has the baro correction for QNH set. What does the altimeter read?
options: The height above mean sea level
The height above the transition altitude
The height above the ground
cards.explain: QNH refers everything to mean sea level, in flight as well as on the ground.

cards.question: A technician selects QNE on an altimeter. Which reference is then used?
options: The ambient pressure at the airport
The ambient pressure at mean sea level on the day
The standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
cards.explain: QNE is always the fixed standard atmosphere value, not a value measured on the day.

cards.question: Where the QNE setting is normally used
options: During takeoff and landing only
On the ground, not in flight
In flight, not on the ground
cards.explain: QNE is the in-flight setting; on the ground the airport settings are used.

cards.question: The advantage of QNE
options: The altimeter reads zero at touchdown
Every aircraft reads its own height above the ground
All aircraft in cruise flight use the same reference pressure
cards.explain: The whole point of QNE is a single common reference for all aircraft in the cruise.

cards.question: What an altimeter in flight indicates with the baro correction for QFE compared with QNH
options: The height above mean sea level with QFE and the height above the ground with QNH
The height above the ground with QFE and the height above mean sea level with QNH
The height above the ground with both corrections
cards.explain: QFE refers the indication to the ground and QNH to mean sea level.

cards.question: The reason why an altimeter set to QFE indicates 0 ft at touchdown
options: Its reference is the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
Its reference is the actual pressure related on mean sea level
Its reference is the actual pressure related on ground level
cards.explain: QFE takes the pressure at ground level as its reference, so the indication is zero on the ground.

cards.question: An altimeter is set to standard pressure. Under which condition is its indicated altitude equal to the true altitude?
options: When the pressure at sea level is really 1013 hPa
When the airport elevation is zero
When the aircraft is above the transition altitude
cards.explain: The conversion from static pressure to altitude only matches the true altitude when the real sea level pressure is the calibration value.

cards.question: A crew keeps 1013 hPa set on the altimeters for the whole cruise. Why does the indication not give the true altitude everywhere along the route?
options: Because the indication is only correct where the pressure at sea level really is 1013 hPa
Because the pressure graph of the standard atmosphere is only linear at low altitudes
Because all aircraft in cruise flight select a different reference pressure
cards.explain: Indicated altitude only equals true altitude where the real sea level pressure is 1013 hPa, and PDF page 464 adds that the altimeters cannot be reset for every point of the route.

cards.question: Why do all aircraft in cruise use one common selected pressure instead of the local pressure?
options: So that each of them indicates its true height above the ground
So that ground control can read the elevation of the airports
So that they all keep the same altitude separation in low and high pressure areas
cards.explain: A common reference keeps the vertical separation between aircraft consistent whatever the local pressure is.

cards.question: An altimeter is left calibrated to 1013 hPa while the real pressure at sea level below the aircraft is lower. What will the instrument indicate?
options: The correct altitude
Too low an altitude
Too high an altitude
cards.explain: With the reference set higher than the real sea level pressure, the instrument over-reads.

cards.question: An aircraft passes the Transition Altitude after takeoff and later the Transition Level before landing. Which setting is made at each point?
options: The actual pressure at the departure airport at the Transition Altitude and 1013 hPa at the Transition Level
1013 hPa at the Transition Altitude and the actual pressure at the destination airport at the Transition Level
1013 hPa at both the Transition Altitude and the Transition Level
cards.explain: The common standard pressure is taken at the Transition Altitude on the way up and given back for the local pressure at the Transition Level on the way down.

cards.question: Two altimeters at the same airport, which lies above sea level, read differently on the ground, one showing zero and the other the elevation of the airport. Which baro corrections are set?
options: QFE on the one showing zero and QNE on the one showing the elevation
QNH on the one showing zero and QFE on the one showing the elevation
QFE on the one showing zero and QNH on the one showing the elevation
cards.explain: QFE is referenced to the ground and reads zero there, while QNH is referenced to mean sea level and shows the airport elevation.

cards.question: The difference between the QNE and the QNH altimeter calibration, both of which refer the altitude to mean sea level
options: QNE uses the actual pressure related to mean sea level while QNH uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
QNE uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa while QNH uses the actual pressure related to mean sea level
QNE uses the actual pressure related to ground level while QNH uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
cards.explain: Both refer the altitude to mean sea level, but QNE always takes the standard pressure while QNH takes the actual one.

cards.question: The airspeed indicator is which type of measuring instrument
options: A differential temperature meter
A differential pressure meter
An absolute pressure meter
cards.explain: The instrument works on the difference between two pressures, so it is a differential pressure meter.

cards.question: The scale of the airspeed indicator is calibrated in
options: Nautical miles
Knots
Kilometres per hour
cards.explain: The printed text gives knots as the unit of the scale.

cards.question: VNE is
options: The maximum allowable speed with flaps extended
The maximum allowed airspeed
The maximum airspeed for cruise flight
cards.explain: VNE is the never exceed speed, which is the maximum allowed airspeed.

cards.question: The green band on the airspeed indicator of a small aircraft shows the
options: Normal Operating Range
Full Flap Operating Range
Caution range
cards.explain: Green marks the normal operating range on the scale.

cards.question: On a helicopter airspeed indicator the red mark shows
options: The range of transition lift
The maximum speed allowed for autorotation
The speed that must never be exceeded
cards.explain: Red marks VNE, the never exceed speed.

cards.question: On a helicopter airspeed indicator the red-white mark shows
options: The maximum speed allowed for autorotation under all conditions
The speed that must never be exceeded
The range of transition lift
cards.explain: The red-white mark is the autorotation speed limit.

cards.question: True airspeed is the speed with which the aircraft moves
options: Through the surrounding air
Relative to the airspeed indicator scale
Over the ground
cards.explain: TAS is defined as the aircraft speed through the surrounding air mass.

cards.question: The speed which is shown on the indicator is called
options: Ground speed
True airspeed
Indicated airspeed
cards.explain: What the instrument displays is the indicated airspeed.

cards.question: A technician traces the pitot line to the airspeed indicator capsule. Which pressure does that line deliver to the capsule interior?
options: Static pressure from the static system
Total pressure from the pitot system
Dynamic pressure from the static system
cards.explain: The capsule interior receives total pressure, which the pitot system delivers.

cards.question: The capsule of an airspeed indicator sits inside a sealed casing. Which pressure acts inside that casing?
options: Static pressure from the static system
Dynamic pressure from the pitot system
Total pressure from the pitot system
cards.explain: The casing is fed from the static system, so static pressure surrounds the capsule.

cards.question: In an airspeed indicator the difference between total pressure and static pressure gives
options: Static pressure
Total pressure
Dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Total pressure minus static pressure is by definition the dynamic pressure.

cards.question: A technician is asked what the indicated airspeed value is used for. Which answer is correct?
options: As a value for thrust and for the maximum cabin pressure
As a value for altitude and for the maximum rate of climb
As a value for lift and for the maximum load on the flaps
cards.explain: The manual lists lift and maximum load on the flaps and airframe among the uses of the IAS.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with a primary flight display instead of a mechanical airspeed indicator. How is airspeed presented?
options: As a speed band on the PFD
As a speed bug on the PFD
As a speed limit marking on the PFD
cards.explain: The third type of airspeed indication listed is the speed band shown on the PFD.

cards.question: In small aircraft the airspeed limits are shown by
options: A movable pointer driven by the air data computer
A digital readout beside the airspeed indicator
Coloured ranges and lines on the airspeed indicator scale
cards.explain: Small aircraft carry the limits as colour markings painted on the instrument scale.

cards.question: An aeroplane is being flown with the airspeed in the yellow band. Which condition applies?
options: It may be used in any air, including hard manoeuvres
It may only be used in smooth air without hard manoeuvres
It may only be used with the flaps extended
cards.explain: The caution range is restricted to smooth air with no hard manoeuvres.

cards.question: The slight increase of VMO with altitude is the result of taking account of
options: The compressibility error of the IAS
The instrument error of the IAS
The static source error of the IAS
cards.explain: The manual attributes the slight rise to the compressibility error of the IAS.

cards.question: Airspeed indicators of jet aircraft do not show the low speed limit because
options: It is already shown by the maximum speed pointer
It is a fixed value and therefore needs no indication
It depends on many factors such as weight and flap position
cards.explain: The low speed limit varies with weight and flap position, so it is not marked on the dial.

cards.question: A crew wants a minimum speed indication in the cockpit. On which aircraft is it available, and where is it shown?
options: Only on aircraft with a glass cockpit, on the speed tape of the PFD
On all jet aircraft, as a coloured band on the airspeed indicator scale
Only on piston engine aircraft, as a red line on the airspeed indicator
cards.explain: The minimum speed indication is a glass cockpit feature shown on the PFD speed tape.

cards.question: How the yellow band on the airspeed indicator of a small aircraft differs from the green band
options: It is the normal operating range, while the green band is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres
It is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres, while the green band is the normal operating range
It is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres, while the green band is the full flap operating range
cards.explain: The green band is the normal operating range while the yellow band is a caution range with conditions attached to its use.

cards.question: A helicopter airspeed indicator carries two essential marked limits. What makes them necessary?
options: The aerodynamic properties of the helicopter
The engine power limits of the helicopter
The maximum take-off weight of the helicopter
cards.explain: The manual gives the aerodynamic properties of the helicopter as the reason for the two marked limits.

cards.question: An aircraft is flown at sea level in standard conditions and its IAS equals its TAS. Which further condition must be met?
options: With negligible instrument error
With negligible static source error
With negligible compressibility error
cards.explain: The manual gives two conditions for IAS and TAS to coincide: standard conditions at sea level and negligible static source error.

cards.question: TAS is obtained from IAS by correcting for instrument error, static source error, dynamic pressure error and
options: Aircraft weight
Magnetic variation
Air density
cards.explain: Air density is the fourth correction listed for deriving TAS from IAS.

cards.question: The air density correction applied to airspeed depends on
options: Pressure and temperature
Temperature and aircraft weight
Pressure and humidity
cards.explain: The manual states air density depends on pressure and temperature.

cards.question: A jet aeroplane climbs from low altitude to high altitude. Which limit governs its maximum speed at the higher altitude?
options: The never exceed speed VNE
The maximum allowed Mach number MMO
The maximum operating velocity VMO
cards.explain: Above a certain altitude the Mach limit MMO takes over from the dynamic pressure limit VMO.

cards.question: Why can the speed limit of a jet aeroplane at low altitude be read directly as an indicated airspeed?
options: Because the limit there depends on dynamic pressure, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a dynamic pressure indicator
Because the limit there depends on dynamic pressure, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a total pressure indicator
Because the limit there depends on the speed of sound, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a dynamic pressure indicator
cards.explain: This page prints that the low altitude limit is a dynamic pressure limit, and PDF page 468 prints that the indicated airspeed is a dynamic pressure indicator, so the limit can be marked as a speed.

cards.question: The change of VMO and of MMO as a jet aeroplane climbs
options: VMO stays constant or increases slightly while MMO decreases
VMO and MMO both decrease
VMO decreases while MMO stays constant or increases slightly
cards.explain: VMO holds or rises a little with altitude while MMO falls, because the speed of sound falls.

cards.question: A helicopter airspeed indicator carries a red mark and a red-white mark. Which limit does each of them give?
options: The red mark the speed that must never be exceeded, the red-white mark the maximum speed allowed for autorotation
The red mark the speed that must never be exceeded, the red-white mark the range of transition lift
The red mark the maximum speed allowed for autorotation, the red-white mark the speed that must never be exceeded
cards.explain: The plain red mark is the never exceed speed and the red-white mark is the autorotation limit.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs while holding a constant indicated airspeed. What happens to the difference between IAS and TAS?
options: It decreases, because the air density decreases
It stays the same, because the IAS is corrected for density
It increases, because the air density decreases
cards.explain: Falling air density with altitude widens the gap between IAS and TAS.

cards.question: An aircraft is flown at sea level in standard conditions, but its static source error is not negligible. Do the indicated airspeed and the true airspeed coincide?
options: Yes, because the static source error only separates them at altitude
Yes, because at sea level the two speeds always coincide
No, because they coincide only when the static source error is negligible as well
cards.explain: The printed condition is both standard conditions at sea level and a negligible static source error, so failing one of them is enough to separate the two speeds.

cards.question: An aircraft is not fitted with an air data computer. What must be provided instead?
options: Correction tables in the aircraft technical log
Correction tables in the Flight Operations Manual
A second airspeed indicator for comparison
cards.explain: Without an air data computer the corrections come from tables in the Flight Operations Manual.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the mach meter
options: To enable flight at the maximum operating mach number and with economic efficiency
To enable flight at the maximum operating velocity and with minimum structural load
To enable flight at the never exceed speed and with maximum rate of climb
cards.explain: The manual gives exactly these two purposes for the mach meter.

cards.question: A technician opens a mach meter on the bench. Which two sensing elements are inside it?
options: Aneroid bellows and a capillary restrictor
Differential pressure bellows and a bimetallic element
Differential pressure bellows and aneroid bellows
cards.explain: The manual lists these two elements as the contents of a mach meter.

cards.question: The mach number M is defined as the relation of
options: Speed flown to speed of sound
True airspeed to calibrated airspeed
Speed of sound to speed flown
cards.explain: Mach number is speed flown divided by speed of sound.

cards.question: Which errors is the indicated mach number Mi subject to
options: Instrument error and compressibility error
Instrument error and static source error
Static source error and density error
cards.explain: These are the two errors stated for Mi.

cards.question: In a jet aircraft the speed limit is shown in the airspeed indicator by
options: A red and white VNE pointer
A red and white VMO / MMO pointer
A red and green VMO / MMO pointer
cards.explain: The manual names the red and white VMO / MMO pointer.

cards.question: On the speed tape of a PFD the speed limit is shown by
options: An amber and black area
A red and white area
A red and black area
cards.explain: The PFD speed tape uses a red and black area.

cards.question: The reason why a mach indication is needed for flight at high altitude
options: Because the limit there is the maximum operating mach number and the speed of sound is a function of altitude
Because the limit there is the maximum operating mach number and the speed of sound is a function of dynamic pressure
Because the limit there is the maximum operating velocity and dynamic pressure is a function of altitude
cards.explain: PDF page 470 prints that at higher altitudes the limit is the maximum operating mach number, and this page prints that the speed of sound is a function of altitude, so the limit cannot be read from an airspeed alone.

cards.question: What does the shock formation caused by compression of the air do to the airflow and the forces on the aircraft
options: It prevents laminar airflow, increases drag and decreases lift
It prevents laminar airflow, decreases drag and decreases lift
It prevents turbulent airflow, decreases drag and increases lift
cards.explain: The page states shock formation stops laminar flow, raises drag and lowers lift.

cards.question: Why can the speed of sound be represented as a function of altitude
options: Because it is a function of static pressure, and under standard conditions pressure is a function of temperature
Because it is a function of density, and under standard conditions density is a function of airspeed
Because it is a function of temperature, and under standard conditions temperature is a function of altitude
cards.explain: The chain given is speed of sound to temperature to altitude.

cards.question: The MMO marking on a stand-alone mach meter is the adjustable version and has to be re-set. Where is this carried out?
options: On the ramp before each flight
In the workshop
In the cockpit by the pilot
cards.explain: The manual calls adjusting the MMO marking a workshop task.

cards.question: How the indicated mach number Mi is obtained compared with the true mach number MT
options: Mi is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure while MT is calculated by the air data computer
Mi is calculated by the air data computer while MT is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure
Mi is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure while MT is calculated from the speed of sound and the outside temperature
cards.explain: Mi comes from the pressures at the instrument while MT is worked out by the air data computer.

cards.question: From which pressures is the indicated mach number Mi calculated
options: Dynamic pressure and cabin pressure
Pitot pressure and accumulator pressure
Pitot pressure and dynamic pressure
cards.explain: The manual names pitot pressure and dynamic pressure as the inputs for Mi.

cards.question: The true mach number MT is calculated by
options: The air data computer
The flight management computer
The central maintenance computer
cards.explain: The manual states the air data computer calculates MT.

cards.question: Two mach values are available on an aircraft, one free of instrument and static source error. Which value is that?
options: The true mach number MT
The indicated mach number Mi
The maximum operating mach number MMO
cards.explain: MT is defined as being without instrument and static source error, unlike Mi.

cards.question: Why do jet aircraft need a pointer or speed tape marking to show the maximum allowed airspeed
options: Because the speed limit is a fixed value as the VNE is in piston engine aircraft
Because the airspeed indicator cannot show indicated airspeed above the speed of sound
Because the speed limit is not a fixed value as the VNE is in piston engine aircraft
cards.explain: The limit varies, so it must be displayed, unlike a fixed VNE.

cards.question: An aircraft approaches its speed limit at low altitude. What sets that limit?
options: The maximum allowed mach number
The static pressure which acts on the aircraft structure
The dynamic pressure which acts on the aircraft structure
cards.explain: VMO is a structural limit set by dynamic pressure.

cards.question: How does VMO behave with increasing altitude when the compressibility error of the IAS is taken into account
options: It always decreases in the same way as MMO
It is either constant or it decreases slightly
It is either constant or it increases slightly
cards.explain: The manual states VMO is constant or rises slightly with altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs steadily and the MMO limit falls. Why does it fall?
options: Because the compressibility error increases
Because the speed of sound decreases
Because the dynamic pressure decreases
cards.explain: The falling speed of sound is the stated reason.

cards.question: Why do all jet aircraft have an independent aural overspeed warning
options: Because the static source error becomes too large at high altitude
Because the airspeed indicator is unreadable at high mach numbers
Because of the danger of aircraft damage during an overspeed
cards.explain: The stated reason is the risk of damaging the aircraft.

cards.question: How is the aural overspeed warning produced
options: From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the master warning system, or by a separate system with a horn from the stall warning
From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the master warning system, or by a separate system with a clacker sound
From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the air data computer, or by a separate system with a clacker sound
cards.explain: These are the two arrangements given for the aural warning.

cards.question: A machmeter is opened and found to contain a differential pressure bellows and an aneroid bellows. Which instruments use these same two sensing elements?
options: The airspeed indicator uses a differential pressure capsule and the vertical speed indicator an aneroid capsule
The altimeter uses a differential pressure capsule and the airspeed indicator an aneroid capsule
The airspeed indicator uses a differential pressure capsule and the altimeter an aneroid capsule
cards.explain: PDF page 468 prints that the airspeed indicator has a differential pressure capsule and PDF page 454 that the altimeter's measuring component is an aneroid capsule, which are the two bellows listed here.

cards.question: A jet aeroplane in high altitude cruise triggers its overspeed warning. Which limit has been exceeded, and does the warning depend on the airspeed indication?
options: MMO, and the detection is taken from the airspeed indication
MMO, and the detection is independent of the airspeed indication
VMO, and the detection is independent of the airspeed indication
cards.explain: PDF page 470 prints that at higher altitudes the limit is the maximum allowed mach number, and this page prints that the overspeed detection is always independent of the airspeed indication.

cards.question: The airspeed indication in the cockpit has failed. What does this mean for overspeed detection?
options: Detection continues, because it is always independent of the airspeed indication
Detection is lost, because it is taken from the airspeed indication
Detection continues only while the aircraft is below the tropopause
cards.explain: Detection is stated to be always independent of the airspeed indication.

cards.question: What does the variometer measure in order to display vertical speed
options: Air temperature changes
Air pressure changes
Vertical acceleration forces
cards.explain: The variometer works from changes in air pressure.

cards.question: In which units is the variometer scale calibrated
options: Knots or m/sec
Ft/sec or m/min
Ft/min or m/sec
cards.explain: The manual gives ft/min or m/sec.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation IVSI stand for
options: Inertial Vertical Speed Indicator
Instantaneous Vertical Speed Indicator
Integrated Vertical Speed Indicator
cards.explain: IVSI is the instantaneous vertical speed indicator, giving undelayed indication.

cards.question: What does the IVSI indicator use to produce its undelayed indication
options: A small pump with a magnetically held piston
A small fan with a spring loaded vane
A small pump with a spring loaded piston
cards.explain: The manual describes a small pump with a spring loaded piston.

cards.question: A diaphragm variometer is stripped for overhaul. What seals the air gap?
options: A rubber lip seal
Badger hair
A felt washer
cards.explain: The manual states the gap is sealed with badger hair.

cards.question: What sets the central position of a diaphragm variometer
options: A permanent magnet
A coiled spring
A hairspring driven by the capillary
cards.explain: A coiled spring sets the central position.

cards.question: The reason why a vertical speed indicator is connected to the static system only
options: Because it works from changes of static pressure acting on its bellows
Because it works from the delay of the total pressure through a capillary
Because it works from the difference between total pressure and static pressure
cards.explain: The instrument senses air pressure changes with static pressure on both sides of its bellows, so it needs no pitot connection.

cards.question: The reason why the outside of the variometer bellows is fed through a capillary
options: So that the same pressure always acts inside and outside the bellows
So that the pressure change outside the bellows is delayed
So that the pressure change inside the bellows is delayed
cards.explain: The capillary holds back the pressure change on the outside, which is what creates the difference the pointer shows.

cards.question: How are the two sides of the differential pressure bellows of a mechanical variometer supplied
options: The outside directly with static pressure, the inside delayed via a capillary
The inside directly with static pressure, the outside delayed via a capillary
The inside directly with total pressure, the outside delayed via a capillary
cards.explain: Static pressure reaches the inside directly and the outside through the capillary.

cards.question: An aircraft holds a constant altitude so static pressure stays constant. What does the mechanical variometer show?
options: Zero, because the same pressure acts inside and outside the bellows
A small descent, because the bellows remain partly compressed
A small climb, because the capillary keeps the outside pressure higher
cards.explain: With equal pressures either side of the bellows the pointer reads zero.

cards.question: An aircraft with an IVSI enters and leaves a turn with a high bank angle. What should be expected?
options: An inaccurate vertical speed indication, because any vertical acceleration affects the piston
A total loss of indication, because the piston is locked by the acceleration
A correct vertical speed indication, because the piston compensates for bank angle
cards.explain: Any vertical acceleration acts on the piston, so turn entry and exit give a wrong reading.

cards.question: What produces the force that moves the diaphragm and the pointer of a diaphragm variometer
options: The difference between static pressure and total pressure
The difference between accumulator pressure and cabin pressure
The difference between static pressure and accumulator pressure
cards.explain: The driving difference is between static and accumulator pressure.

cards.question: How is pressure balanced out in a diaphragm variometer
options: Via a capillary tube between the diaphragm and the casing
Via the air gap between the diaphragm and the casing
Via a calibrated orifice in the centre of the diaphragm
cards.explain: Balancing takes place through the air gap between diaphragm and casing.

cards.question: A precision variometer is required for a glider. Why is the diaphragm type chosen?
options: Because diaphragm variometers are exact
Because diaphragm variometers need no static source
Because diaphragm variometers have the longest time constant
cards.explain: Their accuracy is the stated reason for their use as precision instruments.

cards.question: Why is the pointer movement of a mechanical variometer delayed when the vertical speed changes
options: Because the change is immediate inside the bellows but delayed outside by capillary action and the larger volume
Because the pointer linkage is deliberately damped by a friction brake
Because the change is immediate outside the bellows but delayed inside by capillary action and the larger volume
cards.explain: The capillary and the larger outer volume delay the outside pressure change.

cards.question: The response of a mechanical variometer to a change of vertical speed compared with an instantaneous vertical speed indicator
options: Delayed in the mechanical variometer, and undelayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
Undelayed in the mechanical variometer, and delayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
Delayed in both, because both feed the outside of the bellows through a capillary
cards.explain: PDF page 486 prints that the pointer movement is delayed on a change of vertical speed, and this page prints that the IVSI removes that delay with an acceleration piston.

cards.question: An aircraft begins a descent. How does the IVSI piston give an immediate indication?
options: The negative gravity force closes the capillary so that the outside static pressure changes first
The negative gravity force moves the piston down and lowers the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
The negative gravity force moves the piston up and raises the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
cards.explain: The piston raises bellows pressure ahead of the real static pressure change.

cards.question: A thermometer must read down to minus 150 C. Which filling substance has an application range that reaches this?
options: Mercury
Toluene
Pentane
cards.explain: Only pentane, listed from minus 200 C, covers that low a reading; toluene stops at minus 80 C and mercury at minus 30 C.

cards.question: A mercury thermometer is offered for work at minus 60 C. Why is it the wrong choice?
options: Its application range only starts at minus 30 C
It allows no remote temperature measurement
Its expansion coefficient is temperature-dependent
cards.explain: Mercury is only listed from minus 30 C upwards, so minus 60 C is outside its range.

cards.question: A filling is wanted that reads up to 1000 C without a poison hazard. Which substance fits, and what must be accepted with it?
options: Mercury, with heavy wetting of the thermometer tube
Galinstan, with a health risk from inflammable vapour
Galinstan, with heavy wetting of the thermometer tube
cards.explain: Galinstan is the non-poisonous alloy listed up to 1000 C, and its drawback is heavy wetting of the tube.

cards.question: The airspeed value that the temperature display is used to determine
options: TAS
IAS
EAS
cards.explain: Temperature is one of the inputs needed for true airspeed.

cards.question: The hazard that the temperature display helps the crew detect
options: Possible pitot blockage
Possible engine surge
Possible ice formation
cards.explain: Air temperature is the indication used to judge whether ice can form.

cards.question: What static air temperature (SAT) is
options: The ambient temperature plus the rise from air compression
The actual temperature of the ambient air
The free airstream temperature with a built-in deflection error
cards.explain: SAT is the true ambient air temperature, with no ram rise in it.

cards.question: What total air temperature (TAT) is
options: The ambient temperature minus the temperature generated by air compression
The ambient temperature plus the temperature generated by air compression
The ambient temperature with no allowance for air compression
cards.explain: TAT is ambient temperature plus the heating caused by compression of the air.

cards.question: The temperature value that is determined directly by the measuring probe
options: TAT
RR
SAT
cards.explain: Only TAT comes straight off the probe; SAT and the ram rise are worked out from it.

cards.question: What a TAT measuring probe contains as its sensing elements
options: Two or three temperature dependent capillary tubes
One temperature dependent PTC resistor
Two or three temperature dependent PTC resistors
cards.explain: The probe carries two or three temperature dependent PTC resistors.

cards.question: The engine related use of the temperature display
options: Calculating engine performance and determining engine limits
Calculating engine oil quantity and determining oil limits
Calculating engine vibration and determining balance limits
cards.explain: Air temperature feeds engine performance calculation and the engine limits.

cards.question: What an electronic OAT display needs in order to show a reading
options: An external OAT sensor
An internal cabin thermistor
A direct reading bulb in the cockpit
cards.explain: The electronic display has no sensing element of its own, so an external OAT sensor is required.

cards.question: The aircraft on which the simple OAT indicating system is used
options: Small propeller driven aeroplanes and helicopters
Large commercial jet aeroplanes
Supersonic transport aeroplanes
cards.explain: The simple system is restricted to small propeller driven aeroplanes and helicopters.

cards.question: A fast jet aeroplane cannot use the simple OAT indicating system. What is the reason?
options: It needs a bleed air supply that jets cannot provide
It is only accurate up to an airspeed of 250 kts
It cannot be protected against ice
cards.explain: Its accuracy runs out at 250 kts, which is why it is limited to slow aircraft.

cards.question: In a modern temperature indicating system, the display and the calculation
options: are performed together in the instrument, as in conventional analogue construction
are performed separately, the calculation being done in the computer
are performed separately, the calculation being done in the measuring probe
cards.explain: Modern instruments display digitally and do the calculation separately, in the computer, unlike the conventional analogue indicator that carries its switching inside the instrument.

cards.question: How SAT is obtained in a fast aeroplane
options: It is read directly from the total air temperature probe
It is read directly from a flush skin probe
It is calculated by an air data computer
cards.explain: SAT cannot be measured directly in flight, so the ADC calculates it from other data.

cards.question: Why the TAT is always higher than the SAT during flight
options: The probe heater adds heat to the measurement in flight
Ram air is present at the measuring probe and raises its temperature
The probe is flush with a skin that is warmed by the sun
cards.explain: Ram air at the probe produces the ram rise that lifts TAT above SAT.

cards.question: The built-in error that makes RAT differ from TAT
options: The air is deflected as it flows around the aircraft fuselage
The air is warmed by the probe anti-icing element
The air is brought completely to rest inside the probe neck
cards.explain: The free airstream over the probe is deflected around the fuselage, which is the built-in RAT error.

cards.question: The form of temperature supplied by a probe mounted flush with the aircraft skin
options: SAT
TAT
RAT
cards.explain: A flush probe gives ram air temperature; the TAT probe is the one held off the skin.

cards.question: A temperature probe is carried on a spacing foot clear of the fuselage skin. What is this arrangement for?
options: To keep the probe clear of the skin heating system
To let bleed air be blown back over the skin
To determine the total air temperature out in the airstream
cards.explain: Holding the probe out in the airstream, like a pitot tube, is what lets it sense TAT.

cards.question: Where the switching sits in an analogue temperature indicator of conventional construction
options: In the air data computer, together with the measuring resistor
Directly in the instrument, except for the measuring resistor
Directly in the probe, except for the measuring resistor
cards.explain: Only the measuring resistor sits outside; the rest of the switching is in the instrument.
