cards.question: An artificial horizon gyro whose axis points to the centre of the earth at the north pole is carried down to the equator. How does its axis finish up to an observer on the earth?
options: still vertical
turned through a right angle in the horizontal plane
horizontal
cards.explain: The axis appears to topple during the journey until it is horizontal at the equator.

cards.question: A gyro has worn frame bearings and is also carried east-west across the earth. How do the two error sources add up?
options: the bearing error takes the place of the earth rotation and transport errors
the bearing error is cancelled by the earth rotation and transport errors
the bearing error sits on top of the earth rotation and transport errors
cards.explain: Real errors from construction are error values over and above those due to the earth's rotation and transport.

cards.question: A gyroscope is found with its two frames lined up with each other. What can still be done with it?
options: nothing, an instrument in that state is unusable
it can be used once its frames are re-sprung
it can be used for drift but not for topple
cards.explain: Gimbal lock, where the two frames are aligned, makes the gyroscope unusable.

cards.question: A directional gyro reads correctly in straight flight but shows a heading error whenever the aircraft turns. Which error is that?
options: a real drift error from worn bearings
an earth transport precession error
the cardan error
cards.explain: Gimbal error, known as the cardan error, mainly occurs during a turn and shows up as a direction indication error.

cards.question: An erection system is fitted to a directional gyro. In which direction does it hold that gyro's axis?
options: horizontal
vertical
along the aircraft centre line
cards.explain: The erection keeps the axis horizontal for the directional gyro and vertical for the vertical gyro.

cards.question: What decides whether a given gyro is erected mechanically or by torque motors?
options: the latitude the aircraft is operating at
the type of gyro
the number of frames the gyro is gimballed in
cards.explain: The erection is done by mechanic force of gravity or by electrical torque motors depending on the gyro type.

cards.question: An erection system is set to work against the total topple of a gyro. Which two errors make up that total?
options: real topple and real drift
apparent topple and real topple
apparent topple and apparent drift
cards.explain: Total topple is the sum of apparent topple and real topple.

cards.question: A designer is choosing how big to make the beam cavity of an optical gyro. Why is a larger one wanted?
options: the interference pattern can be measured more easily
the laser needs less power to keep the beams going
the two beams stay in phase over a wider speed range
cards.explain: In general, the larger the beam cavity is, the easier the interference pattern can be measured.

cards.question: At extremely small angular velocities the beams of light still interfere. What is the difficulty then?
options: the interference is difficult to measure
the two beams stop running in opposite directions
the interference pattern no longer forms at all
cards.explain: Beams interfere at extremely small angular velocities, but in such a case they are difficult to measure.

cards.question: An optical gyro is built with mirrors rather than with fibre optics. What does that choice bring with it?
options: easy measurement but a size constrained unit
difficult measurement but a size constrained unit
easy measurement and a very large orbit
cards.explain: Optical gyroscopes with mirrors are easy to measure but are constrained by the size of the unit.

cards.question: The gyroscope block is turned clockwise. What happens to the beam that runs in the direction of that rotation?
options: it travels slightly less far before returning to its starting point
it travels slightly further before returning to its starting point
it stops returning to its starting point at all
cards.explain: The beam moving in the direction of rotation travels slightly further than the one running the other way.

cards.question: One of the two beams has been forced onto the longer course by the rotation. What has become of its frequency?
options: it is slightly lower
it is slightly higher
it is unchanged
cards.explain: The beam on the longer course has the now longer resonator and so a slightly lower frequency.

cards.question: The two wave trains are keeping exactly the same frequencies. What are the bright and dark strips doing?
options: they remain stationary
they wander over the photodiodes
they double in number
cards.explain: As long as the wave trains keep the same frequencies the strips remain stationary.

cards.question: The frequencies of the two wave trains begin to differ. What does the counter then receive?
options: a single bright pulse as the strips cancel at the photodiodes
a steady light level as the strips settle over the photodiodes
alternating light-dark impulses as the strips wander over the photodiodes
cards.explain: When the frequencies differ the strips wander over the photodiodes, which are alternately in light and dark, and those impulses are metered.

cards.question: The photodiodes have told the electronics which way the interference strips are wandering. What is that used for?
options: the path length, carried as a correction to the setting of the mirrors
the rotational direction, carried as a preceding symbol in the pulse count
the rotational speed, carried as a count of the pulses per unit of time
cards.explain: The direction of wander indicates the rotational direction and is taken into account with a preceding symbol when the pulses are added up.

cards.question: Coherent light has been made to interfere inside the optical circuit of a gyro. What can then be measured?
options: the speed of rotation, that is the arc velocity
the temperature of the resonance cavity
the direction of the earth's gravity vector
cards.explain: Because coherent light can interfere, speed of rotation, that is arc velocity, can be measured with the structure of the optical circuit.

cards.question: Which two types of ring cavity have the manufacturers taken
options: two and three-leg ring cavities
three and four-leg ring cavities
four and six-leg ring cavities
cards.explain: There are three-leg and four-leg ring cavities.

cards.question: To which specification does the fibre optic gyro conform entirely
options: ARINC 561
ARINC 705
ARINC 704
cards.explain: The fibre optic gyro conforms entirely to the requirements of the ARINC 705 specification.

cards.question: Which medium do the gas laser gyroscopes that have prevailed in practice use
options: helium/neon
helium/argon
neon/krypton
cards.explain: The gas laser gyroscopes that prevailed use helium/neon as a medium.

cards.question: What determines the frequency of the laser light
options: the number of mirrors in the light path
the current drawn by the laser exciter
the length of the cavity between cathode and anode
cards.explain: The frequency of the laser light is determined by the length of the cavity, cathode to anode.

cards.question: By which three means can laser rays be produced
options: by gas, liquid or semi-conductor lasers
by gas, solid state or semi-conductor lasers
by solid state, liquid or crystal lasers
cards.explain: Laser rays can be produced by gas, solid state or semi-conductor lasers.

cards.question: On what does the sensitivity of a laser gyroscope depend
options: the weight of the gyroscope block
the number of legs of the ring cavity
the size of the circuit
cards.explain: The sensitivity of a laser gyroscope depends on the size of the circuit.

cards.question: In a gyro that winds its light path into a coil, what forms that enclosed path
options: a set of three mirrors
a fibre optic
a quarz bowl
cards.explain: A fibre optic forms the necessary enclosed light path.

cards.question: For which aircraft is the fibre optic gyro now used for position and navigation
options: the largest commercial aircraft of long range, and military aircraft
smaller commercial aircraft of short and medium range, and military aircraft
smaller commercial aircraft of short and medium range only
cards.explain: The fibre optic gyro is used for position and navigation of smaller short and medium range commercial aircraft and in military aviation.

cards.question: Two laser gyros are built to the same sensitivity but with different ring cavities. Which of the two comes out the smaller unit?
options: the four-leg gyro
neither, they come out the same size
the three-leg gyro
cards.explain: For the same sensitivity the dimensions of a four-leg laser gyro are smaller than those of a three-leg gyro.

cards.question: An installation is being changed from a conventional INS platform gyro to a laser gyro. What happens to the wait before the system can be used?
options: it is unchanged, since both need the same warm-up before alignment
it rises, since the laser gyro needs a longer alignment than the platform
it falls away, since the laser gyro has no warm-up and no run-up time
cards.explain: The laser gyro is listed as having neither warm-up time nor gyro run-up time.

cards.question: A ring laser gyro is sitting in the range of very low rotational speeds. What has become of its reading?
options: the low rotational speed of the gyroscope block is no longer measurable
the gyroscope block reports its highest rotation rate instead
the low rotational speed of the gyroscope block is read with doubled accuracy
cards.explain: In the lock-in range the low rotational speed of the gyroscope block is no longer measurable.

cards.question: The gyro block is being deliberately shaken back and forth all the time. How is that kept out of the output?
options: the computer compensates for the self-oscillation when calculating the rates
the photodiodes are blanked whenever the block moves back and forth
the laser exciter is switched off during each back and forth movement
cards.explain: The computer compensates for the self-oscillation when calculating the rotation rates.

cards.question: Path length control is working on a ring laser gyro. What is moved and to what end?
options: the prisms are corrected to bring the two beams back into phase
the mirrors are corrected to attain the maximum possible brightness
the photodiodes are corrected to hold the interference strips still
cards.explain: Via a photodiode and piezo crystals the mirrors are corrected for maximum brightness and thus the optimal path length.

cards.question: A fibre optic gyro is sitting completely still and its two light waves have been brought to interference. What is their relation?
options: they are a quarter wave apart
they are in phase
they are exactly opposed
cards.explain: If there is no rotation the two light waves are in phase at the end of the coil.

cards.question: The fibre optic gyro is now rotated about its vertical axis. Why does a phase displacement appear?
options: the wave running in the direction of rotation has a longer run-time than the other
the wave running in the direction of rotation is slowed down by the fibre
the two waves are no longer of equal intensity when they meet
cards.explain: Under rotation the beam running with the rotation has a longer run-time and the other a shorter one, which is the Sagnac effect.

cards.question: A phase displacement has built up between the two waves in the coil. What does the photodiode actually see?
options: a change in the colour of the interference signal
a break in the interference signal
a change in the intensity of the interference signal
cards.explain: The phase displacement leads to a change in the intensity of the interference signal, which the photodiode captures.

cards.question: What is the fibre optic gyro reference system together with GPS expected to offer general aviation?
options: a costly but extremely precise position and navigation system
an inexpensive, reliable and extremely precise position and navigation system
an inexpensive but only approximate position and navigation system
cards.explain: With GPS the fibre optic gyro reference system should offer an inexpensive, reliable and extremely precise position and navigation system.

cards.question: The input axis of a hemispherical resonator gyro is turned. What does the standing wave do?
options: it dies away until the axis stops turning
it precedes the casing in exact relation to the rotational angle
it grows in amplitude in proportion to the rotational angle
cards.explain: When the input axis turns, the standing wave precedes the casing in exact relation to the rotational angle.

cards.question: Energy is being pumped into the resonator of a hemispherical resonator gyro through the ring forcer electrodes. What is that for?
options: to restore the damping loss and maintain the resonance frequency
to drive the standing wave round against the direction of rotation
to raise the amplitude of the standing wave with the angle of rotation
cards.explain: Via the ring forcer electrodes the damping loss is restored by pumping energy in to maintain the resonance frequency.

cards.question: A fleet planner compares the mean time between failures of the gyro itself with that of the whole inertial reference system. Which of the two is the longer?
options: the gyro, at 150,000 h against 12,000 h for the system
the system, at 150,000 h against 12,000 h for the gyro
they are the same, both being 12,000 h
cards.explain: The HRG has an MTBF of 150,000 h and the IRS one of 12,000 h.

questions.question: What name is given to a gyro whose rotational axis stands upright
options: rate gyro
directional gyro
vertical gyro
questions.explain: A gyro with a vertical axis is called a vertical gyro.

questions.question: The angle of flight direction measured by the directional gyro carries which name
options: the attitude
the course
the drift
questions.explain: The angle of flight direction is the course.

questions.question: Which gyro gives the reference for the attitude indication of an aircraft
options: a rate gyro
a vertical gyro
a directional gyro
questions.explain: The vertical gyro is the reference for the attitude indication.

questions.question: About how long does the gyro of the standby horizon take to spin down
options: about 10 minutes
about 20 minutes
about 2 minutes
questions.explain: The spin down time of the standby horizon gyro is given as about 20 minutes.

questions.question: A technician pulls the caging knob of a standby horizon. What happens inside the instrument?
options: the gyro motor is switched off and allowed to run down
the erection balls are released onto their circular path
the gimbals are caged and stabilized in the normal position
questions.explain: Pulling the caging knob cages the gimbals and stabilizes them in the normal position.

questions.question: A unit on the bench is labelled as a directional gyro. What does that tell a technician about the way its spin axis lies?
options: it is at 45 degrees
it is horizontal
it is vertical
questions.explain: Gyros with a horizontal axis are the ones called directional gyros.

questions.question: To what rate is the normal speed of erection of the vertical gyro limited
options: 2 degrees per minute
12 degrees per minute
20 degrees per minute
questions.explain: Normal speed of erection is limited to 2 degrees per minute.

questions.question: The gyro of a standby horizon with a balance beam is no longer in its horizontal position and the beam mass swings out. What is that displacement used for?
options: as the erection momentum for the gyroscope
as the signal that drops the warning flag
as the braking force on the gyro capsule
questions.explain: The mass displacement is used as erection momentum for the gyroscope.

questions.question: Besides attitude, altitude and airspeed, which two further values can a recent integrated standby system display
options: outside air temperature and wind
drift angle and ground speed
magnetic heading and mach number
questions.explain: Magnetic heading and mach number can be displayed in addition.

questions.question: An aircraft is fitted with an integrated standby instrument system. What has become of the separate standby instruments?
options: they are kept as a second back up
they are no longer needed
they are moved to the overhead panel
questions.explain: With the integrated system the individual original standby instruments are no longer needed.

questions.question: What does an air driven gyro use to generate its erection force
options: level switches holding a fluid
pendulums moved by the airflow
a balance beam turning slowly
questions.explain: The air driven gyro uses pendulums to make an erection force from the airflow.

questions.question: What activates the torque motor of an electrically driven gyro when its axis topples
options: a level switch holding a conductive fluid
a rocker tipped by horizontal acceleration
a pendulum moved by the cockpit airflow
questions.explain: Electrically driven gyros use level switches with a conductive fluid to activate the torque motor.

questions.question: Why must long acceleration periods such as full turns be avoided
options: the erection rate rises above its normal working limit
the gyro motor runs hot in that attitude of the frame
the gyro topple cannot be compensated during that time
questions.explain: During a long acceleration the erection is cut out, so gyro topple cannot be compensated.

questions.question: A vertical gyro is feeding the cockpit indicator. What turns the angular movements at the pivot points into electric signals?
options: conductive level switches
erection torque motors
synchro-transmitters
questions.explain: Synchro-transmitters at the pivot points make the angular movements into electric signals.

questions.question: A vertical gyro has held a motor speed above 75% for more than 30 seconds and its gimbals are erected. What happens next?
options: fast erection ends and the motor runs on at reduced voltage
fast erection begins and the motor runs on at raised voltage
the erectors are switched off for a maximum of three minutes
questions.explain: Those are exactly the conditions that end fast erection and drop the motor to reduced voltage.

questions.question: What is the longest time the pitch erector may stay switched off during strong longitudinal acceleration
options: two minutes
three minutes
30 seconds
questions.explain: The page limits the pitch erector cut-off to a maximum of three minutes.

questions.question: What does the VG valid direct current arriving at the ADI confirm
options: that the vertical gyro is functioning
that the ADI power supply is healthy
that the synchro signals have nulled
questions.explain: The valid direct current is the gyro's statement that it is working.

questions.question: Which kind of movement drives the turn indication on the ADI
options: a synchro receiver
a moving coil
an electric servo motor
questions.explain: It is a moving coil instrument.

questions.question: A technician must identify the drive behind the glideslope pointer of an ADI. What kind of movement will he find?
options: an electric servo motor
a moving coil
a synchro receiver
questions.explain: The glideslope pointer is a moving coil instrument.

questions.question: The ball has moved out in the direction of the turn. What must the pilot do to bring the turn back into balance?
options: raise the rate of turn with rudder towards the ball
lower the bank angle and leave the rudder central
lower the rate of turn with rudder towards the ball
questions.explain: With the ball out into the turn the turn rate must be raised, using rudder towards the ball.

questions.question: The turn needle of a turn and slip indicator stands at full deflection while the ball is centred. What is the aircraft doing?
options: turning at a rate that would complete a circle in two minutes, in balance
turning at a rate that would complete a circle in two minutes, out of balance
turning at a rate that would complete a circle in one minute, in balance
questions.explain: Full deflection is the two minute turn and a centred ball is a coordinated one, so both are being flown.

questions.question: A rate of turn indicator is built with only one free and one constrained degree of freedom and a return spring. What can it therefore show?
options: the attitude the aircraft is holding
the bank angle the aircraft has reached
how fast the aircraft is turning
questions.explain: With the second freedom held by a spring the gyro can only balance precession against spring force, which measures how fast the aircraft turns, not the attitude it holds.

questions.question: A pilot is rolling into a turn and the bank angle is still changing. What is the turn coordinator showing while that goes on?
options: the yaw rate
the resultant force of the turn
the roll rate
questions.explain: While the bank angle is changing the coordinator reads roll rate instead.

questions.question: A rate of turn gyro is held by a linear spring. What can then be said about its precession angle?
options: it is proportional to the angular velocity about the measuring axis
it falls as the angular velocity about the measuring axis rises
it is independent of the angular velocity about the measuring axis
questions.explain: A linear spring makes the precession angle proportional to the angular velocity about the measuring axis.

questions.question: During a turn the loose items in the cabin are being pushed out towards the outside of the curve. Which condition is that?
options: a perfectly coordinated turn
a slip
a skid
questions.explain: With the loose items thrown outward from the centre of the curve the ball also lies to the outside, which Figure 208 labels a skid.

questions.question: A pilot is about to adjust the direction indicator after start-up. Which instrument has to be read first?
options: The magnetic compass
The attitude indicator
The turn indicator
questions.explain: The setting value comes from the magnetic compass, which the direction indicator cannot supply itself.

questions.question: A crew finds the gyro compass reading has moved away from the compass after some minutes of flight. What does the drift of the instrument call for?
options: Re-levelling the inner frame by hand at regular intervals
Synchronising the course indication by hand at intervals
Re-caging the outer frame by hand at regular intervals
questions.explain: Because apparent drift, real drift and cardan error spoil the precision, the course indication has to be resynchronised by hand against the magnetic compass.

questions.question: A heading sensor is mounted well away from the instrument panel and its reading appears on the flight deck. Which gyro is the sensor and what fault must be corrected in it?
options: A directional gyro, whose drift must be compensated
A directional gyro, whose toppling must be compensated
A vertical gyro, whose drift must be compensated
questions.explain: The remote sensor is the directional gyro, and the page states its drift must be compensated.

questions.question: A directional gyro has begun to drift and the slaving momentum is applied to the inner frame axis. Until what point does it continue?
options: Until the inner frame is back in the horizontal
Until the gyro heading matches the standby compass heading
Until the gyro heading matches the flux valve heading
questions.explain: Slaving runs until the gyro agrees with the flux valve, which is the magnetic reference of the system.

questions.question: A chart gives the variation for a position and the compass card carries a deviation. Which pair of directions does each of these angles lie between?
options: Variation between true and magnetic north, deviation between magnetic and compass north
Variation between true and compass north, deviation between true and magnetic north
Variation between magnetic and compass north, deviation between true and magnetic north
questions.explain: Variation separates true from magnetic north and deviation separates magnetic north from compass north.

questions.question: An airport publishes a changed runway designation a few years after the previous one. What has made this necessary?
options: The compass deviation at the airfield has changed
The magnetic poles have moved and magnetic references must follow
The geographic poles have moved and true references must follow
questions.explain: Runway directions are magnetic references, so pole drift forces them to be re-published.

questions.question: An aircraft is to operate in a region close to the magnetic pole. Which heading source must be used there and why?
options: A directional gyro, because the horizontal component is too weak
A flux valve, because the vertical component takes over
A standby compass, because the horizontal component is strongest
questions.explain: Inclination leaves too little horizontal field at high latitude, so a gyro or inertial reference replaces the compass.

questions.question: A compass finds the angle with a mounted, freely rotating permanent magnet. Which method and which compass is this?
options: The mechanical method, a remote reading compass
The electronic method, a remote reading compass
The mechanical method, a direct reading compass
questions.explain: The magnetic needle principle is the mechanical method and gives the direct reading compass.

questions.question: An aircraft suffers a total electrical power loss. Which heading indication is still available?
options: The horizontal situation indicator
The directional gyro
The standby compass
questions.explain: The direct reading standby compass needs no electrical power to show the heading.

questions.question: New electrical equipment has been fitted close to the standby compass. Which compass error will change and what corrects it?
options: Variation, taken out by the compensation magnets
Deviation, taken out by updating the chart value
Deviation, taken out by the compensation magnets
questions.explain: An added aircraft field alters the deviation, and deviation is reduced by the compass compensation magnets.

questions.question: An indication is falsified by the amount of the deviation — what is that heading called?
options: the magnetic heading
the compass heading
the true heading
questions.explain: The falsified indication is named the compass heading.

questions.question: No compensating site is free and the aircraft cannot be turned — which method still works?
options: the markings on the compensating disc
the Standby Compass Calibrator
a bearing plate sighted on a distant object
questions.explain: The SCC works without rotating the aircraft, while the other two methods both need the aircraft turned on a site.

questions.question: An acceleration has tilted a compass out of the horizontal plane — what now acts on its magnet?
options: the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field
the permanent magnetism of the aircraft structure
the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field
questions.explain: Once the compass is off the horizontal the vertical component starts to influence the magnet.

questions.question: An aircraft is held in a 40° banked turn — what happens to the flux valve measuring plane?
options: it can no longer stay horizontal
it stays horizontal because the cardan takes any angle
it is driven back to horizontal by the directional gyro
questions.explain: The cardan only holds the plane level out to about 30°, so at 40° of bank it is exceeded.

questions.question: The excitation coil of a flux valve has gone open circuit — what reaches the magnetic heading reference system?
options: nothing, because the field intensity no longer changes
a signal that gives true heading instead of magnetic
a signal at half of its normal output frequency
questions.explain: Without the excitation the core is never switched in and out of saturation, so the field intensity at the coils is steady and no voltage is induced.

cards.question: Which two tasks are carried out by the gimballed gyros of an aircraft
options: attitude measurement and directional measurement
airspeed measurement and directional measurement
attitude measurement and vibration measurement
cards.explain: The two important functions named for gimballed gyros are attitude measurement and directional measurement.

cards.question: What name is given to a gyro whose rotational axis stands upright
options: rate gyro
vertical gyro
directional gyro
cards.explain: A gyro with a vertical axis is called a vertical gyro.

cards.question: An attitude gyro is running normally in the cruise. Changes in the angle of which two aircraft axes does it measure?
options: the longitudinal axis and the vertical axis
the longitudinal axis and the lateral axis
the lateral axis and the vertical axis
cards.explain: The attitude gyro measures the angle changes of the x-axis and the y-axis.

cards.question: What is the result of the measurement made by the attitude gyro
options: the angle of flight direction
the angle of roll and pitch
the angle of yaw and drift
cards.explain: Measuring the x and y axis angle changes gives the angle of roll and pitch.

cards.question: Which gyro gives the reference for the attitude indication of an aircraft
options: a directional gyro
a rate gyro
a vertical gyro
cards.explain: The vertical gyro is the reference for the attitude indication.

cards.question: Which other name is given to the attitude indication of an aircraft
options: the artificial horizon
the attitude director
the horizon drum
cards.explain: The attitude indication is also called the artificial horizon.

cards.question: A standby horizon is being powered up for a check. From which aircraft supply does its gyro take its drive energy?
options: the main AC generator
the battery system
the cockpit suction pump
cards.explain: The standby horizon gyro is electrically driven from the aircraft battery system.

cards.question: In what way does the erection system of the standby horizon do its work
options: pneumatically
mechanically
electrically
cards.explain: The erection system of the standby horizon works mechanically.

cards.question: To what maximum rate can an erection system influence the gyro axis
options: ten degrees per minute
three degrees per minute
thirty degrees per minute
cards.explain: An erection system can only influence the gyro axis to a maximum of three degrees per minute.

cards.question: A technician pulls the caging knob of a standby horizon. What happens inside the instrument?
options: the gimbals are caged and stabilized in the normal position
the gyro motor is switched off and allowed to run down
the erection balls are released onto their circular path
cards.explain: Pulling the caging knob cages the gimbals and stabilizes them in the normal position.

cards.question: What kind of motor is the gyro of a ball driven standby horizon
options: a three-phase asynchronic internal rotor motor
a single-phase synchronic external rotor motor
a three-phase asynchronic external rotor motor
cards.explain: The gyro is a three-phase asynchronic external rotor motor.

cards.question: The gyro motor of a ball driven standby horizon loses its electrical supply. What shows this on the instrument?
options: a flag
a level switch
an ammeter
cards.explain: A flag monitors the electrical supply to the motor.

cards.question: A unit on the bench is labelled as a directional gyro. What does that tell a technician about the way its spin axis lies?
options: it is vertical
it is horizontal
it is at 45 degrees
cards.explain: Gyros with a horizontal axis are the ones called directional gyros.

cards.question: A gyro on the bench has its rotational axis standing upright. Which measuring task is it built for?
options: turn rate measurement
directional measurement
attitude measurement
cards.explain: The vertical axis gyro is the attitude gyro, so it does attitude measurement.

cards.question: Where must the rotational axis of the attitude gyro always point
options: towards the magnetic north pole
along the flight path
towards the centre of the earth
cards.explain: The attitude gyro axis must always point at the centre of the earth, that is, be vertical.

cards.question: Changes in the angle of which axis are determined when direction is measured
options: the vertical axis
the lateral axis
the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: Direction measurement comes from the angle changes of the vertical axis.

cards.question: A directional gyro is running correctly in level flight. How does its rotational axis lie?
options: parallel to the horizon of the earth
along the lateral axis of the aircraft
straight down at the centre of the earth
cards.explain: The directional gyro axis must always be parallel to the earth's horizon, that is horizontal.

cards.question: In a small aircraft, which instrument has the vertical gyro built into it
options: the attitude indicator
the standby horizon
the suction indicator
cards.explain: In small aircraft the vertical gyro sits inside the attitude indicator.

cards.question: Why must the artificial horizon stay available for as long as possible
options: it is the only indication that shows both roll and pitch together
it is one of the four most important indications in an aircraft
it is the only indication that works without any electrical power
cards.explain: It is named as one of the four most important indications, so it must keep working as long as it can.

cards.question: A standby horizon gyro has run down past the point where it still turns stable. What has happened to its indication?
options: it is frozen at the last attitude
it is no longer usable
it is corrected by the caging knob
cards.explain: The indication stays usable only as long as the gyro runs stable during its spin down time.

cards.question: Why does a standby horizon need a caging mechanism as well as its erection system
options: erection on its own cannot work while the gyro runs at full speed
erection on its own cannot hold the gimbals in the normal position
erection on its own is far too slow to set the gyro up at once
cards.explain: Erection moves the axis only three degrees a minute, so a caging mechanism is needed to erect the gyro immediately.

cards.question: After which event is an immediate erection of the gyro wanted
options: a heavy landing
a long descent
power activation
cards.explain: Immediate erection is wanted for example after power activation.

cards.question: At which gyro speeds is gimbal caging allowed to be used
options: at any speed between standstill and full speed
at full speed or at a complete standstill
only while the gyro is running down from full speed
cards.explain: Caging may be used only with the gyro at full speed or stopped completely.

cards.question: Apart from the horizon drum, what else is turned by the gyro motor of a ball driven standby horizon
options: the erection and erection lock mechanism
the caging knob and the aeroplane symbol
the pendulum stop and the frame stops
cards.explain: The same motor also drives the erection and the erection lock mechanism.

cards.question: What is prevented by the cut-out mechanism of a ball driven standby horizon
options: the gyroscope tipping towards apparent vertical
the gyroscope precessing towards earth vertical
the gyroscope running down after a power failure
cards.explain: The cut-out mechanism stops the gyroscope from tipping towards apparent vertical.

cards.question: An aircraft is loaded heavily so it sits nose high on the ground. How can neutral pitch attitude still be set on the standby horizon?
options: by turning the caging knob to move the aeroplane symbol
by pulling the caging knob to cage the gimbals
by resetting the barometric knob of the instrument
cards.explain: Turning the caging knob raises or lowers the symbol, so neutral pitch can be set whatever the weight.

cards.question: Two gyros stand on a bench, one with its spin axis upright and one with its spin axis lying flat. Which job does each one do?
options: the upright one gives roll and pitch, the flat one gives the course
the upright one gives the course, the flat one gives roll and pitch
the upright one gives pitch only, the flat one gives roll only
cards.explain: The vertical axis gyro is the attitude gyro giving roll and pitch; the horizontal axis gyro is the directional gyro giving the course.

cards.question: Every electrical supply in the aircraft has been lost. Why does the standby horizon still give a usable indication for a while?
options: its erection system needs no power and the gyro runs down slowly
its erection system is fed by the standby inverter during the run down
its gyro is driven by cockpit air which keeps flowing during the run down
cards.explain: The mechanical erection system keeps working with no power while the gyro coasts down, so the indication stays usable.

cards.question: A technician cages the gimbals while the gyro is still coasting down at half speed. What is the likely result?
options: the gyro may be damaged, stability being limited
the gyro will stop at once and need a restart
the gyro will erect at twice its normal rate
cards.explain: Any intermediate speed may damage the gyro because of the limited stability.

cards.question: A standby horizon has just been switched off and the technician wants to cage its gimbals. What should be done first?
options: pull the caging knob twice in succession
wait until the gyro is stopped completely
cage at once before the speed starts to fall
cards.explain: Caging is allowed only at full speed or at a complete standstill, so after switch off the gyro must be left to stop.

cards.question: The gyro axis points at the centre of the earth during unaccelerated flight. What are the two erection balls doing?
options: they are balanced out, so no momentum acts on the gyro axis
they are driven apart, so a momentum acts on the gyro axis
they are held at their stops by the gyro cut-out rocker
cards.explain: With the axis in earth vertical the balls are balanced and no momentum acts on the gyro axis.

cards.question: A horizontal acceleration greater than 1.7 m/s2 acts on a ball driven standby horizon. What happens inside it?
options: a flag drops to show the indication is no longer usable
a torque motor drives the balls apart to correct the axis
a rocker tips and prevents an unbalance of the balls
cards.explain: Above 1.7 m/s2 a rocker tips and keeps the balls from going out of balance.

cards.question: At start-up the gyro axis of a ball driven horizon is found more than 10 degrees out of earth vertical. What must be done?
options: switch the supply off and let the gyro run down
pull the caging knob to erect the gyro rapidly
wait for the erection balls to bring the axis back
cards.explain: Beyond 10 degrees the cut-out mechanism blocks independent erection, so the caging knob must be pulled.

cards.question: Power to a ball driven standby horizon is lost in flight. For how long can the instrument still be used?
options: up to 15 minutes
up to 45 minutes
up to 5 minutes
cards.explain: The gyrating mass lets the standby horizon be used for up to 15 minutes after a power failure.

cards.question: A ball driven standby horizon is switched on with its axis only slightly off earth vertical. Why does it still erect on its own?
options: the erection balls run faster below full gyro speed
the caging knob is pulled by the power up circuit
the cut-out only blocks erection beyond 10 degrees
cards.explain: The cut-out mechanism prevents independent erection only when the axis is more than 10 degrees out of earth vertical.

cards.question: A ball driven standby horizon is held in a long steady horizontal acceleration. Why does its erection stop working?
options: a flag drops, so the erection supply is cut off
the caging knob latches the gimbals in position
a rocker tips, so the balls cannot go out of balance
cards.explain: Above 1.7 m/s2 the rocker of the pendulum accelerometer tips and prevents the ball unbalance that would erect the gyro.

cards.question: A ball driven standby horizon is fed from the battery through a static inverter. What kind of supply does its gyro motor need?
options: single-phase DC
half-wave DC
three-phase AC
cards.explain: The gyro is a three-phase motor, which is why the static inverter is fitted between it and the battery.

cards.question: A standby horizon has lost all power in flight. What sets the limit on how long the crew may keep using it?
options: the rotational energy still stored in the gyro
the air still being drawn through the instrument
the charge still left in the aircraft battery
cards.explain: The gyrating mass carries the gyro on for up to 15 minutes, and that stored energy is what sets the limit.

cards.question: How far can the mass on one end of the balance beam swing out when the gyro is unbalanced
options: up to 10 degrees
up to 85 degrees
up to 30 degrees
cards.explain: The mass on one end can swing out up to 30 degrees in the case of gyro unbalance.

cards.question: In a small aircraft, what generates the airflow that drives the gyro
options: a vacuum or suction pump
a static inverter
an engine bleed tapping
cards.explain: The airflow comes from a vacuum or suction pump.

cards.question: For what do the letters ISIS stand
options: Internal Standby Indicating System
Integrated Standby Instrument System
Integrated Second Instrument Set
cards.explain: ISIS is the Integrated Standby Instrument System.

cards.question: Which three indications are supplied by a recent integrated standby instrument system
options: attitude, heading and mach number
attitude, altitude and airspeed
altitude, airspeed and vertical speed
cards.explain: Recent systems supply attitude, altitude and airspeed indications.

cards.question: How many degrees of freedom does a vertical gyro have
options: one
two
three
cards.explain: A vertical gyro is a gyro with three degrees of freedom.

cards.question: How are vertical gyros driven
options: by cockpit airflow
electrically
by engine bleed air
cards.explain: Vertical gyros are driven electrically.

cards.question: Which switches do electrical gyros carry to deal with aircraft accelerations
options: gimbal caging switches
erection cutout switches
conductive level switches
cards.explain: Electrical gyros have erection cutout switches for this.

cards.question: Which aircraft axis does the roll axis of the vertical gyro correspond to
options: the lateral axis
the longitudinal axis
the vertical axis
cards.explain: The roll axis of the gyro corresponds to the aircraft's longitudinal axis.

cards.question: Which aircraft axis is represented by the pitch axis of the vertical gyro
options: the vertical axis
the lateral axis
the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: The pitch axis of the gyro represents the lateral axis of the aircraft.

cards.question: To what rate is the normal speed of erection of the vertical gyro limited
options: 2 degrees per minute
20 degrees per minute
12 degrees per minute
cards.explain: Normal speed of erection is limited to 2 degrees per minute.

cards.question: How does an improved standby horizon obtain the alternating current it needs to run
options: from a phase converter mounted in the aircraft rack
from a static inverter installed inside the device
from the standby busbar of the aircraft supply
cards.explain: A static inverter built into the device supplies the AC needed for operation.

cards.question: Which mechanism is absent from a pendulum erection standby horizon
options: the gimbal caging mechanism
the ball circulating mechanism
the mechanical cut-out mechanism
cards.explain: These devices do not have a ball circulating mechanism.

cards.question: What takes the place of the ball circulating mechanism in a pendulum erection horizon
options: a balance beam turning at low speed
a pendulum accelerometer and rocker
a pair of conductive level switches
cards.explain: In its place a balance beam rotates at low speed.

cards.question: The gyro of a standby horizon with a balance beam is no longer in its horizontal position and the beam mass swings out. What is that displacement used for?
options: as the erection momentum for the gyroscope
as the signal that drops the warning flag
as the braking force on the gyro capsule
cards.explain: The mass displacement is used as erection momentum for the gyroscope.

cards.question: Besides a large gyro unbalance, what else makes the cut-out mechanism hold the rotational mass in place
options: equivalent horizontal accelerations
a drop of the supply voltage
a rise of the gyro rotational speed
cards.explain: Equivalent horizontal accelerations have the same effect as a 10 degree unbalance.

cards.question: Why does a gyro need a high rotational speed
options: to lower its power consumption
to shorten its erection time
to have enough stability
cards.explain: High rotational speed is what gives the gyro enough stability.

cards.question: The suction pump of a small aircraft is running. Which air is being drawn through the indicators?
options: the bleed air, through a cooling unit
the cockpit air, through a filter
the ram air, through an intake scoop
cards.explain: The pump sucks cockpit air via a filter through the indicators.

cards.question: What shape is given to the gyro body of an air driven instrument
options: it is formed like a small turbine
it is formed like a flat disc
it is formed like a hollow sphere
cards.explain: The gyro body is formed like a small turbine so the airflow can drive it.

cards.question: Which two advantages does an electric motor drive give to the gyros of commercial aircraft
options: more reliability and a stable speed in all flight situations
a simpler filter fit and a lower running temperature
lower weight and a shorter erection time after switch on
cards.explain: Electric drive is stated to be more reliable and to give a stable speed in all flight situations.

cards.question: In what kind of construction are the latest standby horizons built
options: a mechanically caged standby gyro with a horizon drum
an air driven standby gyro with pendulum erection
a solid state electronic standby instrument system
cards.explain: The latest standby horizons are integrated into a solid state electronic standby instrument system.

cards.question: Besides attitude, altitude and airspeed, which two further values can a recent integrated standby system display
options: magnetic heading and mach number
drift angle and ground speed
outside air temperature and wind
cards.explain: Magnetic heading and mach number can be displayed in addition.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with an integrated standby instrument system. What has become of the separate standby instruments?
options: they are kept as a second back up
they are moved to the overhead panel
they are no longer needed
cards.explain: With the integrated system the individual original standby instruments are no longer needed.

cards.question: In which case is a vertical gyro used for an artificial horizon
options: when the gyro must be driven by cockpit airflow
when the gyro has no erection system of its own
when the gyro is not linked mechanically to the dial
cards.explain: The vertical gyro is used where the gyro is not mechanically linked to an instrument's indication.

cards.question: A vertical gyro is mounted in the avionic compartment as an attitude sensor. What else must the installation then have?
options: a suction pump in the cockpit
an indicator in the cockpit
a caging knob in the compartment
cards.explain: With the gyro in the avionic compartment an indicator is needed in the cockpit.

cards.question: What holds the axis of a vertical gyro in the vertical position
options: a caging mechanism
an erection system
a pendulum stop
cards.explain: An erection system holds the gyro axis vertical.

cards.question: The aircraft rolls while a remote vertical gyro is working. By what is the angle of the attitude sensed?
options: by torque motors
by level switches
by synchros
cards.explain: The angle of attitude is sensed by synchros.

cards.question: What does an air driven gyro use to generate its erection force
options: a balance beam turning slowly
pendulums moved by the airflow
level switches holding a fluid
cards.explain: The air driven gyro uses pendulums to make an erection force from the airflow.

cards.question: What activates the torque motor of an electrically driven gyro when its axis topples
options: a pendulum moved by the cockpit airflow
a level switch holding a conductive fluid
a rocker tipped by horizontal acceleration
cards.explain: Electrically driven gyros use level switches with a conductive fluid to activate the torque motor.

cards.question: A force has to be applied to move a gyro axis in a chosen direction. At what angle from that direction must the force act?
options: 180 degrees
45 degrees
90 degrees
cards.explain: Precession means forces must be applied 90 degrees from the result to be achieved.

cards.question: Which error must the normal erection rate compensate, besides precessions from real topple
options: a real topple of 20 degrees per minute
an erection drift of 3 degrees per minute
an apparent topple of 15 degrees per hour
cards.explain: The rate is sufficient to compensate the apparent topple of 15 degrees per hour plus precessions from real topple.

cards.question: An electrical gyro is switched on again after a long power interruption. Which erection rate is used?
options: about 3 degrees per minute
about 20 degrees per minute
about 2 degrees per minute
cards.explain: A faster erection rate of about 20 degrees per minute is activated after a long power interruption.

cards.question: What can a vertical gyro no longer detect once longitudinal accelerations or centrifugal forces act on it
options: the lateral axis of the aircraft
its own rotational speed
the centre of the earth
cards.explain: Under those forces the gyro can no longer detect the centre of the earth.

cards.question: During which manoeuvres must the erection system be switched off
options: during curves or longitudinal accelerations
during climbs and descents at steady speed
during taxiing and engine ground running
cards.explain: The erection system must be switched off during curves or longitudinal accelerations.

cards.question: An erection cutout switch has sensed a roll axis input while the aircraft manoeuvres. For what period does it keep the erection circuit interrupted?
options: for as long as the acceleration lasts
for a fixed period of three seconds
until the gyro is caged by the technician
cards.explain: The switch interrupts the corresponding erection circuit for as long as the accelerations last.

cards.question: Why must long acceleration periods such as full turns be avoided
options: the erection rate rises above its normal working limit
the gyro motor runs hot in that attitude of the frame
the gyro topple cannot be compensated during that time
cards.explain: During a long acceleration the erection is cut out, so gyro topple cannot be compensated.

cards.question: When the attitude of the aircraft changes, what turns around what
options: the aircraft turns around the gyroscope
the gyroscope precesses together with the aircraft
the gyroscope turns around the aircraft
cards.explain: Because the gyro is space stable, any change in attitude is a rotating of the aircraft around the gyroscope.

cards.question: How do the gyro axis and the frame axis lie to one another in horizontal flight
options: at right angles to one another
parallel to one another
at 45 degrees to one another
cards.explain: In horizontal flight the gyro axis and the frame axis are at right angles.

cards.question: A vertical gyro is feeding the cockpit indicator. What turns the angular movements at the pivot points into electric signals?
options: synchro-transmitters
erection torque motors
conductive level switches
cards.explain: Synchro-transmitters at the pivot points make the angular movements into electric signals.

cards.question: What are the voltages between the tapped synchro wires of a locked synchro when the aircraft is in horizontal attitude
options: at half of full value
zero
at a maximum
cards.explain: Those voltages are zero at horizontal attitude of the aircraft.

cards.question: Which two users take the synchro signals of the vertical gyro
options: the flight director and the weather radar unit
the attitude director indicator and the autopilot
the weather radar and the flight director unit
cards.explain: The ADI and the autopilot use the synchro signals.

cards.question: Which two users are switched to the locked synchros of the vertical gyro
options: the autopilot and the weather radar
the weather radar and the flight director
the attitude director indicator and the autopilot
cards.explain: WX and FD are switched to the locked synchros.

cards.question: With which two means can the alignment of the gyro axis be measured
options: a plumb line or a spirit level
a synchro or a pendulum
a level switch or a torquer
cards.explain: The alignment can be measured with a plumb line or a spirit level.

cards.question: A pendulum erection horizon is sitting with a gyro unbalance of 12 degrees. What does its cut-out mechanism do?
options: it holds the rotational mass in its normal position
it lets the rotational mass swing out to full travel
it breaks the electrical supply to the gyro motor
cards.explain: At an unbalance of 10 degrees or more the cut-out mechanism retains the rotational mass in its normal position.

cards.question: A standby horizon is found with no AC feed at all, only 28 V DC. Which type is it and why does it run?
options: a ball driven type, its inverter sits inside the device
a pendulum erection type, its gyro motor runs straight off DC
a pendulum erection type, its inverter sits inside the device
cards.explain: Only the improved pendulum erection horizon is fed with 28 V DC alone, because the static inverter that makes its AC is installed inside the device.

cards.question: The suction regulator of an air driven gyro system fails and the suction rises well above its normal value. What is the danger to the gyro?
options: it will topple to apparent vertical
it will run down earlier than usual
it will run into an overspeed
cards.explain: The regulator is there to prevent gyro overspeed, so losing its control lets the gyro overspeed.

cards.question: A commercial aircraft gyro and a small aircraft gyro are compared. Which has its speed held steady in every flight situation, and why?
options: the commercial one, because its drive is a filtered cockpit airflow
the small one, because its drive comes through a suction regulator
the commercial one, because its drive is an electric motor
cards.explain: Commercial aircraft use electrically driven gyros, which give a stable speed in all flight situations.

cards.question: A gyro instrument is found with a filter and a suction line behind it. In which class of aircraft is it fitted?
options: a small aircraft
a commercial aircraft
an aircraft with no battery
cards.explain: Air driven gyros with a suction pump and filter belong to small aircraft, while commercial aircraft use electric drive.

cards.question: A vertical gyro sits in the avionic compartment and its synchros are working normally. What makes use of the signal they send?
options: the indicator or an indication system
the erection cutout switches
the supply converter of the gyro motor
cards.explain: The synchro signal goes to the cockpit indicator or to an indication system.

cards.question: An artificial horizon is built with its gyro in a remote box and a separate indicator in the cockpit. Which gyro is in the box and how is the attitude passed on?
options: a directional gyro, passed on by synchros
a vertical gyro, passed on by synchros
a vertical gyro, passed on by a linkage
cards.explain: A vertical gyro is used where there is no mechanical link, and the attitude angle it senses goes to the indicator as a synchro signal.

cards.question: The roll level switch of an electrically driven gyro detects the axis in an incorrect direction. What follows?
options: the roll torque motor applies a force and precession corrects it
the caging mechanism locks the gimbals in a normal position
the roll cutout switch opens and the erection circuit is broken
cards.explain: The roll level switch activates the roll torque motor, whose force precesses the gyro back into the correct direction.

cards.question: An aircraft makes normal turns and accelerations in the cruise. Why does the erection system build up no significant error?
options: because the rate it works at is doubled
because the rate it works at is set by hand
because the rate it works at is so small
cards.explain: The erection rate is so small that normal turns and accelerations cannot build a significant error.

cards.question: A vertical gyro has stood without power for a long time and its axis is well off the vertical. Why is a special erection rate needed to get it ready?
options: the normal erection rate works only on the ground
the normal erection rate would be far too slow
the normal erection rate would damage the gimbals
cards.explain: Normal erection is far too slow to bring a badly toppled axis back, so a faster erection rate of about 20 degrees per minute is switched in after a long power interruption.

cards.question: An air driven gyro and an electrically driven gyro are both off the vertical. Which part supplies the correcting force in each?
options: a balance beam in the one, erection balls in the other
level switches in the one, pendulums in the other
pendulums in the one, a torque motor in the other
cards.explain: The air driven gyro erects with pendulums in the airflow, while the electrical gyro erects with a torque motor fed through level switches.

cards.question: Aircraft in a hold fly racetrack patterns rather than continuous turns. What does the shape of that pattern give the erection system?
options: time after each half turn to compensate gyro topple
a steady centrifugal force to erect the gyro against
a continuous cutout of both of the erection circuits
cards.explain: The racetrack gives the erection system enough time after each half turn to compensate any gyro topple.

cards.question: An aircraft is held in one long continuous turn instead of a racetrack. What happens to the attitude reference?
options: the gyro erects faster because of the bank angle
the gyro is caged automatically until the turn ends
the gyro topples and the error is not corrected
cards.explain: The cutout switches hold the erection circuit open throughout the turn, so gyro topple builds up uncorrected.

cards.question: An aircraft settles into a steady turn. What happens to the erection of its vertical gyro, and what follows from it?
options: the torquer is driven harder, so the axis is held upright
the fast rate is switched in, so the axis is held upright
the circuit is cut, so any topple is left uncorrected
cards.explain: The roll cutout switch interrupts the erection circuit for as long as the turn lasts, so gyro topple cannot be compensated.

cards.question: The attitude of the aircraft changes while a vertical gyro is working. Which part of the synchro moves with the airframe?
options: both stator and rotor, around the fixed gyro case
the stator, around the rotor held steady by the gyro
the rotor, around the stator held steady by the gyro
cards.explain: The synchro-stator turns with the aircraft around the synchro-rotor, which the gyroscope keeps stabilised.

cards.question: A deviation voltage from a locked synchro changes its phase and grows in amplitude. What do those two changes each tell you?
options: the phase gives the direction and the amplitude the size
the phase gives the size and the amplitude the direction
the phase gives the axis and the amplitude the rate
cards.explain: Phase shift represents the direction of the deviation and amplitude its dimension.

cards.question: A vertical gyro is sitting on the shelf with no power on it. Which stop keeps the gyroscope out of an extreme inclination?
options: the pitch stop
the pendulum stop
the frame stop
cards.explain: The pendulum stop is the one that prevents an extreme inclination when the gyro is not energised.

cards.question: A vertical gyro has been taken to about 85 degrees of movement around the lateral axis of the aircraft. What holds it there?
options: the pendulum stop
the frame stop
the pitch stop
cards.explain: The pitch stop limits movement around the lateral axis to about +/- 85 degrees.

cards.question: The air bubbles of the level switches have wandered out of the centre of their tubes. What then happens at the torquer?
options: the currents stay equal and no torque is produced
the currents become unequal and torque is produced
the currents are broken and the circuit is deactivated
cards.explain: Off centre bubbles make the currents in the variable windings unequal, so the torquer produces a torque.

cards.question: Why do equal currents in the two variable windings of the torquer leave the gyro axis untouched?
options: the magnetic fields are unequal, so the two torques cancel out
the magnetic fields are equal and opposite, so no torque results
the magnetic fields are equal and additive, so no torque results
cards.explain: With the same currents the magnetic fields are equal but opposite, and the torquer produces no torque.

cards.question: An erection circuit stays active while the aircraft accelerates. Where is the gyro led, and what does the crew see?
options: towards true perpendicular, and a flag in place of the display
towards apparent vertical, and an equally large error on the display
towards the pendulum stop, and a frozen reading on the display
cards.explain: With erection active during acceleration the gyro is led to apparent vertical, and the axis deviation shows as an equally large error on the horizon display.

cards.question: The roll cut out switches of a gyro have failed open circuit so they never cut the erection. Where will the gyroscope be moved during a turn?
options: into apparent vertical
into true perpendicular
onto the pendulum stop
cards.explain: The roll cut out switches are there to prevent the gyroscope being moved into apparent vertical, so without them the turn leads it there.

cards.question: A gyro responds 90 degrees away from an applied force. How is that allowed for in the way the torquers are connected?
options: the pitch torquer puts its torque on the roll axis
the pitch torquer puts its torque on the pitch axis
the pitch torquer puts its torque on the yaw axis
cards.explain: To use precession, the pitch torquer is made to act on the roll axis and the roll torquer on the pitch axis.

cards.question: An aircraft is standing still on the ramp with its vertical gyro powered. Why may the erection circuit work freely here?
options: only the gyro is turning below its normal speed
only the weight is acting as an acceleration
only the cut out switches are disconnected here
cards.explain: In a stationary condition only the earth's acceleration has an effect, which is the condition the erection circuit needs.

cards.question: Which supply voltage is fed to the vertical gyro
options: 90 V AC
28 V DC
115 V AC
cards.explain: The page gives 115 V AC as the voltage supplied to the vertical gyro.

cards.question: How long does the fast erection phase last after the vertical gyro is switched on
options: about 2 - 3 minutes
about 30 seconds
a maximum of three minutes
cards.explain: The page gives about 2 - 3 minutes for the fast erection phase.

cards.question: Where is the vertical gyro that supplies the attitude signals to the ADI installed
options: inside the ADI housing itself
in the electric compartment
in the cockpit overhead panel
cards.explain: The gyro is remote from the indicator and sits in the electric compartment.

cards.question: How many independent vertical gyros are needed so that each pilot has an attitude indication of his own
options: one
two
three
cards.explain: Two independent gyros are needed, one for each pilot's indication.

cards.question: Which other aircraft systems are supplied with attitude information from the vertical gyros
options: the autoflight system and the weather radar system
the instrument landing system and the radio altimeter
the air data system and the instrument warning system
cards.explain: The page names the autoflight system and the weather radar system as further users of the attitude data.

cards.question: Which two kinds of information does the attitude director indicator mainly show
options: attitude and indications from the instrument landing system
heading and indications from the flight director system
attitude and indications from the flight director system
cards.explain: The two main values are the attitude, shown as an artificial horizon, and the flight director indications.

cards.question: To which group of main flight instruments does the attitude director indicator belong
options: the pitot-static group
the Basic T
the engine indicating group
cards.explain: The page places the ADI in the Basic T.

cards.question: What kind of instrument is the slip indicator fitted to the ADI
options: an electric servo motor fed from the vertical gyro
a mechanical ball in a liquid filled curved glass tube
a moving coil movement fed with the yaw rate signal
cards.explain: The slip indicator is purely mechanical: a ball in a liquid filled curved glass tube.

cards.question: Which rate of turn movement does the turn indication on the ADI represent
options: 90°/min
cards.explain: The page gives 180°/min as the rate of turn movement represented.

cards.question: Why is the attitude comparison fitted to the attitude reference system
options: as a means of erecting the gyros faster
as an additional safety feature
as a replacement for the third gyro
cards.explain: It is there as an additional safety feature.

cards.question: Which condition must have applied before switch on for the vertical gyro to run a fast erection phase
options: the gyro had been without current for more than 30 seconds
the erectors had been held at the reduced support rate
the gyro motor had been running above 75% rpm
cards.explain: Fast erection is run only when the gyro has been without current for more than 30 seconds.

cards.question: A vertical gyro has held a motor speed above 75% for more than 30 seconds and its gimbals are erected. What happens next?
options: fast erection begins and the motor runs on at raised voltage
the erectors are switched off for a maximum of three minutes
fast erection ends and the motor runs on at reduced voltage
cards.explain: Those are exactly the conditions that end fast erection and drop the motor to reduced voltage.

cards.question: Which erector is switched off by a strong acceleration along the aircraft's length, and which by a strong horizontal acceleration?
options: the roll erector, and the pitch erector
the pitch erector, and the roll erector
the pitch erector in both of the two cases
cards.explain: Longitudinal acceleration cuts out the pitch erector, horizontal acceleration cuts out the roll erector.

cards.question: What is the longest time the pitch erector may stay switched off during strong longitudinal acceleration
options: three minutes
two minutes
30 seconds
cards.explain: The page limits the pitch erector cut-off to a maximum of three minutes.

cards.question: A flag monitor is checking the gyro supply before it releases the valid voltage. What level must that supply exceed?
cards.explain: The flag monitor requires VG power greater than 90 V before the valid voltage is given out.

cards.question: A technician traces the ADI pitch and roll signals back to the vertical gyro gimbals. What will he find converting the angles into electrical signals?
options: servo motors
moving coils
synchros
cards.explain: Synchros on the gimbals convert the mechanical pitch and roll angles into electrical signals.

cards.question: An ADI receives a gyro valid signal from its vertical gyro. What has the gyro confirmed by sending it?
options: that its gimbals are free of friction
that its synchros are correctly aligned
that it is running at its normal speed
cards.explain: The valid signal is sent only while the gyro is operating at normal speed.

cards.question: Which signal reaches the ADI only once its vertical gyro is up to normal speed and fast erection is complete
options: the roll synchro signal
the pitch synchro signal
the valid signal
cards.explain: The valid signal is withheld until the gyro is up to normal speed and erection is complete, while the synchro signals are produced throughout.

cards.question: One of the two normal vertical gyros has failed in flight. How is that pilot's attitude indication restored?
options: his indicator falls back on the standby horizon signal
a switching transfers the third vertical gyro to his indicator
his indicator is cross-wired to the other pilot's vertical gyro
cards.explain: A switching brings the third vertical gyro onto the indicator that lost its own gyro.

cards.question: A gyro has failed and the spare is to be brought in. To which indicators can that third gyro be switched?
options: to both ADIs at the same time
to one fixed ADI only
to either of the two pilots' ADIs
cards.explain: The third gyro can be switched to whichever of the two ADIs has lost its own source.

cards.question: A student asks why the aeroplane symbol of the ADI follows every movement of the aircraft. What is the answer?
options: it is carried on the instrument housing itself
it is driven by the roll synchro of the vertical gyro
it is mounted on the fork that holds the horizon ball
cards.explain: Being part of the housing, the symbol moves with the airframe it is bolted to.

cards.question: How does the blue and black horizon ball of the ADI behave as the aircraft manoeuvres
options: it turns with the aircraft movement and is kept horizontal by the gyro
it is held still while the pitch and roll scales move around it
it turns contrary to the aircraft movement and is kept horizontal by the gyro
cards.explain: The ball runs counter to the aircraft and the vertical gyro holds it level.

cards.question: What does the VG valid direct current arriving at the ADI confirm
options: that the synchro signals have nulled
that the vertical gyro is functioning
that the ADI power supply is healthy
cards.explain: The valid direct current is the gyro's statement that it is working.

cards.question: What makes the ball of the slip indicator take up the apparent vertical
options: the yaw rate signal fed to a coil behind the ball
the deviation signal of the navigation receiver
the influence of gravity on the ball
cards.explain: Gravity alone settles the ball, which is why it shows the apparent vertical.

cards.question: Which aircraft movement supplies the signal for the rate of turn part of the ADI
options: the pitch rate
the yaw rate
the roll rate
cards.explain: The yaw rate is the signal used for that indication.

cards.question: An aircraft's rotation changes while the ADI turn indicator is being watched. Which change does that movement answer?
options: a change in rotational velocity about the lateral axis
a change in rotational velocity about the vertical axis
a change in the resultant force acting on the aircraft
cards.explain: Its movement answers changes of rotational velocity about the vertical axis.

cards.question: Which kind of movement drives the turn indication on the ADI
options: a synchro receiver
a moving coil
an electric servo motor
cards.explain: It is a moving coil instrument.

cards.question: How much deviation from the localizer do the marks beside the runway symbol stand for
options: about one degree left or right
about three degrees left or right
about one third of a degree left or right
cards.explain: The localizer marks are about one degree of deviation each.

cards.question: A technician must identify the drive behind the glideslope pointer of an ADI. What kind of movement will he find?
options: a synchro receiver
an electric servo motor
a moving coil
cards.explain: The glideslope pointer is a moving coil instrument.

cards.question: What do the flight director bars show the pilot
options: the direction in which the aircraft is to be flown
the deviation of the aircraft from the runway centreline
the direction in which the aircraft is actually moving
cards.explain: The bars command the direction to fly, not the direction being flown.

cards.question: From where does the attitude comparison take the signals it works on
options: directly from the vertical gyro gimbals
directly from the indication
directly from the autoflight system
cards.explain: The signal is derived directly from the indication rather than from the source gyro.

cards.question: How far apart must the pitch or roll indications be before the alert is raised
options: any amount apart at all
several minutes of arc apart
several degrees apart
cards.explain: A difference of several degrees is what triggers the alert.

cards.question: Which system raises the alert when the two attitude indications disagree
options: the instrument warning system
the weather radar system
the autoflight system
cards.explain: The instrument warning system is the one that triggers the alert.

cards.question: An aircraft has primary flight displays in place of ADIs and the two attitudes disagree. What do the crew see?
options: a CHECK ATTITUDE message above the attitude indication on one display
an attitude flag across the attitude indication on both displays
a CHECK ATTITUDE message above the attitude indication on both displays
cards.explain: The message is CHECK ATTITUDE and it appears on top of the attitude indication on both displays.

cards.question: Which sources can serve as the third attitude reference for fault isolation
options: vertical gyro number 1 or the standby horizon
vertical gyro number 3 or the weather radar
vertical gyro number 3 or the standby horizon
cards.explain: The third reference is either vertical gyro number 3 or the standby horizon.

cards.question: A vertical gyro has just reported valid and the voltage on its erectors has dropped. What support rate are the erectors working at now?
options: 2°/min
28°/min
20°/min
cards.explain: Reporting valid marks the end of fast erection, and from then on the erectors run at the reduced rate of 2°/min.

cards.question: Shortly after power up a vertical gyro is reporting invalid while its erectors run at the higher support rate. What does this tell a technician?
options: the gyro has finished erecting and is in normal erection
the gyro motor has failed to reach 75% rpm
the gyro is still in its fast erection phase
cards.explain: Invalid reporting together with the higher erector voltage is the signature of the fast erection phase.

cards.question: A vertical gyro is at full speed with its output synchros energised, yet the flag monitor still withholds the valid voltage. Which remaining condition is missing?
options: the supply has not yet reached its rated alternating voltage
the roll erector has not yet been switched off
fast erection has not yet been completed
cards.explain: Of the four flag monitor conditions only completion of fast erection is still outstanding in this case.

cards.question: An aircraft carries a second autopilot as well as its original one. Which vertical gyro feeds that second system?
options: the first officer's vertical gyro
the third vertical gyro
the captain's vertical gyro
cards.explain: A duplicated system such as a second autopilot takes its attitude from the first officer's gyro, the first system taking the captain's.

cards.question: The aircraft rolls into a bank. How does the horizon ball of the ADI answer that movement?
options: the fork swings the ball the opposite way round
the fork and the ball are both held still
the ball spins about its own axis in the fork
cards.explain: Roll is answered by the fork, which swings the ball the opposite way to the aircraft.

cards.question: The nose of the aircraft is raised. How does the horizon ball of the ADI answer that movement?
options: it is held still while the symbol climbs
it is swung the opposite way round by the fork
it spins about its own axis inside the fork
cards.explain: Pitch is answered by the ball itself rotating about its own axis inside the fork.

cards.question: A pilot flies the flight director bars while watching the horizon ball on the same indicator. What do the two indications give him together?
options: where the aircraft is now and how fast it is turning
how the aircraft is banked and where the runway lies
where the aircraft is now and where it is to be flown
cards.explain: The attitude half states the present attitude and the flight director half commands the attitude to fly, so together they give present state and demand.

cards.question: On an ILS approach the runway symbol is seen rising towards the aeroplane symbol. What is it telling the crew?
options: the radio altitude is decreasing
the localizer deviation is increasing
the glideslope is being captured
cards.explain: The symbol doubles as the radio altimeter indication, and its travel up towards the aeroplane means the radio altitude is falling.

cards.question: An ADI is being used as the aircraft's rate of turn indicator. Which movement feeds that indication and what always accompanies it?
options: the yaw rate, accompanied by the flight director bars
the roll rate, accompanied by the ball
the yaw rate, accompanied by the ball
cards.explain: The turn indication is driven by yaw rate and is always paired with the ball's slip indication.

cards.question: A technician presses the ATT TEST button and the ATT flag comes into view. Is the indicator faulty?
options: no, null monitoring brings the flag in during the test
yes, the flag should stay out of view throughout the test
yes, the flag shows the test voltage never reached the synchros
cards.explain: The flag is expected during the test because null monitoring brings it in.

cards.question: An ADI horizon ball has swung round to a 90° bank attitude. Which condition can produce this on some horizon indicators?
options: the power supply has failed or the valid signal is missing
the attitude test button has been pressed and held in
the expanded part of the pitch scale has been run off
cards.explain: That deliberate tilt is the response to a lost power supply or a missing valid signal.

cards.question: An ADI's two synchro systems null correctly and its gyro reports valid, but the indicator has lost its power supply. Can the attitude still be displayed properly?
options: yes, the synchros hold the ball in its last position
yes, the valid signal alone keeps the display alive
no, it is one of the conditions that must all be met
cards.explain: All four listed conditions must hold together, and the power supply is one of them.

cards.question: An ADI loses the valid signal from its vertical gyro in flight. What can be expected of the attitude indication?
options: the flag stays out of view and the ball holds its last attitude
the flag comes into view and the ball settles back level
the flag comes into view and the ball may tilt right over
cards.explain: Losing the valid signal removes the attitude display valid condition, so the flag appears, and on some indicators the ball is deliberately tilted right over.

cards.question: Two attitude indications disagree and the crew must work out which of them to believe. What does that always need?
options: a repeat of the attitude comparison against the first source
the valid signal taken from each of the two gyros
a third independent source of the same information
cards.explain: Two disagreeing sources can never settle themselves; a third independent source is always needed.
