cards.question: The two attitude indications disagree and vertical gyro number 3 is unserviceable. Which independent source is left for fault isolation?
options: the weather radar system
the autoflight system
the standby horizon
cards.explain: The two named third sources are vertical gyro number 3 and the standby horizon, so with the gyro out the standby horizon remains.

cards.question: Which turn must the aircraft be able to make in one minute when flying a holding pattern
options: a 90° turn
a 360° turn
a 180° turn
cards.explain: The holding pattern turn is defined as 180° in one minute.

cards.question: Which sensor is used to measure how fast the aircraft is turning
options: a rate gyro
an inclinometer
a vertical gyro
cards.explain: The rate of turn sensor is a rate gyro.

cards.question: What damps the movement of the metal ball in the slip indicator
options: a magnetic brake
a liquid
a light return spring
cards.explain: The ball's movement is damped by the liquid it sits in.

cards.question: Of what material is the ball of the slip indicator made
options: glass
metal
plastic
cards.explain: The ball is a metal one.

cards.question: Which turn gives a full deflection of the rate of turn indication
options: a half turn that would take one minute
a complete turn that would take two minutes
a complete turn that would take one minute
cards.explain: Full deflection corresponds to a complete turn in two minutes.

cards.question: What is a complete turn flown in two minutes called
options: a standard turn
a holding turn
a coordinated turn
cards.explain: The manual names that the standard turn.

cards.question: Which degrees of freedom does the rate of turn indicator have
options: one complete and one constrained
two complete and none constrained
one complete and two constrained
cards.explain: It has one complete degree of freedom and one that is constrained.

cards.question: To which aircraft axis is the gyroscope axis of the rate of turn indicator parallel
options: the vertical axis
the longitudinal axis
the lateral axis
cards.explain: The gyro axis lies parallel to the lateral axis.

cards.question: How many degrees of freedom does a rate gyro have
options: three
two
one
cards.explain: A rate gyro has only two degrees of freedom.

cards.question: Which three indicators can be used to fly the required rate of turn
options: the turn and slip indicator, the turn coordinator and the ADI
the turn and slip indicator, the turn coordinator and the standby horizon
the turn and slip indicator, the vertical gyro and the ADI
cards.explain: The three named are the turn and slip indicator, the turn coordinator and the ADI.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with a glass cockpit. How is the rate of turn presented to its crew?
options: on a pointer over a mechanical scale
on a display
by the ball of the inclinometer
cards.explain: In a glass cockpit the rate of turn appears on a display.

cards.question: Which instrument gives the slip indication that always goes with the rate of turn indication
options: an inclinometer, also called the ball
a rate gyro, also called the turn needle
a vertical gyro, also called the horizon
cards.explain: The slip indication comes from an inclinometer, known as the ball.

cards.question: What does the slip indication show the pilot during a turn
options: the direction of the bank
the direction of the resultant forces
the direction of the rate of turn
cards.explain: It shows which way the resultant forces lie during the turn.

cards.question: What do the rate of turn pointer and the ball tell the pilot when they are read together
options: the radius of the turn
the bank angle of the turn
the quality of the turn
cards.explain: Read together they state how good the turn is.

cards.question: The ball of a slip indicator sits exactly in the centre during a turn. Why does that mean the turn is perfectly coordinated?
options: the vertical axis is parallel to the resultant force
the vertical axis is parallel to the true vertical
the rate of turn has reached its full deflection
cards.explain: A centred ball means the aircraft's vertical axis is parallel to the resultant force of the turn.

cards.question: In which direction are the rudder pedals moved whenever the ball has run out of centre
options: towards the direction of the turn
away from the ball
towards the ball
cards.explain: In both of the out of balance cases the pedals go in the direction of the ball.

cards.question: The gyro of a turn indicator precedes against its return spring. On what does that precession force depend?
options: on the gyro stability, which follows the gyro mass
on the stiffness of the return spring itself
on the gyro stability, which follows the gyro speed
cards.explain: The precession force depends on gyro stability, and that stability is proportional to the speed.

cards.question: About which aircraft axis can the frame carrying the gyro axis rotate
options: about the vertical axis
about the lateral axis
about the longitudinal axis
cards.explain: The frame's limited rotation is about the longitudinal axis.

cards.question: By how much is the rate gyro of a turn coordinator turned from its normal position
options: by 90 degrees
by 20 degrees
by 45 degrees
cards.explain: The gyro is canted by 45 degrees.

cards.question: Why is the rate gyro of a turn coordinator canted
options: so that it is also sensitive to the pitch rate
so that it is also sensitive to the roll rate
so that it is no longer sensitive to the yaw rate
cards.explain: Canting the gyro adds sensitivity to roll rate.

cards.question: For what is the rate gyro mainly used
options: as a stable long term attitude reference
as a highly sensitive rotary motion sensor
as a damper for the slip indicator ball
cards.explain: Its main use is as a very sensitive sensor of rotary motion.

cards.question: A force acts on the constrained input axis of a rate gyro. How does the gyro answer it?
options: it precedes around the input axis
it tilts bodily along the spin axis
it precedes around the precession axis
cards.explain: A force on the input axis is answered by precession about the precession axis.

cards.question: By which means can the second degree of freedom of a rate gyro be limited
options: by a spring or by a mechanical stop
by a counterweight or by magnetic braking
by a spring or by movement dependent damping
cards.explain: The page gives a spring or movement dependent damping as the ways of limiting it.

cards.question: Which input to output behaviours can a rate gyro be built to have
options: integral, differential or exponential
proportional, integral or differential
proportional, linear or logarithmic
cards.explain: The three behaviours named are proportional, integral and differential.

cards.question: What is often used in place of the spring in a rate of turn gyro
options: a torsion bar
a damping piston
a torque motor
cards.explain: A torsion bar often replaces the spring.

cards.question: About how many aircraft axes can a rate of turn gyro measure rotary velocity
options: about two, set by its two degrees of freedom
about all three, whatever its orientation
about one only, set by the way it is fitted
cards.explain: All three aircraft axes can be measured, and the gyro's orientation does not matter.

cards.question: How are angular velocity gyroscopes built with integrated features constrained
options: by viscose damping rather than a spring
by a torsion bar rather than a spring
by a spring rather than by damping
cards.explain: They use viscose damping in place of a spring.

cards.question: Which gyro measures angles in the aircraft axes with very high precision
options: an angular velocity gyroscope with integrated features
an attitude gyro with three degrees of freedom
a directional gyroscope with automatic drift compensation
cards.explain: The page states that these gyros measure angles of attitude in the aircraft axes with very high precision, in contrast to attitude gyros.

cards.question: Towards what are devices inside the aircraft drawn when the aircraft slips
options: towards the outside of the curve
towards the nose of the aircraft
towards the centre of the curve
cards.explain: In a slip the devices inside are drawn in towards the centre of the curve.

cards.question: In a turn the ball has moved out towards the inside of the turn. What does that say about the aircraft?
options: the bank angle is too small for the actual rate of turn
the bank angle suits the rate of turn but the speed is too high
the bank angle is too large for the actual rate of turn
cards.explain: A ball out in the direction of the turn means too much bank for the rate of turn being flown.

cards.question: The ball has moved out in the direction of the turn. What must the pilot do to bring the turn back into balance?
options: raise the rate of turn with rudder towards the ball
lower the bank angle and leave the rudder central
lower the rate of turn with rudder towards the ball
cards.explain: With the ball out into the turn the turn rate must be raised, using rudder towards the ball.

cards.question: The ball has moved out opposite to the direction of the turn. What is wrong and what has to be done?
options: the bank angle is too small, so the rate of turn must be raised
the bank angle is too large, so the rate of turn must be raised
the bank angle is too small, so the rate of turn must be lowered
cards.explain: A ball out the other way means too little bank for the rate flown, and the cure is to lower the rate of turn.

cards.question: The needle shows exactly the turn the crew want but the ball lies well out of centre. What do the two indications say about the turn together?
options: the rate is wrong but the turn is coordinated
the rate is right but the turn is not coordinated
the rate and the coordination are both right
cards.explain: The needle sets the rate and the ball sets the coordination, so a good needle with a displaced ball is a turn at the right rate flown out of balance.

cards.question: The gyro of a turn and slip indicator is running below its normal speed. What happens to the rate of turn indication?
options: it loses accuracy because the precession force falls away
it stays accurate because the spring alone sets the deflection
it loses accuracy because the spring force falls away
cards.explain: Low gyro speed means low stability and so a weakened precession force, which is why the indication is accurate only at normal speed.

cards.question: The turn needle of a turn and slip indicator stands at full deflection while the ball is centred. What is the aircraft doing?
options: turning at a rate that would complete a circle in one minute, in balance
turning at a rate that would complete a circle in two minutes, out of balance
turning at a rate that would complete a circle in two minutes, in balance
cards.explain: Full deflection is the two minute turn and a centred ball is a coordinated one, so both are being flown.

cards.question: The aircraft starts to turn about its vertical axis. What then happens inside the rate of turn indicator?
options: the frame is held still and the gyro axis tilts the pointer directly
the gyro axis stays put while the frame is turned by the return spring
the gyro axis precedes and twists the frame against the return spring
cards.explain: The turn about the vertical axis makes the gyro precede, and that precession twists the frame against the spring.

cards.question: A rate of turn indicator is built with only one free and one constrained degree of freedom and a return spring. What can it therefore show?
options: the attitude the aircraft is holding
the bank angle the aircraft has reached
how fast the aircraft is turning
cards.explain: With the second freedom held by a spring the gyro can only balance precession against spring force, which measures how fast the aircraft turns, not the attitude it holds.

cards.question: An aircraft is holding a steady bank angle through a turn. What is the turn coordinator showing at that moment?
options: the yaw rate
the bank angle itself
the roll rate
cards.explain: With the bank angle constant the coordinator reads yaw rate.

cards.question: A pilot is rolling into a turn and the bank angle is still changing. What is the turn coordinator showing while that goes on?
options: the roll rate
the yaw rate
the resultant force of the turn
cards.explain: While the bank angle is changing the coordinator reads roll rate instead.

cards.question: Two aircraft are rolled into a bank at the same moment, one carrying a rate of turn indicator and one a turn coordinator. Whose indication answers the roll in?
options: the one whose gyro lies along the lateral axis
the one whose gyro lies along the vertical axis
the one whose gyro is canted by 45 degrees
cards.explain: Only the turn coordinator's gyro is canted, and that is what makes it answer roll rate while the bank angle is changing.

cards.question: A rate of turn gyro is held by a linear spring. What can then be said about its precession angle?
options: it is proportional to the angular velocity about the measuring axis
it is independent of the angular velocity about the measuring axis
it falls as the angular velocity about the measuring axis rises
cards.explain: A linear spring makes the precession angle proportional to the angular velocity about the measuring axis.

cards.question: During a turn the loose items in the cabin are being pushed out towards the outside of the curve. Which condition is that?
options: a slip
a skid
a perfectly coordinated turn
cards.explain: With the loose items thrown outward from the centre of the curve the ball also lies to the outside, which Figure 208 labels a skid.

cards.question: What other name is given to the direction indicator
options: Position indicator
Heading indicator
Attitude indicator
cards.explain: The page gives heading indicator as the second name for the direction indicator.

cards.question: How many degrees of freedom and which axis does a direction indicator have
options: two degrees of freedom and a horizontal axis
three degrees of freedom and a horizontal axis
three degrees of freedom and a vertical axis
cards.explain: The direction indicator has three degrees of freedom together with a horizontal axis.

cards.question: Which three effects does the indication precision of a gyro compass depend on
options: Apparent drift, inclination and cardan error
Apparent drift, real drift and cardan error
Apparent drift, real drift and parallax error
cards.explain: The page lists exactly these three as the limits on precision.

cards.question: A directional gyro has just been synchronised. For how long does its indication stay relatively exact?
options: 15 - 20 minutes
5 - 10 minutes
5 - 10 seconds
cards.explain: The printed figure for the useful period is 5 - 10 minutes.

cards.question: What are directional gyros used as in remote compass systems
options: Indicators
Sensors
Amplifiers
cards.explain: In a remote compass system the directional gyro is the sensing element.

cards.question: Which two parts carry out the erection task in an electrical directional gyro
options: A pressure switch and a torque motor
A level switch and a flux valve
A level switch and a torque motor
cards.explain: The electrical gyro erects with a level switch driving a torque motor.

cards.question: Which task is the liquid level switch with its torque motor fitted for
options: Drift elimination
Levelling
Monitoring
cards.explain: The level switch and its torque motor are the levelling pair.

cards.question: A directional gyro component list includes a slaving torque motor. What is that motor fitted for?
options: To eliminate drift
To monitor the rpm
To level the frame
cards.explain: The slaving torque motor is listed against drift elimination.

cards.question: Which two kinds of drift does the slaving torque motor eliminate
options: Real drift and pole drift
Apparent drift and real drift
Apparent drift and cardan error
cards.explain: The slaving torque motor is fitted against apparent and real drift.

cards.question: Why does the indication stay steady while the aircraft turns its nose
options: The gyro keeps its own direction stable
The gyro is driven faster during the turn
The gyro is locked to the airframe during the turn
cards.explain: The gyro holds its direction, so the scale moves relative to the aircraft and shows the new heading.

cards.question: A direction indicator has just reached its operational speed. What has to happen before its heading can be used?
options: The heading must be set automatically
The heading must be set from the lubber line
The heading must be set manually
cards.explain: Once the gyro is up to speed the heading has to be adjusted by hand.

cards.question: What property of a space stable gyro allows it to hold the course
options: It maintains the position it has taken up
It aligns itself with the earth's magnetic lines
It returns to the horizontal after every turn
cards.explain: Holding the position it was set to is what keeps the course indication.

cards.question: What must the rotational axis of a gyro compass remain parallel to for its directional information to be read
options: The earth's surface
The aircraft's longitudinal axis
The earth's magnetic axis
cards.explain: The page ties the readable indication to the axis staying parallel to the earth's surface.

cards.question: How is a gyro compass set and from which indication
options: Manually, from the flux valve
Manually, from the magnetic compass
Automatically, from the magnetic compass
cards.explain: The gyro compass is set by hand to match the magnetic compass.

cards.question: Where are the sensor and the indicator of a remote compass system installed
options: The sensor in the cockpit and the indicator anywhere
The sensor anywhere and the indicator in the cockpit
Both the sensor and the indicator in the cockpit
cards.explain: Remote means the sensing unit can sit anywhere while only the display is in the cockpit.

cards.question: An erection system is fitted to a directional gyro. In which plane does it hold the gyro axis?
options: Horizontal
Vertical
Along the lubber line
cards.explain: For a directional gyro the erection system holds the axis horizontal.

cards.question: What is the important difference between a directional gyro and a vertical gyro
options: The directional gyro is never electrical
The directional gyro has no erection system
The directional gyro drifts
cards.explain: Drift is the behaviour that sets the directional gyro apart from the vertical gyro.

cards.question: A commercial aircraft is fitted with electrical directional gyros. How is their drift dealt with?
options: It is compensated automatically
It is compensated by the vertical gyro
It is compensated by the pilot each hour
cards.explain: Electrical gyros in commercial aircraft carry automatic drift compensation.

cards.question: Why is the directional gyro more sophisticated than the gyro compass
options: It is part of the remote compass system, not of the panel
It is part of the standby compass, not of the panel
It is part of the instrument panel, not of a remote system
cards.explain: Being a remote system component rather than a panel instrument is the reason given for its greater complexity.

cards.question: The inner frame of a directional gyro leaves the horizontal. What does the liquid level switch signal?
options: The heading synchro
The torque motor
The slaving amplifier
cards.explain: The level switch output goes to the torque motor.

cards.question: To which axis does the levelling torque motor give momentum
options: The axis of the inner frame
The axis of the gyro rotor
The axis of the outer frame
cards.explain: Levelling momentum is applied to the outer frame axis until the inner frame is horizontal.

cards.question: What produces the signals received by the slaving torque motor
options: The earth magnetic field detector
The heading synchro amplifier
The liquid level switch circuit
cards.explain: The slaving signals come from an earth magnetic field detector.

cards.question: A directional gyro is running up after power-on. What rotor speed must be reached before a valid signal is passed?
cards.explain: The monitoring condition printed for rotor speed is 75%.

cards.question: A pilot is about to adjust the direction indicator after start-up. Which instrument has to be read first?
options: The attitude indicator
The turn indicator
The magnetic compass
cards.explain: The setting value comes from the magnetic compass, which the direction indicator cannot supply itself.

cards.question: A crew finds the gyro compass reading has moved away from the compass after some minutes of flight. What does the drift of the instrument call for?
options: Re-caging the outer frame by hand at regular intervals
Synchronising the course indication by hand at intervals
Re-levelling the inner frame by hand at regular intervals
cards.explain: Because apparent drift, real drift and cardan error spoil the precision, the course indication has to be resynchronised by hand against the magnetic compass.

cards.question: A new course has to be taken up during a turn lasting a couple of minutes. Why does the gyro compass suit this task?
options: Its indication is corrected from magnetic north throughout
Its indication stays exact over such a short period
Its indication is free of drift while the aircraft turns
cards.explain: The short-term accuracy of the gyro is enough for the few minutes a turn onto a new heading takes.

cards.question: A heading sensor is mounted well away from the instrument panel and its reading appears on the flight deck. Which gyro is the sensor and what fault must be corrected in it?
options: A directional gyro, whose toppling must be compensated
A directional gyro, whose drift must be compensated
A vertical gyro, whose drift must be compensated
cards.explain: The remote sensor is the directional gyro, and the page states its drift must be compensated.

cards.question: A directional gyro in a remote compass system is found to have no slaving torque motor fitted. What does this mean for its drift?
options: It cannot be compensated at all
It is removed by the levelling torque motor
It is compensated by other means
cards.explain: The page states drift can also be compensated by other means in remote compass systems.

cards.question: A directional gyro has begun to drift and the slaving momentum is applied to the inner frame axis. Until what point does it continue?
options: Until the gyro heading matches the standby compass heading
Until the gyro heading matches the flux valve heading
Until the inner frame is back in the horizontal
cards.explain: Slaving runs until the gyro agrees with the flux valve, which is the magnetic reference of the system.

cards.question: The servo system of the indicator does not compare correctly. What does the monitoring system of the directional gyro do?
options: It passes no valid signal to the consumer
It passes a valid signal to the consumer anyway
It passes the flux valve heading instead
cards.explain: A correct servo comparison is one of the conditions for a valid signal, so failing it blocks the signal.

cards.question: In which direction do the compass systems always point
options: Magnetic north
Compass north
True north
cards.explain: Compass systems follow the earth's magnetic field, which defines magnetic north.

cards.question: What is the angle between true north and magnetic north called
options: Inclination
Deviation
Variation
cards.explain: Variation is the printed name for the true-to-magnetic north angle.

cards.question: What represents the aircraft longitudinal axis in a heading indication
options: The compass scale
The lubber line
The magnetic needle
cards.explain: The lubber line stands for the longitudinal axis of the aircraft.

cards.question: Which magnetic field lines can a compass use to measure the heading
options: The declining ones
The vertical ones
The horizontal ones
cards.explain: Only the horizontal field lines are usable for heading measurement.

cards.question: Where are all the magnetic field lines horizontal
options: Near the isogonic lines
Near the equator
Near the poles
cards.explain: The field lines run horizontal only in the equatorial region.

cards.question: Which three methods are used to measure the angle between the aircraft longitudinal axis and magnetic north
options: Mechanical, electronic and mathematical
Mechanical, electrical and magnetic
Electronic, mathematical and gyroscopic
cards.explain: The three headings printed on the page are mechanical, electronic and mathematical.

cards.question: Which electrical part does a direct reading compass contain
options: A torque motor
A detector coil
A light
cards.explain: The only electrical item in a direct reading compass is its light.

cards.question: Where is the standby compass usually located
options: At the centerpost between the front windshields
On the centre panel below the front windshields
On the overhead panel above the front windshields
cards.explain: The usual position is the centerpost between the two front windshields.

cards.question: On which law of magnetism is the function of the magnetic compass based
options: All poles attract when they are close enough
Unlike poles attract and like poles repel
Like poles attract and unlike poles repel
cards.explain: The main law of magnetism quoted is that unlike poles attract and like poles repel.

cards.question: What kind of fluid is used in the compass housing to inhibit the movement of the card
options: A mineral or alcohol based fluid
A water or glycol based fluid
A silicone or ester based fluid
cards.explain: The damping medium named is a mineral or alcohol based fluid.

cards.question: To what does the aircraft magnetic field change the direction of magnetic north
options: Grid north
True north
Compass north
cards.explain: The shifted direction is named compass north.

cards.question: What is the difference between magnetic north and compass north called
options: Deviation
Variation
Inclination
cards.explain: Deviation is the printed name for that difference.

cards.question: A magnet has magnetic lines running between its poles. What is the effective area of those lines called?
options: The magnetic field
The magnetic pole
The magnetic axis
cards.explain: The area over which the lines act is the magnetic field.

cards.question: How may the earth be regarded in terms of its magnetism
options: As a giant electromagnet with a wound coil interior
As a giant permanent magnet with a bar magnet interior
As a giant permanent magnet with a hollow interior
cards.explain: The page describes the earth as a giant permanent magnet whose interior is a bar magnet.

cards.question: What does a suspended, free-turning magnetic needle align itself with
options: The earth's magnetic axis
The earth's magnetic lines
The aircraft's longitudinal axis
cards.explain: A free needle takes up the direction of the earth's magnetic lines, which is what makes it usable for navigation.

cards.question: An aircraft is flown to a different part of the world. What does the actual value of the variation depend on?
options: The position on earth
The aircraft's own magnetic field
The heading being flown
cards.explain: Variation is a property of where the aircraft is, not of how it is flown.

cards.question: Between which two directions is the indicated heading measured
options: The lubber line and the aircraft longitudinal axis
The aircraft longitudinal axis and the direction to the north pole
The aircraft lateral axis and the direction to the north pole
cards.explain: Heading is the angle from the aircraft longitudinal axis to north.

cards.question: Why are the different variations at different locations basically no problem
options: Navigation equipment removes the local variation automatically
Navigation equipment, runways and maps all use the magnetic heading
Navigation equipment, runways and maps all use the true heading
cards.explain: Everything is referenced the same way, to magnetic heading, so the local value does not have to be applied.

cards.question: Why must runway headings be updated every few years
options: The variation is zero along the isogonic lines
The position of the magnetic poles is drifting
The position of the geographic poles is drifting
cards.explain: Because the magnetic poles move, anything referenced to them goes out of date.

cards.question: The earth's magnetic field is being resolved at a given latitude. Into which two components is it split?
options: A horizontal and a lateral component
A horizontal and a vertical component
A magnetic and a geographic component
cards.explain: The field is resolved into horizontal and vertical components.

cards.question: An aircraft measures its heading by the electronic method. What determines the angle?
options: A freely rotating permanent magnet
An earth magnetic field detector
A stored variation value
cards.explain: The electronic method senses the field with an earth magnetic field detector.

cards.question: Which compass name is given to the method that uses an earth magnetic field detector
options: Remote reading compass
Standby reading compass
Direct reading compass
cards.explain: A detector-based system is named the remote reading compass.

cards.question: Why is the direct reading compass called the standby compass in commercial aircraft
options: Its indication replaces the gyro indication during every turn
Its indication belongs to the basic T and must always be available
Its indication belongs to the basic T and is the primary one in flight
cards.explain: Being part of the basic T, the heading has to remain available at all times, which is the standby role.

cards.question: Why is the standby compass placed at the centerpost
options: Both pilots can read it and foreign magnetic fields are distant
Both pilots can reach it and direct sunlight is avoided
Only one pilot can read it but foreign magnetic fields are distant
cards.explain: The position suits both crew members and keeps the compass clear of equipment fields.

cards.question: The scale of a standby compass takes up the direction of the field. What turns it?
options: A permanent magnet
An electromagnet
A torque motor
cards.explain: The scale is driven by a permanent magnet aligning with the field.

cards.question: Why is the direct reading compass filled with a fluid
options: To insulate the compass scale from heat
To dampen the compass scale movements
To lubricate the compass scale bearings
cards.explain: The fluid is there as a damping medium for the scale.

cards.question: With what does the freely moving magnet of a compass line up
options: The horizontal components of the earth's field
The longitudinal axis of the aircraft
The vertical components of the earth's field
cards.explain: The compass magnet follows the horizontal components of the earth's field.

cards.question: What does the compass card under the lubber line show
options: The magnetic field against the aircraft's longitudinal axis
The longitudinal axis against the earth's geographic pole
The longitudinal axis against the earth's magnetic pole
cards.explain: The reading at the lubber line is the longitudinal axis direction against the earth's magnetic pole.

cards.question: What condition must be met for the lubber line to represent the aircraft longitudinal axis
options: The compass must be correctly filled
The compass must be correctly compensated
The compass must be correctly installed
cards.explain: The lubber line only stands for the longitudinal axis if the installation is correct.

cards.question: The earth's magnetic field is weak. What does this mean for the compass magnet?
options: A high directive force of the compass magnet
A low directive force of the compass magnet
A high inclination of the compass magnet
cards.explain: A weak field gives the compass magnet only a weak directive force.

cards.question: The damping medium changes volume with temperature. What balances this out?
options: Slots
Washers
Bellows
cards.explain: Bellows take up the expansion and contraction of the damping fluid.

cards.question: What inside the aircraft also affects the direct reading compass
options: A vibration field from electrical equipment
A magnetic field from the earth's interior
A magnetic field from electrical equipment
cards.explain: Equipment running in normal operation sets up a magnetic field inside the aircraft.

cards.question: A standby compass is found to have a compass error from the airframe. What is used to minimize it?
options: Small adjustable weights inside the compass
Small adjustable magnets inside the compass
Copper washers under the mounting plate
cards.explain: The compass compensation consists of small adjustable magnets inside the instrument.

cards.question: Why does the north pole of the magnetic needle show north
options: The geographic south pole of the earth is there
The magnetic south pole of the earth is there
The magnetic north pole of the earth is there
cards.explain: What lies at the earth's north is a magnetic south pole, and unlike poles attract.

cards.question: An aircraft carries a modern inertial reference unit. Why is a compass reference carried as well?
options: Inertial units are accurate for a short time only
Inertial units cannot produce a heading at all
Radio indications are referenced to magnetic north
cards.explain: Even with INS or IRS fitted, indications such as the VOR RMI are referenced to magnetic north.

cards.question: A chart gives the variation for a position and the compass card carries a deviation. Which pair of directions does each of these angles lie between?
options: Variation between true and compass north, deviation between true and magnetic north
Variation between true and magnetic north, deviation between magnetic and compass north
Variation between magnetic and compass north, deviation between true and magnetic north
cards.explain: Variation separates true from magnetic north and deviation separates magnetic north from compass north.

cards.question: An airport publishes a changed runway designation a few years after the previous one. What has made this necessary?
options: The magnetic poles have moved and magnetic references must follow
The compass deviation at the airfield has changed
The geographic poles have moved and true references must follow
cards.explain: Runway directions are magnetic references, so pole drift forces them to be re-published.

cards.question: An aircraft is to operate in a region close to the magnetic pole. Which heading source must be used there and why?
options: A flux valve, because the vertical component takes over
A directional gyro, because the horizontal component is too weak
A standby compass, because the horizontal component is strongest
cards.explain: Inclination leaves too little horizontal field at high latitude, so a gyro or inertial reference replaces the compass.

cards.question: What does growing inclination mean for the indication of a magnetic compass
options: The vertical component weakens and the indication becomes unusable
The horizontal component weakens and the indication becomes unusable
The horizontal component grows and the indication becomes unstable
cards.explain: Inclination takes the field lines out of the horizontal, and the horizontal component the compass needs is halved by 50 degrees of latitude and unusable beyond 70 degrees.

cards.question: A compass finds the angle with a mounted, freely rotating permanent magnet. Which method and which compass is this?
options: The mechanical method, a direct reading compass
The electronic method, a remote reading compass
The mechanical method, a remote reading compass
cards.explain: The magnetic needle principle is the mechanical method and gives the direct reading compass.

cards.question: An aircraft finds its heading from data held in a computer rather than by sensing the field. Which method is this and what does it use?
options: The electronic method, using the field detector fitted at each location
The mathematical method, using the stored variation for each location
The mechanical method, using the magnet mounted at each location
cards.explain: Working from stored variation values in a navigation computer is the mathematical method.

cards.question: An aircraft suffers a total electrical power loss. Which heading indication is still available?
options: The horizontal situation indicator
The directional gyro
The standby compass
cards.explain: The direct reading standby compass needs no electrical power to show the heading.

cards.question: Fluid damping has been accepted so the indicator stays stable under vibration. What has to be accepted along with it?
options: An increase of the installation error
A loss of directive force of the magnet
A time delay after a change of direction
cards.explain: The page calls the delay an unavoidable disadvantage of keeping the indicator steady.

cards.question: New electrical equipment has been fitted close to the standby compass. Which compass error will change and what corrects it?
options: Deviation, taken out by the compensation magnets
Variation, taken out by the compensation magnets
Deviation, taken out by updating the chart value
cards.explain: An added aircraft field alters the deviation, and deviation is reduced by the compass compensation magnets.

cards.question: A compass is about to be compensated — into which classes are the errors to be removed divided?
options: A, B and C errors
B, C and D errors
A, B and D errors
cards.explain: The manual classes the compensated errors as A, B and C.

cards.question: A compass is found to carry a B error — in which directions does it show up?
options: in the north-south direction
in the east-west direction
in all directions
cards.explain: A B error is the east-west error.

cards.question: An engineer is picking out tools for a compass compensation — which ones may be used?
options: only approved antimagnetic tools
only insulated electrical tools
only calibrated torque tools
cards.explain: Compensation may only be done with approved antimagnetic tools.

cards.question: Within what tolerance must the aircraft be aligned to North - South before the SCC is used
options: exactly +/− 5 degrees
exactly +/− 10 degrees
exactly +/− 2 degrees
cards.explain: The printed alignment requirement is exactly +/− 2 degrees of North - South.

cards.question: What is required of the deviation that is left once a compensation has been performed
options: it should be as small as possible
it should be exactly zero on every heading
it should be below one degree on every heading
cards.explain: The requirement is that the deviation is as small as possible.

cards.question: In what steps are the headings checked when a deviation card is made up
options: in steps of 45 degrees
in steps of 30 degrees
in steps of 10 degrees
cards.explain: Headings are checked every 30 degrees.

cards.question: An aircraft is flying over the northern part of the earth — in which direction does the vertical component of the field point there?
options: downwards
upwards
along the meridian
cards.explain: Over the northern part the vertical component points down.

cards.question: On which flight direction does an acceleration or a deceleration leave the heading indication unchanged
options: a westerly direction
a northerly direction
an easterly direction
cards.explain: On a northerly heading an acceleration or deceleration leaves the indication alone.

cards.question: Why does a magnetic compass or a remote compass system have to be compensated at all
options: aircraft ferro- and electro-magnetism sets up fields that cause a deviation
the vertical field component pulls the magnet out of the horizontal plane
the earth's field loses strength as the aircraft climbs away from the ground
cards.explain: Interference fields from the aircraft's own ferro- and electro-magnetism produce the deviation.

cards.question: Some error is still left after a compass has been compensated — where is that remainder written down?
options: on the compensating disc at the airport site
on a deviation card carried on the aircraft
on a label fitted beside the flux valve
cards.explain: The remaining deviation goes on the deviation card that stays on the aircraft.

cards.question: An indication is falsified by the amount of the deviation — what is that heading called?
options: the true heading
the magnetic heading
the compass heading
cards.explain: The falsified indication is named the compass heading.

cards.question: An engineer walks out to compensate a compass — which items that he is carrying can deflect it?
options: his notebook, his pen and his pass
his ear defenders, his gloves and his torch
his glasses, his watch and his mobile phone
cards.explain: Glasses, a watch and a mobile phone are the items named as causing deflection.

cards.question: What does the Standby Compass Calibrator allow to be done without physically turning the aircraft
options: compensate permanent magnetisation errors and complete the deviation card
measure the vertical component of the earth's field at the compass
set the directional gyro to agree with the remote compass heading
cards.explain: The SCC compensates permanent magnetisation errors and completes the deviation card with the aircraft standing still.

cards.question: Which two separate functions does the SCC perform
options: it cancels the local earth's field and adds a rotatable standard field
it rotates the standby compass and records the resulting deviation
it cancels the aircraft's permanent field and adds a vertical field
cards.explain: The SCC cancels the local earth's field and adds a standard field that can be rotated.

cards.question: The aircraft cannot be put exactly on North - South for a standby compass calibration — what is done about the residual misalignment?
options: it is entered on the deviation card
it is taken out on the E−W screw
it is measured and set into the SCC
cards.explain: The misalignment is measured and fed into the SCC itself.

cards.question: A compensation is finished and a small deviation is still there — why can it not be driven to zero?
options: the card is only read in steps of thirty degrees
the earth's field changes while the aircraft is turned
that is nearly impossible with the means for adjustment
cards.explain: Zero cannot practically be reached with the available means of adjustment.

cards.question: The readings have been taken on every checked heading — what is done with each of them?
options: each one is remarked on a deviation card
each one is remarked in the compensation log
each one is set into the remote compensator
cards.explain: Each checked heading's reading goes onto the deviation card.

cards.question: A compass magnet is kept level on its bearing — which component of the earth's field does it then measure?
options: the vertical component
the total resultant field
the horizontal component
cards.explain: Holding the magnet horizontal lets it measure the horizontal component.

cards.question: What decides whether a tilted compass turns to the right or to the left
options: the actual bank angle of the aircraft
the actual airspeed of the aircraft
the actual heading of the aircraft
cards.explain: The direction of the swing depends on the heading the aircraft is on.

cards.question: A compass has been tilted and the vertical component is acting on its magnet — what does the crew see?
options: a frozen heading
a falsified heading
a slowly spinning card
cards.explain: The result at the instrument is a falsified heading.

cards.question: An aircraft decelerates while flying on a southerly heading — what happens to the heading indication?
options: it swings towards the east
it swings towards the west
it is not influenced
cards.explain: South behaves like north, so the indication is not influenced.

cards.question: Why is there no heading error when the aircraft accelerates on a northerly heading
options: the vertical field has no component at all at that position on the earth
the vertical field acts on the magnet the way the horizontal field does
the magnet is held exactly horizontal by its bearing on that heading
cards.explain: Both field components pull the magnet the same way, so nothing moves.

cards.question: Why does a southerly heading behave like a northerly one during an acceleration
options: the pivot point bearing locks the compass scale
the permanent magnet points in the same direction
the vertical component reverses with the hemisphere
cards.explain: On south the permanent magnet still points the same way, so the same reasoning holds.

cards.question: Compensation is being worked from INS/IRS data alongside the aircraft's own heading sources — which source supplies the magnetic heading?
options: the INS/IRS
the standby compass
the remote compass system
cards.explain: The remote compass gives magnetic heading, the INS/IRS gives true heading.

cards.question: A remote compass is 4 ° off the target course on one of the four main headings — what does that mean for the job?
options: it is in tolerance and the 30° headings can be started
it is in tolerance for a main heading but not for a 30° heading
it is out of tolerance and must be adjusted further
cards.explain: The remote compass tolerance is + / − 2 °, so 4 ° is outside it and more adjustment is needed.

cards.question: No compensating site is free and the aircraft cannot be turned — which method still works?
options: a bearing plate sighted on a distant object
the markings on the compensating disc
the Standby Compass Calibrator
cards.explain: The SCC works without rotating the aircraft, while the other two methods both need the aircraft turned on a site.

cards.question: An acceleration has tilted a compass out of the horizontal plane — what now acts on its magnet?
options: the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field
the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field
the permanent magnetism of the aircraft structure
cards.explain: Once the compass is off the horizontal the vertical component starts to influence the magnet.

cards.question: A remote compass system is being explained — which two sensing devices does it use?
options: a sensor for the aircraft's own field and a rate gyro
a sensor for the earth's magnetic field and a directional gyro
a sensor for the earth's magnetic field and a vertical gyro
cards.explain: The system pairs an earth's field sensor with a directional gyro.

cards.question: Where is the indicator of a remote compass system fitted
options: in a wing tip fairing
in the avionics compartment
in the instrument panel
cards.explain: The indicator sits in the instrument panel.

cards.question: What does the flux valve turn the direction of the magnetic field into
options: a proportional electrical signal
a proportional change of resistance
a proportional mechanical rotation
cards.explain: The output is an electrical signal proportional to the field direction.

cards.question: A large aeroplane carries two separate remote compass systems — how are they shared out?
options: one for each pilot
one for each gyro platform
one for each engine
cards.explain: The two systems are split one per pilot.

cards.question: What does the signal detected by the flux valve represent
options: the angle between the directional gyro and the aircraft's longitudinal axis
the strength of the earth's vertical field at the aircraft's longitudinal axis
the direction of the earth's horizontal field to the aircraft's longitudinal axis
cards.explain: The flux valve signal gives the direction of the earth's horizontal field relative to the aircraft's longitudinal axis.

cards.question: A flux valve has to stay level as the aircraft manoeuvres — how is it suspended in its housing?
options: on three rubber mounts
on a needle point bearing
fully cardanically
cards.explain: It hangs in a full cardan suspension.

cards.question: On what do the intensity and the direction of the sensing coil signals depend
options: on how fast the aircraft is turning
on how strong the excitation current is
on where the magnetic field points
cards.explain: Both the intensity and the direction follow the direction of the magnetic field.

cards.question: Under which condition does a coil induce a voltage at all
options: only when the intensity of the magnetic field changes
only when the intensity of the magnetic field is highest
only when the iron core has reached full saturation
cards.explain: A changing field intensity is what induces the voltage.

cards.question: How is the iron core of the flux valve made to change its magnetic state
options: it is frequently turned by a small motor inside the housing
it is frequently demagnetised by a direct current in a sensing coil
it is frequently saturated by an alternating current in an excitation coil
cards.explain: An alternating current in the excitation coil repeatedly saturates the core.

cards.question: What gives the flux valve its name
options: the liquid that flows through its hemisphere
the vent valve that breathes with altitude
the alternate switching of the magnetic field
cards.explain: The field is switched on and off like a valve, which is where the name comes from.

cards.question: An aircraft is held in a 40° banked turn — what happens to the flux valve measuring plane?
options: it is driven back to horizontal by the directional gyro
it stays horizontal because the cardan takes any angle
it can no longer stay horizontal
cards.explain: The cardan only holds the plane level out to about 30°, so at 40° of bank it is exceeded.

cards.question: The excitation current has just fallen away and the core has come out of saturation — what does the magnetic field do?
options: it collapses completely until the core saturates again
it takes the shortest way and bypasses the three coils
it takes an even longer way through the iron and the coils
cards.explain: Unsaturated iron offers a far easier path, so the field runs the longer way through the iron and the coils.

cards.question: The excitation coil of a flux valve has gone open circuit — what reaches the magnetic heading reference system?
options: a signal that gives true heading instead of magnetic
nothing, because the field intensity no longer changes
a signal at half of its normal output frequency
cards.explain: Without the excitation the core is never switched in and out of saturation, so the field intensity at the coils is steady and no voltage is induced.

cards.question: How does the sinusoidal voltage pattern of a flux valve differ from that of an ordinary synchro?
options: it is shifted near to the zero value of the excitation voltage
it is clipped at the saturation level of the iron core
it is shifted near to the peak value of the excitation voltage
cards.explain: In the flux valve the pattern sits near the zero value of the excitation voltage.

cards.question: A compass coupler is getting no setting signal at all — which chain has broken down?
options: the flux valve to control transformer path
the compass coupler to excitation coil feed path
the directional gyro to flux valve drive path
cards.explain: The printed path runs flux valve to control transformer to the directional gyro or compass coupler, so a loss at the coupler points back along that path.

questions.question: A directional gyro is left running for a long flight leg. Which disadvantage shows up?
options: a falsified heading during accelerations and turns
a falsified reading in the region of the magnetic poles
the drift
questions.explain: Drift is the printed disadvantage of the gyro based direction instruments.

questions.question: Where are the amplifiers that raise the voltage of weak signals installed
options: in the housing of the directional gyro
in the integrated instrument system rack
in the automatic direction finder indicator
questions.explain: Weak signals such as the compass rose motor voltage are amplified in the IIS rack.

questions.question: An engineer puts a meter on the excitation supply of a flux valve. Which value should he find?
options: 23.5 V AC
115 V AC
28 V DC
questions.explain: The printed excitation figure for the flux valve is 23.5 V AC.

questions.question: Which errors are adjusted by the screws on the flux valve compensation device
options: the A error only
the A and B errors
the B and C errors
questions.explain: The screws on the compensation device take out the B and C errors.

questions.question: An older document calls one mode the free azimuth mode. Which mode of operation is meant?
options: the fast synchronisation mode
the DG mode
the slaved mode
questions.explain: Free azimuth mode is the other name printed for the DG mode.

questions.question: A helicopter flux valve is to be relocated and the shop asks what rules the choice of place. What governs it?
options: it must be far away from all magnetic fields of the helicopter
it must be close to the gearbox of the helicopter for a rigid mount
it must be inside the cabin of the helicopter to keep the run short
questions.explain: Distance from the helicopter's own magnetic fields decides where the flux valve goes.

questions.question: A pilot glances at the HSI for his heading. Which indication on it is the main one?
options: the compass rose
the course bar
the distance readout
questions.explain: The compass rose is the HSI's main indication.

questions.question: A pilot reads the heading on the ND in front of him. Which compass system supplies it?
options: their own compass system
whichever system the transfer switch selects
the opposite compass system
questions.explain: The HSI or ND is fed by the compass system of its own side.

questions.question: How does the electronic flight instrument system stand in relation to the electronic instrument system
options: It replaces it and shows alert messages
It is a separate system and shows engine data
It is a part of it and shows navigation data
questions.explain: EFIS is part of the EIS and its job is to show navigation data.

questions.question: With respect to which plane does the navigation display present the situation of the aircraft
options: The horizontal plane with respect to the earth's surface
The horizontal plane with respect to the flight path
The vertical plane with respect to the earth's surface
questions.explain: The navigation display works in the horizontal plane referred to the earth's surface.

questions.question: Which computer decides what is to appear on the centralized monitoring displays
options: The system data acquisition concentrator
The flight warning computer
The display management computer
questions.explain: The flight warning computer determines the content of the ECAM displays.

questions.question: Which computer puts the engine parameters and the system page parameters onto the displays?
options: The flight warning computer
The display management computer
The system data acquisition concentrator
questions.explain: Overlaying the engine and system page parameters is the display management computer's job.

questions.question: Which three kinds of warning are generated by the modularized avionics warning electronics assembly
options: Optical, aural and tactile warnings
Optical, tactile and synoptic warnings
Optical, aural and visual warnings
questions.explain: It produces optical, aural and tactile warnings.

questions.question: What happens to the white in the picture when one electron beam of a cathode ray tube fails
options: There is no white in the picture
The white is replaced by amber in the picture
The white turns to grey in the picture
questions.explain: With one beam gone the picture contains no white at all.

questions.question: Which part of the display is affected when one input signal to a display unit is lost
options: Only the indication of the related parameter
The whole of the display unit
Only the warning labels of the display
questions.explain: Only the indication belonging to the missing signal goes away.

questions.question: Under which condition is the head up display meant to give guidance information on the ground and at take-off and landing
options: When the landing gear is extended
When visibility is reduced
When the autopilot is engaged
questions.explain: That guidance is provided for the case of reduced visibility.

questions.question: Which automatic procedure is the head up display used to monitor?
options: The auto approach
The auto land flare
The auto thrust reduction
questions.explain: One stated purpose is to monitor the auto approach.

questions.question: Which ND parameter comes from somewhere other than the navigation systems
options: The ground speed
The heading
The wind velocity
questions.explain: Apart from the heading, all information on the ND is based on data from the navigation systems.

questions.question: A route indication is missing from a navigation display in the sector mode, so which system should be suspected?
options: The instrument landing system
The flight management system
The ground proximity warning system
questions.explain: The route indication in that mode is supplied by the flight management system.

questions.question: Besides an abnormal pushbutton position, which condition is shown by a white light
options: A backup system running
A failure needing awareness
A maintenance operation
questions.explain: White covers a pushbutton in an abnormal position or a maintenance operation.

questions.question: A system is working normally but its pushbutton has been left out of its normal switching position, so what will the crew see on that pushbutton?
options: It will stay dark because no fault exists
It will flash until the fault is cleared
It will be lit even though no fault exists
questions.explain: A pushbutton lights for an abnormal switching state as well as for a local warning, so it is lit with no fault present.

questions.question: A fault is already being annunciated and a second fault then occurs, so what must the crew do for the new one to be indicated?
options: Press the local warning light first
Cancel the master caution light first
Reset the centralised caution panel first
questions.explain: Only after the master caution light has been cancelled can another fault be indicated.

questions.question: A crew is told that a fault exists but not which system has it, so which indication are they looking at?
options: A master caution light
A central warning display message
A centralised caution panel light
questions.explain: The master lights give no information about the system affected, while the panel and the display both name it.

questions.question: A crew member has cleared several caution messages with CLR and then wants to read them again, so what must be done?
options: Press RCL to recall them
Press STS to bring up the status page
Press CLR again to restore them
questions.explain: CLR deletes the messages one by one and RCL is the pushbutton that recalls them.

questions.question: A pilot reading a system page wants the gross weight, so where on that page does he look?
options: On the upper part, among the engine parameters
On the right side, among the inoperative systems
On the lower part, among the permanent data
questions.explain: GW is printed among the permanent data on the lower part of the system page.

questions.question: Two alerts come up together, the first at level 3 and the second at level 1, so what does the more serious of the two report?
options: A configuration to monitor
An abnormal configuration
An emergency configuration
questions.explain: Level 3 is the warning raised by an emergency configuration, while level 1 only covers a configuration to monitor.

questions.question: The cabin altitude has become excessive, so what indications will the crew get?
options: A message on the display with no aural alarm
An aural alarm with a flashing master warning light
A single chime with a steady master caution light
questions.explain: Excess cabin altitude is a level 3 warning and level 3 gives an aural alarm with a flashing master warning light.

questions.question: A single chime sounds and the master caution light comes on, so what does the crew know about the failure?
options: It has no direct influence on the flight
It gives no aural alarm and no warning light
It is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction
questions.explain: A single chime with the master caution light is a level 2, and level 2 failures have no direct influence on the flight.

questions.question: An alert needs the crew to read the engine/warning display to notice it at all, so what does that say about its level?
options: It is a level 2, which gives only a single chime
It is a level 1, which has no attention getter
It is a level 3, which gives only a flashing light
questions.explain: Only a level 1 caution comes without an aural alarm or a warning light, so nothing draws the eye to it.

questions.question: A technician wants to bring the maintenance pages up on the lower EICAS, so why will the display select panel not do it?
options: Because that panel only selects the primary engine parameters
Because that panel only works after the aircraft is powered up
Because that panel only selects synoptics and status information
questions.explain: The EDSP selects synoptics and status information while the maintenance pages come via the CMC.

questions.question: An engine exceedance occurs while the aeroplane stands with its parking brake set, so what becomes of the event?
options: It is lost, since the brake has to be released first
It is lost, since two engines have to be running
It is stored, since that storage is not inhibited
questions.explain: Engine exceedance page storage is printed as not inhibited, so the running and brake conditions do not apply to it.

questions.question: The radio altimeter has failed in flight, so what can still warn the crew about high ground ahead?
options: The basic ground proximity modes
The below glide slope alert of mode 5
The enhanced system terrain functions
questions.explain: The enhanced terrain functions work independently of the radio altitude, while the basic modes need it.

questions.question: The limits of one of the alerting envelopes are exceeded, so what does the enhanced system give the flight crew?
options: Aural alert messages with visual annunciations and displays
An automatic pull-up commanded through the autopilot
A master warning that has to be reset by the crew
questions.explain: Exceeding an envelope limit produces aural messages together with visual annunciations and displays.

questions.question: A system is required to see steep rising ground that the downward looking sensor would find too late, so which protection is needed?
options: The terrain clearance floor protection
The modulation of the alerting envelopes
The terrain data base look ahead protection
questions.explain: Look ahead protection works from the database instead of the downward looking sensor.

questions.question: The terrain awareness display function has been lost, so what happens to the ground proximity warning functions?
options: They fall back to the excessive descent rate mode
They are lost together with the display function
They go on working while the necessary inputs are there
questions.explain: The warning functions keep working as long as their inputs remain available.

questions.question: The crew reduces the descent rate as soon as the first mode 1 message is heard, so which boundary has not been penetrated?
options: The inner alert boundary
The outer alert boundary
The upper alert boundary
questions.explain: The first message comes from the outer boundary, so the inner one has still not been crossed.

questions.question: Which signal is used for the alert boundaries of both the excessive descent rate mode and the excessive terrain closure rate mode besides the radio altitude
options: The computed airspeed
The glide slope deviation
The vertical speed
questions.explain: Mode 1 uses barometric and inertial vertical speed and mode 2 a vertical speed signal, both with radio altitude.

questions.question: Climbing out with gear and flaps up the aircraft loses more height than permitted while staying above the mode 4C filter value, so which message is heard?
options: SINK RATE
DON'T SINK
TOO LOW TERRAIN
questions.explain: That is the mode 3 case, and mode 4C would need the radio altitude to fall below the filter value.

questions.question: Which message is common to a mode 4A penetration at 250 knots and to a mode 4C penetration of the filter value
options: TOO LOW GEAR
TOO LOW TERRAIN
TOO LOW FLAPS
questions.explain: Mode 4A gives TOO LOW TERRAIN when the boundary reached at 250 knots and above is penetrated, and mode 4C gives it for a fall below the filter value.

questions.question: A glide slope deviation message is heard noticeably quieter than the other warnings, so what does that tell the crew?
options: It is a failure of the loudspeaker
It is the soft alert activation
It is the hard alert activation
questions.explain: Only the soft alert is given at about half the normal volume.

cards.question: Where on an aeroplane are the flux valves located
options: at the wing tips, in the vertical stabiliser or in the tail cone
in the nose radome, in the forward cargo bay or in the wheel well
under the cockpit floor, in the engine pylons or in the centre tank
cards.explain: Those three positions are the ones printed for the flux valve on an aeroplane.

cards.question: Where is the flux valve of a helicopter usually installed
options: on the roof of the cabin, in the rotor head or on the upper deck of the engine
on the bottom of the tail boom, the vertical stabilizers or in the vertical fin
under the cockpit floor, in the nose compartment or on the landing gear skid
cards.explain: Those are the printed usual installation places for the flux valve of a helicopter.

cards.question: A directional gyro is left running for a long flight leg. Which disadvantage shows up?
options: a falsified reading in the region of the magnetic poles
a falsified heading during accelerations and turns
the drift
cards.explain: Drift is the printed disadvantage of the gyro based direction instruments.

cards.question: Which disadvantage do magnet compasses and flux valves have
options: a heading which lags behind by a fixed amount in the climb
a falsified heading during accelerations and turns
a drift which grows with the running time of the unit
cards.explain: Accelerations and turns are what falsify the magnetic sensing devices.

cards.question: What do the two acronyms in the name ADF RMI stand for
options: Automatic Direction Finder and Radio Magnetic Indicator
Airborne Direction Finder and Radio Magnetic Instrument
Automatic Deviation Finder and Remote Magnetic Indicator
cards.explain: ADF is Automatic Direction Finder and RMI is Radio Magnetic Indicator.

cards.question: What do the arrows in the ADF RMI point to
options: the magnetic north found by the flux valve
the course selected on the compass rose
tuned broadcast stations
cards.explain: The ADF arrows point at whichever broadcast stations have been tuned.

cards.question: Which three units does a remote compass with ADF/RMI have
options: a flux valve, a compass coupler and an ADF/RMI
a directional gyro, a compass coupler and a compass controller
a flux valve, a directional gyro and an ADF/RMI
cards.explain: Those three are the units listed for the remote compass with ADF/RMI.

cards.question: Where are the amplifiers that raise the voltage of weak signals installed
options: in the automatic direction finder indicator
in the integrated instrument system rack
in the housing of the directional gyro
cards.explain: Weak signals such as the compass rose motor voltage are amplified in the IIS rack.

cards.question: Which errors are adjusted by the screws on the flux valve compensation device
options: the A error only
the B and C errors
the A and B errors
cards.explain: The screws on the compensation device take out the B and C errors.

cards.question: How is the A error of a remote compass system compensated
options: by turning the adjustment screws of the compensation device
by turning the flux valve
by turning the N − S potentiometer of the remote compensator
cards.explain: The A error is taken out by rotating the valve itself, not by a screw or a potentiometer.

cards.question: Which units make up a remote compass system with a compass coupler
options: flux valve, DG, compass controller and compass coupler
flux valve, DG, ADF RMI and compass coupler
flux valve, DG, compass controller and remote compensator
cards.explain: Those four are the units listed for the coupler based system.

cards.question: With which control can any desired heading be set
options: the SET HDG knob
the DG − SLAVED switch
the synchronizing knob
cards.explain: The SET HDG knob is the one for setting a heading of choice.

cards.question: Fast synchronisation is unserviceable on a compass system. Which unit holds the control logic?
options: in the compass coupler
in the directional gyro
in the compass controller
cards.explain: The fast synchronisation logic sits inside the coupler.

cards.question: To which value does fast synchronisation raise the update rate of the magnetic heading
options: 7 °/min.
cards.explain: Fast synchronisation runs at seven hundred degrees a minute.

cards.question: A flux valve is to go at a wing tip rather than near the cabin. Why is that place chosen?
options: to keep them inside the pressurised area so they can be reached in flight
to exclude the influence of magnetic interference fields as far as possible
to bring them as close as possible to the heading indicators they supply
cards.explain: The locations are chosen to keep magnetic interference fields away from the valve.

cards.question: A helicopter flux valve is to be relocated and the shop asks what rules the choice of place. What governs it?
options: it must be far away from all magnetic fields of the helicopter
it must be close to the gearbox of the helicopter for a rigid mount
it must be inside the cabin of the helicopter to keep the run short
cards.explain: Distance from the helicopter's own magnetic fields decides where the flux valve goes.

cards.question: Why is the heading of a flux valve falsified while the aircraft accelerates
options: the valve swings so that it is also affected by the vertical magnetic field
the valve output is damped so that it follows the change far too slowly
the valve loses part of its excitation while the aircraft is accelerating
cards.explain: The swing lets the vertical component of the earth's field reach the valve.

cards.question: Which two units are combined to build a remote compass system that shows the correct heading
options: a directional gyro and a magnet compass
a flux valve and a directional gyro
a flux valve and a magnet compass
cards.explain: The flux valve and the directional gyro together make the remote compass system.

cards.question: From which unit does the indicator of a remote compass system receive the stable heading information
options: from the magnet compass
from the directional gyro
from the flux valve
cards.explain: Stable heading comes to the indicator from the directional gyro.

cards.question: How is the difference between the magnetic field direction and the indicated heading used
options: it drives the compass rose of the indicator directly
it changes the excitation voltage of the flux valve
it adjusts the DG through a torque motor
cards.explain: The difference signal is fed to a torque motor which moves the gyro.

cards.question: The slaving torque motor applies a torque to the gyro. What does this produce in it?
options: a rigidity which locks the DG to magnetic north
a gyro precession which changes the DG direction
a friction brake which holds the DG direction
cards.explain: Torque on a gyro acts as precession and so moves the gyro's direction.

cards.question: A crew has one ADF RMI on the panel. Which two kinds of information does it give them?
options: the magnetic heading and the distance to the station
a radio navigation indication and the magnetic heading
a radio navigation indication and the aircraft attitude
cards.explain: The one indicator carries both the radio navigation picture and the magnetic heading.

cards.question: What does the slaving annunciator show the pilot
options: the difference between the selected course and the indicated heading
the difference between the indicated heading and the flux valve signal
the difference between the excitation voltage and its nominal value
cards.explain: The annunciator displays how far the indicated heading is from what the flux valve says.

cards.question: Where is the difference between the indicated heading and the flux valve signal detected in this architecture
options: inside the flux valve
inside the compass coupler
inside the ADF RMI
cards.explain: In this architecture the detection happens in the indicator itself.

cards.question: A pilot reaches for the synchronizing knob on the ADF RMI. What can he change with it?
options: the mode in which the system operates
the indication of the compass rose
the rate at which the torque motor runs
cards.explain: The knob acts on what the compass rose shows.

cards.question: What is protected by the fuse fitted in the integrated instrument system rack
options: the transformer which supplies the flux valve excitation
the amplifier which raises the compass rose motor voltage
the torque motor which is fitted inside the directional gyro
cards.explain: That fuse is there for the excitation transformer of the flux valve.

cards.question: In which form does the detected field direction reach the control transformer in the indicator
options: as a single-phase signal
as a direct current signal
as a three-phase signal
cards.explain: The flux valve passes its direction information on as a three-phase signal.

cards.question: A slaving control transformer is fitted in an ADF/RMI. What is its rotor connected to?
options: the synchronisation knob
the compass card
the slaving torque motor
cards.explain: The rotor of the slaving CT is driven directly by the compass card.

cards.question: The north found by the flux valve matches the position of the compass rose. What appears at the slaving CT output?
options: a steady direct voltage
no signal at all
a signal of maximum size
cards.explain: Agreement between the two gives a null at the control transformer.

cards.question: In which condition of flight does the information from the flux valve contain no errors?
options: when flying a steady turn at a constant bank angle
when flying straight ahead without acceleration
when flying at a constant height in any manoeuvre
cards.explain: Unaccelerated straight flight is the condition in which the valve is error free.

cards.question: Which precision of heading indication is possible all the time with the remote compass system
cards.explain: Two degrees either way is the printed precision of the remote compass system.

cards.question: Where is the amplified error signal from the control transformer sent
options: to the compass rose motor
to the slaving torque motor
to the flux valve signal coils
cards.explain: The amplified error signal drives the slaving torque motor on the gyro.

cards.question: After switch on the gyro is not aligned with magnetic north. How long can the automatic alignment take?
options: up to 9 minutes
up to 90 minutes
up to 90 seconds
cards.explain: Working off a large error at the slow torquing rate can take as long as ninety minutes.

cards.question: The annunciator needle of the ADF/RMI sits at its central position. What does this mean?
options: the slaving amplifier has failed
the system is in the free azimuth mode
the slaving CD is zeroed out
cards.explain: Centre position of the moving coil annunciator means the slaving CD is nulled.

cards.question: What does the annunciator on the ADF/RMI display
options: the excitation voltage supplied to the flux valve
the output voltage of the slaving torque motor
the output voltage of the slaving amplifier
cards.explain: The moving coil annunciator reads the slaving amplifier output.

cards.question: Between which two units can a remote compensator be switched
options: flux valve and directional gyro
compass coupler and compass controller
flux valve and compass coupler
cards.explain: The remote compensator sits in the line between the flux valve and the coupler.

cards.question: A meter is put on the supply output of a remote compensator. Which kind of voltage is there?
options: an extremely constant three-phase voltage
a variable low frequency AC voltage
an extremely constant DC voltage
cards.explain: The compensating supply is a very constant direct voltage.

cards.question: How is the compensation device carrying the B and C error adjustment screws fitted
options: it is wired in series with the excitation coil
it is screwed into the compass coupler
it is screwed onto the flux valve
cards.explain: The compensation device is mounted directly on the flux valve.

cards.question: A compensation device is to be fitted to a flux valve. In which case is this done?
options: only in the case of a failed remote compensator
only in the case of persistent interference fields
only in the case of a drifting directional gyro
cards.explain: It is reserved for interference fields that will not go away.

cards.question: A newer type of compass system is fitted. Where is the fuse for the flux valve excitation transformer additionally installed?
options: in the flux valve housing
in the compass controller
in the compass coupler
cards.explain: On newer couplers the protecting fuse is also carried in the coupler.

cards.question: The synchronising annunciator is deflected. Along which path is the difference being reported?
options: DG − coupler − autoflight system
flux valve − coupler − HSI
flux valve − coupler − DG
cards.explain: It watches the chain from the valve through the coupler to the gyro heading.

cards.question: Which two signals are coupled together in the compass coupler in the slaved mode
options: the flux valve signal and the selected VOR course
the flux valve signal and the DG platform heading
the DG platform heading and the autoflight heading
cards.explain: Slaved mode brings the valve signal and the gyro heading together in the coupler.

cards.question: Flux valve and gyro headings disagree in a coupler system. Which device balances them out?
options: a differential synchro
a slaving torque motor
a control transformer
cards.explain: The differential synchro in the coupler takes out the difference.

cards.question: How does a coupler system compare with the ADF/RMI system for indication behaviour and precision?
options: it is less precise but reacts faster
it is more precise but reacts slower
there is no difference between them
cards.explain: The two systems behave and perform the same way.

cards.question: The system is in its run-up phase. What happens to the update rate of the differential synchro?
options: it is increased to 700°/min.
it is reduced to 0.2°/min.
it is held at 2°/min.
cards.explain: Run-up uses the much higher rate so the system lines up quickly.

cards.question: Which source provides the directional information in the DG mode
options: only the short-term stable gyro platform
only the long-term stable flux valve
the gyro platform and the flux valve together
cards.explain: In DG mode the gyro alone supplies the direction.

cards.question: What is the state of the synchronising annunciator in the DG mode
options: it is switched off
it shows the drift rate
it stands at its centre
cards.explain: There is nothing for it to compare in DG mode, so it is switched off.
