cards.question: How does the fast synchronisation control logic raise the update rate
options: by switching in a second torque motor
by bypassing the differential synchro
by switching the amplification factor
cards.explain: A change of amplification factor is what gives the higher rate.

cards.question: After which length of switch-off pause does switching on in SLAVED mode start the fast synchronisation
options: about 2 seconds
about 2 minutes
about 10 seconds
cards.explain: A pause of roughly two minutes before a SLAVED start triggers the logic.

cards.question: What is gained by holding the torquing rate of the directional gyro to its printed maximum
options: drift is still compensated but accelerations cannot move the indication
alignment is faster but the gyro cannot be moved by its own drift
turns are still compensated but drift cannot move the indication
cards.explain: The rate is fast enough for drift but too slow for the short acceleration errors to get through.

cards.question: An aircraft is in a long accelerating climb and the flux valve signal is briefly false. Why does the indicated heading stay good?
options: the flux valve signal is cut off automatically whenever speed changes
the torque motor reverses and drives the gyro back to its old heading
the gyro can be torqued only slowly, so a brief error cannot move it
cards.explain: The slow torquing rate means a short lived false signal has no time to shift the indication.

cards.question: In the cruise the slaving annunciator keeps fluctuating around zero. What does this tell the pilot?
options: the gyro is still running up and the heading is not yet usable at all
the gyro has lost its stable direction and the valve is being ignored
the gyro has the correct stable direction and the valve is correcting it
cards.explain: Fluctuation about zero is the sign of a healthy system doing its normal correcting.

cards.question: The slaving annunciator shows a long term deflection to one side. What should be concluded?
options: there is an error in the system
the gyro drift is being corrected normally
the flux valve is seeing an acceleration error
cards.explain: A deflection that lasts, rather than one that fluctuates, means a system error.

cards.question: Why can the compass rose of the ADF RMI show any heading just after power up
options: the flux valve needs several minutes before it delivers any signal
the slaving annunciator is held at zero during the whole run-up
the direction taken up by the gyro after run-up may be any direction
cards.explain: The rose follows the gyro, and the gyro runs up pointing anywhere.

cards.question: The system has just been switched on and the heading shown is wrong. Why does it take time to become correct?
options: the slaving torque motor may move the gyro by only 2° per minute
the compass rose motor is deliberately damped during the run-up
the flux valve must first warm up before it delivers its excitation
cards.explain: A large initial error can only be worked off at the slow torquing rate.

cards.question: A pilot uses the synchronizing knob shortly after start up. What is the effect?
options: the slaving annunciator is switched off for the rest of the flight
the time until the heading indication is correct becomes much shorter
the torquing rate of the gyro is raised to 700° per minute
cards.explain: Minimising the difference by hand saves the slow automatic torquing.

cards.question: Why is the flux valve signal coupled with the gyro heading instead of being sent straight to the indicator
options: it is far too weak to drive the compass rose motor of the indicator
it can fluctuate wildly for a short time under the influence of acceleration
it is a three-phase signal which the compass card cannot accept at all
cards.explain: Acceleration makes the raw valve signal jump about, so the gyro steadies it.

cards.question: Which unit supplies which kind of stability to the heading signal of a remote compass with ADF/RMI
options: long-term stability from the flux valve, short-term from the gyro
long-term stability from the coupler, short-term from the gyro
long-term stability from the gyro, short-term from the flux valve
cards.explain: The valve holds the long term truth, the gyro the short term steadiness.

cards.question: An aircraft accelerates on take off and then cruises for hours. Which unit takes out which error?
options: the coupler takes out the acceleration errors and the valve the drift
the valve takes out the acceleration errors and the gyro the drift
the gyro takes out the acceleration errors and the valve the drift
cards.explain: The gyro covers the short acceleration errors, the flux valve the slow drift.

cards.question: An engineer does not want to wait for the automatic alignment. How is the stator of the control transformer adjusted?
options: by holding the mode switch in the SLAVED position
by depressing and rotating the synchronisation knob
by depressing and rotating the course selector knob
cards.explain: The stator is set by hand with the synchronisation knob.

cards.question: Which errors are offset by the two precision potentiometers of the remote compensator
options: the A error alone
the B and C errors
the A and B errors
cards.explain: The N − S and E − W settings together deal with the B and C errors.

cards.question: A flux valve is indexed, that is prefixed. What does this mean when the A error is to be compensated?
options: it must not be twisted in its mounting
it must be twisted only with the compensator switched off
it must be twisted until the B error is also at zero
cards.explain: An indexed valve is not allowed to be turned, so that way of taking out the A error is barred.

cards.question: What makes it unnecessary to update the gyro by torquing in a system with a compass coupler
options: the gyro used in such a system has no drift to be corrected
the differences are balanced out by a differential synchro
the flux valve signal is passed to the indicator on its own
cards.explain: Because the coupler itself removes the difference, the gyro need not be torqued.

cards.question: What becomes of the two signals in the coupler when the DG mode is selected
options: the heading signal still passes through, the valve signal is switched off
the heading signal is switched off, the valve signal still passes through
the heading signal still passes through, the valve signal is amplified more
cards.explain: Only the flux valve signal is cut; the heading still runs through the coupler.

cards.question: The flux valve fails during flight. Which mode of operation has to be used?
options: the DG mode
the fast synchronisation mode
the slaved mode
cards.explain: With no usable valve signal the system has to run on the gyro alone, which is DG mode.

cards.question: The system has been in DG mode for a long time and the heading has slowly wandered. What must the crew do?
options: wait for the synchronising annunciator to null it out
switch briefly to the slaved mode and straight back again
correct the indication with the SET HDG knob
cards.explain: In DG mode nothing corrects the drift automatically, so it is set out by hand.

cards.question: A remote compass system is found in which the gyro is never torqued. Which arrangement must it have?
options: an indicator in which a control transformer balances the signals
a coupler in which a torque motor balances the signals
a coupler in which a differential synchro balances the signals
cards.explain: Only the coupler arrangement with a differential synchro removes the need to torque the gyro.

cards.question: Fast synchronisation has been running for well over its minimum time. What else must happen before it is complete?
options: the synchronisation error must have come down to 2° per minute
the synchronisation error must have come down to 2° or less
the synchronising annunciator must have been off for 2 minutes
cards.explain: Both the time and an error within two degrees are needed before it finishes.

cards.question: Which state of the fast synchronisation is required for the superflag signal to appear
options: fast synchronisation must have been run at least once
fast synchronisation must not be in operation
fast synchronisation must be in operation at the time
cards.explain: One of the listed conditions for the superflag is that fast synchronisation is not running.

cards.question: Which two conditions concerning the gyro and the servo circuit must hold for the superflag signal to appear
options: the DG or INS is valid and the servo circuit is nulled out
the DG or INS is valid and the servo circuit is complete
the DG is in free azimuth and the servo circuit is complete
cards.explain: Validity of the gyro or INS and a complete servo circuit are two of the listed conditions.

cards.question: The maintenance monitor responded only briefly during a flight. What does that mean for the compass system?
options: its heading output must be treated as invalid
it must be put into the DG mode for the rest of the flight
its functioning is not affected
cards.explain: A temporary response is printed as having no effect on how the system works.

cards.question: A compass system is switched off for half a minute and then switched on again in SLAVED. Does fast synchronisation run?
options: no, the switch-off pause was too short for it
no, it runs only when the mode is left in DG
yes, every switch-on in SLAVED will start it
cards.explain: A pause of about two minutes is needed, so half a minute does not trigger the logic.

cards.question: After a changeover from DG to SLAVED the heading lines up within seconds instead of minutes. Why is that?
options: the update rate has been raised to 700°/min. for the changeover
the update rate has been raised to 20°/min. for the changeover
the gyro has been torqued at its full rate for the changeover
cards.explain: Switching DG to SLAVED starts the fast synchronisation, which runs at the much higher rate.

cards.question: What shows the pilot that the signal from his compass system is not valid
options: a heading warning flag
the synchronising annunciator
the compass superflag
cards.explain: Loss of validity is shown by the heading warning flag.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation HSI stand for
options: Horizontal Situation Indicator
Horizontal Stabiliser Indicator
Heading and Situation Instrument
cards.explain: HSI is the Horizontal Situation Indicator.

cards.question: A pilot glances at the HSI for his heading. Which indication on it is the main one?
options: the distance readout
the course bar
the compass rose
cards.explain: The compass rose is the HSI's main indication.

cards.question: A pilot reads the heading on the ND in front of him. Which compass system supplies it?
options: their own compass system
whichever system the transfer switch selects
the opposite compass system
cards.explain: The HSI or ND is fed by the compass system of its own side.

cards.question: Which compass system do the RMIs show
options: the system feeding the autoflight computer
the opposite compass system
their own compass system
cards.explain: The RMI deliberately carries the heading of the other side's system.

cards.question: To which autoflight system is the heading of compass system 1 provided
options: to both autoflight systems together
to autoflight system number 2
to autoflight system number 1
cards.explain: The autoflight systems are fed straight across, one for one.

cards.question: To what besides the other heading sensor can the heading transfer switch connect a user
options: to a third unit if one is available
to the flux valve signal taken on its own
to the autoflight system of the other side
cards.explain: Where a third unit exists the transfer switch can reach it too.

cards.question: A heading leaves the compass coupler on its way to the HSIs. Which heading is it?
options: the free azimuth platform heading
the uncorrected flux valve heading
the gyro supported magnetic heading
cards.explain: What leaves the coupler is the magnetic heading after the gyro has steadied it.

cards.question: To which compass system is the flight recorder normally switched
options: to both systems in turn
to compass system 1
to compass system 2
cards.explain: The flight recorder normally sits on compass system 2.

cards.question: How are the ADF RMIs normally switched to the two compass systems?
options: crosswise
both to system 1
both to system 2
cards.explain: The ADF RMIs are fed across, each from the other side's system.

cards.question: From which viewpoint does the HSI present the situation of the aircraft
options: as seen from the side
as seen from above
as seen from behind
cards.explain: The HSI gives a plan view, the aircraft seen from above.

cards.question: To which kind of ground station is the course selected on an HSI related
options: an ADF broadcast station
a DME ground station
a VOR ground radio station
cards.explain: The selectable course on the HSI belongs to a VOR station.

cards.question: The white bar on an HSI has moved away from the centre. What is it telling the crew?
options: there is a deviation in the distance to the station
there is a deviation from the selected heading
there is a deviation from the selected course
cards.explain: The bar is the course deviation indication of the HSI.

cards.question: What can the HSI show with respect to a DME ground station
options: the distance to it
the deviation from it
the bearing to it
cards.explain: From a DME station the HSI takes the distance.

cards.question: Which kind of system do all the further indications on an HSI belong to
options: navigation systems
attitude reference systems
autoflight systems
cards.explain: Every extra indication on the HSI is a navigation system indication.

cards.question: A pilot compares the heading on the ND with the heading on the RMI in front of him. Which sources is he comparing?
options: his own compass system against the opposite one
the opposite compass system against the flight recorder
his own compass system against the autoflight system
cards.explain: Because the two displays are fed from opposite systems, the comparison is a cross check of both.

cards.question: A heading warning flag has appeared on one side, so what can the pilot do about it?
options: use the synchronizing knob to re-set the compass rose by hand
use the heading transfer switch to take the other heading sensor
use the compass controller to take the free azimuth heading instead
cards.explain: The transfer switch is the printed way of getting a valid heading back.

cards.question: An HSI loses its heading while the RMI beside it still shows one. Which compass system has gone?
options: the one belonging to the opposite side of the cockpit
the one selected with the heading transfer switch
the one belonging to that side of the cockpit
cards.explain: The HSI is fed by its own system and the RMI by the other one, so the failure is on its own side.

cards.question: One of the two compass systems fails in flight. What happens to the consumers that were fed by it?
options: they can all be switched to the system that is still working
they hold the last valid heading until the system is reset
they are fed directly from the flux valve of the failed system
cards.explain: Every affected consumer can be moved over to the surviving system.

cards.question: What is achieved by exciting the synchros from various voltage sources
options: a receiver is always supplied even when the coupler itself has failed
a receiver is always fed from two independent buses at the same time
a receiver is always on a transmitting synchro fed by its own bus
cards.explain: Spreading the excitation keeps each receiver and its synchro on a common bus.

cards.question: An HSI is showing a compass rose, a course bar and a distance. Which of these comes from the compass system?
options: the distance
the course bar
the compass rose
cards.explain: The rose is the heading indication; the course bar and the distance are navigation system indications.

cards.question: What is meant by a glass cockpit
options: the instruments are fitted behind one large glass panel
the instrument glasses are replaced by a scratch free type
computers and displays are used instead of instruments
cards.explain: Glass cockpit means instruments have given way to computers and displays.

cards.question: What is the system used for flight monitoring in a glass cockpit called in many aircraft
options: CDS
EFIS
EIS
cards.explain: The flight monitoring displays are commonly called EFIS.

cards.question: Which three items are the components of a typical electronic instrument system
options: Display units, control panels and pressure sensors
Display computers, display units and control panels
Display computers, control panels and warning horns
cards.explain: The three listed components are the display computers, the display units and the control panels.

cards.question: A system is fitted with as few display computers as it is allowed to have, so how many is that?
options: Two
Three
Four
cards.explain: The text gives at least two display computers as the minimum.

cards.question: How many indication display screens represent the display system in the cockpit
options: Four
Eight
Six
cards.explain: The cockpit carries six indication display screens.

cards.question: What do the letters ECAM stand for
options: Electronic central alert monitor
Electronic centralized aircraft monitor
Engine centralized aircraft monitor
cards.explain: ECAM is the electronic centralized aircraft monitor.

cards.question: How many display management computers are installed and what do they do with the data they receive
options: Two computers, forwarding the data to the display units
Three computers, forwarding the data to the warning computers
Three computers, forwarding the data to the display units
cards.explain: Three identical display management computers take in the data and pass it to the display units.

cards.question: An engineer counts the flight warning computers of the system, so how many does he find?
options: One
Three
Two
cards.explain: Two identical flight warning computers are fitted.

cards.question: A crew is flying an aircraft with a glass cockpit. How is their flight monitoring done?
options: by one display for each pilot
by two displays shared by both pilots
by two displays for each pilot
cards.explain: Each pilot has two displays for flight monitoring.

cards.question: Where are the many engine parameters shown in a glass cockpit
options: on the related engine control panel
on two central displays
on two displays for each pilot
cards.explain: Engine parameters go on the two central displays.

cards.question: Where are the alerts of the central warning panel presented in a glass cockpit
options: on a printed caption board
at the related control panel
in a display
cards.explain: Those alerts move from the panel onto a display.

cards.question: The engine data and the auto flight system data reach a display computer, so in which form do they arrive?
options: One is digital and one is analogue
Both are digital
Both are analogue
cards.explain: Navigation, auto flight and engine inputs are all listed as digital.

cards.question: Why does a large aircraft carry a third display computer
options: To convert analogue inputs
To drive the control panels
For redundancy
cards.explain: The third computer is fitted on large aircraft for redundancy.

cards.question: How does the electronic flight instrument system stand in relation to the electronic instrument system
options: It replaces it and shows alert messages
It is a separate system and shows engine data
It is a part of it and shows navigation data
cards.explain: EFIS is part of the EIS and its job is to show navigation data.

cards.question: How many control panels serve the centre displays and what is selected on them
options: Two panels, used to select the system to be monitored
One panel, used to select the computer to be monitored
One panel, used to select the system to be monitored
cards.explain: A single control panel serves the centre displays and selects the system to be monitored.

cards.question: Which further information is presented on the electronic instruments besides the navigation data
options: The condition of the air conditioning system
The limits of the engine parameters
The activities of the auto flight system
cards.explain: The electronic flight instruments also show what the auto flight system is doing.

cards.question: How are the six indication display screens divided between the electronic flight instruments and the central monitoring displays
options: Two flight instrument displays and four monitoring displays
Three flight instrument displays and three monitoring displays
Four flight instrument displays and two monitoring displays
cards.explain: Four of the six are flight instrument displays and two are central monitoring displays.

cards.question: Which two displays make up the centralized monitoring pair on an Airbus aircraft
options: The engine and warning display and the system display
The engine and warning display and the navigation display
The primary flight display and the system display
cards.explain: The pair is the engine and warning display together with the system display.

cards.question: Which of the two EICAS displays on a Boeing aircraft carries the engine and warning indications
options: The auxiliary EICAS display
The upper EICAS display
The lower EICAS display
cards.explain: The upper EICAS is the engine and warning display and the auxiliary one is the system display.

cards.question: Which kind of information does the primary flight display supply
options: Flight monitoring information and parameters
Flight planning information and parameters
Engine monitoring information and parameters
cards.explain: The primary flight display is the flight monitoring display.

cards.question: Which parameter is listed among those supplied by the primary flight display?
options: Fuel on board
Hydraulic pressure
Radio altitude
cards.explain: Radio altitude is one of the parameters listed for the primary flight display.

cards.question: Which annunciation is listed among the parameters of the primary flight display
options: The flight mode annunciation
The engine mode annunciation
The flight phase annunciation
cards.explain: The flight mode annunciation is one of the listed primary flight display parameters.

cards.question: With respect to which plane does the navigation display present the situation of the aircraft
options: The horizontal plane with respect to the flight path
The horizontal plane with respect to the earth's surface
The vertical plane with respect to the earth's surface
cards.explain: The navigation display works in the horizontal plane referred to the earth's surface.

cards.question: A flight warning computer works on the data it receives, so which three kinds of output does it generate?
options: Alert messages, synthetic voice and engine parameters
Alert messages, aural alerts and system pages
Alert messages, aural alerts and synthetic voice
cards.explain: The three outputs are the optical alert messages, the acoustic aural alerts and the voice announcements.

cards.question: An announcement in spoken words is heard in the cockpit, so which of the three warning outputs is this?
options: Aural alert
Synthetic voice
Alert message
cards.explain: The voice announcement is the synthetic voice output, while the acoustic one is the aural alert.

cards.question: Which computer decides what is to appear on the centralized monitoring displays
options: The system data acquisition concentrator
The display management computer
The flight warning computer
cards.explain: The flight warning computer determines the content of the ECAM displays.

cards.question: To which two sets of computers does a system data acquisition concentrator forward its data
options: The flight warning computers and the display management computers
The display management computers and the control panels
The flight warning computers and the other concentrator
cards.explain: The concentrator feeds both the flight warning computers and the display management computers.

cards.question: Which computer puts the engine parameters and the system page parameters onto the displays?
options: The system data acquisition concentrator
The display management computer
The flight warning computer
cards.explain: Overlaying the engine and system page parameters is the display management computer's job.

cards.question: Which three kinds of warning are generated by the modularized avionics warning electronics assembly
options: Optical, aural and tactile warnings
Optical, tactile and synoptic warnings
Optical, aural and visual warnings
cards.explain: It produces optical, aural and tactile warnings.

cards.question: Through which item of equipment are the warnings of the avionics warning electronics assembly generated
options: Through the control panel
Through the display select panel
Through the interface unit
cards.explain: The warnings are generated by way of the EFIS/EICAS interface unit.

cards.question: Which three items are controlled by the avionics warning electronics assembly itself?
options: The master warning light, the aural warn speaker and the display units
The master warning light, the aural warn speaker and the stick shaker
The master caution light, the aural warn speaker and the stick shaker
cards.explain: Those three are the items it drives directly.

cards.question: An aircraft without a glass cockpit is being compared with one that has it. What does flight monitoring use on the older aircraft?
options: two displays for each pilot and some other navigation indicators
two central displays and the indicators of a central warning panel
the basic T instruments and some other navigation indicators
cards.explain: Without displays the job is done by the basic T instruments plus other navigation indicators.

cards.question: On which display is the crew told that a value somewhere in the aircraft has gone out of limit
options: On one of the two engine and system data displays
On the primary flight display of each pilot
On the navigation display of each pilot
cards.explain: One of the two engine and system displays additionally carries the alerts for out of limit conditions.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with only the minimum number of display computers, so what does it lack compared with a large aircraft?
options: The computer that handles the analogue inputs
The computer that drives the centre displays
The computer that is there for redundancy
cards.explain: The minimum fit is two computers, so the third one carried for redundancy on large aircraft is missing.

cards.question: Which part inside a second generation display unit makes a picture out of the data it is sent
options: Its integrated display computer
Its integrated symbol generator
Its integrated control panel
cards.explain: These units are sent data rather than video, so the symbol generator built into them draws the picture.

cards.question: Which Boeing display does the same job as the Airbus system display
options: The auxiliary EICAS display
The upper EICAS display
The engine and warning display
cards.explain: The auxiliary EICAS does the job that the system display does on the other manufacturer's fit.

cards.question: Which path is taken by the signal that produces an amber caution
options: From the sensors and computers direct to the warning computer
From the sensors and computers through the data concentrator to the warning computer
From the sensors and computers through the display computer to the warning computer
cards.explain: An amber caution reaches the flight warning computer by way of the system data acquisition concentrator.

cards.question: Both system data acquisition concentrators are lost, so which colour of warning can still be generated?
options: The amber cautions
The red warnings
Neither colour
cards.explain: Red warnings reach the warning computer without passing through the concentrator, so they survive its loss.

cards.question: The engine and warning screen stays blank but the aural alerts are still heard, so which computer is suspected?
options: The display management computer
The flight warning computer
The data acquisition concentrator
cards.explain: The warnings are still being generated, so the fault lies in the computer that feeds the display unit.

cards.question: The stick shaker does not operate although the conditions for it are met, so which unit is first suspected?
options: The avionics warning electronics assembly
The EICAS display select panel
The EFIS and EICAS interface unit
cards.explain: The stick shaker is one of the items the warning electronics assembly controls directly.

cards.question: The master warning light comes on but no message reaches the screens, so which item is suspected?
options: The EICAS display select panel
The avionics warning electronics assembly
The EFIS and EICAS interface unit
cards.explain: The light is driven directly and works, so the path through the interface unit to the screens is at fault.

cards.question: What appears on the display in place of a parameter whose input signal is not available
options: A flag
An amber box
A dash
cards.explain: The indication disappears and a flag is shown instead.

cards.question: What does a cathode ray tube display unit do first when it detects an internal overheat
options: It switches the display off
It switches the strokes off
It switches the raster colours off
cards.explain: The first step is to switch off the raster colours.

cards.question: What is left on the screen after the first step of the overheat reaction
options: Only the raster, with all information still given
Only strokes, with the warnings removed
Only strokes, with all information still given
cards.explain: Only the strokes remain but none of the information is lost.

cards.question: Why does switching the raster colours off help a display unit that is running hot?
options: Less light is needed from the backlight
Less heat is produced then
Less current is drawn by the cooling fan
cards.explain: Dropping the raster colours makes the tube produce less heat.

cards.question: What does the display unit do as the second step of its overheat reaction
options: It switches the display to the cross side computer
It switches the raster colours off
It switches the display off
cards.explain: The second step is to switch the display off altogether.

cards.question: Which two causes are given for an overheat of a display unit?
options: An internal failure or a problem in the power supply
A high cabin temperature or a problem in the cooling system
An internal failure or a problem in the cooling system
cards.explain: The two causes given are an internal failure and problems in the cooling system.

cards.question: What happens to the white in the picture when one electron beam of a cathode ray tube fails
options: There is no white in the picture
The white is replaced by amber in the picture
The white turns to grey in the picture
cards.explain: With one beam gone the picture contains no white at all.

cards.question: What becomes of the information that is normally presented in the colour of a failed electron beam
options: It is shown as a flag instead
It is shown in white instead
It will not be shown
cards.explain: Information carried by the missing colour simply disappears from the screen.

cards.question: What does the display do when the red electron beam fails
options: It loses only the white
It switches itself off
It turns monochrome
cards.explain: A failed red beam makes the whole display go monochrome.

cards.question: Which electron beam has failed when the crew sees the whole display in one colour
options: The blue beam
The red beam
The green beam
cards.explain: Only the failure of the red beam makes the display go monochrome.

cards.question: Which part of the display is affected when one input signal to a display unit is lost
options: Only the indication of the related parameter
The whole of the display unit
Only the warning labels of the display
cards.explain: Only the indication belonging to the missing signal goes away.

cards.question: Where does a helicopter crew find the engine alerts and where the navigation picture
options: Both of them on the centre instrument panel
The alert on the outboard panels and the picture on the centre panel
The alert on the centre panel and the picture on the outboard panels
cards.explain: Engine and warning indications sit in the centre while the flight and navigation displays sit in front of the crew.

cards.question: Where does the information of a primary flight display appear when that display goes blank in flight
options: On the navigation display
On the opposite primary flight display
On the centre engine display
cards.explain: The information of a failed primary flight display is switched automatically onto the navigation display.

cards.question: A pilot's primary flight display goes dark, so what must he do before the information comes back?
options: Select the cross side computer on his control panel
Nothing, because the failed screen restarts on its own
Nothing, because the transfer happens on its own
cards.explain: The takeover by another screen is automatic, so no crew action is needed to get the information back.

cards.question: A display unit that switched itself off because of overheat has cooled down again, so what happens next?
options: The picture comes back without any crew action
The picture stays off until the crew resets it
The picture comes back without the raster colours
cards.explain: Once it is back within the limits the unit activates its display again on its own.

cards.question: Which failure fits a screen that has lost its colours but still shows every item of information
options: A total loss of the display unit
The first step of the overheat reaction
The second step of the overheat reaction
cards.explain: Losing the raster colours while keeping all the information is the first overheat step.

cards.question: What comes next when a screen has already dropped its raster colours and the cause has not been cleared
options: The screen drops its strokes as well
The screen switches to the cross side computer
The screen switches itself off
cards.explain: The two step reaction goes on to its second step, in which the display is switched off.

cards.question: A pilot reports that the green symbols have gone and nothing on the screen looks white any more, so what has happened?
options: One electron beam of the tube has failed
The raster colours have been switched off
An input signal to the display has been lost
cards.explain: Loss of one beam removes both the white and everything drawn in that beam's colour.

cards.question: Why is the display turned monochrome rather than left with its remaining colours when the red beam fails
options: Because the warning labels are red and must not be allowed to disappear
Because the remaining colours would produce too much heat
Because the warning labels are red and must not be allowed to flicker
cards.explain: Warnings are drawn in red, so losing that beam would hide them unless the whole picture is made monochrome.

cards.question: Why is a failure of the red beam treated differently from the failure of another beam?
options: Because the information it carries must never be lost
Because it carries more of the picture than the others
Because it produces more heat than the others
cards.explain: The red beam draws the warning labels, which may not be allowed to disappear.

cards.question: Two screens have lost a beam and only one of them went monochrome, so what separates the two cases?
options: The monochrome one lost the beam that draws the green symbols
The monochrome one lost the beam that draws the warnings
The monochrome one lost two beams instead of one
cards.explain: Only the loss of the beam that draws the red warning labels turns the whole picture monochrome.

cards.question: What is wrong when a single scale on the primary flight display is replaced by a flag
options: The input signal for that parameter is not available
The display unit has started its overheat reaction
One electron beam of the display tube has failed
cards.explain: A flag in place of one parameter is the sign that the input signal for it is missing.

cards.question: Several indications are gone and flags stand in their place, so what does this tell the engineer?
options: The display unit has an electron beam failure
The signals for those parameters are missing
The display unit has begun to overheat
cards.explain: Flags are the signature of missing input signals, not of a fault inside the display unit.

cards.question: One screen has lost some of its symbols and another shows flags in their place, so are the causes the same?
options: Yes, both of them come from a failure inside the display unit
No, the flags come from missing signals and the lost symbols from a failed beam
No, the flags come from a failed beam and the lost symbols from missing signals
cards.explain: A flag marks a missing input, while symbols that vanish without a flag point to a beam failure in the tube.

cards.question: Which display units normally show the ND contents
options: The lower display unit
The inboard display units
The outboard display units
cards.explain: The two inboard display units normally carry the navigation display contents.

cards.question: Which movement of the pilot is avoided by the use of a head up display
options: Lowering his head from the cockpit window to the control pedestal
Lowering his head from the cockpit window to the displays below
Turning his head from the cockpit window to the overhead panel
cards.explain: The pilot no longer has to lower his head to the conventional displays below the window.

cards.question: Under which condition is the head up display meant to give guidance information on the ground and at take-off and landing
options: When the landing gear is extended
When the autopilot is engaged
When visibility is reduced
cards.explain: That guidance is provided for the case of reduced visibility.

cards.question: Which automatic procedure is the head up display used to monitor?
options: The auto approach
The auto land flare
The auto thrust reduction
cards.explain: One stated purpose is to monitor the auto approach.

cards.question: How does the head up display help the pilot at an airfield that has no instrument landing system
options: It gives the pilot the glide slope deviation
It gives the pilot the localizer deviation
It gives the pilot information for the visual approach
cards.explain: Where no instrument landing system exists the head up display supports the visual approach.

cards.question: Visibility is poor on the approach, so why can the pilot keep his eyes on the outside world?
options: The information is presented on a screen at head height
The information is read out to him by a synthetic voice
The information is presented on a screen below the window
cards.explain: Because the screen sits at head height he can read the guidance without looking down into the cockpit.

cards.question: Why does the picture seen on the head up display change as the aircraft goes from take-off to cruise?
options: Because the display depends on the selected control panel
Because the display depends on the flight configuration
Because the display depends on the available input signals
cards.explain: The pilot is given different displays according to the flight configuration.

cards.question: Which segment of the head up display image is used while the automatic system flies the aircraft down to the runway
options: The ground roll information segment
The approach trajectory deviation segment
The system messages segment
cards.explain: Monitoring an automatic approach calls for the segment that shows how far the aircraft is off the trajectory.

cards.question: Why a parameter can be absent from a display at one point in the flight and present at another
options: Because much data is only shown in the flight phase it belongs to
Because the control panel is reset between the flight phases
Because the display units are tested one after the other in flight
cards.explain: The flexibility of the screen lets much data be displayed only during the respective flight phase.

cards.question: A mechanic finds a glass cockpit aircraft with no separate DME or marker indicator fitted, so what does that tell him?
options: Those indications are only on the standby panel
Those indications are handled by the EFIS
Those two systems are not installed
cards.explain: The DME indicator and the marker lights are both in the list of instruments the EFIS replaces.

cards.question: A trainee asks why a glass cockpit needs no separate flight mode annunciator, so what is the answer?
options: The ND carries that zone itself
The PFD carries that zone itself
The control panel carries that zone itself
cards.explain: The flight mode annunciator is replaced by the EFIS and appears as a zone of the PFD.

cards.question: Which display is affected by four of the five basic EFIS control panel functions
options: The lower display unit
The PFD
The ND
cards.explain: Mode, range, TCAS and additional information selections all act on the ND, leaving only baro correction for the PFD.

cards.question: A pilot selects TCAS on the EFIS control panel, so where does the traffic picture appear?
options: On the standby instrument
On the PFD
On the ND
cards.explain: Selection of the TCAS indication is a basic function and the indication appears on the ND.

cards.question: A mechanic moves to a new aircraft type and finds an unfamiliar switch on its EFIS control panel, so how should he treat it?
options: As a basic function common to every type
As a type specific additional function
As a function that acts on the standby instruments
cards.explain: Beyond the common basic functions, many types carry some type specific additional functions.

cards.question: An outboard display unit goes blank in flight, so what happens to the PFD picture?
options: It is moved to the standby attitude instrument
It is lost until the display unit is replaced
It can be switched to the inboard display unit
cards.explain: On failure of the outboard display the PFD can be switched automatically or manually to the inboard DU.

cards.question: In which two ways the PFD can reach the inboard display unit after an outboard display failure
options: Manually from either seat
Automatically or manually
Automatically after a delay
cards.explain: The switching to the inboard DU can be done automatically or manually.

cards.question: A pilot wants his navigation picture on the lower display unit, so how does he get it there?
options: It appears there automatically
He selects it on the source select module
He switches it there manually
cards.explain: The captain's or F/O's ND can be switched onto the lower display unit manually.

cards.question: Both outboard display units fail, so what does the crew lose on the inboard screens?
options: The normal navigation pictures
The normal warning indications
The normal engine indications
cards.explain: The inboard units normally show the ND, so taking the PFDs onto them costs the crew those navigation pictures.

cards.question: On which display unit is the PFD normally shown
options: The inboard pair
The lower one
The outboard one
cards.explain: The PFD is normally presented on the outboard display unit.

cards.question: From which viewpoint the navigation display presents the aircraft situation
options: From above
From behind
From the side
cards.explain: The ND shows the situation of the aircraft seen from above.

cards.question: Which conventional instrument is fully replaced by the navigation display
options: The HSI
The ADI
The RMI
cards.explain: The ND fully replaces the horizontal situation indicator.

cards.question: During which part of the flight the ND ILS mode indicates its parameters
options: During the taxi out
During the ILS approach
During the initial climb out
cards.explain: The ILS mode indicates ILS parameters during the ILS approach.

cards.question: A pilot selects the ILS mode on his ND, so which two deviations does he then see?
options: Glideslope and vertical speed
Localizer and track
Localizer and glideslope
cards.explain: The ILS mode of the ND indicates localizer and glideslope deviation.

cards.question: Which three items are added in the navigation sector mode of the ND
options: The range selection, the localizer scale and the waypoint
The waypoint, the glideslope scale and the route indication
The waypoint, the range selection and the route indication
cards.explain: The nav sector mode additionally displays waypoint, range selection and route indication.

cards.question: A pilot's PFD appears on the inboard screen in flight, so what has most likely happened?
options: The baro correction has been changed
The control panel has been reset
The normal display unit has failed
cards.explain: The PFD is switched to the inboard display unit on failure of its normal one.

cards.question: What the small aircraft symbol on the navigation display is there for
options: To show the aircraft type being flown
To act as a reference for the picture
To show the attitude of the aircraft
cards.explain: The small aircraft symbol is used as a reference and is normally in the centre of the screen.

cards.question: Which navigation point does the basic waypoint data on the ND refer to
options: The last one passed
The destination one
The next one
cards.explain: The waypoint data gives information about the next navigation point.

cards.question: A trainee asks what ground speed on the navigation display means, so what is the answer?
options: The speed limit on the ground
The speed through the air
The speed above the ground
cards.explain: Ground speed is printed as the speed above the ground.

cards.question: Which ND parameter comes from somewhere other than the navigation systems
options: The heading
The ground speed
The wind velocity
cards.explain: Apart from the heading, all information on the ND is based on data from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Which aircraft system supplies the parameters shown in the ND ILS mode
options: The flight management computer system
The air data computer system
The instrument landing system
cards.explain: The ILS mode indicates parameters coming from the instrument landing system.

cards.question: A route indication is missing from a navigation display in the sector mode, so which system should be suspected?
options: The flight management system
The ground proximity warning system
The instrument landing system
cards.explain: The route indication in that mode is supplied by the flight management system.

cards.question: Why the loss of one display unit need not cost the pilot his primary flight picture
options: Because the PFD can be switched to another display unit
Because the PFD is drawn on a second display unit as well
Because the standby instruments take over the PFD picture
cards.explain: The PFD can be switched automatically or manually to the inboard display unit when its own unit fails.

cards.question: Which system supplies the AFCS information shown on the PFD
options: The navigation system
The autoflight system
The air data system
cards.explain: The AFCS information on the PFD comes from the autoflight system.

cards.question: The pressure setting on a PFD will not change, so which control should be suspected first?
options: The range selection on the EFIS control panel
The baro correction on the EFIS control panel
The mode selection on the EFIS control panel
cards.explain: The pressure setting on the PFD is the baro correction, which is set from the EFIS control panel.

cards.question: Which two deviations are shown together on the PFD in the ILS mode
options: The localizer and the vertical speed
The glide slope and the radio height
The localizer and the glide slope
cards.explain: The ILS mode displays localizer and glide slope alongside the source and the marker.

cards.question: A mechanic is asked why there is no separate ILS indicator in an EFIS cockpit, so what should he say?
options: The ILS picture is only available on the ground
The PFD takes that job in the ILS mode
The ILS is only monitored from the standby instrument
cards.explain: The PFD itself is used as the display for the instrument landing system.

cards.question: Why the wind indication stays on the navigation display whatever mode is selected
options: Because the control panel cannot reach that part of the screen
Because it is only drawn by the air data computer
Because it is one of the basic items always present
cards.explain: Wind direction and velocity is one of the basic pieces of information present no matter what is selected.

cards.question: A pilot changes the ND mode and loses an indication he wanted, so what does that tell him about it?
options: It is not one of the basic always present items
It is only driven by the flight management system
It is only shown while the autopilot is engaged
cards.explain: Only the listed basic pieces of information are present no matter what is selected on the control panel.

cards.question: The navigation systems feeding an ND are lost but the heading is still drawn, so what does that say about the heading?
options: It is drawn by the flight management computer
It is navigation data like every one of the others
It is the one item that is not navigation data
cards.explain: Apart from the heading, all information on the ND is based on data from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Why the localizer deviation can be read on the PFD and on the ND at the same time
options: Because both displays can present ILS parameters
Because the ND copies the whole PFD picture in that mode
Because the ILS feeds only the navigation display units
cards.explain: The PFD has an ILS mode and the ND has an ILS mode, and both show the localizer indication.

cards.question: Why selecting the navigation sector mode changes what the pilot can read on the display
options: Because that mode adds flight management data
Because that mode removes the compass rose from the picture
Because that mode moves the picture onto the lower display unit
cards.explain: The nav sector mode adds the waypoint, range selection and route indication, all from the FMS.

cards.question: A pilot swaps from the ILS mode to the navigation sector mode, so what replaces the ILS parameters on his display?
options: Flight management information
Radio altimeter information
Inertial reference information
cards.explain: The ILS mode shows ILS parameters while the nav sector mode adds information from the flight management system.

cards.question: A pilot reduces the display range on the ND, so what happens to the small aircraft symbol?
options: It moves towards the edge of the screen
It is removed until the range is restored
It stays in the centre of the screen
cards.explain: The small aircraft symbol is used as a reference and is normally displayed in the centre of the screen.

cards.question: How do the pushbuttons appear while everything is operating normally
options: Steady white
Steady green
Dark
cards.explain: All pushbuttons are dark during normal operation.

cards.question: Which colour is used when an immediate action is necessary
options: Amber
Red
White
cards.explain: Red is the colour used when an immediate action is necessary.

cards.question: Which colour indicates the normal operation of a backup system
options: White
Green
Blue
cards.explain: Green indicates the normal operation of a backup system.

cards.question: Which colour indicates the normal operation of a temporarily used system
options: Amber
Blue
Green
cards.explain: Blue indicates the normal operation of a temporarily used system.

cards.question: Where is the centralised caution panel installed
options: On the centre pedestal
At the pilots' eye level
On the overhead panel
cards.explain: The centralised caution panel is installed at the pilots' eye level.

cards.question: Where is the local warning light of a system covered by the centralised caution panel fitted
options: On the glareshield
On the centralised caution panel
On the overhead panel
cards.explain: The local warning light sits on the overhead panel while the centralised panel sits in view.

cards.question: What two forms of information do central warning displays give the flight crew
options: Text and aural information
Graphic and tactile information
Text and graphic information
cards.explain: The displays provide text and graphic information.

cards.question: What kind of system is ECAM
options: A central warning system
A flight management system
An autoflight system
cards.explain: ECAM is a central warning system.

cards.question: Which two displays make up ECAM in the cockpit
options: The primary flight display and the system display
The engine/warning display and the navigation display
The engine/warning display and the system display
cards.explain: ECAM is present as the E/WD and the SD.

cards.question: Apart from calling up pages and messages, which display property is set from the ECAM control panel
options: The contrast ratio
The refresh rate
The brightness
cards.explain: The control panel is used to control the brightness of the ECAM display units.

cards.question: What is simulated when the TO CONFIG pushbutton is used
options: The emergency electrical configuration
The approach configuration
The take-off power configuration
cards.explain: The TO CONFIG pushbutton simulates the T/O power configuration.

cards.question: Which two kinds of page does the system display show
options: The system and status pages
The engine and warning pages
The memo and alert pages
cards.explain: The SD shows the system and the status pages.

cards.question: How many system pages exist for the system display
options: Twelve
Eight
Five
cards.explain: One of twelve system pages can be shown.

cards.question: What happens to the related system when an illuminated pushbutton is pressed
options: Its light test is only started
Its warning is only acknowledged
Its switching state is changed
cards.explain: Pressing the illuminated pushbutton changes the state of the switch behind it.

cards.question: A pushbutton on the overhead panel has just lit up, so what does that tell the crew?
options: The pushbutton lamp is being tested by the crew
The system has returned to its normal switching state
A local warning or an abnormal switching state exists
cards.explain: A pushbutton lights only for a local warning or for an abnormal switching state.

cards.question: Why are the pushbutton lights given a colour code
options: To make abnormal conditions easy to identify
To show which bus supplies each panel
To group the pushbuttons by aircraft system
cards.explain: The colour code exists to help in the easy identification of abnormal conditions.

cards.question: An engine fire has broken out, so what colour will the associated pushbutton light show?
options: Red
White
Amber
cards.explain: An engine fire needs immediate action, and immediate action is coded red.

cards.question: Besides an abnormal pushbutton position, which condition is shown by a white light
options: A backup system running
A failure needing awareness
A maintenance operation
cards.explain: White covers a pushbutton in an abnormal position or a maintenance operation.

cards.question: A pushbutton shows a steady blue legend, so what is the crew being told?
options: A backup system is operating normally
A system has been left in an abnormal position
A temporarily used system is operating normally
cards.explain: Blue is reserved for the normal operation of a temporarily used system.

cards.question: A pushbutton shows a steady green legend, so what is the crew being told?
options: A temporary system is operating normally
A backup system is operating normally
A failure needing awareness has occurred
cards.explain: Green is reserved for the normal operation of a backup system.

cards.question: Which shortcoming of the master caution and master warning lights led to a centralised panel
options: They do not stay on long enough to be seen
They cannot be cancelled once they are on
They do not say which system is affected
cards.explain: The master lights give no information about which system is affected or which local light is on.

cards.question: What does the centralised caution panel tell the crew about a fault
options: Which particular system it is in
How many flight hours remain before rectification
Which circuit breaker has tripped
cards.explain: The panel indicates a fault in a particular system.

cards.question: How is the master caution light cancelled
options: By switching off the affected system
By pressing its light cover
By pressing the local warning light
cards.explain: The master caution light is cancelled by pressing its light cover.

cards.question: Why does the crew cancel the master caution light rather than leave it on?
options: So that the local warning light goes out
So that the centralised panel can be tested
So that another fault can be indicated
cards.explain: Cancelling the light frees it so that a further fault can be indicated.

cards.question: What does the information on a central warning display describe
options: The flight phase being computed
The present failure condition
The maintenance action already carried out
cards.explain: The displays describe the present failure condition.

cards.question: An engineer compares the central warning systems of two different aircraft types, so what will he mostly find?
options: The same function under different names
Different functions under the same name
The same name and the same hardware
cards.explain: Central warning systems in different types generally share the function but not the name.

cards.question: Under what condition is the symbol ADV displayed
options: When a status page becomes available
When ECAM is working as a mono display
When a caution message is cancelled
cards.explain: ADV appears when ECAM is working as a mono display, that is with only one display.

cards.question: One of the two ECAM displays has failed, so which symbol appears in the lower part of the engine/warning display?
options: STS
ADV
RCL
cards.explain: With only one ECAM display left, ECAM works as a mono display and ADV is shown.

cards.question: Which two pages are combined in the cruise page
options: The engine and fuel pages
The air and hydraulic pages
The engine and air pages
cards.explain: The cruise page consists of the engine and air pages.

cards.question: A memo message has to be read, so which display and which part of it does the crew use?
options: The lower part of the engine/warning display
The upper part of the engine/warning display
The lower part of the system display
cards.explain: Memo messages are in the lower part of the E/WD.

cards.question: Which three things can be done to warnings and messages from the ECAM control panel
options: Cancel, delete or call them up again
Dim, enlarge or colour them
Record, print or transmit them
cards.explain: The panel cancels, deletes or calls up again the warnings and messages.

cards.question: In which position must the slats and flaps be for the take-off configuration check to pass
options: Fully extended
Fully retracted
In the T/O range
cards.explain: The check requires the slats and flaps to be in the T/O range.

cards.question: What condition of the speed brakes is required by the take-off configuration check
options: They must be retracted
They must be extended
They must be armed
cards.explain: The check requires the speed brakes to be retracted.

cards.question: What condition of the wheel brakes is required by the take-off configuration check
options: They must be released
They must be parked
They must not be overheated
cards.explain: The check requires the wheel brakes not to be OVHT.

cards.question: The take-off configuration check is run with a cabin door still open, so what will the crew find?
options: The master caution will be inhibited
The normal message will not appear
The check will be bypassed automatically
cards.explain: Door closed is one of the items checked, so an open door prevents the normal result.

cards.question: A continuous aural alert is sounding and the crew wants it silenced, so which ECAM control panel pushbutton is used?
options: EMER CANC
CLR
RCL
cards.explain: The EMER CANC pushbutton cancels the aural warnings.

cards.question: What happens when the ALL pushbutton is pressed and held
options: The system pages are called up at one second intervals
The system pages are frozen on the display
The status page is called up again after five seconds
cards.explain: Pressing and holding ALL calls up the system pages at one second intervals.

cards.question: What happens when the ALL pushbutton is pressed only briefly
options: The displayed system page is deleted
The system page moves forward by one page
The system pages cycle continuously
cards.explain: A brief press moves the system page forward by one page.

cards.question: When does the light in the CLR pushbutton come on
options: When warning, caution or status messages appear
When the recall function has just been used
When the system pages are being cycled by the crew
cards.explain: The CLR light comes on when warning, caution or status messages appear on the ECAM display.

cards.question: Which message is removed each time the CLR pushbutton is pushed
options: The oldest warning in the list
The warning at the top
Every warning at once
cards.explain: Each push of CLR deletes the warning at the top.

cards.question: What reappears on the display after the last clearance has been made with CLR
options: The caution messages
The memo messages
The status page
cards.explain: After the last clearance the memo messages reappear.

cards.question: How long after the status pushbutton is used do the normal messages return when no status messages are present
options: After 5 seconds
After 10 seconds
After 2 seconds
cards.explain: With no status messages present the normal messages are displayed again after 5 seconds.

cards.question: The brightness of the engine/warning and system displays has to be changed, so which panel is used?
options: The ECAM control panel
The centralised caution panel
The EICAS display select panel
cards.explain: Brightness is controlled from the ECAM control panel.

cards.question: How many system pages can be shown on the system display at any one time
options: Four
Two
One
cards.explain: Only one of the twelve system pages can be displayed at any one time.

cards.question: Which two air temperatures are shown among the permanent data on a system page
options: TAT and SAT
TAT and EGT
SAT and ITT
cards.explain: The permanent data includes TAT and SAT.

cards.question: Which item is shown as an alternative to the G-load among the permanent data
options: The gross weight
The selected altitude
The static air temperature
cards.explain: The permanent data ends with G-load or selected altitude.

cards.question: A pilot needs the total air temperature while a system page is up, so where is it shown?
options: On the engine/warning display
On the upper part of the page
On the lower part of the page
cards.explain: TAT is one of the permanent data items on the lower part of the system page.

cards.question: A system is working normally but its pushbutton has been left out of its normal switching position, so what will the crew see on that pushbutton?
options: It will flash until the fault is cleared
It will be lit even though no fault exists
It will stay dark because no fault exists
cards.explain: A pushbutton lights for an abnormal switching state as well as for a local warning, so it is lit with no fault present.

cards.question: A pushbutton has stayed dark for the whole flight, so what does that say about its system?
options: It is a backup that has taken over the load
It is normal and in its usual switching state
It has failed but needs no action at once
cards.explain: A pushbutton lights only for a local warning or an abnormal switching state, so a dark one means neither is present.

cards.question: A pushbutton carries an amber FAULT legend, so how urgent is the crew action?
options: Action is needed but not at once
Action is needed at once
Action is not needed at all
cards.explain: Amber is used when action is required but not necessarily at once.

cards.question: Several pushbuttons are lit at once and the crew must choose where to start, so which colour takes priority?
options: Red
White
Amber
cards.explain: Red marks the failure needing immediate action while amber needs awareness but no immediate action.

cards.question: A pushbutton is lit in a colour that reports normal operation, so which two colours could it be?
options: Red or amber
Amber or white
Green or blue
cards.explain: Green and blue are the two colours printed against normal operation, of a backup system and of a temporarily used system.

cards.question: A system has been selected off and no fault exists, so which colour will its pushbutton show?
options: Amber
Green
White
cards.explain: A pushbutton left in an abnormal position is coded white, and no failure is being reported.

cards.question: Which two colours on a pushbutton both report a failure of some kind
options: Red and amber
Green and blue
White and green
cards.explain: Red and amber are the two colours printed against a failure, the first needing immediate action and the second only awareness.

cards.question: A fault occurs in a system whose local light is on the overhead panel out of the pilot's sight, so how does the crew learn which system it is?
options: The master caution light names the affected system
The centralised caution panel names the affected system
The overhead local light is repeated on the glareshield
cards.explain: The master light says only that something is wrong, so the panel at eye level is what identifies the system.

cards.question: A fault is already being annunciated and a second fault then occurs, so what must the crew do for the new one to be indicated?
options: Cancel the master caution light first
Reset the centralised caution panel first
Press the local warning light first
cards.explain: Only after the master caution light has been cancelled can another fault be indicated.

cards.question: A crew is told that a fault exists but not which system has it, so which indication are they looking at?
options: A central warning display message
A centralised caution panel light
A master caution light
cards.explain: The master lights give no information about the system affected, while the panel and the display both name it.

cards.question: A pilot sees STS in the lower part of the engine/warning display but no status page is being shown, so where will that status page appear once it is called up?
options: On the engine/warning display
On the system display
On the centralised caution panel
cards.explain: STS says a status page is available and the status page is displayed on the SD.

cards.question: A page made up of the engine and air pages is on the system display, so where is the aircraft in its flight?
options: In the take-off run
In cruise flight
In the approach
cards.explain: The cruise page, which consists of the engine and air pages, is the one shown in cruise flight.

cards.question: A crew member has cleared several caution messages with CLR and then wants to read them again, so what must be done?
options: Press CLR again to restore them
Press STS to bring up the status page
Press RCL to recall them
cards.explain: CLR deletes the messages one by one and RCL is the pushbutton that recalls them.

cards.question: The status pushbutton has been pressed and after a short time the normal messages return on their own, so what does that tell the crew?
options: No status messages are present
The status page has been cleared by CLR
The ECAM is working as a mono display
cards.explain: The normal messages come back by themselves only when there are no status messages to show.

cards.question: A level 3 alert has triggered an aural warning and the master warning lights, and the crew uses EMER CANC, so what is left showing on the ECAM?
options: Nothing at all is left on the display
The warning message on the display stays
Only the system page is cancelled
cards.explain: EMER CANC removes the aural warnings, the master warning lights and the caution messages, so a warning message itself is not in that list.

cards.question: The light in the CLR pushbutton is on and nobody has pushed it yet, so what is on the ECAM display?
options: A warning, caution or status message
Only the permanent data of the system page
Only the memo messages of the systems
cards.explain: The CLR light comes on only when warning, caution or status messages are present.

cards.question: A pilot wants to step through every system page in turn, so what must be done with the ALL pushbutton?
options: Press it twice in quick succession
Press it briefly once
Press and hold it
cards.explain: Pressing and holding ALL calls up the system pages one after another at one second intervals.

cards.question: STS is showing on the engine/warning display and the crew presses the status pushbutton, so what appears?
options: The normal messages, since no status messages exist
The status page with its messages
The cruise page with its engine data
cards.explain: STS means a status page is available, so pressing the pushbutton brings that page up rather than returning the normal messages.

cards.question: A pilot wants to see a second system page while one is already up, so what happens to the page already displayed?
options: It stays, because the second page opens on the E/WD
It is replaced, because only one can be shown at a time
It stays, because two pages can be shown side by side
cards.explain: Only one of the twelve system pages can be displayed at any one time.

cards.question: A pilot reading a system page wants the gross weight, so where on that page does he look?
options: On the lower part, among the permanent data
On the upper part, among the engine parameters
On the right side, among the inoperative systems
cards.explain: GW is printed among the permanent data on the lower part of the system page.

cards.question: Which aircraft condition is associated with a level 3 alert
options: A configuration to monitor
An abnormal configuration
An emergency configuration
cards.explain: Level 3 is the warning raised for an emergency configuration.

cards.question: Which aircraft condition is associated with a level 2 alert
options: An abnormal configuration
An emergency configuration
A configuration to monitor
cards.explain: Level 2 is the caution raised for an abnormal configuration.

cards.question: What priority do level 3 warnings carry
options: A medium priority
The highest priority
The lowest priority
cards.explain: Level 3 warnings are the warnings with the highest priority.

cards.question: How quickly must the crew react to a level 3 warning
options: Before the next scheduled check
Before the next flight phase
Immediately
cards.explain: A level 3 warning is a real emergency and the crew must react immediately.

cards.question: What influence does a level 2 caution have on the flight
options: A direct and immediate influence
No direct influence
An influence only during the approach
cards.explain: Level 2 cautions have no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: What is required of the crew when a level 2 caution appears
options: An immediate reaction
Greater attention
No reaction at all
cards.explain: A level 2 caution calls for greater attention.

cards.question: On which display do level 1 cautions appear
options: The system display
The engine/warning display
The centralised caution panel
cards.explain: Level 1 cautions appear on the E/WD.

cards.question: Which indications are absent for a level 1 caution
options: Memo messages and status messages
Aural alarms and warning lights
Text messages and system pages
cards.explain: There are no aural alarms or warning lights for a level 1 caution.

cards.question: Which flight phase does the flight warning system select by default when it has no data
options: The preflight phase
The approach phase
The cruise phase
cards.explain: With the data unavailable the FWS defaults to the cruise phase.

cards.question: Which parameters are permanently displayed on the upper EICAS
options: The status information
The primary engine parameters
The secondary engine parameters
cards.explain: The upper EICAS permanently displays the primary engine parameters.

cards.question: How many EFIS/EICAS interface units are fitted
options: Four
Three
Two
cards.explain: There are three EFIS/EICAS interface units.

cards.question: Which two parameters are the primary engine parameters on the EICAS display
options: N2 rotor speed and fuel flow in kilogrammes
N1 rotor speed and exhaust gas temperature
Oil pressure and oil temperature in degrees
cards.explain: The page names N1 rotor speed and EGT as the primary engine parameters.

cards.question: Which colour is used for a Level A warning message in the alert message field
options: White
Red
Amber
cards.explain: Level A warning messages are printed as showing in red.

cards.question: How many manual snapshots can be stored for each system
options: Up to 3
Up to 5
Up to 10
cards.explain: Storage is available for up to 5 manual snapshots per system.

cards.question: A snapshot has just been taken because a parameter went outside its preset value, so where is it kept?
options: In the manual event non-volatile memory
In the auto event non-volatile memory
In the real time data storage buffer
cards.explain: Auto snapshots go to the auto event non-volatile memory.

cards.question: Which alert level is classified as a warning rather than a caution
options: Level 2
Level 1
Level 3
cards.explain: Level 3 carries the title warnings while levels 2 and 1 are cautions.

cards.question: An alert is classified as a level 3 rather than a level 2, so what does that say about the aircraft?
options: There is a real emergency on board
There is no direct influence on the flight
There is a system that is not needed
cards.explain: Level 3 is printed against a real emergency, while a level 2 is a failure with no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: The aircraft has gone into an abnormal configuration without any emergency, so which alert level is produced?
options: Level 3
Level 2
Level 1
cards.explain: An abnormal configuration is the condition behind a level 2 caution.

cards.question: In what manner does the master warning light behave for a level 3 warning
options: It stays dark
It flashes
It stays steady
cards.explain: The master warning light flashes for a level 3 warning.

cards.question: What may appear on the system display in addition to a level 3 warning
options: A system page, if one is available
A cruise page, if one is available
A status page, if one is available
cards.explain: If available, a system page may also appear on the SD.

cards.question: An alarm sounds and the master warning light begins to flash, so which level has been reached?
options: Level 3
Level 2
Level 1
cards.explain: An aural alarm with a flashing master warning light is the level 3 signature.

cards.question: How many chimes are sounded for a level 2 caution
options: One
None
Three
cards.explain: A level 2 caution is given with a single chime.

cards.question: What kind of system does a level 1 caution draw attention to
options: A serviceable system temporarily switched off
A defective system needed for the flight to continue
A defective system not required for the flight to continue
cards.explain: Level 1 cautions point at a defective system which is not required for the flight to continue.

cards.question: A caution message has appeared on the engine/warning display with no sound and no light, so which level has been reached?
options: Level 3
Level 1
Level 2
cards.explain: Level 1 is the only level with no aural alarm and no warning light.

cards.question: A brakes channel fault is annunciated as a level 1 caution, so what does that say about continuing the flight?
options: That system is required to continue
The flight has to be ended at once
That system is not required to continue
cards.explain: Level 1 cautions cover a defective system which is not required for the flight to continue.

cards.question: From which system does the flight warning system take its compressed or not compressed signal
options: The landing gear system
The air data system
The brake control system
cards.explain: The gear compressed or not compressed information comes from the L/G system.

cards.question: Which number is given to the default flight phase of the flight warning system
cards.explain: The default is the cruise phase, numbered 8.

cards.question: Which four items can be shown on the lower EICAS
options: Primary engine parameters, synoptics, memo messages and maintenance pages
Secondary engine parameters, system pages, status information and alert messages
Secondary engine parameters, synoptics, status information and maintenance pages
cards.explain: The lower EICAS can show secondary engine parameters, synoptics, status information and maintenance pages.

cards.question: Which panel brings synoptics and status information onto the lower display unit
options: The ECAM control panel
The EICAS display select panel
The centralised caution panel
cards.explain: Synoptics and status information are selected with the EICAS display select panel (EDSP).

cards.question: Through which unit are the maintenance pages called up on the lower EICAS
options: The CMC
The EDSP
The EIU
cards.explain: The maintenance pages are called up via the CMC.

cards.question: Which data appears on the lower EICAS immediately after power-up
options: The status information
The secondary engine data
The primary engine data
cards.explain: After power-up the lower EICAS shows the secondary engine data.

cards.question: Which data bus supplies the EICAS display units
options: An ARINC 573 data bus
An ARINC 629 data bus
An ARINC 429 data bus
cards.explain: The display units are supplied via an ARINC 429 data bus.

cards.question: A message shows in the alert message field in amber and indented, so which level is it?
options: Level D memo
Level B caution
Level C advisory
cards.explain: Only the Level C advisory messages are both amber and indented.

cards.question: Why is information that is not required removed from the EICAS display
options: To reduce the heat produced by the screens
To save electrical power in the display units
To maintain a quiet, dark flight deck
cards.explain: Removing unneeded information is what keeps the flight deck quiet and dark.

cards.question: What makes an automatic snapshot occur for a system
options: Parameters that exceed preset values
Selection of the real time display mode
A request made by the maintenance crew
cards.explain: An auto snapshot is taken when parameters go beyond their preset values.

cards.question: What causes a manual snapshot of the real time format to be taken
options: An action by the flight or maintenance crew
A report sent to the printer or to ACARS
A parameter that goes out of its limits
cards.explain: A manual snapshot follows an action by the flight or maintenance crew.

cards.question: Two alerts come up together, the first at level 3 and the second at level 1, so what does the more serious of the two report?
options: A configuration to monitor
An emergency configuration
An abnormal configuration
cards.explain: Level 3 is the warning raised by an emergency configuration, while level 1 only covers a configuration to monitor.
