cards.question: The cabin altitude has become excessive, so what indications will the crew get?
options: A single chime with a steady master caution light
A message on the display with no aural alarm
An aural alarm with a flashing master warning light
cards.explain: Excess cabin altitude is a level 3 warning and level 3 gives an aural alarm with a flashing master warning light.

cards.question: An engine fire breaks out in flight, so what must the crew do about it?
options: React immediately, as it is a real emergency
Note it and continue, as the flight is not affected
React before the next flight phase begins
cards.explain: Engine fire is a level 3 warning and a level 3 warning is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction.

cards.question: A level 3 warning and a level 1 caution are annunciated at the same moment, so which one is handled first?
options: Either one, since the two carry the same priority
The warning, which has the highest priority
The caution, which has the highest priority
cards.explain: Level 3 warnings are the warnings with the highest priority.

cards.question: A single chime sounds and the master caution light comes on, so what does the crew know about the failure?
options: It has no direct influence on the flight
It gives no aural alarm and no warning light
It is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction
cards.explain: A single chime with the master caution light is a level 2, and level 2 failures have no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: A failure needs greater attention but no immediate reaction, so which aural alert will the crew hear?
options: No sound at all
A single chime
A continuous alarm
cards.explain: Greater attention without an immediate reaction is a level 2, and a level 2 is given with a single chime.

cards.question: A defective system is annunciated with a single chime rather than silently, so what does the crew know about it?
options: It is a level 2, needing greater attention
It is a level 1, needing greater attention
It is a level 3, needing an immediate reaction
cards.explain: A single chime marks a level 2, which calls for greater attention, while a level 1 would have been silent.

cards.question: A system that the flight does not need has become defective, so what will the crew hear?
options: Nothing, as there is no aural alarm
A continuous alarm from the master warning
A single chime from the master caution
cards.explain: A defective system not required to continue the flight is a level 1 caution, and level 1 has no aural alarm.

cards.question: An alert needs the crew to read the engine/warning display to notice it at all, so what does that say about its level?
options: It is a level 2, which gives only a single chime
It is a level 3, which gives only a flashing light
It is a level 1, which has no attention getter
cards.explain: Only a level 1 caution comes without an aural alarm or a warning light, so nothing draws the eye to it.

cards.question: A recorder fault and a stall warning occur in the same flight, so how do the two alerts differ in what the crew gets?
options: One gives no sound or light while the other gives both
One gives a single chime while the other gives no sound
Each one gives an aural alarm but only one gives a light
cards.explain: A recorder fault is a level 1 with no aural alarm or warning light, while a stall warning is a level 3 with an aural alarm and a flashing master warning light.

cards.question: An instructor asks what separates a warning from a caution in practice, so what is the difference in the reaction required?
options: A caution needs an immediate reaction, a warning does not
A warning needs an immediate reaction, a caution does not
Each one needs the same immediate reaction from the crew
cards.explain: The level 3 warning is a real emergency needing an immediate reaction, while the level 2 caution has no direct influence on the flight.

cards.question: Which indication is common to all three alert levels when it is available
options: A chime sounding from the loudspeaker
A light coming on at the eye level
A system page on the system display
cards.explain: Each of the three levels is printed with the note that a system page may also appear on the SD if available.

cards.question: A technician wants to bring the maintenance pages up on the lower EICAS, so why will the display select panel not do it?
options: Because that panel only works after the aircraft is powered up
Because that panel only selects the primary engine parameters
Because that panel only selects synoptics and status information
cards.explain: The EDSP selects synoptics and status information while the maintenance pages come via the CMC.

cards.question: An aircraft has just been powered up and no selection has been made, so what is seen on the two EICAS display units?
options: Primary engine data above and secondary engine data below
Primary engine data above and the status information below
Secondary engine data above and primary engine data below
cards.explain: After power-up the upper unit shows the primary and the lower unit the secondary engine data.

cards.question: All three interface units have failed, so what will the EICAS display units show?
options: Nothing, as their data comes through them
Primary engine data only, taken direct from the engines
Maintenance pages only, taken direct from the CMC
cards.explain: The display units are fed by one of the three EIUs, and all the important systems supply their data to those units.

cards.question: A pilot needs the secondary engine parameters while a synoptic is up on the lower EICAS, so what must happen on that display?
options: The synoptic must be deselected to show them
The synoptic and the parameters appear together
The upper display must be used to show them
cards.explain: The lower EICAS carries the secondary parameters, synoptics, status and maintenance pages in turn, while the upper one is permanently the primary parameters.

cards.question: A synoptic is wanted on the lower EICAS straight after power-up, so what must be done?
options: It must be selected on the display select panel
It is already there after power-up
It must be called up through the maintenance computer
cards.explain: After power-up the lower unit shows the secondary engine data, so a synoptic has to be selected on the EDSP.

cards.question: The upper EICAS display unit is showing data that cannot be deselected, so what is on it?
options: The synoptics of the systems
The primary engine parameters
The secondary engine parameters
cards.explain: The upper EICAS permanently displays the primary engine parameters, the selectable items being on the lower unit.

cards.question: Every indication that is not needed has been removed from the main EICAS display, so which two groups are still shown?
options: The landing gear status and the flap indications
The cabin altitude and the duct pressure readouts
The primary engine parameters and the fuel system data
cards.explain: Those two groups are the ones stated to show at all times.

cards.question: A caution and an advisory both show in amber in the alert message field, so how is the advisory told apart?
options: It is underlined
It is flashing
It is indented
cards.explain: The advisory is the amber message that is indented.

cards.question: An engine exceedance occurs while the aeroplane stands with its parking brake set, so what becomes of the event?
options: It is lost, since two engines have to be running
It is stored, since that storage is not inhibited
It is lost, since the brake has to be released first
cards.explain: Engine exceedance page storage is printed as not inhibited, so the running and brake conditions do not apply to it.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the GPWS
options: To warn the flight crew of another aircraft on a conflicting track
To warn the flight crew when the aircraft comes too close to the ground
To warn the flight crew of a windshear encountered on approach
cards.explain: The system warns the crew when the aircraft mistakenly comes too close to the ground.

cards.question: By which two means is the basic GPWS warning given to the pilot
options: A master caution and a single chime
A flashing display and a stick shaker
An aural alert and annunciator lights
cards.explain: The warning is an aural alert plus annunciator lights in front of the pilot.

cards.question: On which display does the enhanced ground proximity warning system show the surrounding terrain
options: On the primary flight display
On the navigation display
On the engine indication display
cards.explain: The terrain picture is presented on the navigation display.

cards.question: Which three parts are the main parts of a ground proximity warning system
options: One warning computer, indications and inhibit switches
One warning computer, a radio altimeter and a speaker
Two warning computers, indications and a control panel
cards.explain: The computer, the indications and the inhibit switches are the main parts.

cards.question: A basic GPWS is checked, so at which radio altitude does its operative range begin?
options: 30 ft
50 ft
10 ft
cards.explain: The printed operative range of the basic GPWS begins at 30 ft radio altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with the enhanced system, so which two functions does it have on top of the basic modes?
options: Radio altitude callouts, and the modulation of alerting envelopes
Terrain awareness alerting and display, and terrain clearance floor
Windshear alerting for take-off, and excessive bank angle alerting
cards.explain: Those two are the additional functions listed for the enhanced system.

cards.question: The enhanced computer needs the height above the ground for its warning calculation, so which unit supplies it?
options: The digital air data computer
The instrument landing system
The downward looking radio altimeter
cards.explain: The downward looking radio altimeter is the primary sensor for the warning calculation.

cards.question: A ground proximity alert sounds in the flight deck, so what kind of voice is heard?
options: A rising tone sequence
A recorded crew voice
A synthetic voice
cards.explain: The aural alert uses a synthetic voice.

cards.question: An operator asks where a ground proximity warning system is only rarely found, so which aircraft are meant?
options: Twin-engined aeroplanes
Helicopters
Four-engined aeroplanes
cards.explain: The page states the system is rarely installed in helicopters.

cards.question: Where else are GPWS alert messages presented in some aircraft
options: On the primary flight displays
On the navigation displays
On the engine indication display
cards.explain: Some aircraft add alert messages on the primary flight displays.

cards.question: In which aeroplanes is the ground proximity warning system installed
options: In all of them except the very small ones
In the very small ones only
In all of them without any exception
cards.explain: Every aeroplane except the very small ones carries the system.

cards.question: Which signal are the terrain functions of the enhanced system independent of
options: The radio altitude
The barometric altitude
The glide slope deviation
cards.explain: The enhanced terrain functions do not depend on the radio altitude.

cards.question: A crew is told their fit is the advanced version, so what does it do that the basic one does not?
options: It sounds its alerts with a synthetic voice
It shows the terrain around the aircraft
It lights annunciators in front of the pilot
cards.explain: The terrain picture is what the advanced system adds.

cards.question: From which sources does the GPWC receive its inputs
options: From an air data computer and various navigation systems
From the autopilot and the flight control computers
From the flight data recorder and the engine computers
cards.explain: Its inputs come from an air data computer and from the navigation systems.

cards.question: Only some aeroplanes carry one of the three main parts of the system, so which part is it?
options: The warning computer
The indications
The inhibit switches
cards.explain: The inhibit switches are the part fitted to some aeroplanes only.

cards.question: Which kind of accident is the enhanced system intended to prevent
options: Runway incursion on landing
Loss of control in flight
Controlled flight into terrain
cards.explain: Its stated purpose is to help prevent CFIT accidents.

cards.question: With what does the enhanced system compare the aircraft position
options: With an internal database
With the radio altitude signal
With the weather radar picture
cards.explain: The aircraft position is compared with an internal database.

cards.question: Which two sources can supply the aircraft position used in that comparison
options: The ADC or the IRS
The FMS or the GPS
The ILS or the VOR
cards.explain: The position comes from the FMS or the GPS.

cards.question: Windshear alerting is fitted to an aircraft, so which mode number does it carry?
options: Mode 6
Mode 7
Mode 5
cards.explain: Windshear alerting is mode 7.

cards.question: What does the enhanced system do with the variety of aircraft parameters it accepts
options: It transmits them to the ground station
It records them for later readout
It applies alerting algorithms to them
cards.explain: The parameters are taken in and alerting algorithms are applied to them.

cards.question: Which two products were introduced in the late 1980s
options: MARK VI for digital aircraft and MARK I for analogue aircraft
MARK V for digital aircraft and MARK VII for analogue aircraft
MARK II for analogue aircraft and MARK III for digital aircraft
cards.explain: The two late 1980s products were MARK V for digital and MARK VII for analogue aircraft.

cards.question: Which two introductions improve the terrain awareness and the warning times of the enhanced system
options: The terrain display and the terrain data base look ahead protection
The terrain clearance floor and the modulation of the envelopes
The altitude callouts and the alert for an excessive bank angle
cards.explain: Terrain display and terrain data base look ahead protection are the named improvements.

cards.question: Why can the warning time be short when the aircraft flies towards steep terrain
options: The aural message volume is reduced to one half below 300 feet
The primary sensor is a downward looking radio altimeter
The alerting boundaries are computed from the barometric height
cards.explain: The warning is calculated from a downward looking sensor, which sees steep terrain late.

cards.question: Rising ground is approached at 2600 ft radio altitude, so why does the basic GPWS stay quiet?
options: Its boundaries are computed from the barometric altitude
Its automatic operation begins only at a lower radio altitude
Its aural alerts are suppressed with the landing gear up
cards.explain: The aircraft is still above the radio altitude at which the basic system begins to operate automatically.

cards.question: The radio altimeter has failed in flight, so what can still warn the crew about high ground ahead?
options: The enhanced system terrain functions
The below glide slope alert of mode 5
The basic ground proximity modes
cards.explain: The enhanced terrain functions work independently of the radio altitude, while the basic modes need it.

cards.question: The crew sees the surrounding high ground pictured on the navigation display at 3000 ft, so which system provides it?
options: The weather radar system
The enhanced system
The basic warning system
cards.explain: The basic system works only below 2500 ft, while the enhanced terrain picture is independent of the radio altitude.

cards.question: Which GPWS function keeps working when the radio altitude signal is no longer available
options: The terrain awareness alerting and display
The unsafe terrain clearance mode
The excessive terrain closure rate mode
cards.explain: The enhanced terrain functions are independent of the radio altitude while the basic modes need it.

cards.question: The limits of one of the alerting envelopes are exceeded, so what does the enhanced system give the flight crew?
options: An automatic pull-up commanded through the autopilot
Aural alert messages with visual annunciations and displays
A master warning that has to be reset by the crew
cards.explain: Exceeding an envelope limit produces aural messages together with visual annunciations and displays.

cards.question: A stable non-precision approach is flown in low visibility with the gear down and the landing flaps out, so why does the early system stay silent?
options: It is inhibited below 500 feet
It expects the aeroplane to land
It has lost its radio altitude input
cards.explain: In the landing configuration the early system expects a landing and issues no warning.

cards.question: A system is required to see steep rising ground that the downward looking sensor would find too late, so which protection is needed?
options: The modulation of the alerting envelopes
The terrain clearance floor protection
The terrain data base look ahead protection
cards.explain: Look ahead protection works from the database instead of the downward looking sensor.

cards.question: The aircraft is recognised as landing at one of the troublesome airports held in the database, so what does the system do?
options: It adjusts the warning modes for that airport
It changes over to the terrain display only
It switches off all of its aural warnings
cards.explain: At such an airport the warning modes are adjusted, and only under specific conditions.

cards.question: A terrain clearance floor function is found on an aircraft, so which generation of the system is installed?
options: The enhanced system
The MARK I system
The MARK V system
cards.explain: The terrain clearance floor belongs to the enhanced system only.

cards.question: Which unit is the control unit of the EGPWS
options: The air data computer
The display management computer
The enhanced computer
cards.explain: The EGPWC is the control unit of the system.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 1 alert on
options: An excessive terrain closure rate
An altitude loss after take-off
An excessive descent rate
cards.explain: Mode 1 is the excessive descent rate mode.

cards.question: Which aural message is generated when the aircraft penetrates the outer alert boundary of mode 1
options: PULL UP
DON'T SINK
SINK RATE
cards.explain: The outer boundary gives the SINK RATE message.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 2 alert on
options: An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An excessive terrain closure rate
An excessive descent rate
cards.explain: Mode 2 covers an excessive rate of closure with the terrain.

cards.question: For how long after take-off is the mode 2B configuration valid
options: For the first 60 seconds
For the first 90 seconds
For the first 30 seconds
cards.explain: Mode 2B applies for the first 60 seconds after take-off.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 3 alert on
options: An excessive rate of descent
An altitude loss after take-off
An unsafe clearance from terrain
cards.explain: Mode 3 is the altitude loss after take-off mode.

cards.question: A DON'T SINK message is heard in the flight deck, so which mode has generated it?
options: Mode 4
Mode 3
Mode 1
cards.explain: Mode 3 gives the DON'T SINK message.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 4 alert on
options: An excessive rate of descent
An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An altitude loss after the take-off
cards.explain: Mode 4 covers unsafe terrain clearance.

cards.question: How many submodes does mode 4 have
options: Three
Four
Two
cards.explain: Mode 4 has three submodes.

cards.question: Which condition does mode 5 alert on
options: An unsafe clearance from the terrain
An excessive rate of descent near ground
A deviation below the glide slope beam
cards.explain: Mode 5 covers a deviation below the glide slope.

cards.question: How many levels of mode 5 operation does the computer provide
options: One
Three
Two
cards.explain: There are two levels of mode 5 operation.

cards.question: Which additional protection does mode 6 provide
options: An alert for an excessive rate of closure with the terrain
A comparison of the aircraft position with a terrain database
A selectable menu of radio altitude callouts during the approach
cards.explain: Mode 6 offers selectable radio altitude callouts on the landing approach.

cards.question: Which part of the system operations is independent of the other functions
options: The built-in test equipment function
The terrain awareness display function
The warning function
cards.explain: The warning function is the one stated to be independent of the others.

cards.question: The descent continues after the first mode 1 message and the inner alert boundary is penetrated, so what is heard then?
options: PULL UP
TERRAIN TERRAIN
TOO LOW TERRAIN
cards.explain: The inner boundary gives the PULL UP message.

cards.question: Which three inputs define the two alert boundaries of mode 1
options: Barometric altitude, glide slope deviation and gear position
Radio altitude, computed airspeed and the position of the flaps
Barometric vertical speed, inertial vertical speed and radio altitude
cards.explain: Those three inputs define the two mode 1 boundaries.

cards.question: What does the computer produce besides the aural message in both mode 1 cases
options: A discrete output to drive the visual annunciations
A terrain picture on the navigation display
A command to the autopilot to level the aircraft
cards.explain: A discrete output drives the visual annunciations in both cases.

cards.question: In which flight conditions can the aircraft be when a mode 2 alert is generated
options: In descent or level flight only
In the landing configuration only
In descent, level flight or climb
cards.explain: Mode 2 alerts are possible in descent, in level flight and in the climb.

cards.question: A mode 2 alert boundary is being computed, so which two signals are combined?
options: Barometric altitude and glide slope deviation
Airspeed and the position of the flaps
Vertical speed and radio altitude
cards.explain: Vertical speed and radio altitude are the two signals used.

cards.question: When is the mode 2A alert generated
options: With the flaps set to the landing position on an approach
In any configuration other than the one defined for 2B
Within the first sixty seconds following the take-off
cards.explain: Mode 2A covers every configuration that is not a mode 2B configuration.

cards.question: Which aural message comes first when the aircraft penetrates the mode 2A alerting boundaries
options: SINK RATE
TERRAIN TERRAIN
PULL UP
cards.explain: The first mode 2A message is TERRAIN TERRAIN.

cards.question: The aircraft goes on penetrating the mode 2A boundaries after the first message, so which message is repeated until it leaves the envelope?
options: TERRAIN TERRAIN
PULL UP
DON'T SINK
cards.explain: PULL UP is repeated until the aircraft exits the warning envelope.

cards.question: What makes the upper alert boundary of mode 2A vary
options: The rate of closure with the terrain
The speed of the aircraft
The position of the landing flaps
cards.explain: The upper boundary of this mode varies with aircraft speed.

cards.question: Within how many dots of the localizer or glide slope centreline does the mode 2B configuration apply during an ILS approach
options: Within plus or minus 3 dots
Within plus or minus 1 dot
Within plus or minus 2 dots
cards.explain: The printed figure is plus or minus 2 dots.

cards.question: Which messages are suppressed when both gear and flaps are in the landing position in mode 2B
options: The TERRAIN messages
The PULL UP messages
The TOO LOW GEAR messages
cards.explain: In that configuration the PULL UP messages are suppressed.

cards.question: In which two flight phases does mode 3 provide its alerts
options: During the cruise and during a precision approach
Immediately after take-off and during a missed approach
During the final approach and the landing roll
cards.explain: The two phases are immediately after take-off and during a missed approach.

cards.question: Until when do the mode 3 visual annunciators remain active
options: Until a positive rate of climb is established
Until the warning envelope has been left
Until the landing gear has been retracted
cards.explain: They stay active until a positive rate of climb exists.

cards.question: Which configuration must exist after take-off before the computer initiates a mode 3 alert
options: The gear up and the flaps not at landing
The gear down and the flaps at landing
The gear up and the flaps set to landing
cards.explain: The alert needs the gear up and the flaps away from the landing position.

cards.question: With reference to what is the insufficient terrain clearance of mode 4 detected
options: The phase of flight and the speed
The glide slope and the localizer
The vertical speed and the bank angle
cards.explain: Detection is made with reference to the phase of flight and the speed.

cards.question: When is mode 4A active
options: During take-off with the gear and the flaps still retracted
During cruise and approach with the landing gear not at landing
During an ILS approach with the flaps in landing position
cards.explain: Mode 4A covers cruise and approach with the gear not in the landing configuration.

cards.question: At which speed does a mode 4A penetration with the landing gear up give the TOO LOW GEAR message
options: At 159 knots or below
At 250 knots and above
At 190 knots or below
cards.explain: The printed speed for that message is 190 knots or below.

cards.question: The airspeed builds up during the cruise, so what happens to the mode 4A upper boundary?
options: It decreases linearly
It increases linearly
It stays constant
cards.explain: The boundary increases linearly with airspeed.

cards.question: In which configuration does mode 4B give the TOO LOW FLAPS message
options: With the gear up below one hundred and fifty nine knots
With the gear and the flaps both still fully retracted
With the gear down and the flaps not at landing
cards.explain: That message belongs to the gear down, flaps not at landing case.

cards.question: On what is mode 4C based
options: A minimum terrain clearance floor that increases during take-off
A deviation of the flight path below the glide slope beam
A fixed boundary of five hundred feet during the approach
cards.explain: Mode 4C uses a minimum terrain clearance floor that rises during take-off.

cards.question: An ILS approach is being flown, so on which course does mode 5 give its alerts?
options: A front course ILS approach
A back course ILS approach
A non-precision radio approach
cards.explain: Mode 5 works on a front course ILS approach.

cards.question: How loud is the soft alert GLIDE SLOPE message
options: About one half of the other alert volume levels
About twice the other alert message volume levels
The same as the other alert message volume levels
cards.explain: The soft alert is at approximately one half, minus 6dB, of the other levels.

cards.question: A hard alert activation occurs on an approach, so below which radio altitude is the aircraft?
options: 500 feet
300 feet
245 feet
cards.explain: The hard alert belongs to radio altitudes below 300 feet.

cards.question: How far below the glide slope must the aircraft be for the hard alert activation
options: More than 2 dots
More than 3 dots
More than 1.3 dots
cards.explain: The hard alert needs more than 2 dots below the glide slope.

cards.question: The terrain awareness display function has been lost, so what happens to the ground proximity warning functions?
options: They are lost together with the display function
They fall back to the excessive descent rate mode
They go on working while the necessary inputs are there
cards.explain: The warning functions keep working as long as their inputs remain available.

cards.question: An installation carries only the modes that are basic system requirements, so which basic GPWS alerting mode is missing?
options: Mode 4
Mode 6
Mode 5
cards.explain: The basic GPWS covers modes 1 to 6 while only modes 1 to 5 are the basic requirements, so mode 6 is the one left out.

cards.question: A warning lamp stays dark although the aural message is heard, so which computer function is suspect?
options: The alert output processing
The terrain awareness display
The input signal processing
cards.explain: The warning lamp drivers belong to the alert output processing.

cards.question: A replacement enhanced computer is being fitted, so what has to be set so that it works with the right modes?
options: The program pins, before it is installed
The maintenance pages, after the installation
The inhibit switches, before the first flight
cards.explain: The modes are selected by program pins before the computer is installed.

cards.question: The crew reduces the descent rate as soon as the first mode 1 message is heard, so which boundary has not been penetrated?
options: The inner alert boundary
The outer alert boundary
The upper alert boundary
cards.explain: The first message comes from the outer boundary, so the inner one has still not been crossed.

cards.question: An aircraft descends rapidly towards flat ground with the gear up, so which mode produces the first alert?
options: Mode 3
Mode 1
Mode 5
cards.explain: An excessive descent rate is the trigger of mode 1.

cards.question: Both the landing gear and the flaps are in the landing position when the mode 2B envelope is penetrated, so which message is repeated?
options: TERRAIN
TERRAIN TERRAIN
PULL UP
cards.explain: With gear and flaps at landing the repeated message is TERRAIN.

cards.question: The mode 2B envelope is penetrated with the landing gear down but the flaps still up, so which message is heard first?
options: PULL UP
TOO LOW TERRAIN
TERRAIN TERRAIN
cards.explain: With either gear or flaps not at landing the initial message is TERRAIN TERRAIN.

cards.question: The flaps are at the landing position and the aircraft is within two dots of the localizer on an ILS approach, so which submode boundary applies?
options: Mode 4B
Mode 2A
Mode 2B
cards.explain: That configuration is one of those listed for mode 2B.

cards.question: Which signal is used for the alert boundaries of both the excessive descent rate mode and the excessive terrain closure rate mode besides the radio altitude
options: The glide slope deviation
The computed airspeed
The vertical speed
cards.explain: Mode 1 uses barometric and inertial vertical speed and mode 2 a vertical speed signal, both with radio altitude.

cards.question: Which aural message follows a continued penetration in both the excessive descent rate mode and the excessive terrain closure rate mode
options: TERRAIN TERRAIN
SINK RATE
PULL UP
cards.explain: Mode 1 gives PULL UP at the inner boundary and mode 2 repeats PULL UP on continued penetration.

cards.question: A go-around is flown with the gear up and the flaps away from landing when a larger altitude loss than permitted is detected, so which alert is initiated?
options: The mode 3 alert
The mode 1 alert
The mode 4 alert
cards.explain: That is exactly the condition printed for the mode 3 alert.

cards.question: A computer has to decide how much height may be lost before a mode 3 alert is given, so what does it do?
options: It calculates the amount of permitted loss
It compares the loss with a fixed boundary
It reads the loss from the terrain database
cards.explain: The computer itself calculates the permitted loss before alerting.

cards.question: Which mode works from the altitude above sea level rather than from a terrain closure rate
options: Mode 2
Mode 3
Mode 1
cards.explain: Only the mode 3 computation is stated to use altitude above sea level information.

cards.question: Climbing out with gear and flaps up the aircraft loses more height than permitted while staying above the mode 4C filter value, so which message is heard?
options: DON'T SINK
TOO LOW TERRAIN
SINK RATE
cards.explain: That is the mode 3 case, and mode 4C would need the radio altitude to fall below the filter value.

cards.question: The mode 4A boundary is penetrated at 250 knots with the landing gear still retracted, so which message does the computer generate?
options: TOO LOW TERRAIN
TOO LOW GEAR
TOO LOW FLAPS
cards.explain: Above the 190 knot case the penetration of that boundary gives TOO LOW TERRAIN.

cards.question: Just after take-off with gear and flaps up the radio altitude falls below the long term filter value, so which message is generated?
options: TOO LOW GEAR
TOO LOW TERRAIN
DON'T SINK
cards.explain: That decrease below the filter value gives TOO LOW TERRAIN.

cards.question: An approach is flown at 140 knots with the gear down and the flaps still up, so which submode watches the terrain clearance?
options: Mode 4B
Mode 4A
Mode 4C
cards.explain: Mode 4B is the submode that applies once the landing gear is lowered.

cards.question: Which message is common to a mode 4A penetration at 250 knots and to a mode 4C penetration of the filter value
options: TOO LOW TERRAIN
TOO LOW FLAPS
TOO LOW GEAR
cards.explain: Mode 4A gives TOO LOW TERRAIN when the boundary reached at 250 knots and above is penetrated, and mode 4C gives it for a fall below the filter value.

cards.question: The aircraft is more than two dots below the glide slope at 250 feet radio altitude, so which mode 5 activation has been reached?
options: The hard alert activation
Only the soft alert activation
Neither of the two activations
cards.explain: Below 300 feet radio altitude and more than 2 dots below the glide slope are the printed conditions of the hard alert activation.

cards.question: The aircraft drifts 1.5 dots below the beam centre at 800 feet radio altitude, so which activation occurs?
options: The soft alert activation
No alert activation at all
The hard alert activation
cards.explain: It is beyond 1.3 dots so the soft alert comes, while the hard alert needs below 300 feet and more than 2 dots.

cards.question: A glide slope deviation message is heard noticeably quieter than the other warnings, so what does that tell the crew?
options: It is the hard alert activation
It is the soft alert activation
It is a failure of the loudspeaker
cards.explain: Only the soft alert is given at about half the normal volume.

questions.question: The approaching option is set so that the aural comes at decision height + 100 feet, so which call-out is then given?
options: approaching minimums
plus hundred
approaching decision height
questions.explain: The plus hundred call-out is the one whose altitude selection is decision height + 100 feet.

questions.question: Which further aeroplane parameters the GPWC checks near such an airport
options: Ground speed, roll attitude and calculated flight path angle
Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation
Vertical speed, true heading and terrain elevation data
questions.explain: Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation are all on the printed list.

questions.question: Which sources terrain awareness uses for latitude and longitude
options: GPS or FMS
GPS or WXR
ADIRS or ADC
questions.explain: Latitude and longitude come from GPS or FMS.

questions.question: What the EGPWC compares with its terrain database to find a threat
options: The aeroplane speed and flap setting
The aeroplane position and track
The aeroplane pitch and roll
questions.explain: Position and track are compared with the database.

questions.question: The aeroplane stays inside the terrain warning envelope, so how is PULL UP given?
options: Twice and then once per 20% height loss
Continuously
Every seven seconds
questions.explain: PULL UP repeats continuously for as long as the warning envelope is penetrated.

questions.question: What the alert discretes of the look-ahead function are provided for
options: To inhibit the weather radar transmitter
To reset the radio altimeter output
To energise the terrain display relays
questions.explain: The discretes energise the terrain display relays.

questions.question: The aeroplane is near a listed airport but the glide slope deviation and runway heading fail to match, so what does the GPWC conclude?
options: A modulation condition exists anyway
The terrain database must be in error
No modulation condition exists
questions.explain: Position alone is not enough; the extra parameters must also confirm the condition.

questions.question: Both GPS and FMS position data are lost in the cruise, so which EGPWS function can no longer work?
options: The barometric altitude correction in the ADC
The look-ahead comparison with the terrain database
The radio altimeter height measurement function
questions.explain: Without latitude and longitude there is no position to compare with the terrain database.

questions.question: An area along the track is painted solid yellow rather than in a dot pattern, so what has happened?
options: The caution envelope has been violated
The warning envelope has been violated
The clearance floor has been penetrated
questions.explain: Solid yellow is reserved for ground that violates the caution envelope.

questions.question: The terrain display relays have been energised by the alert discretes, so what do the navigational displays then carry?
options: The terrain test pattern in cyan
The weather radar picture as before
The conflicting ground in yellow or red
questions.explain: Once the relays are energised the conflicting ground is painted solid yellow or solid red.

questions.question: Which colour marks a failure of the computer itself
options: Yellow
Red
Green
questions.explain: The computer fail LED is red.

questions.question: The yellow LED is lit on the front panel while the green one stays on, so where should the engineer look first?
options: At the power supply to the computer
Inside the computer itself
At the equipment feeding the computer
questions.explain: Yellow marks an external fault while green still says the computer is good, so the trouble is outside it.

questions.question: One of the two vibration sensors of an engine sits in the compressor area, so where is the other one?
options: In the combustion chamber area
In the accessory gearbox area
In the turbine area
questions.explain: The second of the two sensors is in the turbine area.

questions.question: In which two formats is the vibration value put on an EICAS display
options: In a digital and a bar graph format
In an analog and a digital format
In an analog and a colour coded format
questions.explain: The display gives the value both in analog and in digital form.

questions.question: The cockpit vibration reading creeps up over several flights with no other symptom, so what does the trend suggest?
options: The sensor wiring is open circuit
The indicator calibration has drifted
A rotor imbalance is developing
questions.explain: A rising trend in the vibration level is read as a developing rotor imbalance, the first sign of damage.

questions.question: The vibration sensor near the N1 rotor shaft of an engine has failed, so which part of the engine has lost its pick-up?
options: The accessory gearbox area
The turbine area
The compressor area
questions.explain: The sensor near the N1 rotor shaft is the one in the compressor area, so that area is the one left unmonitored.

questions.question: Why can an electromagnetic vibration sensor work without any outside supply
options: Because relative motion induces its voltage, as in a generator
Because its coil is fed from the engine tachometer circuit
Because its springs store the energy of each vibration cycle
questions.explain: The sensor generates its own voltage by induction, the way a generator does.

questions.question: An indicator carries a REL AM scale and two readings are taken a week apart, so what can be done with them?
options: They can be read as rotor speed values
They can be compared to follow the trend
They can be read as absolute amplitudes
questions.explain: With no units on the scale the readings are only useful compared with each other as a trend.

questions.question: How can one sensor signal be turned into separate N1 and N2 vibration indications
options: By comparing its frequency with the two rotor speed signals
By switching the filter between the forward and the aft pick-up
By comparing its amplitude with the two stored limit values
questions.explain: The frequency of the vibration signal is compared with the two rotor speed signals to sort it into N1 and N2.

questions.question: Which three components make up the main rotor rpm monitoring system
options: A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and a triple tachometer
A magnetic pick up, an rpm indicator and an rpm warning unit
A magnetic pick up, an rpm warning unit and a master caution light
questions.explain: These three are the components of the system.

questions.question: The rotor rpm falls below the operating range, so what is given to the crew?
options: A visual and an audio warning
A visual warning only
A removal of the rpm indication
questions.explain: Going outside the range either way sets off both visual and audio warning.

questions.question: Why is a main transmission fault easier to judge than a tail rotor gearbox fault
options: The transmission carries only a light, the gearbox constant indications
Both carry constant indications but only the gearbox has a light
The transmission carries constant indications, the gearbox only a light
questions.explain: Main transmission values are indicated all the time, while the other gearboxes give nothing but a caution light.

questions.question: A helicopter without EFIS was started without the bending load indicator being calibrated, so what is now in doubt?
options: The accuracy of the mast moment indication
The aural warning of the rotor rpm
The supply to the strain gauge bridge
questions.explain: Without the pre-start calibration the indicated mast moment can no longer be trusted.

questions.question: Which two methods are basically used to measure the fuel quantity
options: An ultrasonic system and a flow meter system
A capacitor system and an ultrasonic system
A capacitor system and a float switch system
questions.explain: Capacitors and the ultrasonic principle are the two methods given.

questions.question: A small aeroplane is being fitted with a fuel quantity system, so which of the two measuring methods is open to it?
options: The one using capacitors
The one using the ultrasonic principle
Either of the two methods
questions.explain: The ultrasonic method is for larger aeroplanes only, which leaves the capacitor method.

questions.question: A tank is deep and awkwardly shaped, so what does that mean for the probes put in it?
options: Several of them, cut to different lengths
Several of them, all cut to one length
One of them, laid flat at several levels
questions.explain: Size and shape decide how many probes are needed, and because they must reach from bottom to top they end up different lengths.

questions.question: Why does a capacitive probe give a different reading as the tank fills
options: Because the spacing between its tubes changes
Because the area of its tubes changes
Because the material between its tubes changes
questions.explain: Filling the tank swaps air for fuel between the tubes, and that material change alters the capacitance.

questions.question: Which units are used to show the fuel quantity on a large commercial aircraft
options: Units of weight
Units of volume
Units of pressure
questions.explain: On large commercial aircraft the fuel quantity is shown in units of weight.

questions.question: Which property of air and fuel the capacitance method of quantity measurement makes use of
options: Their differing boiling points
Their differing dielectric constants
Their differing electrical resistances
questions.explain: The capacitance method uses the differing dielectric constants of air and fuel.

questions.question: Why the amount of fuel carried is indicated in units of weight
options: The energy available from the fuel depends on weight
The tank capacity is certified in terms of weight
The energy available from the fuel depends on volume
questions.explain: The energy present in the form of fuel is dependent on weight, so weight is indicated.

questions.question: What makes a direct weight indication of the fuel necessary on a large commercial aircraft
options: Fuel density is constant so the weight can be read straight from the volume
Fuel is always loaded by volume and the tank gauges are marked in litres only
Fuel can be half the take-off weight and the approved weights need it
questions.explain: Fuel can be up to one half of take-off weight, so direct weight indication is needed for the approved take-off and landing weights.

questions.question: How the capacitive bridge of a fuel quantity indicator is rebalanced in service
options: Manually, by the crew turning a trimming knob
Automatically, by amplifying the difference signal
Automatically, by switching in reference condensers
questions.explain: Fuel quantity capacitive bridges are balanced automatically by amplifying the difference signal.

questions.question: When the cadensicon sensor takes its measurements of K and D
options: As fuel enters the tank
Only when the tank is nearly empty
Only once the engines have been started
questions.explain: The cadensicon measures K and D separately as fuel enters the tank.

questions.question: Water has collected between the plates of a capacitance probe, so how does the probe capacitance compare with the same probe covered in fuel?
options: The same
Slightly lower
Much higher
questions.explain: Water is given a far larger dielectric constant than fuel, and the capacitance rises with the dielectric constant of whatever fills the probe.

questions.question: Refuelling has to stop before a tank overflows, so what is built into the fuel quantity computer system for this?
options: A totaliser that sums all of the master systems
A trimming condenser at the cockpit indicator
A preselection of the wanted load with a shutoff
questions.explain: The system integrates a preselection of the desired volume together with a shutoff on reaching it or shortly before overflowing.

questions.question: Which kind of signal the tank units of this liquid level metering system transmit
options: A radio frequency signal
A light pulse
An ultrasonic signal
questions.explain: The tank units transmit an ultrasonic signal.

questions.question: A tank of an ultrasonic system is opened for inspection, so how many tank units will be found in it?
options: Exactly two units
Numerous units
A single unit
questions.explain: Each tank contains numerous tank units.

questions.question: Which property of the fuel the capacitance of a tank unit responds to, unlike an ultrasonic tank unit
options: Its dielectric constant
Its temperature in flight
Its density in the tank
questions.explain: Capacitive measurement works from the differing dielectric constants, while the ultrasonic unit works from a reflected signal.

questions.question: A densitometer in one tank of an ultrasonic system has failed, so which calculation is lost first?
options: The fuel weight for that tank
The fuel height in that tank
The water level in that tank
questions.explain: Height still comes from the tank unit, but without the density from the densitometer the processor unit cannot work out that tank's fuel weight.

questions.question: A tank unit reads correctly on the tester but the cockpit indication is still wrong, so which further tester function would be used on the wiring?
options: Measuring contact resistances
Simulating the probe capacities
Measuring the tank unit currents
questions.explain: Besides measuring and simulating capacities the tester measures contact resistances, which is what a wiring check needs.

cards.question: What makes the EGPWS give Mode 6 alerts and call-outs
options: The aircraft climbing above predefined altitudes
The aircraft descending below predefined altitudes
The aircraft exceeding a predefined airspeed
cards.explain: Mode 6 is triggered by the aircraft descending below predefined altitudes such as DH and minimums.

cards.question: Which indications Mode 6 alerts and call-outs give to the crew
options: Aural messages and ARINC 429 outputs only
Visual warnings and aural messages only
Visual warnings and ARINC 429 outputs only
cards.explain: Mode 6 produces aural messages and ARINC 429 outputs but no visual indication.

cards.question: Which flight phases the Mode 7 windshear alerting covers
options: Cruise and initial descent
Take-off and final approach
Taxi and initial climb
cards.explain: Mode 7 alerts during take-off and final approach.

cards.question: Between which heights above ground the windshear detection is active
options: 50 and 2500 feet AGL
10 and 1500 feet AGL
200 and 1000 feet AGL
cards.explain: Detection is active between 10 and 1500 feet AGL.

cards.question: An airport needs envelope modulation, so how is it held in the GPWC memory?
options: By their runway heading alone
By their ICAO four-letter code
By their latitude and longitude
cards.explain: Those airports are held in memory identified by latitude and longitude.

cards.question: What the terrain awareness alerting function uses to predict a conflict ahead
options: The radio altimeter signal with the nearest runway length
The aircraft position and altitude with an internal database
The weather radar returns with the aircraft ground speed
cards.explain: Geographic position and altitude are compared with the internal terrain database.

cards.question: Terrain awareness is working normally, so which two systems supply its aeroplane data?
options: The ADC and the ILS
The ADIRS and the GPS
The FMS and the WXR
cards.explain: Aeroplane data comes from the ADIRS and the GPS.

cards.question: Which alerting envelopes the terrain alerting function computes
options: A look-up envelope and a lateral offset envelope
A caution-level envelope and a warning-level envelope
A take-off envelope and a final approach envelope
cards.explain: Two envelopes are computed, one for caution level and one for warning level.

cards.question: From where the decision height used by the minimums call-out is taken
options: A fixed preset inside the radio altimeter
The setting on the EFIS control panels
The runway elevation in the terrain database
cards.explain: The minimums call-out uses the decision height set on the EFIS control panels.

cards.question: An approaching minimums call-out is selected, so how far above the decision height does it normally come on?
options: 100 feet
130 feet
80 feet
cards.explain: The approaching minimums call-out normally comes on 80 feet above the decision height.

cards.question: The approaching option is set so that the aural comes at decision height + 100 feet, so which call-out is then given?
options: approaching decision height
approaching minimums
plus hundred
cards.explain: The plus hundred call-out is the one whose altitude selection is decision height + 100 feet.

cards.question: The windshear pre-alert comes up on take-off, so which indications does it give?
options: Aural outputs and a cockpit siren
Visual and ARINC 429 outputs
Aural, visual and ARINC 429 outputs
cards.explain: The caution, or pre-alert, gives visual and ARINC 429 indications only.

cards.question: What the measured windshear value represents
options: The vector sum of inertial and air mass accelerations
The rate of change of barometric altitude
The difference between ground speed and airspeed
cards.explain: The value is the vector sum of inertial versus air mass accelerations along and across the flight path.

cards.question: Which further aeroplane parameters the GPWC checks near such an airport
options: Ground speed, roll attitude and calculated flight path angle
Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation
Vertical speed, true heading and terrain elevation data
cards.explain: Radio altitude, magnetic track and glide slope deviation are all on the printed list.

cards.question: Which navigational signals the envelope modulation feature can use
options: Updated VOR and DME range and bearing signals
Localizer and glide slope beam deviation signals
GPS or updated flight management system signals
cards.explain: The feature uses GPS or updated FMS navigational signals.

cards.question: Which sources terrain awareness uses for latitude and longitude
options: GPS or WXR
GPS or FMS
ADIRS or ADC
cards.explain: Latitude and longitude come from GPS or FMS.

cards.question: Which of the terrain awareness input quantities is worked out by the EGPWC itself
options: Barometric altitude
Ground track
Flight path angle
cards.explain: Only the flight path angle is noted as calculated by the EGPWC; the others are received.

cards.question: What the EGPWC compares with its terrain database to find a threat
options: The aeroplane pitch and roll
The aeroplane position and track
The aeroplane speed and flap setting
cards.explain: Position and track are compared with the database.

cards.question: How the terrain display shows terrain height relative to the aeroplane
options: By solid contour lines
By numeric height labels
By different coloured dots
cards.explain: Terrain height relative to the aeroplane is shown by different coloured dots.

cards.question: The caution level aural has just been heard and the envelope is still penetrated, so when does it come again?
options: Every seven seconds
Every three seconds
Without any pause
cards.explain: The caution message repeats every seven seconds while the envelope is penetrated.

cards.question: The aeroplane stays inside the terrain warning envelope, so how is PULL UP given?
options: Continuously
Twice and then once per 20% height loss
Every seven seconds
cards.explain: PULL UP repeats continuously for as long as the warning envelope is penetrated.

cards.question: What the alert discretes of the look-ahead function are provided for
options: To inhibit the weather radar transmitter
To reset the radio altimeter output
To energise the terrain display relays
cards.explain: The discretes energise the terrain display relays.

cards.question: By which three dimensions the terrain alerting envelopes are sized
options: A look-ahead distance, an altitude offset and a lateral distance
A ground speed, a flight path angle and a roll attitude
A runway distance, a radio altitude and a ground track angle
cards.explain: The three sizing dimensions are look-ahead distance, altitude offset and lateral distance.

cards.question: At the height where the call-outs begin the operator rejects the aural TWENTY FIVE HUNDRED, so what is the other option there?
options: The aural TOO LOW TERRAIN
The aural MINIMUMS MINIMUMS
The aural RADIO ALTITUDE
cards.explain: At 2500 feet the alternative to TWENTY FIVE HUNDRED is the aural RADIO ALTITUDE.

cards.question: The aeroplane is at 300 feet radio altitude and the roll is increased steadily, so at which angles does the call-out occur?
options: 15, 30 and 45 degrees
35, 40 and 45 degrees
10, 20 and 30 degrees
cards.explain: Above 130 feet the bank angle call-out comes at 35, 40 and 45 degrees.

cards.question: On a low go-around at 60 feet radio altitude the pilot rolls to 20 degrees, so what does Mode 6 do?
options: It gives the aural MINIMUMS, MINIMUMS
It gives no roll call-out at that height
It gives the aural BANK ANGLE, BANK ANGLE
cards.explain: 60 feet lies between 30 and 130 feet and 20 degrees is larger than 10 degrees, so the call-out is given.

cards.question: At 200 feet radio altitude the aeroplane is rolled to 20 degrees but nothing is heard, so why is that?
options: Above 130 feet at least 45 degrees is needed
Above 130 feet at least 35 degrees is needed
Above 130 feet roll call-outs are inhibited
cards.explain: Above 130 feet the first bank angle call-out is at 35 degrees, so 20 degrees gives nothing.

cards.question: A windshear warning is triggered on take-off, so how do its indications differ from those of the pre-alert?
options: An ARINC 429 output is added
A visual indication is added
An aural indication is added
cards.explain: The warning adds the aural to the visual and ARINC 429 indications the caution already gives.

cards.question: A shear indication comes up on take-off with no sound at all, so which level of Mode 7 has been reached?
options: The terrain caution
The warning
The pre-alert
cards.explain: Only the warning has an aural, so a silent visual indication is the caution or pre-alert.

cards.question: On final approach at 900 feet AGL the head wind increases quickly and a severe up draft is met, so what does Mode 7 do?
options: It stays quiet, because the gear is not yet down
It alerts, because the height is inside the active band
It alerts only after the aeroplane is below 500 feet
cards.explain: 900 feet lies inside the printed 10 to 1500 feet AGL detection band, so Mode 7 gives its alert.

cards.question: Severe shear is met at 1800 feet AGL in the climb but nothing is annunciated, so why is that?
options: Detection is inhibited during any climb
Detection stops above 2500 feet AGL
Detection stops above 1500 feet AGL
cards.explain: The active band ends at 1500 feet AGL, so 1800 feet is outside it.

cards.question: The aeroplane is near a listed airport but the glide slope deviation and runway heading fail to match, so what does the GPWC conclude?
options: A modulation condition exists anyway
No modulation condition exists
The terrain database must be in error
cards.explain: Position alone is not enough; the extra parameters must also confirm the condition.

cards.question: Why is the top radio altitude limit of the mode 2 alert area lowered at some locations?
options: To let the aeroplane fly closer to the terrain without alerts
To let the aeroplane approach without lowering the gear
To let the aeroplane descend faster without any alerts
cards.explain: Lowering the mode 2 area lets the aeroplane fly closer to the terrain without alerts.

cards.question: An approach needs mode 5 annunciations higher than normal and with the gear still up, so which change makes that possible?
options: The alert area is lowered and a gear down requirement added
The descent rate limit is increased and the alert area raised
The alert area is increased and the gear down requirement removed
cards.explain: Mode 5 modulation increases the alert area limits and removes the gear down requirement.

cards.question: Both GPS and FMS position data are lost in the cruise, so which EGPWS function can no longer work?
options: The look-ahead comparison with the terrain database
The radio altimeter height measurement function
The barometric altitude correction in the ADC
cards.explain: Without latitude and longitude there is no position to compare with the terrain database.

cards.question: An aural is heard and exactly seven seconds later the same words come again, so which envelope is still penetrated?
options: The clearance floor envelope
The warning envelope
The caution envelope
cards.explain: A seven second repeat is the caution level; the warning level repeats continuously.

cards.question: What happens to the look-ahead distance as the aeroplane accelerates and why
options: It stays fixed, because altitude alone sets it
It decreases, to keep the envelope narrow
It increases, to keep the alerting time about equal
cards.explain: The distance grows with ground speed so that alerting times stay roughly the same.

cards.question: Which colour paints ground that violates the terrain caution envelope
options: 100 per cent yellow
100 per cent red
50 per cent magenta
cards.explain: Caution envelope violations are painted solid yellow.

cards.question: Which colour paints ground that violates the terrain warning envelope
options: 100 per cent red
100 per cent yellow
50 per cent green
cards.explain: Warning envelope violations are painted solid red.

cards.question: What the TCF alert function builds around the intended runway
options: An increasing terrain clearance envelope
A circular windshear detection envelope
A fixed glide slope deviation envelope
cards.explain: TCF builds a terrain clearance envelope that grows with distance from the runway.

cards.question: Which two sources feed the navigational displays through the select relays
options: The EGPWC and the WXR transceiver
The ADIRS and the flight management system
The GPWC and the radio altimeter
cards.explain: The two sources are the EGPWC and the weather radar transceiver.

cards.question: Under which condition terrain is kept off the display
options: When it lies more than 2000 ft below reference altitude
When it lies more than 1000 ft above reference altitude
When it lies more than 2000 ft above the runway
cards.explain: Terrain more than 2000 ft below reference altitude is not painted.

cards.question: On which three quantities the terrain clearance floor alerts are based
options: Aircraft heading, runway length and barometric altitude data
Aircraft location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude
Ground speed, flight path angle and nearest terrain elevation
cards.explain: Location, nearest runway centre point and radio altitude are the three inputs.

cards.question: When the terrain clearance floor is active during take-off
options: When the flaps have been retracted
When mode 4 protection is not available
When the landing gear is still down
cards.explain: In the take-off mode TCF covers the gap where mode 4 protection is missing.

cards.question: The aeroplane moves further away from the airport, so how does the height of the clearance envelope change?
options: It stays the same at every distance
It increases as the distance increases
It decreases as the distance increases
cards.explain: The envelope gets higher the further the aeroplane is from the airport.

cards.question: Which aeroplane data the EGPWC compares with the clearance envelope data
options: Heading, ground speed and radio altitude
Latitude, longitude and barometric altitude
Latitude, longitude and radio altitude
cards.explain: Latitude, longitude and radio altitude are compared with the envelope data.

cards.question: On which data bus standard the terrain and weather display data is carried
options: ARINC 453
ARINC 429
ARINC 629
cards.explain: The display data runs on ARINC 453 buses.

cards.question: Which equipment receives the data from the terrain weather select relays
options: The flight warning computers
The air data computers
The display electronics units
cards.explain: The relays feed the display electronics units, which drive the NDs.

cards.question: What happens when the TERR switch is selected a second time
options: The relay deenergises and the weather radar is connected
The relay deenergises and a test pattern is shown
The relay stays energised and the terrain stays shown
cards.explain: A second selection deenergises the relay and reconnects the weather radar.

cards.question: The aeroplane is in level flight and an area ahead is painted high density red, so where does that ground lie?
options: Between 1000 and 2000 ft above it
More than 2000 ft below the aeroplane
More than 2000 ft above the aeroplane
cards.explain: In level flight the reference altitude is the aircraft altitude, so high density red is more than 2000 ft above it.

cards.question: An area along the track is painted solid yellow rather than in a dot pattern, so what has happened?
options: The warning envelope has been violated
The caution envelope has been violated
The clearance floor has been penetrated
cards.explain: Solid yellow is reserved for ground that violates the caution envelope.

cards.question: A QFE approach is flown into a field with an extreme surface temperature, so why does the EGPWS need no special procedure?
options: Corrected barometric altitude is used instead
The radio altimeter replaces the air data input
Its computed altitude copes with both conditions
cards.explain: The geometric altitude function covers temperature extremes and QFE operation together.

cards.question: Why the terrain awareness function still works properly after a wrong altimeter subscale setting
options: Its computed altitude is not susceptible to that error
The radio altimeter replaces every altitude input
The air data computer recomputes the corrected value
cards.explain: Geometric altitude is immune to an incorrect altimeter setting, so terrain awareness is unaffected.

cards.question: The aeroplane flies through a strong inversion layer, so why can the corrected barometric altitude mislead the EGPWS?
options: It freezes at the last valid value
It can be in error against the true height
It is replaced by uncorrected altitude
cards.explain: Under non-standard conditions such as inversions the corrected barometric altitude differs from the true altitude.

cards.question: The landing gear is lowered in the descent, so how does the lower edge of the medium density yellow band change?
options: From 500 ft below to 250 ft below the reference altitude
From 1000 ft below to 500 ft below the reference altitude
From 250 ft below to 500 ft below the reference altitude
cards.explain: With the gear up the band reaches 500 ft below, with the gear down only 250 ft below.

cards.question: The landing gear is up and ground lies 400 ft below the reference altitude, so in which band is it painted?
options: Medium density yellow
Light density green
Medium density green
cards.explain: With the gear up the medium density yellow band runs down to 500 ft below, so 400 ft below falls in it.

cards.question: TERR is selected on an EFIS control panel, so what does the select relay do?
options: It deenergises and connects weather data to the display units
It energises and connects terrain data to the display units
It energises and connects the hazard bus to the display units
cards.explain: Selecting TERR energises the relay and connects terrain data to the display units.

cards.question: What the transfer relays do while the weather radar is on and the caution criteria become fulfilled
options: They drop the terrain bus and switch to the weather bus
They drop the weather bus and switch to the terrain bus
They connect both buses to the display units at once
cards.explain: With the criteria fulfilled the relays swap the weather bus out for the terrain bus.

cards.question: A predictive windshear alert arrives while the terrain picture is up, so which picture is then shown?
options: The terrain test pattern
The terrain one, with the shear data on it
The weather one, with the shear data on it
cards.explain: A shear alert overrides the terrain picture and reverts to the weather display.

cards.question: The terrain display relays have been energised by the alert discretes, so what do the navigational displays then carry?
options: The weather radar picture as before
The conflicting ground in yellow or red
The terrain test pattern in cyan
cards.explain: Once the relays are energised the conflicting ground is painted solid yellow or solid red.

cards.question: A siren is followed by the same word three times during the climb-out at 300 feet, so which mode has alerted?
options: Mode 5
Mode 7
Mode 2
cards.explain: Only the mode 7 warning begins with a siren and repeats its word three times.

cards.question: The short level 1 test aural sequence begins with glideslope INOP, so what does that tell the engineer?
options: The glide slope lamp itself has failed
No valid glide slope input is present
The test was started below 2000 feet
cards.explain: The INOP annunciation in the sequence means the glide slope input is missing.

cards.question: A level one test is run from the front panel of the computer, so why is the GPW module used instead for an operational test?
options: The front panel test only checks the power supply
The front panel test gives out no aural messages at all
The flight deck annunciations cannot be seen there
cards.explain: From the computer front panel the flight deck annunciations are out of sight.

cards.question: An engineer looks at the front of the ground proximity warning computer, so how many status LEDs are fitted there?
options: Five LEDs
Three LEDs
Two LEDs
cards.explain: Three status LEDs are fitted on the front panel.

cards.question: When the status LEDs on the front panel of the GPWC turn on
options: When a fault has been detected
When the computer is powered
When a self-test has been started
cards.explain: The LEDs come on whenever the computer has power.

cards.question: Which colour marks the external fault indication on the computer front panel
options: Green
Red
Yellow
cards.explain: The external fault LED is yellow.

cards.question: The green LED on the computer front panel is on, so what does that say?
options: The computer is serviceable
An external fault is present
The computer has failed
cards.explain: Green is the computer OK indication.

cards.question: Which colour marks a failure of the computer itself
options: Red
Yellow
Green
cards.explain: The computer fail LED is red.

cards.question: Level 2 reports No Faults but the engineer must still see what went wrong on earlier flights, so which level is needed?
options: Level 6
Level 3
Level 4
cards.explain: Current faults are level 2; the history of earlier legs is level 4.

cards.question: The yellow LED is lit on the front panel while the green one stays on, so where should the engineer look first?
options: At the equipment feeding the computer
At the power supply to the computer
Inside the computer itself
cards.explain: Yellow marks an external fault while green still says the computer is good, so the trouble is outside it.

cards.question: What the engine vibration indication lets you identify
options: A fuel control fault
An oil filter blockage
A rotor imbalance
cards.explain: The vibration indication reveals a rotor imbalance.

cards.question: An engine vibration reading is seen in the cockpit, so how is its level expressed?
options: Usually in units
Usually in millimetres per second
Usually as a percentage of maximum
cards.explain: The cockpit indication is normally given in units.

cards.question: Which kind of transducer is used as an engine vibration sensor
options: A strain gauge bridge
A tachometer generator
An accelerometer
cards.explain: The vibration sensors on an engine are accelerometers.

cards.question: A technician counts the vibration sensors fitted to one engine, so how many does he normally find?
options: Two
Four
One
cards.explain: Two sensors per engine is the usual fit.

cards.question: Which two types of accelerometer are used as engine vibration sensors
options: The electromagnetic type and the piezoelectric-crystal type
The piezoelectric-crystal type and the strain gauge type
The electromagnetic type and the variable reluctance type
cards.explain: Only these two accelerometer types are used on engines.

cards.question: What makes a piezoelectric crystal generate a voltage
options: A current passed through the crystal
A force applied to the crystal
A magnet moved across the crystal
cards.explain: Applying force to the crystal is what produces the voltage.

cards.question: A test switch is fitted to an analogue vibration display, so how much of it can be checked?
options: The sensor wiring only
The filter setting only
The entire indicator
cards.explain: The test switch checks the whole indicator.

cards.question: A glass cockpit display shows the engine vibration, so how many vibration indications are given per engine?
options: Two
One
Four
cards.explain: Two indications are given for each engine.

cards.question: An EICAS display shows the engine vibration, so how many values are given for each engine?
options: Four
Two
One
cards.explain: Only one value per engine is shown on this display.

cards.question: Why a rotor imbalance matters to the engineer
options: It can be the first sign of engine damage
It shows the engine is running overspeed
It always means a bearing has already failed
cards.explain: An imbalance can be the earliest sign that the engine is being damaged.

cards.question: What the engine vibration sensors deliver to the computer
options: Electrical signals
Pneumatic pressure signals
Hydraulic pressure signals
cards.explain: The sensors send electrical signals to the computer.

cards.question: What the computer does with the data it receives from the sensors
options: It passes it unchanged to the flight data recorder
It turns it straight into a cockpit warning indication
It filters it for indication and trend monitoring
cards.explain: The computer collects and filters the data for both indication and trend monitoring.

cards.question: Which other parts carry vibration sensors on many helicopter types?
options: Flight control actuators
Rotors and gearboxes
Fuel pumps and filters
cards.explain: On many helicopters the rotors and gearboxes also carry vibration sensors.

cards.question: Which quantity of the rotor system is sensed by an engine vibration pick-up
options: The radial acceleration of the rotor system
The axial displacement of the rotor system
The rotational speed of the rotor system
cards.explain: The accelerometer senses acceleration in the radial direction.

cards.question: One of the two vibration sensors of an engine sits in the compressor area, so where is the other one?
options: In the turbine area
In the accessory gearbox area
In the combustion chamber area
cards.explain: The second of the two sensors is in the turbine area.

cards.question: How is the permanent magnet carried inside an electromagnetic vibration sensor
options: It is held on a base plate by an inertia mass, with a coil around it
It is held in the centre by a fixed coil, with two springs around it
It is held in the centre by two springs, with a fixed coil around it
cards.explain: Two springs hold the magnet centrally and the coil is the fixed part around it.

cards.question: The housing of an electromagnetic vibration sensor shakes with the engine, so what does the magnet inside do?
options: It moves up and down with the housing
It stays almost still because of its inertia
It turns with the rotor system
cards.explain: Inertia keeps the magnet nearly stationary while the housing and coil move.

cards.question: What produces the AC output voltage of an electromagnetic vibration sensor
options: The difference in motion between the coil and the magnetic field
The force of the two springs acting on the permanent magnet
The pressure of an inertia mass on the base plate
cards.explain: Relative motion between coil and field induces the voltage, as in a generator.

cards.question: What is the job of the attuned filter inside an analogue vibration indicator
options: It screens out the undesired frequencies
It amplifies the undesired frequencies
It rectifies the critical frequencies
cards.explain: The attuned filter removes the frequencies that are not wanted.

cards.question: What does the marking REL AM on a vibration indicator tell the technician
options: That the scale carries no units and only follows a trend
That the scale shows the speed difference of the rotors
That the scale is graduated in mils of displacement
cards.explain: REL AM means an unitless scale meant only for trend following.

cards.question: Which two rotor systems are covered by the two vibration indications of one engine
options: The N2 rotor system and the accessory drive system
The N1 rotor system and the N2 rotor system
The N1 rotor system and the fan rotor system
cards.explain: One indication is for N1 and the other for N2.

cards.question: From how many sensor signals does the monitoring unit make the two vibration indications
options: From one single sensor signal on its own
From one sensor signal for each indication
From the two sensor signals added together
cards.explain: Both indications come from a single sensor signal.

cards.question: Which of the two engine vibration sensors is normally used for this display indication?
options: Whichever reads higher
The aft one
The forward one
cards.explain: The forward sensor is the one normally used.

cards.question: The forward vibration sensor of an engine fails, so what does the monitoring unit do?
options: It freezes the last indicated value
It removes the N2 indication only
It switches over to the aft one
cards.explain: On failure of the forward sensor the unit changes over to the aft sensor.

cards.question: In which two formats is the vibration value put on an EICAS display
options: In an analog and a digital format
In a digital and a bar graph format
In an analog and a colour coded format
cards.explain: The display gives the value both in analog and in digital form.

cards.question: A technician studies the vibration display, so what is put on it beside the value itself?
options: The sensor and filter functions in use
The stored limit values for the engine
The rotor speeds used for the comparison
cards.explain: The sensor and filter functions being used are shown with the value.

cards.question: The cockpit vibration reading creeps up over several flights with no other symptom, so what does the trend suggest?
options: The indicator calibration has drifted
The sensor wiring is open circuit
A rotor imbalance is developing
cards.explain: A rising trend in the vibration level is read as a developing rotor imbalance, the first sign of damage.

cards.question: The vibration sensor near the N1 rotor shaft of an engine has failed, so which part of the engine has lost its pick-up?
options: The accessory gearbox area
The turbine area
The compressor area
cards.explain: The sensor near the N1 rotor shaft is the one in the compressor area, so that area is the one left unmonitored.

cards.question: A vibration signal reaches the monitoring unit with a high voltage but a low frequency, so what has it been told?
options: A small acceleration at a fast vibration
A large acceleration at a slow vibration
A large rotor speed at a slow acceleration
cards.explain: Voltage carries the acceleration level and frequency carries the vibration frequency, so high voltage with low frequency is a big acceleration vibrating slowly.

cards.question: Why can an electromagnetic vibration sensor work without any outside supply
options: Because relative motion induces its voltage, as in a generator
Because its coil is fed from the engine tachometer circuit
Because its springs store the energy of each vibration cycle
cards.explain: The sensor generates its own voltage by induction, the way a generator does.

cards.question: A technician wants the indication of a low frequency vibration on an older system, so which switch does he use?
options: The one that picks the engine
The one that picks the sensor
The one that picks the filter
cards.explain: Frequency band is set by the filter switch, not by the sensor switch.

cards.question: An indicator carries a REL AM scale and two readings are taken a week apart, so what can be done with them?
options: They can be read as absolute amplitudes
They can be read as rotor speed values
They can be compared to follow the trend
cards.explain: With no units on the scale the readings are only useful compared with each other as a trend.

cards.question: An older vibration system must show the oscillations of the add-on components, so which filter position is used?
options: The low frequency one
The high frequency one
The broad band one
cards.explain: Add-on components give the low oscillations, so the low frequency filter is selected.

cards.question: An analogue vibration indicator is driven by a moving coil, so what must be done to the alternating sensor signal before it can drive that movement?
options: It must be digitised
It must be rectified
It must be attenuated
